stories.Headline: How AI is changing procurement and supply chains
stories.Summary:
Sifted reported on November 12, 2026 that Magentic, a procurement and supply chain automation company, deploys AI agents to run procurement and supply chain processes for its customers. The same day, Seadronix announced that it had secured its first government vessel supply reference in the global defense market. Seadronix is an AI maritime solutions provider led by CEO Byeolteo Park, and its win concerns the NAVISS Bridge AI ship monitoring and navigation system. That system will be installed on the Republic of Singapore Navy's next-generation Sentinel-class Offshore Patrol Vessels, which are purpose-built for maritime security missions. The vessels are being built by Fassmer, a German shipbuilder that specializes in special-purpose and defense vessels.

Singapore's Ministry of Defence officially named Seadronix's AI system in the vessels' specifications, which it published on October 2. Seadronix is the only non-European company chosen for the vessels' sensor suite, listed alongside Thales, Saab, Safran and Terma. On the Magentic side, its agents extract data from emails, documents, files and CAD drawings, then use that data to verify pricing and purchase orders and secure cost savings within enterprise systems. The agents also identify and close value leakage, meaning the hidden loss of capital when a company overpays or fails to negotiate savings. For one client, Magentic ran agents on 1m purchase orders a year, checking pricing accuracy, supplier choice, renegotiation chances and rerouting to cheaper existing contracts.

Magentic's CEO, Robin Van Aeken, said everyone wants this work to run autonomously, but customers must first go on a human-in-the-loop journey in which agents learn from users. He said direct procurement is complex and localised, traditionally owned by manufacturing plants and by senior category managers who have known their three suppliers for 30 years. According to him, legacy ERP systems record only the final price paid, and none of the negotiation, context or supplier performance behind it. He said that in the first three months after one customer went live Magentic saved $1.2m, and that the total reached $4.2m over the six months after that. Seadronix's CTO, Hankeun Kim, called the Singapore selection a defining milestone, saying a place beside European suppliers shows its AI delivers the capabilities and reliability maritime security missions demand.

Boston Consulting Group data shows that only 35% of procurement teams have adopted AI, even though better supply chain management is crucial. According to LeanDNA, 64% of manufacturers spend 10% or more of their manufacturing budget reacting to supply chain disruptions, through last-minute production changes or emergency sourcing. Van Aeken said modernising procurement is critical for growth, including in European manufacturing, which competes aggressively with cheaper, lower-cost manufacturing. Magentic works with enterprises in the automotive, oil and gas, and food and beverage industries.

On the defense side, the article describes the selection as a strong endorsement, because equipment on government vessels must perform reliably over decades of service. Magentic's research on the cost of waste comes from World Commerce and Contracting, which found that value leakage costs enterprises that manage contracts and supply chains around 9% of annual turnover. To build trust with new clients, Magentic typically starts with outcome-based pricing, charging only a percentage of savings generated during a pilot phase. It then moves to a customised subscription model once daily operations are fully automated.

Seadronix's Singapore work extends beyond the patrol vessels, covering a smart port collaboration with the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore. It also includes a fireboat demonstration with the Singapore Civil Defence Force and a memorandum of understanding with the Defence Science and Technology Agency on an unmanned surface vessel. Seadronix describes the Sentinel-class win as a dual-use milestone, with AI proven on commercial and government vessels now extending into defense. Van Aeken expects procurement teams to change, with automation shifting them from administrative work to more strategic tasks.

He said the procurement team of the future finds more win-wins with suppliers, does more value engineering and pre-empts more disruptions. He hopes procurement will grow into a more strategic function, a partner to the CFO, to manufacturing and to engineering, rather than being too much of a cost centre. Seadronix's NAVISS Bridge is slated for installation on the Sentinel-class vessels, but the announcement gives no installation dates or number of vessels. The articles also give no delivery timetable for the vessels, no contract value for Seadronix, and no date by which Magentic's agents are expected to run fully autonomously.

stories.Headline: The Nvidia spy scandal exposes networks operating in Singapore that help Chinese tech companies access advanced US AI chips and circumvent export controls (Owen Walker/Financial Times)
stories.Summary:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has acknowledged an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed International. United States intelligence officials suspect that Alice Huang acted as a Chinese intelligence asset. The admission has prompted an internal investigation by the Nvidia board, which announced the probe on a Sunday. It has also united Democrats and Republicans in Congress in demanding tighter controls on exports of artificial intelligence hardware. The news broke in the days before 11 November 2026, as lawmakers returned to Washington for the lame-duck session.

Federal investigators are examining whether Megaspeed served as a conduit for bypassing United States export controls and diverting restricted, high-performance AI processors to buyers in Beijing. Megaspeed purchased $2 billion worth of Nvidia products between 2023 and 2024. Senator Elizabeth Warren and other legislators want to attach three new semiconductor export bills to must-pass defence legislation before the end of the year. These include an AI monitoring act that would bar exports of H200-class and more advanced chips to China for a set period, a chip security act, and the MATCH Act. A floor vote is seen as possible in the second week of December, with a presidential signature after mid-December, and the proposals would mandate stricter end-user verification and impose severe penalties on manufacturers whose products turn up in unauthorized jurisdictions.

The Nvidia board has said its independent investigation will examine whether corporate secrets or national security parameters were compromised during the relationship. The probe is expected to review the chief executive's communications and the specific terms of the Megaspeed contracts. Jensen Huang has publicly apologised for the affair but has not addressed the espionage allegations about his associate. United States intelligence agencies concluded earlier this year that Alice Huang was gathering information on the American AI sector for China's Ministry of State Security. Authorities suspect she used her relationship with Huang and her position at Megaspeed to help move advanced hardware to China, where it could train military and commercial AI models.

Republican Representative Jim Banks and Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren issued a bipartisan statement urging immediate action on export controls for AI semiconductors bound for China. According to reports from intelligence briefings, President Donald Trump was told that Huang was associating with a suspected Chinese operative before the executive was allowed aboard Air Force One for a trade mission to Alaska. Democratic lawmakers call this gross negligence, arguing that the administration ignored warnings and kept collaborating closely with Nvidia on federal technology initiatives. Republican defenders reply that the president relied on the company's internal compliance assurances and that Huang was himself the target of an intelligence operation exploiting human vulnerabilities. A former senior American official said some restrictions could also appear in economic and technology exchanges between the United States and China, and industry analysts warn that firms may have to audit their distributors, raising compliance costs.

Alice Huang, who is not related to the Nvidia executive, previously worked as a journalist for Chinese state television before moving into Asian finance, with roles at HSBC and Citic Securities. By 2023 she had become a controlling shareholder and director at Megaspeed. Corporate filings show its balance sheet growing from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion a year later, as it became one of Nvidia's largest regional clients and a listed cloud partner. Singapore does not strictly prohibit selling advanced hardware to Chinese entities, but deals involving American-designed components must comply with Washington's extraterritorial export laws, and the case shows how hard multi-jurisdictional supply chains are to monitor. Nvidia, valued in the trillions of dollars, dominates the design of the processors behind generative AI, and Washington has steadily tightened sales of them to China.

The proposals are expected to be folded into the National Defense Authorization Act, which supporters see as the most viable vehicle before the new Congress convenes in January. The Nvidia board's inquiry into the chief executive's communications and the Megaspeed contracts is still under way. The articles do not say when it will finish or what it might conclude. Nor do they say whether federal investigators will bring any charges, or whether Alice Huang has responded to the allegations. Markets have already moved, with SK hynix, which supplies more than 50% of Nvidia's HBM memory, facing doubts over its plan to expand a plant in Dalian, China, while AMD shares jumped 13%.

stories.Headline: Meta is launching its "smallest and most efficient" AI model: Muse Ember.
stories.Summary:
Meta Superintelligence Labs released a new AI model called Muse Ember on Monday, November 9, 2026, describing it as the lab's lightest and most cost-efficient model so far. Meta said Ember was designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day, such as tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction and long document parsing. The model is hosted by Meta, with access through the Meta Model API and Muse Code, and its weights are private. Ember is the fourth model under the Muse brand, following Spark, Glimmer and Wonder. Meta says Ember was the first model it trained using Muse Wonder Full, its largest model.

Ember costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, while cached input costs $0.004 per million, and Meta lists no long-context pricing tier. It has a context window of one million tokens and can produce up to 512K output tokens, four times the 128K cap on both Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna. The model accepts text, images, audio and video natively, so agents can read screenshots, charts, scanned documents, voice memos, meeting recordings and video without a separate model. It can also operate desktop applications from screenshots. Haiku 5.5 charges $0.50 and $2.50 above 100K prompt tokens, and GPT-6 Luna doubles its input rates above 272K input tokens.

Meta is responsible for the release, and it summed up the design by saying Muse Wonder plans while Muse Ember handles the volume. The company emphasized cost per task, using the composite benchmark score from Artificial Analysis to present Ember as cheaper and smarter than rivals such as Anthropic's Haiku and OpenAI's Luna. Meta positions Ember below its larger models, with Wonder handling the hardest problems and Spark covering coding and agentic workflows. Ember takes repeatable coding and agent tasks at scale. In a customer-support setting, a heavier model would set rules for an issue and Ember would then apply them across tens of thousands of cases.

The benchmark figures reported come partly from Artificial Analysis and partly from Meta's internal suite, all at maximum reasoning effort. Ember scores 36 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, level with Claude Haiku 5.5 at max effort and ahead of GPT-6 Luna at 28. On AutomationBench-AA, which covers 657 Zapier business workflows, Ember completes 37.8 percent of tasks, against 20.2 percent for Luna and 13.9 percent for Haiku. Ember leads Terminal-Bench 4.0 with 40.9 against 39.2 for Haiku and 16.4 for Luna, but loses FrontierCode 2.0-AA, scoring 27.2 against Haiku's 34.9. Its output cap and pricing mainly benefit developers running repetitive agent work at high volume.

Ember's cost advantage comes from the number of tokens used per task, since its list prices match those of Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna. On Meta's chart, Ember at max effort scores 35.8 at $0.136 per task, while Haiku 5.5 at max scores 36.2 at $0.411. Luna's best setting scores 27.8 at $0.152 per task, and Artificial Analysis summarised the result as matching Haiku at a third of the cost per task. Ember also leads the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, 46 to 37 to 31, and scores 61.6 on Agents' Last Exam against 57.1 and 57.0. Ember ties GPT-6 Luna on GDP.pdf-AA at 22.8 and edges Haiku on OSWorld 2.1, 69.5 versus 68.9 on partial credit.

Ember follows the mid-weight Spark, released in April, Spark's open source twin Glimmer, released in August, and the Wonder frontier model, released in October. The flagship consumer product, the Muse Agent, was released in September and met unexpected success, with features such as Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier in November. Ember was released on November 9, 2026, after Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7, 2026 and GPT-6 Luna on September 22, 2026. Ember is also cost-competitive with open source rivals such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash. Its PerceptionBench score with tools is 80.6, compared with 78.6 for Haiku and 62.8 for Luna.

The articles describe no further release schedule for Ember or for other Muse models, and they do not say whether Meta plans an open source counterpart like Glimmer. Ember's parameter count is not disclosed, and the weights are closed, so there is no local GPU, laptop or quantized option. Because Ember is hosted only on Meta's infrastructure, developers must use the Meta Model API or Muse Code to try it. The articles also leave open how customers will compare the model in practice, since the cost and accuracy figures come from Meta's own chart and internal suite alongside Artificial Analysis. Ember trails Haiku on mergeable real-repo coding, and the articles do not say whether Meta plans to close that gap.

stories.Headline: 🔥 Jensen Huang and the future of the AI boom
stories.Summary:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on Wednesday, 11 November 2026, after the company's board launched an investigation into his behavior and its possible national security implications. Huang, now 63, had run the company for the 33 years since he co-founded it in 1993. He left after two reported extramarital affairs, one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee. The board named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive and appointed Harvey Jones as chairman. Nvidia has not replied to repeated requests for comment on the episode.

Kress will serve as interim chief executive until the board finds a permanent replacement, while Jones takes over as chairman of the board. CNBC reported that Huang has agreed to testify before Congress following his resignation. Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That figure is up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012.

Nvidia's board is responsible for choosing a successor, and it must do so without a succession policy, because the company refused to put one in place. Colette Kress and Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees after the announcement, and CNBC published what they said. Huang publicly apologized for being unfaithful to his wife on the Sunday before he resigned, according to the reporting. Nvidia did not respond to the repeated requests for comment that CNBC made. Huang had earlier built the company with no second-in-command, which leaves the board looking for a leader of a firm run by one singular figure.

Kevin Cramer, a Republican senator from North Dakota who sits on the Senate Banking Committee, told CNBC just before the resignation that Huang looked vulnerable to extortion and blackmail. Many US lawmakers demanded investigations, and some demanded Huang's resignation. Former Cisco chief executive John Chambers said that how companies handle a crisis determines their future, and that this will show whether Nvidia is a great leadership team beyond one person. Michael Dell called Huang a visionary of the AI age, and Chris Miglino of the neocloud Axe Compute said the industry would be years behind without him. Tomás Puig of Alembic said Nvidia prepaid two years of invoices after the 2023 collapse of Silicon Valley Bank, when his firm was down to weeks of cash.

Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 to make chips for computer graphics, and in the early 2000s he and other executives saw that the chips could serve computationally intense projects. The company became the first to pass a $5 trillion market cap, and in the five years to 2026 it sold nearly 14 million flagship AI chips, which hold 85% of the market. Nvidia has backed the neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius with equity and financial guarantees, and it invested nearly $10 billion across Europe in the last year. In August it said it would provide up to $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio. The woman involved was identified by US intelligence as recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, according to The New York Times, and she has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer.

The next test is Nvidia's quarterly report on Tuesday, when analysts expect revenue of $109.2 billion. The board still has to pick a permanent chief executive, and the articles do not say who it will choose or how long that will take. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, but the articles give no date for the hearing or say what he will be asked. It remains open whether the ecosystem of neoclouds and startups that leaned on his sign-off will stay on course, since one source said project finance deals waited on his approval even while he was flying. The articles also leave open what the national security investigation will find, and Azeem Azhar asked whether the dependent ecosystem will stay on the road.

stories.Headline: AMD or Nvidia: Which AI Chip Stock Would I Buy With $1,000 Today?
stories.Summary:
Advanced Micro Devices and Intel were compared in a Motley Fool article by Harsh Chauhan, published on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, which weighed which AI chip stock is the better buy. Both stocks have gained this year, despite what the article calls a brutal recent sell-off in semiconductor shares. AMD shares have jumped 137% in 2026, while Intel has recorded gains of 60% as of the time of writing. Both companies benefit from demand for AI-oriented chips, which major hyperscalers deploy in data centers for both training and inference workloads. A second Motley Fool article, published on November 11, 2026, separately discussed SpaceX as a potential member of the $5 trillion club by 2029.

Intel's data center and AI segment revenue rose 78% year over year in the third quarter, reaching $7.3 billion. AMD's data center segment grew 97% year over year to $8.5 billion in the previous quarter, so AMD now outsells Intel in that segment. AMD expects revenue of $17 billion in the current quarter at the midpoint of its guidance, a 66% year-over-year increase, while Intel's $15.5 billion guidance implies a jump of just 13%. AMD projects revenue growth of more than 80% in 2027, which is more than double the company's long-term growth forecast. AMD trades at 30 times forward earnings per Morningstar, against 35 times for Intel, and AMD's earnings per share are projected to rise 118% in 2027 versus 20% for Intel.

AMD CEO Lisa Su spoke on the latest earnings call about the company's visibility into 2027, saying it continues to strengthen. She recalled that last quarter AMD expected annual server revenue to grow more than 70% and data center segment revenue to more than double for the year. Since then, she said, customers have expanded their Epyc and Instinct deployment plans, and AMD has secured more supply to support that growth. She said AMD now expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027, and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than projected 90 days earlier. Intel management also spoke on its own earnings call, noting that it expects server CPU industry shipments to increase by more than 30% in 2026 and 2027.

The article's author, Harsh Chauhan, concluded that AMD is growing significantly faster than the end market, which indicates it is taking market share from Intel. He described AMD as the better semiconductor stock to buy right now, especially since it is cheaper than Intel on a valuation basis. He added that analysts have become significantly more bullish on AMD's long-term earnings per share growth following its latest quarterly report. He noted that Intel's earnings per share could also increase impressively over the long run, but said AMD's lower valuation makes it the better buy. Chauhan has no position in any of the stocks mentioned, while The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends both Advanced Micro Devices and Intel.

AMD sells both server central processing units and graphics processing units, which helps explain why it is outselling Intel in the data center segment. Intel, by contrast, seems more inclined toward server CPUs after its Gaudi series of data center GPUs failed to find much favor among customers. AMD expects stronger data center growth from the increasing adoption of its latest MI455X graphics cards, which it has begun shipping in volume to customers, along with its Epyc server CPUs. Intel's data center and AI revenue growth has been accelerating in recent quarters, even though AMD's growth is stronger. The Motley Fool's Stock Advisor team did not include Advanced Micro Devices among its 10 best stocks to buy now, and its total average return stands at 852% versus 203% for the S&P 500.

The articles do not say whether AMD's guidance for the current quarter and for 2027 will be met, so those projections remain forecasts. Analysts expect AMD to clock significantly stronger earnings growth than Intel in 2027, with estimates of 118% for AMD against 20% for Intel. The articles leave open how long the recent semiconductor sell-off will last or whether the two stocks will keep their 2026 gains. In the second article, SpaceX and Tesla formed independent committees in October to explore a merger that would be based on a combined market value of roughly $3.4 trillion. Reaching $5 trillion from there would take about 47% appreciation, though the article stresses that a merger is not guaranteed and would create complications for shareholders.

stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, FuelCell Energy, a Nasdaq-listed company trading as FCEL and based in Danbury, Connecticut, announced that it is taking part in a project called StabilityMax. The project is a three-year collaboration led by the National Laboratory of the Rockies, which belongs to the U.S. Department of Energy. Argonne National Laboratory also participates in the effort alongside FuelCell Energy and the lead laboratory. The partners aim to develop and validate integrated power system architectures built for the fast-changing energy needs of artificial intelligence data centers. The announcement came as a press release distributed through GlobeNewswire on the morning of November 10.

StabilityMax will produce a testing and modeling framework that evaluates how fuel cells, energy storage, advanced controls and power electronics can work together. The goal is to deliver reliable and responsive power to AI data centers, which are driving unprecedented electricity demand and rapid swings in consumption. FuelCell Energy will develop a fuel cell test facility in Connecticut, creating a testbed that the national laboratories will support for evaluating integrated power solutions. The National Laboratory of the Rockies will build data center load profiles and simulation models that capture the dynamic power demands of modern computing infrastructure. Argonne National Laboratory will add techno-economic and lifecycle analyses to help identify commercially appealing and cost effective deployment strategies.

Shankar Achanta, FuelCell Energy's Chief Product and Technology Officer, said AI infrastructure is creating unprecedented demand for reliable, flexible and resilient power. He explained that StabilityMax joins the company's operating experience and fuel cell technology with the expertise of leading national laboratories. According to Achanta, the work will show how integrated power systems can serve the evolving needs of AI data centers and will help optimize system designs. He added that it will also validate performance under real-world conditions and support future deployment of fuel cell-based solutions for digital infrastructure. Eric Strayer, the company's Head of Global Sales, said FuelCell Energy is already working with customers and partners deploying power solutions for digital infrastructure.

Strayer said the project will supply valuable data and operating experience that can inform future deployments, since load profiles change with each new generation of chips. He said the insights will help refine designs and strategies for integrating fuel cells, energy storage and power electronics in data center environments. Zhiwen Ma, the Principal Investigator at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, said fuel cells collocated with data centers offer unique solutions to the power demands of AI infrastructure. Ma said the project will help demonstrate how integrated fuel cell systems can respond rapidly to data center needs while limiting impacts on the utility grid and ratepayers. The parties most directly affected are AI data centers, the utility grid and the ratepayers who depend on it.

StabilityMax is one part of a broader initiative by the National Laboratory of the Rockies to support the growing energy needs of AI-enabled digital infrastructure. Through new modeling tools, planning platforms and test environments, the laboratory is helping accelerate the power systems needed for efficient fuel cell-powered data centers. The project builds on FuelCell Energy's ongoing development of integrated power solutions for digital infrastructure. Earlier this year, the company announced a collaboration with Siemens on a layered architecture that combines multiple technologies operating across different timescales to meet AI data center power needs. FuelCell Energy describes itself as a U.S. clean energy technology company delivering continuous, scalable baseload power, with global deployments approaching one gigawatt.

Insights from StabilityMax are expected to further inform system design and deployment strategies for future digital infrastructure applications. The collaborators plan to use the framework and testbed to optimize designs, validate performance and support future deployment of integrated power solutions. The project runs for three years, though the articles give no specific milestones or timelines for its outcomes. They also give no cost or funding amount for the project or for the Connecticut test facility. The articles do not say when the Connecticut facility will be ready or what fuel cell capacity it will hold.

stories.Headline: Cisco deploys Mythos 5 in AI Defense to boost AI-focused red team testing
stories.Summary:
Cisco announced on November 9, 2026, that its AI Defense product will add Anthropic's Claude Mythos to its adaptive AI red teaming framework, making it among the first AI security products to do so. The announcement appeared on the Cisco blog and was written by Amy Chang and Vikram Varakantam. The model is described as Claude Mythos 5, and it is meant to strengthen the framework where an attacker's reasoning matters most. Cisco says it paired that frontier reasoning with responsible controls so that red team engagements can reflect adversary capability without compromising customer security. The article that bears the Mythos headline gives no further figures beyond these framing details.

The deployment is built around three controls: authorization to test only targets the customer is permitted to test, attribution to a named operator, and full auditability. The model sits inside AI Defense with a fixed job, a registered target, and objectives defined by the human user. Customers do not get an open interface to Claude Mythos, and they cannot prompt it freely. They inform the target and the objective, and Cisco's agentic red teaming framework carries out the engagement within those bounds. During planning, the model's reasoning produces attack ideas, and when those ideas become concrete payloads the benefit is sharper still, under safeguards built for authorized testing.

Cisco's blog post makes the case for the move in its own words, and Michael Moore, Cybersecurity Lead at Anthropic, supplied a supporting statement. Moore said enterprises are building AI agents into their core operations and want to test them thoroughly before production. He said that by bringing Claude Mythos to Cisco AI Defense, Cisco can help security teams red team their agents with advanced reasoning that plans tests and generates attack ideas for each system. Cisco says it regards this as an early instance of a broader shift, in which the frontier capabilities most relevant to security are made available to defenders under verified, controlled access. Cisco contrasts that approach with withholding those capabilities from everyone.

The people affected are Cisco's customers, who exist across virtually every industry and use agentic AI in correspondingly diverse ways. Cisco says businesses are eager to adopt agentic technologies while security teams work to keep pace. It adds that organizations must now account for how agents behave once connected to a complex, interconnected system of tools, skills, and sensitive resources. Every environment is different, so Cisco says security teams need a way to find risks specific to their own deployments before attackers do. Separately, Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 reported that attackers are using AI-enabled red teaming tools such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI to carry out offensive operations autonomously.

Cisco describes AI Defense as the first enterprise AI security offering to combine asset visibility, supply chain scanning, algorithmic red teaming, and runtime guardrails in a single unified solution. When agents emerged, Cisco says it was the first to introduce adaptive red teaming and adaptive guardrail capabilities. AI Defense offers two kinds of testing, standard and adaptive. Standard red teaming covers thousands of categories, content types, and adversarial techniques in minutes, including prompt injection and jailbreaks, sensitive data exposure, and harmful content generation, with reports mapped to Cisco's Integrated AI Security and Safety Framework and to OWASP, MITRE, and NIST standards. Adaptive testing lets users define custom criteria in plain language, after which the framework analyzes the target, tailors attacks, refines tactics from the target's responses, and reports its findings.

The adaptive reports come with recommended follow-up actions, and customers can guard against specific risks by building custom adaptive guardrails in Policy Studio. The Cisco text provided breaks off mid-sentence while describing how the deployment operates, so the rest of the safeguards are not given. The article does not say when the Mythos capability will be available, how it will be priced, or which customers will receive it first. It also leaves open how the controls will be verified or audited in practice. Unit 42 notes that the author of ARTEX recently made the repository closed-source and stopped public development to prevent misuse, and says emerging alternatives are rapidly filling that void.

stories.Headline: What Does CoreWeave (CRWV) Winning A New AI Training Deal Mean?
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave reported quarterly financial results on Tuesday, and a Washington Examiner commentary said the company crushed expectations across every metric as it drove rapid utilization of its accelerated computing services. The commentary was written by James Rogan, a former U.S. diplomat who later worked in law and finance for more than thirty years. It framed the report as a test of true demand for the computing services at the heart of the artificial intelligence revolution. Separately, The New Stack carried an article headed to say that CoreWeave tests AI integrations on its cloud before customers migrate. The text of that second article available here consists almost entirely of website navigation and sign-up forms, so none of its substance can be reported.

Net income losses continue at CoreWeave, which the commentary attributes primarily to heavy depreciation and ballooning quarterly debt service obligations. Those obligations now approach $1 billion in net interest expense, which the commentary calls a key risk. At the end of June, the company held a cash position of $5.5 billion against $35 billion in debt. Its debt currently yields 16 percent, a level the commentary says is consistent with junk status. In August, the company put its capital spending guidance at $35 billion to $39 billion, against only around $13 billion in 2026 revenue.

The people responsible for closing that gap are CoreWeave's management, and the commentary says they must convince the market that they can fund it at manageable rates. The commentary notes that CoreWeave has to pay for chips and data center capacity before customers are obligated to start paying for compute capacity. It adds that the backlog of business is growing, but so is the capital investment necessary to deliver it. Nebius, another major NeoCloud company, is due to report its own results on Thursday. The writer discloses owning shares in CoreWeave, Nvidia, Nebius and Google.

Financial markets are increasingly concerned about true demand for AI computing services, and Rogan says these two reports should bring some clarity this week. Analysts anticipate strong revenues for Nebius, which is expected to keep aggressively deploying its new inventory of Nvidia accelerated computing clusters. Over the past few weeks the share prices of both companies have dropped sharply, as the market worries whether they can keep accessing capital at competitive rates. Startups that rent clusters can reach the market without building a multibillion-dollar data center, while the hyperscalers Google, Amazon and Microsoft use NeoClouds to meet customer demand their own data centers cannot. The commentary warns that distress at either company could freeze the market for new syndicated debt supporting independent data center builds, and could spread across valuations for all alternative infrastructure providers.

The commentary describes CoreWeave and Nebius as perhaps the leading companies in the NeoCloud business, which rents access to clusters of advanced chips typically designed by Nvidia. Customers use those chips to train AI models and to run them to answer queries, a process known as inference. Many companies in the AI ecosystem carry heavy debt loads, and the NeoClouds are particularly debt-heavy. Anthropic, a leading developer of frontier AI models, is expected to go public next week at a valuation of around $1.4 trillion. That valuation has dropped by several hundred billion dollars over the past few weeks, and Tuesday's higher-than-expected October Consumer Price Index inflation numbers led the market to forecast a more aggressive interest rate policy by the Federal Reserve.

The immediate next event is Nebius reporting its quarterly results on Thursday, which analysts expect to show strong revenues. Anthropic is expected to go public next week, though its valuation has already slipped by several hundred billion dollars. Management at CoreWeave still has to show the market how it will fund the gap between $35 billion to $39 billion in planned capital spending and about $13 billion in 2026 revenue. The articles leave open whether the NeoClouds can keep raising capital at rates that avoid financial distress. They also leave open what the new AI training deal named in the headline involves, because the available text does not describe it.

stories.Headline: Nscale considers delaying its New York IPO until next year, The Telegraph reports
stories.Summary:
Nscale, the London-based AI cloud company backed by chip giant Nvidia, is considering delaying its planned New York stock market listing, according to a report in The Telegraph published on Tuesday, November 10. Reuters relayed that report, which said executives at the data-centre developer are assessing whether to pause their efforts to go public until next year. Reuters did not report a specific reason for the possible delay, and the company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Telegraph has put the possible value of the listing at $35 billion, and some reports describe it as being as high as that figure. The report arrived days after Reuters reported that Microsoft had declined an option to expand its existing agreement with Nscale.

Nscale filed for the initial public offering in September, when it sought about $3.5 billion in funding, including $2 billion from Nvidia. The company plans to list on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol NSCL. In October, Bloomberg reported that Nscale was seeking a valuation of roughly $30 billion, well below the $35 billion ceiling the Telegraph has mentioned. Nscale's last private funding round valued the company at about $15 billion. Microsoft and Anthropic accounted for about 85% of the $103.4 billion in signed and active contracts that Nscale reported at the end of August.

Nscale's executives are the ones weighing the delay, according to the Telegraph, which said they are assessing whether to pause the listing until next year. The company has not publicly confirmed or denied that it is considering a postponement. It did not respond to Reuters outside regular business hours when asked for comment on the report. Reuters said it did not report a reason for the possible delay, so the company's motives remain unstated in the coverage. The articles attribute no on-the-record statement from any Nscale official about the timing of the listing.

Some investors told Bloomberg in October that a valuation of $16 billion to $19 billion would attract more buyers than the roughly $30 billion Nscale was seeking. They cited construction delays and a cooling market for AI infrastructure listings. Microsoft is directly affected, having declined last week to expand its Nscale contract for more computing power at a Texas data center. Reuters described that decision as part of a broader pullback that has exposed the neoclouds built on Microsoft's contracts. Financing for the sector has also tightened, with lenders pulling back from AI debt.

Microsoft withdrew as anchor tenant of Nscale's planned data center in Loughton, Essex, where grid operators do not expect to supply power until the 2030s. Nscale's site in Norway is reportedly about six months behind schedule. CoreWeave, the largest listed neocloud, was due to report its third-quarter results after the close on Tuesday. Reuters tied the Nscale report to Anthropic's own listing plans, which it called a key test of Wall Street's faith in the AI boom. Anthropic on Tuesday filed an updated prospectus for its IPO, seeking a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, slightly short of some investors' expectations.

Executives at Nscale are still assessing whether to pause their efforts to go public until next year, so no decision has been reported. It remains unclear whether the company will keep its September filing in place or hold the NYSE listing back. The articles do not say what valuation Nscale would accept if it proceeds, given the gap between the roughly $30 billion it sought and the $16 billion to $19 billion some investors favored. Nscale has not yet responded to Reuters' request for comment on the Telegraph report. Anthropic's offering continues to move ahead, and the reports describe it as a key test of Wall Street's faith in the AI boom.

stories.Headline: ModelOp Named a Market Shaper in the 2026 Gartner® Emerging Market Quadrant for AI FinOps Tools - Startup Vendors
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, two companies announced that Gartner had positioned them as Market Shapers in its Emerging Market Quadrant for AI FinOps Tools, Startup Vendors. ModelOp, which calls itself the Enterprise AI Command Center for Fortune 500 and Global 2000 organizations, made its announcement from Park City, Utah. Coralogix, which describes itself as the data and AI platform for observability, made its own announcement from Boston. Both announcements were distributed through GlobeNewswire and carried by The Manila Times that day. Gartner published the report on October 28, 2026, and the announcements describe the Coralogix recognition as part of an October 2026 report.

ModelOp says it is one of four vendors in the Market Shapers quadrant, among 18 vendors recognized in the report. The quadrant examines vendors in fast-changing technology markets, assessing their Potential for Market Disruption and Potential to Execute. Gartner defines AI FinOps tools as solutions that measure, attribute, forecast, control and optimize AI costs, and it characterizes Market Shapers as vendors with strong cost optimization insights and automation pursuing end-to-end proactive AI cost management. ModelOp delivers its AI FinOps capabilities through its Enterprise AI Command Center, powered by the ModelOp AI Delivery Engine, known as MADE. Its listed capabilities include use case-level cost attribution, a usage dashboard, portfolio analysis, AI discovery of shadow assets and business value monitoring, with integrations spanning Microsoft Agent 365, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Quick, OpenAI and tools based on the Model Context Protocol.

Dave Trier, chief executive of ModelOp, said enterprise AI faces a financial accountability crisis, because companies deploy more models and autonomous agents than ever while counting tokens does not show executives whether investments pay off. He argued that the real question is the business value of specific use cases, which is why ModelOp ties AI costs to the use case, the business owner and the expected outcome. He added that AI FinOps must be part of how enterprises govern and operate AI, rather than a dashboard added afterward. Trier also said the next phase of enterprise AI will be defined by measurable returns, not by the number of agents deployed. ModelOp states its belief that its placement reflects its approach of bringing AI usage, cost and business value into the same system of record that manages AI governance and delivery.

Ariel Assaraf, chief executive and co-founder of Coralogix, said AI is changing the economics of running modern software, and that managing AI spending requires visibility into the systems and workflows driving it. He said the company believes its recognition reflects the growing importance of connecting AI observability with financial accountability as enterprises operationalize at scale. Coralogix cited Gartner as saying the market is shifting beyond cost reporting toward AI economics management, and that organizations must connect token consumption, compute and other costs to measurable business outcomes. As one example of its reach, Coralogix says a global professional services firm uses it to monitor approximately 19,500 coding-agent users, with visibility across users, models and repositories. Its AI FinOps capabilities include budget controls, consumption forecasting and automated safeguards against unexpected spending, and it tracks token usage across models, teams and workflows.

ModelOp says this is its third Gartner recognition of 2026, following two earlier research recognitions. In June it was named a Visionary in the Gartner Magic Quadrant for AI Governance Platforms. In the companion Critical Capabilities for AI Governance Platforms report, it received the highest score for the AI Agent Governance use case. The company says it has been building its enterprise AI delivery and governance foundation since 2018, covering lifecycle automation, risk management, policy enforcement, operational monitoring and AI FinOps. Coralogix says its platform is built on a streaming-first architecture that unifies logs, metrics, traces and AI observability, and it describes enterprises as moving from AI experimentation to production-scale deployments with multi-model environments and expanding token consumption.

Coralogix says it will keep investing in AI-native observability, real-time data infrastructure and autonomous investigation capabilities, and it has made the full report available for download from its website. ModelOp points readers to its website and blog for more detail on its AI FinOps capabilities. Both companies attribute the placement to their own view, and Gartner's disclaimer states that its publications are opinions rather than statements of fact and do not endorse any vendor. The articles do not say how the other vendors in the quadrant were placed, nor do they name the 18 vendors recognized in the report. They also give no word from Gartner on the announcements, no placement details for Coralogix beyond its Market Shaper status, and no further timeline for either company.

stories.Headline: IBM and Microsoft Launch AI Agent Platform
stories.Summary:
IBM and Microsoft announced a new artificial intelligence agent platform called Imagine Enterprise on Tuesday, November 10, 2026. The two companies launched it jointly, with IBM based in Armonk, New York, and Microsoft in Redmond, Washington. It combines more than 6,000 prebuilt AI agents and related assets from IBM Consulting with Microsoft's cloud infrastructure. The platform is meant to help banks, insurers and retailers automate business processes, and it initially targets financial services, insurance and retail. The announcement describes it as an agentic platform for building, running and governing agents that help people carry out industry-specific processes.

Forward-deployed engineers from both companies will work directly with qualifying customers to integrate agents into existing software and move them from testing into production. The 6,000 figure covers agents and other assets, so it does not count only agents that can be deployed. IBM's contribution comes from Consulting Advantage, its existing platform for developing and deploying AI applications, along with Process Studio, Context Studio and Advantage Core. Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio and GitHub Copilot supply agent development and coordination tools, while Microsoft Fabric connects enterprise data. Microsoft Entra manages identities and access permissions, Purview supports data governance, and Defender provides security, with Azure and Microsoft 365 infrastructure also part of the supporting technology.

Mohamad Ali, Senior Vice President and Head of IBM Consulting, said clients no longer want AI that merely helps people do the same work slightly faster. He said they want to build an agentic business. Ali added that Microsoft and IBM are helping organizations bring human expertise and digital labor together in a way that can scale across the enterprise. He said the aim is to turn AI from a productivity aid into a real competitive advantage. The platform is designed to connect with existing company systems and to adapt agents to an organization's own information and processes, so customers do not have to start from scratch.

Sneha Shah, Chief AI Strategist and Head of SEI Next, said the company's work with IBM Consulting and Microsoft is helping it explore how emerging capabilities could support critical processes and be responsibly scaled over time. SEI is a financial technology, operations and asset management provider, and it is working with IBM Consulting, supported by Microsoft, to explore emerging and agentic technologies. Its goals include better business operations and better experiences for employees and clients. The announcement does not identify a completed Imagine Enterprise deployment at SEI or give measured results from the new platform. The platform particularly targets organizations in regulated industries, and its governance features include controls, observability and AI-compliance support.

The partnership extends Microsoft's efforts to expand AI adoption across its existing enterprise software customer base. Microsoft has 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats, but fewer than 7% carry paid Copilot licenses, according to PYMNTS reporting from September. Microsoft 365 Copilot costs $30 per user monthly, while newer agent capabilities are billed according to usage. Microsoft has also introduced agents that operate within corporate Microsoft 365 environments, with their own identities, memory and email addresses. The launch comes as businesses increase AI investments but remain cautious about giving software independent authority.

PYMNTS Intelligence's November report, titled The Agentic Edge Index, found agentic AI in use at 89% of large U.S. enterprises. Even so, 78% of those enterprises would limit agents to read-only access to company directories. Another 18% would let agents perform tasks with human approval, while 2% would permit independent execution. The same report found that 51% of executives see organizational barriers, including staffing, business processes and corporate culture, as greater obstacles to AI adoption than technology. The articles give no launch pricing, availability dates or customer list for Imagine Enterprise, and the engineering support applies only to qualifying engagements.

stories.Headline: Google Launches Gemini Decisions API With Gemini Decision 1 at $0.10/M Tokens
stories.Summary:
Google has launched the Gemini Decisions API, powered by a new model called Gemini Decision 1, with the identifier gemini-decision-1, according to a report published on 11 November 2026. The model does not write text. Instead, it scores up to 1,000 typed questions against one shared input and returns calibrated probabilities, which developers can use to drive branching choices inside agents such as routing, policy checks, tool selection and grading. Google prices it at $0.10 per million input tokens, and no output tokens are billed because output usage is always zero. It is available only through Google's hosted Gemini Developer API in v1beta, with no open weights or self-hosting.

Each request contains a model ID, a shared input and a map of questions, and the shared input can mix text, images, video, audio and PDFs. The documentation defines three question types. A yes/no type returns the probability of yes, bounded between 0.01 and 0.99, a choice type picks one of 2 to 255 options and returns normalized probabilities for each, and a score type rates the input on 2 to 255 ordered rubric levels and returns a probability-weighted score. Every answer carries a confidence value from 0 to 1, and Google suggests sending low-confidence cases to a fallback or a human reviewer. The context window is 262,144 tokens shared across the input and all questions, and the shared input is billed once per request, with each question adding only its own instruction and criteria tokens.

All benchmark figures are self-reported by Google, and refusals and safety blocks count as incorrect. Gemini Decision 1 leads seven of the nine accuracy benchmarks in the table, including 92.2% on JevBench against 90.0% for TypeSafe Jev 1.14, and it posts the lowest calibration error, 0.0250 compared with 0.0494 for Jev 1.14. Its weakest result is a 58.7% Macro-F1 on Amazon ESCI, and it trails Jev 1.14 on When2Call, 79.9% to 82.0%. On cost, the total for the seven shared evaluations is $0.88, against $0.68 for Jev 1.14, $0.93 for OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna and $4.14 for Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, which Google says makes it nearly five times cheaper than Flash-Lite. Google also reports median model compute of 50 to 100 milliseconds and 150 to 250 milliseconds end to end, for inputs up to 16K tokens.

The model is positioned against TypeSafe Jev 1.14, OpenAI Decisions running GPT-6 Luna, and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. Standard models decode an answer token by token and leave the code to parse it, whereas Gemini Decision 1 scores the candidate options in a single forward pass. Latency stays nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions, and Google lists no charges for thinking tokens, transcription or OCR. The comparison table shows GPT-6 Luna allowing 1 to 400 questions per request with a context of 1,050,000 tokens, while Jev 1.14 has no fixed question cap and offers 64K per request, or 262K with an opt-in header. The articles do not say what Google plans to do next with the API beyond its current v1beta availability.

stories.Headline: Nebius Group (NASDAQ: NBIS) stock price forecast: AI infrastructure growth drives Wall Street's bullish outlook
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group shares rallied sharply on November 11, 2026, ahead of the company's third-quarter earnings release scheduled for before the U.S. market opened on November 12. The recovery followed stronger-than-expected results from CoreWeave, which reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 bn, up 168%, and a revenue backlog of roughly $132.5 bn. Nebius shares rebounded 12-15% in premarket trading on November 11, reaching about $150-154 after closing at $134 on November 10. CoreWeave's strong earnings helped restore confidence in AI infrastructure stocks, and Simply Wall St reported that the news sharpened attention on Nebius' large Microsoft contract and its GPU build out. The articles describe the third-quarter release as the immediate catalyst for the stock.

Wall Street expects Nebius to report third-quarter revenue of approximately $907 mn, up 521% year over year from $146.1 mn in the third quarter of 2025. Second-quarter 2026 revenue was $582.3 mn, so the expected sequential growth is 56%. Analysts anticipate a quarterly loss of roughly $0.60-0.70 per share as infrastructure investment accelerates. Investment bank price targets range from $144 to $399, with a broader analyst consensus near $297. At a premarket share price near $150, the $296.73 average target implies about 98% potential appreciation over 12 months, a figure the article describes as an expectation and not a guaranteed return.

The company is responsible for the results and the expansion plan, and the articles report its commitments rather than direct statements. Nebius announced a five-year agreement with Meta in March 2026, covering $12 bn of dedicated computing capacity, with deliveries scheduled to begin in early 2027. The arrangement includes commitments for up to $15 bn of additional capacity, bringing its potential total value to approximately $27 bn. Nebius has also indicated that it holds more than $40 bn in long-term customer commitments. Beinsure reports that investors will focus on whether data center capacity comes online on schedule, financing is sufficient and contracts become recognized revenue.

Among the banks, Morgan Stanley rates the stock Equal Weight with a $144 target from August 2026, while Piper Sandler is Neutral at $185 as of October 21. Citigroup holds a Buy rating at $265 as of November 4, Bank of America a Buy at $310 as of October 22, and Goldman Sachs a Buy at $328 as of August 25. Exane BNP Paribas rates the stock Outperform at $399 as of September 24. Citigroup cut its target from $324 to $265 in early November, and Piper Sandler cut its target from $237 to $185 while keeping a Neutral rating. Across 13 analyst ratings, the consensus includes nine Buy recommendations, three Holds and one Sell, and Simply Wall St's community narrative by Womble puts fair value at $259.97 per share.

The articles give financing as the background to the expansion, since rapid growth requires heavy spending on GPUs, power infrastructure, cooling systems and data center construction. In October, Nebius secured a $3.5 bn senior secured financing facility from Citi, with an initial maturity of 364 days and interest starting at Term SOFR plus 2.75%. In August, the company completed an approximately $5.75 bn convertible senior notes offering. Beinsure notes that debt financing increases interest expenses, that convertible securities can create potential shareholder dilution, and that a prolonged period of elevated U.S. interest rates would make future expansion more expensive. The stock has also fallen substantially from its August highs, and Beinsure reports that Microsoft has increased scrutiny of certain AI infrastructure projects, which it says should not be confused with confirmation that contracts will be terminated.

Nebius will publish its third-quarter results before the U.S. market opens on November 12, and revenue approaching $907 mn would confirm rapid business expansion. Beinsure says the market is likely to place greater weight on management's capacity deployment schedule, financing strategy and 2027 outlook than on the headline figure. Its three developments to watch are capacity delivery, financing costs, and utilization and margins. Under the bullish case, the higher bank targets of $265-328 become more defensible, while delays, higher financing costs or changes in customer spending could keep the stock nearer the $144-185 range. Simply Wall St adds that investors await clarity on utilisation, cash burn and Microsoft-related workloads, and the articles leave open whether Nebius can turn contracted demand and its $3.5 bn facility into sustainable cash generation.

stories.Headline: #AmazingChina | AI in eyes of global media leaders - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
The 7th World Media Summit was held in Beijing from Nov. 5 to 9, 2026, where media professionals from around the world discussed artificial intelligence and its effect on news production. Xinhua News Agency and the Beijing municipal government jointly organized the gathering under the theme "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action." About 500 representatives from nearly 330 media organizations, think tanks, government bodies and international organizations took part, coming from 112 countries and regions. Participants explored how to use AI to improve news production while avoiding ethical pitfalls that could undermine trust in their content. They stressed that adopting the technology must go together with upholding journalistic principles, and that international cooperation is essential.

On Saturday the summit released the Global Media Initiative for the Joint Development of AI Application Standards, which Xinhua launched with major media outlets and other professional organizations. The initiative aims to safeguard the authenticity of information, protect data security and uphold media ethics, so that public trust in the media is maintained. Participants plan to work together for about two years to develop a set of standards addressing different media uses of AI, validated by media outlets. The initiative also calls for a global database of AI applications. During the summit, two life-sized robot news anchors, described as the world's first bionic humanoid robot news anchors, made their official debut and greeted the audience in fluent English.

Fu Hua, president of Xinhua News Agency, urged media professionals at the opening ceremony to share new technologies and applications, exchange experience in using them, and close gaps in AI research, development and understanding. He said the industry should lead the way in giving all media professionals a fair chance to benefit from AI. Speaking to executives at the high-level dialogue, he said Xinhua is willing to strengthen dialogue with all parties to advance the industry's development and promote exchanges and cooperation. He added that media practitioners should make good use of AI while safeguarding the credibility of mainstream media. He also said Xinhua looks forward to deeper cooperation with fellow media organizations, to promote closer people-to-people ties and advance relations between countries.

Reuters President Paul Bascobert called AI a resource that increases speed, efficiency and scale, but said it must meet journalistic standards and that tasks may be automated while judgment may not. He said the most important aspects of journalism are done by people, including gaining trust, reading people and understanding nuance in conversation. Toshimitsu Sawai, president of Japan's Kyodo News, called generative AI an assistive tool, warned of copyright infringement, misinformation and out-of-control model behavior, and said humans bear final responsibility for content. AFP Chairman and CEO Fabrice Fries described "augmented journalism," in which reporters spend less time on routine production and more on observing reality and explaining complex developments, while CNN's Kostas Oikonomou called collaboration between media companies a strategic necessity. Tatiana Valovaya of the UN Office at Geneva said AI's opportunities and risks are too consequential to be left to a handful of countries or companies, and representatives from the Global South, including Mohammed Alyami, Aminath Namza and Wong Chun Wai, urged that developing countries share in AI's benefits and in shaping its governance.

Newsrooms everywhere are under pressure, Fries said, with audiences expecting faster coverage, more formats, more languages and more explanations. AI is finding its way into virtually every stage of news production, from story planning and information gathering to fact-checking, proofreading and the generation of news images and videos. Bascobert noted that news delivery has evolved from carrier pigeons and telegraphs to digital technologies, while the core task of getting the facts, checking them and reporting them has not changed. Valovaya listed serious challenges, including synthetic content, information manipulation, privacy threats, algorithmic bias and unequal access to technology. A China-Africa AI media training program for Tanzanian media professionals also took place in Dar es Salaam on Nov. 1, 2026.

Participants in the standards initiative plan to work for about two years on the standards, which will be validated by media outlets. Alyami, whose Union of News Agencies of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation is among the first participants, hopes the initiative becomes a practical avenue for sharing expertise and building capacity, with standards that outlets of different sizes and resources can apply. The articles do not say which outlets beyond the first participants will join, or what the global database of AI applications will contain. They also do not describe how the standards will be enforced once developed, or when the robot news anchors might be used in actual reporting. Sumeyra Teymur of Haberler.com has expressed interest in humanoid robots covering dangerous situations such as earthquakes and conflicts, but no plans are reported.

stories.Headline: Cloudflare Jumps 11%, Nebius Surges 9% as AI Cloud Stocks Defy NVIDIA's Slide; CoreWeave Rallies 6% on Wayve Deal
stories.Summary:
AI cloud stocks rose on Monday, November 9, 2026, even as NVIDIA fell. Cloudflare traded at $297.22, up 11% in afternoon trading, as buyers kept piling in after its third-quarter earnings beat. Nebius Group rose 9% to $140.70 ahead of its own quarterly report. CoreWeave gained 6% to $49.18 after signing a multi-year cloud computing deal with British autonomous driving startup Wayve. NVIDIA, meanwhile, slid 5% to $177.40, while the articles say AI shares were drawing buyers back after last week's post-midterm selloff.

Under the deal reported on November 9, Wayve will use CoreWeave's NVIDIA Blackwell-based infrastructure to train and test its driving models. Wayve already uses Weights & Biases, which CoreWeave acquired in 2025, and financial terms were not disclosed. Cloudflare reported revenue of $782.51 million for the third quarter, up 39.2% from a year earlier and above the $738.30 million consensus. Adjusted earnings of $0.38 per share beat the $0.3434 estimate, and the company reported a 17.5% adjusted operating margin. Management raised its full-year 2026 revenue outlook to $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion and guided fourth-quarter revenue to $845 million to $846 million.

Cloudflare reported its results after the close on November 5, and CEO Matthew Prince called it the company's best quarter ever. He credited the company's fastest revenue growth in nearly four years, achieved while profitability expanded. On the earnings call, Prince presented Cloudflare as the first agentic cloud, with developers building AI agents on its Workers platform. Nebius is expected to report before the market opens on November 12, and its investors are likely to focus on capacity guidance, 2027 run-rate projections and infrastructure spending. CoreWeave did not disclose financial terms of the Wayve agreement, and its own quarterly earnings are also coming up.

NVIDIA's decline was described as running on a separate track from the cloud names. Yahoo Finance reported on November 9 that NVIDIA is investigating CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Oracle gained 3% to $119.16, a smaller rise than the neocloud names, and IREN rose 2% to $21.98, also trailing Nebius and CoreWeave. Analysts expect Nebius to post revenue of $905 million to $907 million, which would mean growth of more than 500% from a year earlier. They also expect an adjusted loss of 69 cents to $1.11 per share, and options pricing implies a post-earnings move of 17% or more.

Cloudflare runs a global edge network that sells security, networking and developer tools on a subscription basis to millions of organizations. That model ties its growth to developer adoption and security demand across a broad customer base. Nebius and CoreWeave rent GPU computing capacity to AI labs, hyperscalers and enterprises, and both buy their chips from NVIDIA. CoreWeave reported a revenue backlog of approximately $104 billion as of June 30, while Nebius disclosed $37.5 billion in remaining performance obligations. Oracle pairs its AI cloud with an enterprise software franchise, and IREN owns the land, power and data centers behind its shift from crypto mining.

The next test for Cloudflare is whether its growth can stay near the pace management guided for the fourth quarter. The bulls can point to accelerating revenue, the 17.5% adjusted operating margin and a higher full-year outlook. On the other side, Cloudflare's reported gross margin fell to 71.2% from 74%, and $4.4 billion in convertible notes remain outstanding. For Nebius, the upcoming report could decide whether its run-up holds against high expectations, and the articles suggest a conservative approach may be warranted until results are released. The articles leave open how long NVIDIA's slide will last and what the reported investigation into Huang's ties will find.

stories.Headline: Meta, TikTok join Google to push back on Indonesia’s planned AI copyright law revisions
stories.Summary:
Meta and TikTok joined Google on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, in pushing back against proposed revisions to Indonesia's copyright law at a parliamentary hearing in Jakarta. The revisions would require digital platforms to pay publishers for displaying news content, and they would also set rules for artificial intelligence. If the bill is passed, Indonesia could become the first country in Southeast Asia to incorporate AI in its copyright law. Reuters exclusively reported the planned revisions in July, citing a draft of the bill. The Reuters report on the hearing was written by Stanley Widianto and edited by Emelia Sithole-Matarise.

The bill would oblige digital platforms to pay publishers for displaying news content, which is the provision Google and Meta objected to most directly. It would also write rules for AI into Indonesia's copyright law, a step few governments have taken as they grapple with the technology. Those rules touch on the use of human-created work to train AI models, which is one of the central questions governments face. The articles do not give the amount of any payment, the mechanism for setting it, or the specific wording of the AI rules. The articles also do not say when the revised law could take effect if it is approved.

Agung Pamungkas, Google's Indonesia government affairs and public policy manager, told the hearing that requiring platforms to pay compensation for showing links to publishers' news content would limit Indonesians' access to news. Berni Moestafa, Meta's public policy head in Indonesia, said compensation requirements meant publishers could lose readership traffic as well as potential advertising and subscription revenue. Berni added that directing readers to an article is different from reproducing or republishing the article itself. Noudhy Valdryno, TikTok's head of public policy in Indonesia, addressed lawmakers separately on the AI provisions of the bill. He said disclosure requirements should not apply where AI is used only in an assistive capacity rather than to fully create content.

Noudhy also urged lawmakers to preserve safe-harbour protections for platforms. His reasoning was that platforms cannot reliably determine copyright ownership or licences for the material they carry. The objections therefore came from three of the largest digital platforms operating in Indonesia, each raising a different concern. Publishers are the group the payment proposal is meant to benefit, though the articles quote no publisher at the hearing. The articles also do not name any lawmaker who responded to the platforms, or any government body that has taken a position.

Governments around the world are grappling with how AI affects copyright rules, including the use of human-created work to train AI models. Indonesia's draft would put the country among the first to act on that question in law, and the first in Southeast Asia. The draft became public in July, when Reuters reported its contents exclusively after seeing a copy of the bill. By November 11, the arguments had moved to a formal parliamentary hearing where Google, Meta and TikTok each spoke. The articles supply no further history of the copyright law itself or of earlier attempts to revise it.

The bill is still a proposal, and the hearing on November 11 was one stage in its consideration by parliament. If it is passed, Indonesia could become the first Southeast Asian country to include AI in its copyright law. The articles do not say when a vote might be held, or whether the proposed payments for news content will be kept, amended or dropped. They also leave open whether lawmakers will accept TikTok's request to exempt assistive uses of AI from disclosure, or to preserve safe-harbour protections. Whether publishers or other groups will testify, and how the final text might differ from the draft, is likewise not stated.

stories.Headline: Nvidia spy allegations likely to spur laws to tighten China's access to AI chips
stories.Summary:
Congress is now more likely to pass legislation tightening China's access to AI chips, according to lawmakers and advocates, after news that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence agent. Reuters reported the story from New York on November 9, citing both lawmakers and outside advocates who favor the measures. Three chip-related measures are slated for possible inclusion in the annual defense authorization bill for fiscal year 2027, which began in October. The articles say Huang's affair has added new urgency to concerns that China's access to advanced chips could undermine United States national security. They also point to his close relationship with President Donald Trump as a factor that sharpens those concerns.

The first measure is the AI Overwatch Act, which would give Congress power over exports of advanced chips. The second is the Chip Security Act, which would require businesses to track their chips in order to combat smuggling. The third is the Match Act, which would push United States allies to restrict more chipmaking equipment going to China. The House Foreign Affairs Committee advanced all three bills earlier this year, and they now sit in the Senate National Defense Authorization Act management package. Representative Bill Foster of Illinois, a Democrat, said the Chip Security Act he introduced with Republican Representative Bill Huizenga of Michigan passed unanimously out of the House committee.

Nvidia declined to comment on the matter, and its position is described mainly through earlier statements and through a former congressional staffer. The company has said it complied with export laws. Until the Department of Justice brought indictments tied to chip smuggling last year, Huang and Nvidia had argued that no such smuggling existed. One former congressional staffer, who had direct contact with the company over several months, said Nvidia is considered the biggest opponent of both the Chip Security Act and the AI Overwatch Act. The White House did not comment on the measures, though the articles describe winning its support as the main obstacle that the bills must clear.

In a joint statement on Monday, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Republican Senator Jim Banks of Indiana said Huang's confirmation of the relationship made the national security concerns even more urgent. They called on Congress to take decisive action and pass key bills such as the AI Overwatch Act in the defense bill, to cut off pathways through which China reaches advanced chips. Foster posted on X on Monday that Congress has the tools to keep powerful AI chips from the wrong hands, and urged lawmakers to get his bill across the finish line. Chris MacKenzie, a spokesman for Americans for Responsible Innovation, a Washington nonprofit that favors the measures, said backing Nvidia in a fight with Congress would be costly for the White House. The Information Technology Industry Council, whose members include Nvidia, has opposed the measures, arguing they could undermine United States competitiveness and complicate export control policy, and its spokeswoman declined to comment on the current Nvidia situation.

The articles give some background on how the debate reached this point. In March, Warren and Banks urged the Department of Commerce to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses to China and to conduct a full security review. Headlines linked from the pages indicate that the story had been developing for days, including a report that key Republicans sought a briefing from Huang over the spy allegations. Other linked reports say Nvidia announced a probe into Huang, that the company's shares slid as its board examined the matter, and that Congress would investigate. The pages also point to coverage of Huang's earlier ties to a Singapore company in a spy probe, and of Nvidia boosting chip tracking in Southeast Asia to fight smuggling.

What happens next depends largely on whether the three measures stay in the defense authorization package and on whether the White House comes around to supporting them. The articles say the fiscal year 2027 defense authorization bill is the vehicle under consideration, but they give no vote dates or timetable for action in the Senate. They do not say whether the White House will support the measures, since it did not comment, or how Nvidia will respond beyond its stated compliance with export laws. They also leave open whether the Department of Commerce will act on the senators' March request about Nvidia's export licenses. The outcome of the probes mentioned in linked headlines, and any consequences for Huang or the company, are not described in the articles themselves.
