stories.Headline: Indian organisations see AI returns but risk readiness declines: Kyndryl
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl released its third annual Readiness Report on November 11, 2026, finding that Indian organisations are seeing stronger returns from artificial intelligence while their readiness to manage the surrounding risks is falling. Sixty per cent of Indian organisations investing in AI and machine learning now report positive returns, which is an increase of three percentage points from 2025. At the same time, the share that consider themselves completely ready to manage external risks dropped by eight percentage points to 27 per cent. The report draws on responses from 3,700 senior business leaders across 21 countries, including 200 leaders in India. Coverage of the findings highlights a growing gap between how widely AI is being adopted and how prepared enterprises are to cope with its risks.

Eighty-five per cent of Indian organisations are now deploying AI in workflows that go beyond pilot projects, according to the report. The proportion of businesses still at the experimentation stage has fallen by 15 percentage points to 56 per cent. Cybersecurity is the leading worry, with 68 per cent of Indian respondents naming cyberattacks as a top external risk, yet only 35 per cent say they are completely prepared to manage them. That readiness figure is a drop of 10 percentage points from the previous year, while globally only 26 per cent of organisations reported complete readiness against cyberattacks. Seventy-one per cent of Indian leaders rated their IT infrastructure as mostly or fully modernised, but 59 per cent said significant re-architecture would still be needed to support AI at scale.

Kyndryl, the technology services company, is the author of the report, and Martin Schroeter, its Chairman and CEO, commented on the findings. He said organisations are increasingly focused on making their early AI returns sustainable. He added that their technology infrastructure, workforce capabilities and governance frameworks are struggling to keep pace with the speed of adoption. The report itself frames the findings around the challenges businesses face as AI moves from experimentation to large-scale deployment. Its summary also points to a distinction between having modern technology infrastructure and having systems that can support enterprise-wide AI deployment.

The surveyed Indian leaders themselves described several difficulties in scaling AI, and these views are what the report records from the people it affects. Seventy per cent of them said their organisations have more AI pilots than they can realistically scale, and 58 per cent said innovation often stalls after the proof-of-concept stage. Half of the surveyed organisations significantly changed their AI strategy over the past year, while 31 per cent reported an AI investment failure. Thirty-seven per cent of respondents experienced disagreements between their chief human resources officer and their chief technology or information officer over AI strategy. Despite the security concerns, three in four leaders said AI was helping their organisations identify threats faster, and the report also raised concerns about AI-driven disruption to established business models.

The report offers some background on how Indian organisations are already putting AI to work. Eighty per cent of them are using AI agents to automate workflows that previously required coordination across multiple teams or systems. This is the third annual edition of the Readiness Report, which gives a basis for comparison, with the 60 per cent returns figure measured against 2025. The proportion of organisations considering themselves completely ready for external risks has fallen by eight percentage points, and the cyberattack readiness figure has fallen by 10 points. Globally, the share of organisations fully prepared for cyberattacks is down by 11 percentage points to 26 per cent.

The articles do not describe any specific actions that Kyndryl or the surveyed organisations plan to take after the release of the report. The only forward-looking element is the statement from Schroeter that organisations are focusing on making their early AI returns sustainable. What the report means for the 59 per cent of leaders who expect significant re-architecture is not spelled out, including how much it would involve or how long it might take. The articles also do not say how organisations plan to close the readiness gap on external risks and cyberattacks. Whether the 70 per cent of leaders with more pilots than they can scale will manage to move those projects forward is left open.

stories.Headline: Google's AI chip expansion opens new doors for Samsung, SK hynix
stories.Summary:
Google is pushing to sell its custom AI chips beyond its own data centers, and this is creating openings for Samsung Electronics and SK hynix to diversify demand for high-bandwidth memory away from Nvidia. The Korea Herald reported on November 11, 2026, that the US tech giant is expanding its tensor processing unit business to serve cloud providers and companies building AI infrastructure. On Monday, Google unveiled two new TPU systems, the TPU 8i Max and the TPU 8tx, which expand its eighth-generation lineup to four models. The 8i Max combines two chips in a single package, doubling both computing performance and HBM capacity. The 8tx targets AI workloads that require stronger data security.

Google says it now has nearly 100 TPU customers, including companies that deploy the processors inside their own data centers. Oracle plans to offer Google's chips through its cloud platform next year, and Alphabet expects TPU system sales to rise substantially after they contributed to Google Cloud's third-quarter growth. Counterpoint Research forecasts that HBM bit demand for custom AI server chips will grow 35-fold between 2024 and 2028, driven partly by Google's TPU expansion. Samsung and Broadcom, Google's major TPU development partner, signed a memorandum of understanding in July covering HBM, foundry manufacturing and advanced packaging. The potential cooperation is valued at more than $200 billion through 2030, though that estimate spans several businesses and includes no confirmed HBM orders.

On the Korean side, SK hynix is seeking a role earlier in chip development, after a February meeting between SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won and Google CEO Sundar Pichai. Following that meeting, the memory maker proposed jointly designing customized HBM for future TPUs, and Chey also met Broadcom CEO Hock Tan to discuss next-generation AI chips. Counterpoint says Google is working with Taiwan's MediaTek on its TPU 8t, partly to move away from Broadcom's turnkey model. In that model the design partner also handles memory purchases, and Counterpoint estimates it adds a markup of 15 to 20 percent to HBM costs. Counterpoint research associate David Wu said that by bringing chip design and HBM procurement in-house, starting with the code-named Zebrafish, Google removes the intermediary fee and lowers its overall cost.

Counterpoint research director Hwang Min-sung called the shift a major opportunity for memory suppliers to create a high-value business. An industry source said the bigger story is not Google's latest chip specifications but that Google is turning TPUs into a business serving customers outside its own data centers. A second industry source cautioned that winning a new customer does not necessarily mean shipping more HBM right away, because so much future capacity is already committed. That source added that the real competition is over who gets into the next chip design and secures production slots early enough to turn the relationship into long-term orders. The affected parties are Samsung and SK hynix, whose HBM demand has been concentrated around Nvidia's dominant GPU ecosystem.

The Korea Herald explains that HBM4 and HBM4E let suppliers tailor memory components to specific AI processors, which could secure higher-value, longer-term contracts through earlier involvement in chip design. Securing new orders may nonetheless be difficult, because production capacity is already heavily committed. SK hynix said in October that agreements with 14 major customers cover volumes equivalent to more than half its total production capacity for 2027 and 2028, including products beyond HBM. Seoul Economic Daily reported separately that Samsung Electronics and SK hynix both rose more than 5% in premarket trading on Nextrade on the 10th. As of 8:12 a.m., SK hynix traded at 1.213 million won, up 6.78%, while Samsung Electronics stood at 201,000 won, up 5.85%.

That rise followed a rebound on Wall Street the day before, when all three major indexes climbed more than 2%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at 52,389.75, the S&P 500 at 7,549.94 and the Nasdaq Composite at 25,253.14. AMD surged 13.26%, Marvell Technology rose 9.49%, Broadcom 8.78% and Micron Technology 6.25%, while SK hynix's American depositary receipts gained 5.53%. Nvidia fell 4.27% amid controversy surrounding Chief Executive Jensen Huang, and its closing market value shrank by about $192.1 billion in one day. Kiwoom Securities analyst Han Ji-young said the sharp recent correction has already priced in much of the concern about the AI industry and chipmakers' earnings outlook, and that the US consumer price index for October and CoreWeave's earnings could trigger a recovery in sentiment.

stories.Headline: New York's AI Safety Law Hits OpenAI, Anthropic Today
stories.Summary:
New York State opened a corporate registration portal on the 10th, local time, ahead of putting its RAISE Act into practice, an AI safety and transparency law aimed at the biggest developers of advanced artificial intelligence. The law covers frontier AI developers with annual revenues above $500 million, and OpenAI and Anthropic are named among the representative companies it reaches. Covered companies must register with state authorities by January 1, 2027, and must report major safety incidents within 72 hours of the event. One article says the law takes effect early next year, while another says enforcement began on the same day the portal opened, so the articles differ on the timing. Governor Kathy Hochul also launched a new research center at Binghamton University (SUNY) that day to support the oversight effort.

The law places three core obligations on covered companies, starting with public disclosure of their safety management systems on their own websites. Those disclosures must describe how each company identifies and manages the risks its AI systems pose, and companies must also issue model transparency reports. Companies must notify authorities within a set deadline when a major safety incident occurs, and that deadline is 72 hours. Violations can bring penalties of up to $1 million, about 1.3 billion won, for a first violation and up to $3 million, about 4 billion won, for repeat violations. The $500 million revenue threshold is about 670 billion won, and the registration deadline of January 1, 2027, applies to every covered company.

Enforcement falls to the newly established Division of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust, known as DIGIT, which oversees large AI research labs and checks whether companies meet their statutory safety duties. State authorities said they can take enforcement action against companies that fail to register, but they did not disclose the specific method. Governor Hochul launched the New York AI Responsibility and Research Center at Binghamton University on the same day the portal opened. The center will independently assess whether advanced AI systems operate safely, examine their security and operational methods, and review corporate safety policies together with DIGIT. She first announced plans for the center in January, backed by $55 million, about 73 billion won, in donations and capital.

Speaking at a briefing that day, Hochul criticized technology companies for justifying harm in the name of the AI development race. She said the tech moguls describe their envisioned AI future as inevitable and warn that anyone who does not join in will be left behind. She added that the state is building a sensible regulatory model that puts communities before corporations and people before powerful technology. Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic has issued a public statement about the New York deadline, though both have previously voiced support for thoughtful regulation in congressional testimony. Anthropic priced its IPO at $70 to $78 per share ahead of a November 19 debut, and OpenAI has just turned ChatGPT into a business discovery tool.

The articles place the law among other state measures, starting with California's SB 53, which took effect in January and requires frontier developers to establish and disclose safety policies and protect whistleblowers. SB 53 also requires major safety incidents to be reported within 15 days, compared with New York's 72 hours. Illinois's SB 315 takes effect early next year and adds a requirement for independent audits of compliance with safety standards. New York has also enforced a law since last year requiring AI companion services to remind users periodically that they are talking to an AI and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal thoughts or signs of self-harm. Last month it enacted a chatbot safety law for minors that restricts impersonation of humans, emotional manipulation, unconditional agreement and encouragement of suicide or eating disorder behaviors, taking effect June 1 of next year.

The new rules are expected to raise cost and compliance burdens for large developers, since disclosures, transparency reports and incident reporting systems all require standing staff and internal controls. Companies operating in several states will likely need to design their response systems to meet the strictest reporting deadline, because the deadlines diverge between 72 hours and 15 days. If regulators and independent research institutions come to review corporate safety policies jointly, demand for external verification of AI safety assessments is also expected to grow. One article says the exact fine structure remains under regulatory review and names the Department of Financial Services as the overseer, which conflicts with the other article's penalty figures and its naming of DIGIT. That article also says the agency has not disclosed how many investigators it has assigned or what its audit schedule looks like, and it reports that Colorado and Massachusetts have working groups studying the issue.

stories.Headline: Adobe brings AI agents and new creative tools to Photoshop, Premiere, and Firefly
stories.Summary:
Adobe announced a broad expansion of AI features across its creative products at its MAX 2026 conference, which opened in Miami on the 10th. The update reaches Firefly, its generative AI app, and the Creative Cloud programs Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator and InDesign. At the centre of the Firefly update is the Adobe Creative Agent, which now works more widely across the app. Adobe also released a Model Context Protocol that lets other chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini use Adobe features. Forrest Key, Adobe's vice president for Firefly and agentic AI, introduced the Firefly features in his keynote.

The Creative Agent can be directed in natural language through the beta Firefly AI Assistant, and it is now available in Firefly Boards for developing mood boards, storyboards and concepts. Custom settings let users define formats, colours, brand guidelines, characters and products once and apply them across every project. A Plan Mode lets users review, edit and approve the agent's proposed steps before work begins, or let it proceed independently. A model selector lets users pick a model for a session or leave the choice to the system. The number of AI models in Firefly has grown to 36, including ByteDance's Dreamina and Seedance 2.5, Runway's Gen-4.5, Kuaishou's Kling 4.0, Google's Nano Banana 2.1 and OpenAI's GPT.

Forest Key said Adobe wants to offer every creator an agent that supports the creative process from first exploring an idea to bringing it into the world, with the creator's taste, style and vision leading. He described Firefly as the AI creative studio where the best models, the tools creators already trust and an agent acting as a creative partner come together. In his keynote, he said the company's goal is to help everyone create, whether they are new to digital creation or already professionals. Adobe described the Creative Agent as a partner that works alongside users while leaving creative decisions in their hands. Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for Creative Cloud, said the update will let professionals focus on the decisions that shape their own work, with precision, control and flexibility.

Adobe cited its latest Creators' Toolkit Report, which found that 78 per cent of creators said creative AI had accelerated the growth of their business or following. Customers have already used the Creative Agent for batch portrait retouching and for turning product images into short social videos. Firefly now offers models from Adobe, Topaz Labs and partners including ByteDance, Google, Kling, OpenAI and ElevenLabs, so users need not move between separate applications. In Premiere, a generative remove feature in beta erases unwanted objects from footage, using a masking approach in which users designate the target themselves. Photoshop officially launched Relight, which allows fine adjustment of lighting in an image even after a shoot is finished.

Adobe describes Firefly as its effort to bring more of its creative software into one interface as creators work across image, video, audio and design. The company's broader message is that creative work increasingly involves repeated tasks and multiple deliverables, not just one-off outputs. Customers can build custom workflows with Firefly Graph, which is in beta and includes an AI Assistant, for tasks such as character studies, shot lists and applying brand guidelines across campaign assets. Firefly Builder, in private beta, is described as moving into Figma's territory, turning concepts into interactive prototypes such as websites, presentations or apps from natural language prompts. Quick Actions adds ready-to-use workflows such as Remove Object, Thumbnail Generator and Build Product Ad, and Firefly Design in beta combines illustration, image editing, animation, 3D and print on one canvas.

Edit Text, Retouch, Relight and Quick Actions are now generally available in Firefly, while the other newly announced tools remain in beta. Firefly Builder is available in private beta through a waitlist, and Premiere gained a Color Mode that lets users adjust video colour directly in the program. Always-on agents are shown only as a preview, and Adobe says they will handle recurring tasks such as organising incoming assets, checking quality and preparing content for different channels while the user is away. The articles give no dates for when the beta tools or the always-on agents will reach general release. They also give no pricing, no word on which Firefly features need a paid plan, and no date for when Builder's waitlist will open further.

stories.Headline: Law firm founder on AI, patent drafting and changing client expectations - Managing Intellectual Property
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, October 29, the Brooklyn Entertainment & Sports Law Society, known as BESLS, hosted a Film and TV panel titled "The Impact of AI on IP." The event brought together prominent intellectual property attorneys to discuss how artificial intelligence is reshaping the legal and commercial landscape of IP. The panel featured Brooklyn Law School alumni Meeka Bondy, class of 1994, who founded Meeka J. Bondy, PLLC and previously worked at Perkins Coie and HBO. It also included Erica Carter, class of 2015, founder of Carter Advisory, PLLC and formerly of Epic Games and Sesame Workshop, along with Stacy Lager of the National Hockey League. Matt Gamble, a 2027 J.D. candidate at Brooklyn Law School, wrote up the discussion for the Brooklyn Sports & Entertainment Law Blog on November 9, 2026.

The panelists explained that studios generally hold the copyright interests in the fictional characters they create, but that an actor's name, image, and likeness, along with their voice, raise different legal considerations. They noted that rights of publicity vary by state, which makes protecting an individual difficult. Contract language also matters more because of AI, and the panelists discussed provisions granting companies rights to exploit performances across media "now known or not yet created." They expect future contract negotiations to address AI-generated performances and replications more explicitly, including compensation and consent terms. A company wanting to reproduce a single performance indefinitely may face demands for much higher upfront pay or limits on future use.

The panelists themselves are the main voices in the account, and each spoke from their own professional experience. Carter drew on her time at Sesame Workshop, where the company controlled the IP for characters like Elmo, yet the relationship between a character and the human talent behind it remained important. She observed that AI can replicate voice actors' performances without new recordings or studio sessions, which creates tension between a company's ownership interests and the creative contributions of human talent. Lager described the NHL's protective approach to its brand, stressing that licensees cannot simply use valuable IP however they want. The panelists said that effective licensing requires anticipating how IP might be used, reproduced, and misused long after an agreement is signed.

Others affected include actors, athletes, and the labor organizations that represent them. The panel said athletes have a strong interest in protecting their name, image, and likeness from unauthorized AI-generated products that could compete with their existing endorsement opportunities. Actors and other performers may likewise seek greater control over AI reproductions of their work. Labor organizations like SAG play an important role in setting baseline protections, but the panelists stressed that collective bargaining agreements often fall short of the maximum protections available. Individual talent and their teams must negotiate extra safeguards, and their success depends on their leverage, which is limited for the vast majority of actors and athletes.

The panel also covered the background on licensing, authenticity, and employment. For AI-related licensing agreements, the panelists highlighted the scope and duration of permitted uses, approval rights, ownership of derivative works, and indemnification for infringement claims, along with transparency and clear identification of AI-generated content. The panelists were largely skeptical that AI-generated content would diminish the value of established entertainment, and Carter put it as "Elmo is Elmo." They noted that today's consumers still place significant value on authenticity, though unchecked unauthorized reproductions could create commercial competition and complicate exclusive arrangements. Companies must now balance aggressive protection of their rights against the reputational risks of pursuing individual consumers, and AI's ability to generate content around the clock raises questions about future demand for human labor in fields like animation and voice performance.

Looking ahead, the panel concluded with advice for law students preparing to enter industries where AI increasingly shapes legal practice. Each panelist encouraged future attorneys to understand how AI works and how companies develop it, noting that the most effective lawyers are those willing to learn alongside the industry they serve. The panelists discussed possible revenue-sharing arrangements for artists whose existing work contributes to AI-generated products, but no arrangement was settled. The first article, from Managing Intellectual Property, is a Five minutes with interview in which Raluca Vasilescu of Cabinet M Oproiu discusses how AI is changing client expectations of patent attorneys. Its substance is not visible, because the content is limited to subscribers, so what she said about overhyped technology and the next generation's needs remains open.

stories.Headline: Protest against AI in schools, search block planned outside Google's Chicago office Wednesday
stories.Summary:
Dozens of parents, children and teachers protested outside Google's Cambridge, Massachusetts office on Wednesday, 11 November 2026, against a plan to cut off Google Search for schools that decline its artificial intelligence. The protest was part of an organized set of rallies that also targeted Google offices in other cities, including New York, Chicago and Los Angeles. Demonstrators chanted "Kids over tech!" and "Books, not Chromebooks!" as they marched past the company's sign.

Two days earlier, on Monday, 9 November, Massachusetts Senator Edward Markey sent a letter to Alphabet chief executive Sundar Pichai demanding that Google reverse the policy. The Boston Globe reported on the protest, while Tech Times UK covered the senator's letter. Under the arrangement Google announced, Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Google Search stay disabled for kindergarten through 12th-grade accounts until administrators explicitly switch them on. Schools that reject Google's AI offerings will therefore lose access to its foundational search engine. Google said it would no longer automatically turn on its Gemini chatbot for the many schools that use Google Classroom.

Education executive Chris Phillips set out the changes in a blog post on 3 November, and the company is also introducing Guided Learning features that give structured explanations rather than immediate answers. A limited pilot programme involving US schools is scheduled to begin later in November. Google has not budged on bundling search with AI, and a spokesperson told CBS News that AI features are so closely integrated with Search that the company cannot offer the search service separately. Spokesperson Jackie Berté said Google hears the concerns of parents and teachers about students using AI to shortcut learning, and shares the goal of helping students learn. She said the Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will remain off by default until schools decide which services to enable.

Berté added that the company is building these experiences in partnership with educators and listening closely to ensure its products support students and teachers. Google is also developing new restrictions on the school version of Gemini, including a function that lets teachers review chatbot transcripts. Markey wrote that the policy is not a choice but an ultimatum that effectively forces schools to enable generative AI, and he asked whether schools can disable AI Overviews, Gemini and Guided Learning while keeping Search. Sudbury parent Tom Rogan called the policy a breaking point for some families, and Matt Bach, head of the Massachusetts Teachers Association, said classrooms do not need Google. The protest was joined by the leaders of both the Massachusetts Teachers Association and the AFT Massachusetts, along with the Massachusetts AI Action Network, Sociedad Latina and the Becca Schmill Foundation.

Deb Schmill, founder of that foundation, said she knows of no evidence that these products work and that scores have only declined since technology entered classrooms. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has also accused Google of using its market position to push public schools toward AI services. Google's products are widely used in American classrooms, where many schools issue its low-cost Chromebook laptops to every student alongside the Classroom learning platform. In August, Google turned on the Gemini app by default for all schools that use Classroom.

Last week, a day before the search policy was announced, a North Carolina family sued Google, contending their 13-year-old daughter made plans to end her life after months of using Google AI on her school-issued Chromebook. Markey cited a lawsuit alleging that Gemini helped a minor develop a suicide plan, and his letter says the student reached it through Google Search despite restrictions on standalone services, though the allegations have not been established in court. New York and Los Angeles, the two largest school districts, have banned AI chatbots for some or all grades, while Boston has trained AI ambassadors to teach students to work with AI. Google has until 30 November to answer Markey's questions, including its research into the effects of AI tools on children's mental health, safety and learning.

The articles do not say whether Google will revise the policy, and the company has announced no change in response to the senator's request. The limited pilot of Guided Learning in US schools is due to begin later in November, though the articles give no further detail on where it will run. Some protesters said that even if Google rolls back its policy, schools should use the moment to move away from the company entirely. The articles do not say how many schools have opted out of AI or how many administrators have enabled Search.

stories.Headline: Texas Paused Data Center Permits Before the Election. Here's Why That Context Matters for AI Investors.
stories.Summary:
Last week's elections, held in early November 2026, put new Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, and AI stocks have fallen since, dragging the S&P 500 lower. Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect of Texas, has pledged a moratorium on data center building, and Georgia and Ohio's new governors plan to halt permits as well. The market initially seemed to welcome the results on Wednesday, with Amazon and Alphabet rising, before reversing sharply on Thursday. Texas had already paused data center permits before the vote, which is the context the article's headline stresses. The Motley Fool piece, written by Jennifer Saibil and published on Monday, November 9, 2026, describes investors worrying that new legislation could hinder data center growth and slow AI development.

On Thursday, Nvidia fell 8% and Broadcom fell 9%, while the S&P 500 dropped more than 4% and the tech-focused Nasdaq composite fell 5.5%. Hinojosa's pledge would pause building until the legislature can meet and pass into law what she calls real protections for people. Texas accounts for 25% to 30% of the data center capacity planned for development by 2030. In the first few months of 2026 alone, almost 200 data centers asked to be connected to the electric grid. About 90% of the large energy consumers requesting massive amounts of power came from data centers, and those requests totaled five times the amount needed to power the whole state at its record demand.

Hinojosa is the central figure, having promised the moratorium so that government can work with the people to see what their needs are. Her stated condition is that the pause continues until lawmakers pass real protections into actual law, since she sees that as the only way to assure people are protected. Texas's current governor has already started an audit to assess how much energy data centers use and how that affects residents' energy consumption and bills. State lawmakers have questioned whether companies can be compelled to take part in that audit without a law being passed. The article suggests the incoming state government under Hinojosa may pass the laws needed to make the audit happen.

Investors are the group most clearly affected, particularly those holding so-called pick and shovel companies such as Nvidia and Broadcom, which could suffer if data center development is paused. The author notes that much of Nvidia's rapid growth story depends on the continued pace of data center construction. Nvidia has reported accelerating growth, including revenue that doubled in the fiscal second quarter of 2027, which ended July 26. That growth rate will slow if construction slows, and the author expects many AI and AI-adjacent companies to be in the same position. Separately, Simply Wall St reported that regulators and local authorities are reviewing operating permits for several Nebius Group AI facilities, with some approvals still pending as of early November 2026, and commentators have questioned whether this could affect its next expansion phase.

The article says the market did not react to Texas's original permit pause because it did not yet know how seriously lawmakers would take the issue. It adds that the market had been worried about AI spending for months while continuing to climb, leaving some of the biggest spenders behind. Heavy spending has pushed many top tech companies into negative free cash flow. Companies with robust platforms already in place, such as Amazon and Alphabet, are described as well positioned against smaller rivals that still need to build out. Nebius, which builds AI infrastructure across the US, the UK and other markets and has a market cap of $35.5 billion, runs on thin margins of 3.1%, and Simply Wall St says it has partnerships with Nvidia and others.

The articles say new governments entering office with an agenda critical of AI development could cause the AI bubble to pop. They also say a new Congress and the broader implications of the new governments were weighing on sentiment after Thursday's reversal. What the Georgia and Ohio governors will actually do about permits, and when, is not spelled out beyond their plans to halt them. The articles do not say when Hinojosa takes office, how long her moratorium would last, or whether the Texas legislature will pass the laws needed to compel participation in the audit. It also remains unresolved when the pending approvals for Nebius's facilities will be decided, and whether tighter rules would limit connected power across several regions at once.

stories.Headline: GITEX World RobotiX 2026 brings humanoid debuts and next-gen embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Dubai
stories.Summary:
GITEX World RobotiX is a new launch event within GITEX GLOBAL, announced on November 10, 2026, and set to bring the world's robotics pioneers and embodied AI leaders together in Dubai next month. It will run from 8 to 11 December at Dubai Exhibition Centre, Expo City Dubai. The event will show how machines that perceive, reason and act in the physical world are transforming manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, hospitality and smart infrastructure. Visitors can expect interactive humanoids, machines doing industrial tasks, multilingual robot assistants and wearable exoskeletons. GITEX GLOBAL 2026 opens a day earlier, on 7 December, with the GITEX Summit at Dubai World Trade Centre.

The four-day exhibition at Expo City Dubai runs alongside Expand North Star, the startup and investor event, and is billed as the 46th edition of GITEX GLOBAL. It brings together more than 6,000 enterprise and startup exhibitors with tens of thousands of government leaders, executives, investors and buyers from 180 countries. Unitree, which holds 31 percent of the global humanoid market, leads participation, alongside UBTECH, AiMOGA, DEEP Robotics and Micropolis Robotics. Lumos Robotics will bring its MOS 2, a wheeled AI Worker with dual arms that handles payloads of up to 50 kg and runs for more than eight hours. Its NIX S3 will perform a live dance showing 21 degrees of freedom, while Besomi will introduce six robots called the Besomi Rangers.

The event is organised by inD, which runs the 46th edition of GITEX GLOBAL. Mazen El-Kurdi, CTO of Mangobot, said the aim is less to look at robots and more to experience working alongside them. Cecile Wei of Lumos Robotics said its demonstrations show that robots must do more than move and should perform useful tasks reliably in real environments. Hazem Ghazal, General Manager of Lootah Robotics, said the company is building an integrated robotics ecosystem rather than simply supplying individual robots. Tingxiang Fan, co-founder and CTO of Light Origins, said the company believes its bunny-shaped robot is ready to enter consumers' homes.

Mohammad Hani, CEO of Besomi Robotics & AI, said he wants young engineers to ask how things work and then build the next generation of robotics technologies in the UAE. Sandy Liu of the Chengdu Humanoid Robot Innovation Centre said the walking, interaction, performance and education abilities of its robots turn Physical AI into a usable business tool. Nick Zhang of JWIPC said the NVIDIA Thor module gives embodied intelligence a high-compute edge brain that runs multi-modal models locally. Raydiculous will debut in the Middle East with its TP01 humanoid, which speaks English and Arabic, and DINOBOT, a bipedal walking bionic dinosaur. Light Origins will show its bunny-shaped robot publicly for the first time, with live demos of household scenarios.

Counterpoint Research reports that more than 22,000 humanoid robots shipped worldwide in the first half of 2026, a 300 percent rise on the previous year. It expects shipments to exceed 50,000 units by the end of the year. Dubai is pursuing its Robotics and Automation Program, which targets deploying 200,000 robots over ten years to 2032. UBTECH's humanoids are already deployed in car factories and are being tested by Airbus, while Micropolis Robotics supplies autonomous patrol robots to Dubai Police. Lumos Robotics says its first-generation MOS robots ran for over 1,000 hours without failure at Mitsubishi Electric's Changshu factory, handling materials, inspecting quality and driving screws.

The exhibition opens after the GITEX Summit on 7 December, with the expo running through 11 December in Dubai. Lootah Robotics will show robots from Unitree, AGIBOT, Pudu Robotics, UBTECH and EngineAI, and Besomi will run a live Robotics & AI Lab with training on the Arduino VENTUNO platform. JWIPC will launch controllers built on NVIDIA's Thor module, which it says delivers up to 2,070 TFLOPS of FP4 computing performance. Songying Technology will demonstrate ORCA OS and ORCA Lab, and Vecow will unveil rugged edge AI platforms and introduce its new UAE team. The articles do not say how many exhibitors or visitors will attend the robotics event specifically.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Goes for Microsoft’s Crown With New Claude-Powered Office Tools
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, Anthropic unveiled a set of AI-powered office tools at an event in San Francisco. Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets launched in beta, and Claude Dashboards, which had entered beta in October, became generally available under the new name Claude Data. The Verge reported a third tool, Claude Meetings, that can join a meeting, take notes and turn a presentation into a one-minute explainer video, while Gizmodo said it is coming soon. Whiteboards and Sheets are open to all paid plans, and The Verge said Meetings will be available to Teams and Enterprise subscriptions. The company also introduced interactive connectors that open partner apps inside Claude.

Anthropic describes Whiteboards as a shared board where a team brainstorms with Claude, which can turn a spoken, messy plan into a timeline with owners and dates. In a retro meeting, for example, everyone can add notes, and Claude can group them by theme and draft action items for each person. Sheets lets Claude build and edit spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, formatting and drop-downs, often from a single prompt such as a request for a campaign tracker or hiring budget. It outlines each edit so changes can be tracked, and for now it offers only simple spreadsheet functionality, with more planned. Files can be exported to .xlsx or CSV, used through Claude for Excel, or continued in partner tools including Airtable, Asana, monday.com and Smartsheet.

Claude Data lets teams ask questions of company data held in tools like Amazon Redshift, BigQuery and ClickHouse. A data team can certify queries so that charts built on them carry a certified badge, and certified queries and live sharing are both in beta. With live sharing, colleagues see current numbers even without access to the underlying connectors, but they can only view the results of approved queries. The product also now supports design systems, caching with per-dashboard refresh cadences, and tracked changes with rollback to a specific version. Named partners include Amplitude, Mixpanel, Omni, PostHog and Sigma.

For administrators, all three tools are on by default on Team plans. On Enterprise plans, Whiteboards and Sheets are off by default, while Claude Data switches on by default on November 19, 2026. Settings can be changed under Organization settings > Artifacts. The tools work on web, desktop and mobile, and Claude Data requires a data connector such as a warehouse or CRM. The interactive connectors let apps from companies including Adobe, Atlassian, Box and Notion open beside a conversation or in full screen.

Nicholas Lin, who works on product at Anthropic, told The Verge that Claude Code changed how engineers work a year ago and that knowledge workers are now the gap the company hopes to close. He said there is still a lot of friction in adopting AI for non-developers. Lin added that Claude Cowork, another tool for non-engineers, is essentially a wrapper for Claude Code aimed at the technical parts of Anthropic's non-technical audience. Anthropic said in its own announcement that its aim is to keep documents, boards, sheets and dashboards inside Claude so teams can keep editing together. Gizmodo's Ece Yildirim called Sheets the most direct threat to Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets, noting it works almost exactly like those apps.

The new tools join existing ones such as Claude Docs, Slides, Design and Motion, and arrive two and a half years after Artifacts first debuted. Lin said Anthropic launched Model Context Protocol about two years ago and its marketplace has grown to more than 9,000 plugin options, and the company now wants those connections to be deeper. The Verge noted that Google's Gemini and, in some cases, OpenAI's ChatGPT can already join meetings and take live notes. It also said Anthropic faces pressure to generate revenue ahead of an IPO that could be the most valuable public debut ever, with a separate headline citing a $1.4 trillion target. Gizmodo reported that the company is reportedly looking to debut on the stock market on November 19, despite jitters around the broader AI industry, and that the Nasdaq had its worst month in over a year last month.

stories.Headline: Fireworks AI Breach Widens to Expose Customer Billing Data and Incomplete Model Weights
stories.Summary:
Fireworks AI said on Monday that its investigation into a security incident first reported early last month had uncovered further malicious activity. The new activity affected account and billing information, alongside secrets, datasets and incomplete models for what the company called a "limited set of accounts." The company said it first detected unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials on October 6, 2026, at 9 a.m. PDT. That access let an unauthorized third party reach environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts.

Notion, a customer of Fireworks, separately published its own notice about the incident and its effect on some workspaces. The latest Fireworks bulletin says attackers reached its development environment through an unnamed third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks research and development machines on October 23, 2026. On October 24, the third party used that access to reach Fireworks development machines and run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact. The breach exposed resource metadata, including resource identifiers, display names, descriptions and creation time. It also exposed billing information, including billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment history, account balance and credit usage.

A subset of incomplete model weights and datasets belonging to certain customers was also accessed. Fireworks AI said payment card numbers are not stored by the company and were not affected by the incident. It said that, as of October 25, it had not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the platform customers use. The company said it is alerting customers whose data was impacted. After the first detection, it revoked the compromised internal credentials and rotated service account tokens, along with affected Fireworks API keys and keys created by the threat actor.

It also said it has isolated affected systems to prevent further unauthorized activity and lateral movement, tightened access controls, and improved its logging and monitoring. Fireworks AI said the evidence points to a financially motivated cybercriminal group aiming to sell tokens from unauthorized access to large language models to illicit routing gateways. In its first notice, the company said it had found evidence only that environment variables, including API keys and tokens stored as secrets, were captured in certain accounts. At that point it saw no signs that customer models, datasets, training data, inference traffic or personal information were accessed. Notion said its security team found that fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces may have been affected.

Some unattributable Notion AI chat sessions may have been exposed, meaning chats not labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts held no tool call results. Notion said no other data from within a workspace is affected and that it continues to monitor the incident. Notion said it used Fireworks for classification jobs behind its Insights feature and as a general inference provider serving open-weight models inside its product. Fireworks told Notion on November 6 that malicious actors may have accessed potential customer data, and it confirmed the new dataset on November 8. Notion says it disconnected its systems from Fireworks on November 3, deleted all data in the Fireworks system, stopped sending data and traffic there, and halted all training runs.

Notion has contacted the owners of affected workspaces, who can review the data under a Security incident review option in the sidebar, on a desktop browser. Notion recommends treating the data as exposed and rotating any passwords, API keys or credentials that anyone pasted into Notion AI during the period. Notion also said that volunteer customers in its Learning and Early Access Program had in the past contributed data to experiments training task-specific models on Fireworks. The activity is assessed to be part of an emerging threat known as LLMjacking, in which a victim's LLM is hijacked through stolen credentials and access is resold, leaving the legitimate owner to pay the bill. Last week, Google warned that threat actors are increasingly targeting AI infrastructure for LLMjacking in North America, South America and Asia Pacific.

The targeted sectors include financial services, retail, technology and transportation. Google also warned that LLMjacking attacks are costing some enterprises up to $1 million in cloud charges. Fireworks is described by Notion as one of the most-used global AI infrastructure platforms, powering tens of thousands of customers and used by hundreds of thousands of developers. Notion said the Insights feature has been disabled while it investigates, and that it is no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks.

Notion said workspaces that have not heard from it, through either the owner or the member, are not affected and need no action. It also pointed readers to Fireworks' official security updates for the latest on the incident. The articles do not say how many Fireworks accounts were affected, how many customers had billing data or incomplete model weights taken, or the name of the third-party cloud provider. They also do not say whether the intruders have sold any stolen tokens or data.

stories.Headline: Portland parents protesting use of AI in schools
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, concerned parents and advocates with a group called OR Unplugged spent the day protesting outside Google's Downtown Portland office. Their message was that technology in the classroom should be reined in, and that for some of them artificial intelligence should be removed from schools altogether. KOIN 6 News reporter Joey Vacca reported the protest from Portland, Oregon, posting the story on November 11, 2026. The demonstration was one of several protests planned outside Google offices across the country on that same Wednesday. Parents gathered in front of the Downtown Portland office, where KOIN photographed them.

The articles give no formal rule, law or policy being changed by the protest itself, only the demands the protesters voiced. The group's outreach coordinator, Kathy Masarie, summed up its position with the motto "skills before screens." The group's central demand is to limit technology in classrooms and, for some members, to remove AI entirely. Google, for its part, described changes it is making, starting with a pilot this month of Guided Learning capabilities in Search. Next year, Google says, the Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable.

Masarie is the person speaking for the protesters, and she said AI is outsourcing students' learning to technology instead of building their skills. She also said the group was protesting outside Google because the company had threatened to cut schools off from searching on its platform if they declined to use its AI. A Google spokesperson responded with a statement saying the company hears the concerns of parents and teachers about students using AI to shortcut learning. The spokesperson said Google shares the same goal of helping students learn. Google added that it is building these experiences in partnership with educators and listening closely to make sure its products support students and teachers.

Masarie was not convinced by Google's response and said tech companies have been telling the public for years that they are installing protections and barriers. She said a whole group is now checking these so-called protections and finding that they do not work. According to her, a parent who turns a feature on believes the child is safe, and a school that turns it on believes the same, but they are not. Parent Nataliya Pirumova said she is not entirely opposed to technology in class, so long as it is used properly. She said it makes sense to include AI literacy courses so students can understand how the technology works, and that AI is not going away.

For background, the articles say the Portland protest was part of a wider effort, with several protests planned outside Google offices across the country on the same day. Google's statement says the company wants to improve Search for the classroom and is responding to feedback it has heard from educators. According to that statement, the Guided Learning capabilities are meant to walk students step by step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Google also said its planned change to school controls is meant to address that educator feedback. Masarie's account of repeated assurances from tech companies, and of a group now testing the protections, is the other history the articles offer.

Looking ahead, Google said it is starting to pilot its Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month, which the articles date to November 2026. The company said that next year it will update its approach to school controls, so that the Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search are off by default. Under that plan, schools would decide which of those services to enable. The articles do not say whether the protesters will take further action after Wednesday, or whether OR Unplugged will respond to Google's announced changes. They also do not say how Google would answer the claim that it threatened to cut schools off from searching on its platform, or what the groups doing the checking have found.

stories.Headline: Drug Ads Can Influence AI Treatment Recommendations, Study Finds
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai found that a clearly labeled drug advertisement can shift which treatment an AI model recommends. The findings appeared in the November 11 online issue of The Lancet Digital Health. The team tested 12 AI models from major technology companies, including Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic, using physician-written clinical cases. When a case was preceded by an advertisement for a drug, the models became more likely to select the advertised drug. The study asked what happens when commercial advertising appears alongside a clinical question, as people increasingly turn to AI for health information.

The researchers ran 33 clinical scenarios and analyzed 258,559 AI responses, assessing both the treatment selected and whether it was consistent with clinical guidance. The advertised drug was selected in 47.6 percent of responses when an ad was present, compared with 35 percent without one. In four cases, models moved from choosing the advertised drug zero percent of the time to choosing it 100 percent of the time once the ad was introduced. The design isolated the effect of advertising, with a real, clearly labeled drug advertisement placed immediately before each case. Patient information and treatment choices stayed unchanged, and only the presence of the advertisement varied.

First author Mahmud Omar, a lecturer in the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at the Icahn School of Medicine, who leads research on generative AI in clinical care, said he found it surprising how reasonable the answers often appeared. He explained that a model could recommend an appropriate treatment, yet its preference among several reasonable options changed after it saw the ad. Because the final answer could still look medically sound, he said the influence could be easy to miss in typical research evaluations and in personal use by patients and physicians. Senior author Girish N. Nadkarni, chair of the Windreich Department and Chief AI Officer of the Mount Sinai Health System, said an answer can be clinically reasonable and still raise a question about why the AI arrived at it. He added that as AI becomes part of how people get health information, clinical guidance must be distinguishable from commercial influence, with transparency about when advertising is part of the interaction.

The investigators stressed that the findings do not mean pharmaceutical advertising will necessarily cause AI models to recommend unsafe or inappropriate treatments. In the study, advertisements did not clearly increase recommendations for unsupported supplements or clearly suboptimal drugs. The researchers also examined how often the models acknowledged an advertisement or repeated information from it. In a subset of free-text responses, models explicitly mentioned the ad in only 29.9 percent of responses, while they repeated information or claims from it more often. The people affected include patients and physicians who use AI for health information, since the influence could be easy to miss in their personal use.

Mount Sinai physician-scientists have been leading research on the safety, reliability, and real-world effects of generative AI in clinical care, and the study builds on that work. Nadkarni's roles include directing the Hasso Plattner Institute for Digital Health and holding the Irene and Dr. Arthur M. Fishberg Professorship of Medicine. The paper is titled Pharmaceutical advertising and drug recommendations by consumer-facing artificial intelligence: A controlled study, and carries the DOI 10.1016/j.landig.2026.101114. The researchers did not examine whether changes in AI recommendations ultimately affected prescriptions, patient decisions, costs, or health outcomes.

The researchers say the findings point to several practical steps for AI developers and health systems. These include testing AI systems with and without promotional content to see whether recommendations change, and clearly disclosing when advertising is presented to an AI system. They also include keeping promotional material separate from clinical advice. The findings may carry implications for regulators as they consider how existing rules on pharmaceutical advertising apply when promotional content is incorporated into AI-generated health information. The research team plans to extend the work through its ongoing evaluation of AI and human-AI interaction in real-world clinical cases.

stories.Headline: WhatsApp to make connections richer, use AI to save time; privacy unchanged: CEO Kunal Shah
stories.Summary:
WhatsApp chief Kunal Shah set out three priorities for the Meta-owned messaging platform in a post on X, which PTI reported on Wednesday, November 11, and which Trak.in dated to November 10. He said WhatsApp will make connections richer, let users finish tasks such as paying bills inside chats, and use AI to improve efficiency, while personal messages and calls stay end-to-end encrypted. Shah took charge of the platform in June this year and said he spent the months since listening to users about what they wanted. In his words, what he heard was simple: help people stay close to those who matter to them, and get more done on WhatsApp. He said that is what the company will build.

On the first priority, Shah said WhatsApp will make voice notes, groups, stickers and video simpler and more expressive, because how people feel close keeps changing. He noted that users send over 10 billion voice messages and over 4 billion stickers every day. The second priority is to cut the extra steps that follow when a task starts in a chat but has to be finished elsewhere, such as paying a bill, borrowing money or staying connected while travelling. WhatsApp is working with financial services and telecom partners so that finishing something feels as easy as starting it, he said. Trak.in noted that Shah gave no specific new financial partners or launch dates for additional services.

The third focus area is artificial intelligence, which Shah said should quietly find what users need, get things done and make sure they never miss a booking or an appointment. He said the best technology saves people time so they can return to the connections that matter. Trak.in reported that Shah gave no timeline for consumer-facing AI capabilities. Shah also said WhatsApp handles over 100 billion messages and 2 billion calls every day, and that the platform must stay simple, reliable and private. Trust takes years to earn and a moment to lose, he said, adding that he does not take that lightly and that the quality bar would not change.

Meta appointed Shah, the founder of fintech platform CRED, as WhatsApp's global head in June, and he succeeded Will Cathcart, who had led the service since 2019. As part of the move, Meta led a funding round of about Rs 8,550 crore, or about USD 900 million, in CRED. That round placed the Bengaluru-headquartered company at a valuation of Rs 43,239 crore, or USD 4.5 billion. Trak.in said WhatsApp has more than three billion users worldwide, including over 500 million in India, its largest market.

Trak.in also described moves already under way in India. WhatsApp introduced prepaid mobile recharges for Jio, Airtel and Vi in April 2026, and in September Meta announced a gradual rollout of bill payments through Bharat Connect. That service is expected to give access to 22,722 billers across 30 categories, including electricity, water, insurance and loan repayments. Meta has already introduced Business AI for eligible Indian small businesses, which can handle customer queries, recommend products and help manage appointments in native Indian languages. The company has also indicated that UPI payments within AI-assisted chats are forthcoming, and UPI processed approximately 2,547 crore transactions in October 2026.

stories.Headline: Rescale Expands Agentic Digital Engineering with Customizable AI Agents for R&D Teams
stories.Summary:
Rescale, which calls itself the digital engineering platform for the AI era, announced new agentic digital engineering capabilities on Nov. 10, 2026, from San Francisco through PR Newswire. The tools let research and development and engineering teams customize AI agents to their own standards, so every result remains reviewable and traceable. At the center of the release are Agentic Projects, which give engineers a way to customize agents and build reusable agentic workflows. Rescale also introduced Rescale Desktop, expanded Model Context Protocol connectors, and persistent memory for its assistant Edison. Kairos Power and Oak Ridge National Laboratory are named as users of agentic workflows on the platform for advanced nuclear reactor design and manufacturing.

Teams can define each Agentic Project with their own context, skills, tools and guardrails, share projects across teams, and keep approved learnings through project memory. Expanded engineering intelligence capabilities connect data across requirements, design, simulation, test and process systems into foundational knowledge graphs. As agents run workflows, the platform generates project-specific work graphs that provide traceability and capture learnings, which enrich agent context and preserve knowledge. Rescale Desktop extends the platform to engineers' local machines, and the Model Context Protocol connectors include Rescale availability on the Claude and Codex directories. Edison, described as the AI assistant and agent orchestrator, now has persistent memory so engineers can describe their intent in natural language.

Jacob Surber, Rescale's vice president of product, said customers build aircraft, vehicles and reactors, so the agents supporting that work must deliver reliable results. He said Agentic Projects supply context that grows with every iteration, calling it a material advance toward an engineering harness built for how these teams work. Rescale says the capabilities together give agents a harness that makes them execute to the same standards as experienced engineers. The company says this helps organizations build the trust in agentic outcomes needed to transform operations. A new dataset creation agent, uncertainty quantification, Auto Tune and a local design explorer are also part of the launch, along with new cluster performance metrics and a priority score for administrators.

Ed Blandford, chief technology officer and co-founder of Kairos Power, said the company depends on quick learning cycles of designing, building and testing, then carrying lessons into the next round. He said much of the difficulty in scaling nuclear energy comes down to manufacturing, and that agents managing setup, execution and reporting free his engineers for judgment and rigor. Ryan Dehoff, director of the Manufacturing Demonstration Facility, said industry engineers and lab researchers solve problems side by side there. He said nuclear innovation demands speed and rigor at once, and that agents allow Oak Ridge expertise to scale beyond its facility. Tech Times noted that Kairos's headline gain is a projection and not a measured result, and that an audit trail does not by itself show a model is valid.

Kairos Power and the Department of Energy's Manufacturing Demonstration Facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, with support from Rescale AI developer engineers, built a digital agentic scaffolding on the platform. The work is part of a collaboration to test advanced manufacturing and construction methods for Hermes 2, Kairos Power's 50-megawatt fluoride-salt-cooled reactor. Agents exercised thermal, flow and shielding simulation and reporting workflows for the reactor cavity and bioshield plug designs, with engineers approving each agent action. Kairos Power projects that workflows built from past simulations could raise end-to-end simulation analysis efficiency by up to 3x while keeping the data traceability regulatory compliance requires. Oak Ridge is encoding its simulation and additive manufacturing expertise in agents on the platform so engineers can adopt advanced methods to address industry challenges.

Rescale says the launch also shows how agentic digital engineering works with its AI physics solution to make surrogate models easier to build. Uncertainty quantification builds trust that engineers are using an appropriate surrogate model and flags predictions that should be confirmed with a full-fidelity simulation. Tech Times reports that Hermes 2 is Kairos's demonstration plant in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, where Kairos broke ground on April 17, 2026. Kairos says the plant will deliver up to 50 megawatts of electricity to the Tennessee Valley Authority grid and has targeted 2030 for power production. Tech Times adds that Rescale's release notes date Agentic Projects to Oct. 26, the Edison rename to Oct. 19, Rescale Desktop to Nov. 5, and uncertainty quantification and the dataset agent to Nov. 6.

Organizations can learn more about the new capabilities at rescale.com. Tech Times says teams weighing engineering AI agents should ask what each approval step actually checks and how surrogate predictions get rechecked against full simulations. It also says they should ask what outside AI assistants can reach through the connectors. The release gives no measured figure for the Kairos workflow, so the threefold efficiency gain remains a projection. The release also does not say whether the 50-megawatt figure for Hermes 2 is thermal or electric, though Kairos describes it as electric output.

stories.Headline: Growing AI Use Raises Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks
stories.Summary:
Kaspersky has published a survey showing that growing use of artificial intelligence for personal advice, health questions and everyday planning is raising worries about privacy and cybersecurity. The survey covered respondents across the Middle East, Türkiye and Africa region, known as META, and was reported by Pakistan Observer and The Patriot on 12 November 2026. Nearly 79 percent of respondents said they use AI services, including chatbots and tools for making images and videos. Experts warned that sharing sensitive information with these platforms could expose users to data leaks, misuse by third parties and cyberattacks. The IAPP also published an analysis on 12 November 2026 on how Italy is handling AI, privacy and cybersecurity.

Searching for and summarising information was the most common use of AI, cited by 74 percent of those surveyed. Writing texts followed at 50 percent, generating images from written prompts at 42 percent, and editing personal photos at 41 percent. Another 32 percent turned to AI to create videos, while 37 percent used it for health-related questions and 41 percent sought advice on personal matters. Planning weekends, holidays or events drew 29 percent, and creating meal menus and diet plans drew 23 percent. Almost one in 10 respondents had already met incorrect AI-generated information, and 24 percent believed AI could give inaccurate answers.

Seifallah Jedidi, Kaspersky's Head of Consumer Channel for the Middle East, Türkiye and Africa, is the named spokesperson. He urged consumers to understand the limits of AI services and the risks linked to them. He said even widely used platforms can have vulnerabilities that lead to data leaks. According to him, information shared with these platforms may be processed under the relevant service and its policies, or may be reached by third parties. He urged users to verify AI-generated content, avoid sharing confidential information and stay alert to fraudulent AI services designed to spread malware.

Kaspersky experts advised users to avoid giving sensitive, confidential or private information to AI services in order to reduce cybersecurity risks. They warned that phishing web pages, malicious software and fake websites often imitate genuine platforms or deceive users with fake tools. The company also recommended checking each platform's data-handling policies. It advised consulting reliable sources before relying on AI for medical, financial, legal or educational advice. Users of AI services are the people affected, particularly those who share health details or personal matters with chatbots.

The IAPP analysis, written by Ludovica Mosci, Manager of Privacy Compliance EMEA at The Walt Disney Company, describes Italy as one of Europe's most interventionist jurisdictions on privacy, AI and cybersecurity. Two legislative decrees recently completed Italy's transposition of the EU AI Act into national law. Legislative Decree No. 160, adopted on 9 September, introduced corporate and individual criminal liability provisions. Legislative Decree No. 179, adopted on 8 October and in force from 23 October, clarifies the roles and responsibilities of Italy's national AI supervisory authorities. In July, the data protection authority, the Garante, concluded its investigation into Character Technologies, the U.S.-based provider of the Character.AI companion app, which also touched on minors' online protection.

The articles do not say what follows from the Kaspersky survey, and they give no sign of any regulatory response to its findings. They describe Italy's cybersecurity position as one of no new regulatory developments, with 2026 marking the move from legislative implementation to operational compliance and active supervision under the NIS2 Directive and the Digital Operational Resilience Act. They say the Garante has continued its scrutiny of AI providers, including a decision on an AI-powered plug-in for sentiment analysis of employees. The IAPP excerpt does not set out the outcome of the Character.AI investigation or of the employee plug-in decision. Kaspersky also points to its Kaspersky Premium security solution, which it says protects users in everyday digital activities through AI-based technologies.

stories.Headline: Quantinuum and RIKEN Expand Partnership to Accelerate the Commercialization of Quantum-AI Hybrid Supercomputing in Japan
stories.Summary:
Quantinuum has upgraded its Reimei quantum computer at the RIKEN research institute in Japan to the company's System Model H2, and the upgrade was announced this week. The announcement came as Quantinuum disclosed an expanded partnership with RIKEN and with SoftBank Corp. in early November 2026. Quantinuum issued an 8-K press release confirming the news on November 10, 2026, according to coverage dated that week. Reimei originally ran on the earlier H1 version of Quantinuum's technology before the work was completed at RIKEN. The expanded cooperation is meant to advance quantum-AI hybrid supercomputing in Japan and to move that work toward commercial use.

The upgraded Reimei is now a 56-qubit machine, replacing the original H1 system, which offered 20 qubits when it was deployed in February 2025. The two organizations signed a Memorandum of Understanding covering advanced scientific and industrial applications, along with joint development of a fault-tolerant quantum computer described as "Made with Japan." That development effort will involve Japanese universities and domestic component suppliers, and it will draw on what was learned deploying and operating Reimei at RIKEN. Under a separate agreement, Quantinuum, RIKEN and SoftBank will explore connecting quantum computing directly with AI data centers in Japan. The partners will also assess infrastructure readiness and study how connected systems could support commercial quantum-AI hybrid computing services.

Dr. Rajeeb Hazra, the chief executive of Quantinuum, said Japan's quantum ambitions need both advanced capabilities today and a lasting commitment to what comes next. He said the Reimei upgrade widens what Quantinuum can explore with RIKEN across electronics, energy and life sciences. Hazra added that the companies are building on this work to develop a fault-tolerant machine with Japanese universities and suppliers, while exploring with SoftBank how industry could gain access through Japan's AI data centers. Takenori Kobayashi, a vice president and head of the product research and development division at SoftBank Corp., said Japan has built a strong base for hybrid quantum and supercomputing through the NEDO-supported JHPC-quantum project. He said SoftBank's responsibility is to turn those achievements into industrial value and to advance a Quantum AI Datacenter linking quantum computing with AI and high-performance computing.

The upgraded system supports two active research projects that involve RIKEN's own machines and outside partners. The first uses RIKEN's ROQUO GPU supercomputer together with quantum data from Reimei to train an AI model for magnetism simulations. Preliminary findings indicate that this model can deliver more precise predictions than AI models trained only on classical simulations. The second project links Reimei, RIKEN's Fugaku supercomputer and an evolutionary AI agent from NVIDIA running on ROQUO to simulate a complex photoactive biomolecule. The filing says a better grasp of how such biomolecules respond to light could drive more efficient solar cells and other industrial applications, and it notes the research aligns with a planned $1 billion partnership under the U.S. Genesis Mission.

Reimei is operated as part of the JHPC-quantum project, which is funded by NEDO, the New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization, an organization under Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry. The original H1 version was installed at RIKEN in Wako, Saitama, and it was Quantinuum's first on-premise delivery of a system. Quantinuum was founded in 2021 when Honeywell spun out its Quantum Solutions division and merged it with the UK startup Cambridge Quantum Computing. Honeywell holds a 54 percent stake in Quantinuum, and IBM is also an investor. The company reports a global workforce of about 800 employees, and more than 70 percent of its technology team hold PhDs or Master's degrees.

The partners will now carry out the separate agreement under which they assess infrastructure readiness for connecting quantum computers with AI data centers in Japan. Their work toward a "Made with Japan" fault-tolerant quantum computer will continue with Japanese universities and domestic component suppliers. The two research projects on the upgraded Reimei platform are described as ongoing, and the articles give no completion dates for either. The articles do not say when a fault-tolerant machine might be built, what it would cost, or how many qubits it would have. They also give no timeline for commercial quantum-AI hybrid services, and they do not say which AI data centers might be connected or what SoftBank's role will cost.

stories.Headline: HK ranks 11th in digital and AI competitiveness
stories.Summary:
The International Institute for Management Development, a Switzerland-based institute, released its World Digital and AI Ranking 2026 on Wednesday, covering 70 economies. Hong Kong placed 11th in the world and fourth in Asia. South Korea's science ministry said the country moved up eight spots from last year to tenth place. The United States took first place after climbing three spots, while last year's leader, Canada, dropped to fifth.

In Hong Kong's case, the city ranked second globally for workforce development, fifth for efficiency and 10th for technology and infrastructure, three of the five factors in the benchmark. At the sub-factor level it came first in the world for technological framework, practices, and education and training. It also finished in the global top 10 for talent, societal attitudes and regulatory framework. South Korea improved in all five categories, which are governance, technology infrastructure, efficiency, human resources development, and societal attitudes and values, and placed third in both technology infrastructure and efficiency. Among other Asia-Pacific economies, Singapore was second, China seventh and Japan 19th.

A spokesman for the Hong Kong government said the result recognises the city as one of the world's most competitive economies in digital and AI development. The spokesman said the government is fully committed to turning Hong Kong into an international innovation and technology centre, following the directions in the First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. The statement said the city will strengthen the institutional framework for innovation and technology development and move faster to align with key national technology strategies. It will also develop a new paradigm of three major innovation and technology parks and five key research and development institutions.

According to Xinhua, the spokesperson added that Hong Kong will build a comprehensive industrial ecosystem covering research and development, commercialisation, pilot production and mass production. The city also plans to advance new industrialisation and use AI technology to empower different sectors of the economy. The ranking measures an economy's capacity to develop, adopt, deploy and govern digital technologies and AI in a way that produces lasting economic and societal value. The articles do not say when the next edition will be published.
