stories.Headline: OpenAI faces civil racketeering charges over $30bn data center planned in Effingham County, Georgia
stories.Summary:
The civil racketeering lawsuit over OpenAI's planned Project Camellia data center in Effingham County, Georgia was filed by residents against the company, two of its affiliates and several county officials. The complaint alleges that the defendants kept residents in the dark about the project. It is the third lawsuit related to Project Camellia filed since the 3.2 GW campus was announced in July. Among the allegations are civil conspiracy, improper zoning procedures, and civil racketeering involving false statements, perjury, and forgery. The complaint does not detail specific statements that might constitute racketeering.

The project is a $30 billion data center campus planned on a 1,440-acre parcel at the Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub near Rincon. It would have four data center buildings with a total footprint of 4.4 million square feet, or 408,775 square meters. Construction could start in 2028 if final permission is granted. A Supervisors' board decision that had been due on November 4 has been shifted to November 19. Tom's Hardware reports the site is expected to cost between $20 billion and $30 billion, built across five phases.

The lawsuit was filed by the law firm Savage Turner Pinkney Savage Sprouse & Gilluly on behalf of three Effingham County residents, identified as Dr. Michelle Finch-Mincey, Lehman Mincey Jr. and Raymond Carver. The named defendants include county commissioners Damon Rahn, Forrest Floyd, Roger Burdette, Jamie DeLoach, Elizabeth Helmly and Phil Kieffer, County Manager Tim Callanan, and Industrial Development Authority CEO Brandt Herndon. Also named are the Industrial Development Authority, OpenAI, Octans GA LLC, which operates the data center for OpenAI, and Savannah Industrial Development LLC. OpenAI was contacted for comment, and the articles do not report a response.

The plaintiffs say offers to buy nearby properties have been reduced or withdrawn, and that the project has affected their property values, so they seek civil damages. The complaint alleges the defendants used non-disclosure agreements and misleading public statements to keep residents unaware of the project's nature for as long as possible. Residents say the county tried to secure land, tax incentives and zoning approvals without informing them until key decisions were final and contracts signed. The plaintiffs describe the actions as affecting residents of Effingham County, whose property values they say have declined.

OpenAI has promised that the project will not raise the community's utility costs, since it will pay for all required infrastructure upgrades, and that it will use minimal water through a closed-loop system. The Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act was originally conceived to counter organized crime, but Georgia's version is less stringent than the federal one. Georgia's RICO statute was used in the 2023 election case against Donald Trump and 18 others over the 2020 presidential election results in the state, and in Young Thug's trial. Georgia State University professor Volkan Topalli, quoted in Atlanta Magazine, said critics consider the state version too encompassing. Developers say they use NDAs to avoid running afoul of insider trading rules, though West Feliciana Parish in Louisiana closed a data center deal without one.

Two other lawsuits related to the project were filed earlier this year, one over zoning and another over the Effingham County Industrial Development Authority's role in advancing the development. None of the three cases has yet reached court. The articles do not say whether the November 19 board decision will proceed as scheduled or how the courts will rule on the claims. They also do not report whether OpenAI or the county has responded to the allegations in court.

stories.Headline: Ulster County Bans Government Use of AI Surveillance
stories.Summary:
Ulster County Executive Jen Metzger issued an executive order on October 22 banning the use of Flock cameras and other AI-assisted video surveillance technologies in county government. The order, titled "Prohibiting the Use of Flock Cameras and other AI-Assisted Video Surveillance Technologies" and designated Executive Order No. 5, took effect immediately upon its announcement. It bars any department or employee under the county executive's office from buying or deploying such systems, from helping to develop them, and from aiding private individuals or corporations in implementing them. Flock systems, made by Flock Safety, include security cameras, license plate readers and data-sharing networks, many of which use generative AI and machine learning to identify people, track them and build databases.

The ban covers buildings and property under the county executive's authority, including the Ulster County Courthouse, the Sheriff's Office, UCAT public transit facilities, county public works departments and public recreational areas such as rail trails. It does not reach facilities controlled by towns and villages, such as the New Paltz Town Hall, the New Paltz Courthouse or the New Paltz Police Headquarters, and it does not apply to private individuals or businesses. In her order, Metzger argued that protecting public safety and individual rights go hand in hand in a democracy and that the rapid, unregulated growth of the AI sector threatens that balance. She wrote that tech companies dominate AI development without independent oversight, that multiple security breaches have occurred in these companies' systems, and that collected information could be shared outside county government without authorization.

New Paltz Town Supervisor Tim Rogers said he agrees with Metzger's assessment that unregulated AI in security matters can weaken public safety and democratic principles, and he warned that civil liberties could be trampled if for-profit companies are left to operate without limits. He also said the town has no current plan to adopt Flock technology, citing its high cost, and that to his knowledge the New Paltz Police Department does not use it. Rogers acknowledged that surveillance can deliver local benefits, arguing that cameras like those Lowe's operates on Route 299 help deter shoplifting and theft. The New Paltz Oracle reports that the town has three AI surveillance systems in and around its territory, two of them Flock cameras owned by Lowe's facing its parking lot, and that the owner of the third remains undisclosed. Rogers said Lowe's is not required to register these cameras with the town and that no site plan or building review involves Flock cameras, so private companies remain outside local regulation, just as they do at the county level.

stories.Headline: Stony Brook FinTech Workshop Explores AI’s Impact on Finance, Announces New Industry Partnership
stories.Summary:
Stony Brook University held its FinTech Workshop on November 6 in the New Computer Science Building, where researchers and industry leaders discussed how artificial intelligence is changing financial analysis, software development and investment decisions. The event was organized by Karina Torres Castro, manager of research and innovation and assistant research professor in mechanical engineering, and it included the announcement of a new AI Innovation Lab in partnership with the financial technology company Broadridge. Students and faculty will work alongside industry experts in the lab to tackle challenges in AI and finance. The workshop included academic research presentations, industry perspectives and a panel discussion, and it was sponsored by the College of Engineering and Applied Sciences, the Long Island Manufacturing Extension Partnership, the Center of Excellence in Wireless and Information Technology and the AI Innovation Institute.

Amy Erickson, executive director of the Long Island Manufacturing Extension Partnership, said AI-driven financial modeling can help small and mid-sized manufacturers reduce waste and make better investment decisions without replacing skilled workers. She described the workshop as the first of several AI-focused programs her organization is rolling out for regional manufacturers. Andrew C. Singer, dean of the college, welcomed participants and introduced keynote speaker Robert J. Frey, research professor and founder of the university's Quantitative Finance Program. Frey, who has held leadership roles at Renaissance Technologies and other financial firms, compared the rise of AI with earlier technological advances that disrupted industries, saying some adjustments can be painful in the short term. He argued that stagnation is not the answer.

At Broadridge, AI is taking on more complex software development tasks, including some once assigned to entry-level employees. Roger Burkhardt, the company's chief technology officer of capital markets and AI, said the career ladder is changing and that new employees may be expected to define problems, evaluate AI-generated code and recognize security vulnerabilities. He encouraged students to experiment with AI development tools while learning to assess their output, and he said critical thinking and communicating with users are lasting skills. Jill Scher, managing director at CBIZ Advisors, began her accounting career in 1994 working with paper ledgers and red pencils, and she now uses AI to analyze financial statements and prepare for client meetings. Frey said that when AI is used properly, students will see it as a force multiplier that increases productivity rather than replacing them.

Pawel Polak, a faculty member in the Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, presented research on an international competition that attracted more than 1,000 registered participants to develop AI agents capable of writing code, forecasting financial trends and simulating markets. Some agents significantly improved the speed of existing software, but others struggled with unfamiliar problems. Teams that incorporated financial knowledge and agents required to explain their predictions generally performed better on new tasks, and Polak said human involvement definitely helps. Lav Varshney, professor of electrical and computer engineering and inaugural director of the AI Innovation Institute, argued that opaque "black box" AI may be less helpful because its inner workings are unknown. He described research using explicit, verifiable rules, with one possible application being financial transactions that fail to settle as expected, a context where traceability matters in regulated industries.

The afternoon panel, moderated by Yvette Wohn, inaugural chair of the Department of Technology, AI and Society, included Polak, Burkhardt, Scher and Melissa Brown, managing director of investment decision research at SimCorp. Brown said her team helps investors understand how unexpected economic developments might affect their portfolios, and she described an exercise considering what could happen if the Federal Reserve lost its independence. She said that work once took hours of searching historical data but now can be done by asking AI to identify similar past circumstances, which "takes five minutes rather than a day." Scher said some clients arrive with AI-generated tax analyses and ask her to confirm them, even when those analyses may overlook changing regulations or individual circumstances. Samir Das, chair of the Department of Computer Science, closed the workshop by announcing the AI Innovation Lab, which he said will focus on experiential learning and on how universities and industry can work together.

stories.Headline: Exploring How Autistic Individuals Interact With Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Stony Brook University and the University of Cincinnati studied how autistic people use ChatGPT, and their findings were published in the Association for Computing Machinery Interactive Health Conference. The study was led by Renkai Ma, an assistant professor at the University of Cincinnati's School of Information Technology, with coauthor Ben Zhang from Stony Brook's Department of Technology, AI and Society. The article is dated November 11, 2026, and it extends earlier research the team published in the proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2026. That earlier study analyzed posts from six major social media platforms about using chatbots for mental health support. The researchers gathered 3,984 posts from Reddit, X and Tumblr, published between January 2023 and September 2025, focusing on firsthand accounts from people who identified as autistic.

The article describes four ways autistic users benefited from ChatGPT, including communication, planning and emotional support. Some users called the chatbot a bi-directional translator between neurodivergent and neurotypical people, helping them adapt messages and interpret replies. Users also relied on it to offload executive tasks such as planning, organizing and getting started. For emotional regulation, some valued expressing difficult feelings without fear of judgment or pressure to mask. The researchers also say these benefits are linked to risks, including automated masking, over-reliance and reinforced beliefs when the chatbot's agreeable responses make them sound credible.

The article attributes its findings to Ma and Zhang, who are quoted describing how autistic users turned to ChatGPT during acute distress and to get unstuck on tasks. Ma said autistic people felt that readers were connecting with ChatGPT rather than with them, and that they had lost the ability to communicate on their own. The authors argue that heavy reliance on chatbots can push autistic users to hide their natural way of communicating. The researchers also recommend that a chatbot separate emotional validation from factual verification, so it can acknowledge distress while checking the facts behind a fear. The article was written with Salomé Davoudiasl listed as its author.

The findings matter to autistic users who turn to chatbots for everyday support, and to the neurotypical people who receive messages drafted or rewritten by them. The article notes that some users worried about losing their own voice when the chatbot wrote for them. Users described messages that sounded less like them after rewriting to fit neurotypical expectations. The article does not give a count of how many users have experienced these effects beyond the 3,984 posts analyzed.

To address these concerns, the authors propose what they call beneficial frictions, such as asking users to set their priorities before the chatbot suggests a plan. They also propose tools that help neurotypical readers interpret direct messages from autistic colleagues. The researchers say these ideas will direct their future research. The article does not say when that research will begin, how the proposed tools would work, or whether any chatbot developer has adopted these recommendations.

stories.Headline: Quectel Wireless Solutions: Quectel SP900BF-AP Smart Module Sets the Pace for Edge AI with 100 TOPS of Computing Power
stories.Summary:
Quectel Wireless Solutions announced the SP900BF-AP on November 11, 2026, in Munich, as a smart module that lets robots, inspection systems and edge gateways run large AI models on the device itself. The module is built on the Qualcomm Dragonwing IQ-9075 Processor and delivers up to 100 TOPS of on-device AI compute. It lets industrial OEMs embed advanced AI directly into their products, which reduces latency, bandwidth costs and data privacy risks tied to cloud processing. Processing data locally lets manufacturers run real-time robotics and automated inspection while keeping sensitive production data under their own control. Quectel describes the module as one that offers long-term hardware availability to meet the extended product lifecycles industrial customers require.

The module has an octa-core Qualcomm Kryo CPU running at up to 2.36 GHz, an Adreno 663 GPU, a Hexagon DSP and a dedicated NPU. Memory options reach 36 GB of LPDDR5X and 256 GB of UFS storage, and the module supports real-time multi-stream video processing and multiple displays. Quectel commits to a product lifecycle of up to 10 years, which it says helps customers reduce inventory, maintenance and upgrade costs. The module is designed to run Ubuntu and Yocto Linux, with support for those systems still in development. PCIe, USB 3.1, UART, SPI and I²C interfaces let OEMs add 4G/5G or Wi-Fi to suit each deployment.

Quectel Wireless Solutions is responsible for the module, and Raymond Wang, its Product Head for Smart, said that the value of AI must ultimately be proven on the industrial front line. Wang said Quectel is providing a complete, ready-to-use edge intelligence solution rather than only a high-performance module. He said this helps customers avoid complex low-level development and speed up their AI-driven transformation. The SP900BF-AP was developed through close collaboration between Quectel and Qualcomm Technologies, which combined modular design with system-level optimisation. Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. and its subsidiaries own the Qualcomm branded products referenced in the release.

The module targets industrial OEMs and manufacturers who run autonomous mobile robots, production-line inspection and edge AI gateways. For autonomous mobile robots, the module offers four-camera support, 3D perception and on-device navigation. For production-line inspection, it enables real-time defect detection without transferring sensitive data off-site. For edge AI gateways, it runs large language and vision-language models such as Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma and LLaVA locally to reduce bandwidth requirements and keep data secure. Industrial equipment stays in the field for years, which is why the module is planned for a long service life.

Quectel is a global end-to-end IoT solutions provider with a worldwide team of over 10,000 professionals. Its portfolio spans cellular, GNSS, satellite, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth modules, high-performance antennas, value-added services and full turnkey offerings including ODM services and system integration. The release notes that Quectel has regional offices and support across the globe. The SP900BF-AP has completed key technical validation. Engineering samples are now available to selected customers for solution evaluation and joint development.

Attendees at Electronica can find the SP900BF-AP and the complete Quectel IoT solutions portfolio on stand C2.601 at the show. The articles do not give the price or a commercial launch date for the module. They also do not say when Ubuntu and Yocto Linux support will be finished or which customers will receive the engineering samples. Quectel's media contact is listed as media@quectel.com, and the source version of the release is on businesswire.com.

stories.Headline: What California’s new law means for legal teams using AI and whether other states could follow suit
stories.Summary:
California has become the first state to regulate how attorneys use artificial intelligence through a statute, and the law takes effect January 1, 2027. The law is Senate Bill 574, which Senator Tom Umberg, chair of the state's Senate Judiciary Committee, introduced in February 2025. It passed both chambers on the last day of the legislative session after two rounds of amendments in the Senate and four in the Assembly. Governor Gavin Newsom signed the bill on September 30, 2026. The measure was reported by Ironclad and republished by ABC17 News in November 2026.

The law allows attorneys to use generative AI to assist in the practice of law but forbids them from delegating the practice of law to it. Attorneys may not enter confidential, personal identifying, or other nonpublic information into an AI system unless access is limited to them and authorized people who must keep it confidential. Personal identifying information includes dates of birth, witness addresses and phone numbers, and medical and financial details. Attorneys must take reasonable steps to verify AI output and correct errors or hallucinations before using it, including in contract review. Attorneys who use AI must disclose it on documents submitted to a court, while for content shared with the public they only need to consider disclosure.

The articles identify Senator Tom Umberg as the bill's author and Governor Gavin Newsom as the official who signed it. The articles say the law puts into writing many practices careful lawyers already followed, such as checking citations and protecting client information. The articles do not say who opposed the bill or what specific objections were raised. The articles state that the law affects attorneys and firms inside California and those who practice with courts there, and that arbitrators are also limited by its provisions. Court filings in California face tighter citation rules whether or not AI was involved.

Companies and firms outside the state may be affected if they work with California courts, according to the articles' framing of the law's reach. The articles do not identify specific individuals or groups that filed comments or testimony. The State Bar of California first issued AI guidance for attorneys in 2023, and the Judicial Council followed in 2025 with rules governing how judges and court staff use generative AI. In May 2026 the State Bar updated its guidance to address agentic AI, which can carry out tasks with little human direction. The articles describe Ironclad, a legal technology company, as the source of the analysis, and it is republished through the Stacker content exchange.

The articles do not give further history of earlier legislative efforts on AI in the legal profession. The articles do not say whether other states will follow California's approach, though they pose that question. They do not describe enforcement mechanisms, penalties for violations, or how courts will process disclosures in practice. The articles also leave open how the law's distinctions between court filings and public-facing content will be applied in detail.

stories.Headline: Rajnath Singh calls for stronger defensive capabilities to maintain 'element of surprise' in future warfare; launches UDAAN-developed AI applications
stories.Summary:
The Indian Air Force has begun using homegrown artificial intelligence applications to strengthen its operations, an initiative announced by defence minister Rajnath Singh at the Air Force Commanders' Conference in New Delhi on Thursday. The applications were developed in-house by the IAF's AI Centre of Excellence under the Unit for Digitisation, Automation, Artificial Intelligence and Application Networking, known as UDAAN. The launch was made at a time when Singh also urged the armed forces to be ready for emerging threats. Singh spoke about maintaining the element of surprise against adversaries while staying alert to unexpected enemy moves. The announcement was reported on November 12, 2026, by news outlets including The Economic Times and The Times of India.

The applications are deployed on the Air Force's secure network and are meant to automate tasks across operations, administration and aerospace safety. They are aimed at speeding up work in three key areas: military operations, administrative functions and aerospace safety. According to an official ministry of defence release, the tools form part of the IAF's wider effort to bring artificial intelligence into its functioning. The initiative is intended to improve efficiency through technology-driven solutions. Singh's remarks at the conference also called for capabilities that leave adversaries with little time to react or recover.

Singh called on the armed forces to strengthen both offensive and defensive capabilities to maintain the element of surprise against conventional and emerging threats. He said Indian forces must never be caught off guard by an unexpected enemy move. He further called for stronger intelligence and surveillance mechanisms, better integration among military systems and early identification of potential threats. Singh said operational preparedness must be raised so that personnel remain alert, agile and ready to respond to emerging challenges. The defence minister's statements were made at the conference where the applications were launched.

Singh noted that warfare is increasingly extending beyond traditional battlefields, with missiles, drones and advanced weapon systems playing a significant role. He referred to the Russia-Ukraine and Israel-Hamas conflicts when pointing to the growing importance of drones and air defence systems. He urged IAF commanders to prepare for threats involving kamikaze drones, surveillance and counter-drone operations. The armed forces, and in particular IAF commanders, are the audience for these calls to readiness. Singh also said future victories would depend on more than the number of aircraft deployed.

Singh called for dedicated doctrines and architectures for emerging domains of warfare, including electronic, cyber and space. He said technological preparedness would shape the outcome of future conflicts. The IAF's AI applications are expected to affect personnel across operations, administration and aerospace safety. The reports do not give further details on which units or personnel will use the tools first. The articles provide no figures on the cost, number of users or timeline for wider deployment of the applications.

The background given is that the IAF has been working to integrate artificial intelligence into its functioning and improve efficiency through technology. Singh's comments referred to recent conflicts in Russia-Ukraine and Israel-Hamas as examples of how warfare is changing. The articles also describe the conference as a regular gathering of Air Force commanders where such priorities are discussed. No further history of the IAF's AI programme is given in the reports. The conference was held in New Delhi on Thursday, November 12, 2026.

The articles do not say when the applications will be extended beyond their initial deployment or whether further AI tools will be launched. They also do not state how the new doctrines for electronic, cyber and space warfare will be developed or when. It is not clear from the reports how the IAF will measure whether the applications have improved efficiency. The articles leave open how the call for stronger offensive and defensive capabilities will be translated into specific programmes. Further official details on these matters have not been released in the reports.

stories.Headline: Lafayette City Council rejects proposed new downtown AI bar - KATC
stories.Summary:
Lafayette City Council members voted late on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, to reject a proposed high-tech bar in downtown Lafayette. The decision came amid concerns about safety in the downtown area. The owner had planned to use artificial intelligence bartenders to staff the club. Entrepreneur Quintin Borel had hoped to open a bar called "Plush" in the former "Bliss" cocktail lounge. He said it would use technology to change the patron experience.

Under the plan, bar-goers would scan a barcode and order a drink from their seats. A machine would make the cocktail, and a server would deliver it to the customer. Borel said the system would reduce disturbance and traffic movement, allowing him to organize the venue as he wanted. He said his focus was the satisfaction of the guests themselves. The articles give no further terms, dates or figures for the proposal.

Borel defended the concept, saying it added convenience and kept the flow of customers orderly. The Downtown Development Authority's board approved a resolution a couple of weeks earlier asking the council to vote no. Kevin Blanchard, the authority's CEO, said weekend conditions after midnight downtown were not safe. He said the area had seen a lot of chaos and violence on the streets for some time. Blanchard said the authority had raised that concern for a while.

The articles do not describe how other residents or businesses reacted to the vote. They also do not say how the rejection affects Borel's plans beyond his intention to open Plush. Blanchard's remarks focused on weekend nights after midnight, and the articles do not name any specific incidents. The articles say the downtown area has faced ongoing safety concerns, which the Development Authority has cited in opposing the bar. The articles give no further background on the council's earlier handling of the proposal.

It is not yet known what Borel plans to do next. The articles do not say whether he will appeal the decision, revise the concept, or seek another location. They also do not state whether the council will consider similar proposals in the future. The articles leave open how the downtown safety concerns will be addressed.

stories.Headline: Warby Parker bets on Google AI glasses for growth, but privacy fears still loom
stories.Summary:
Warby Parker is entering the smart glasses market in partnership with Google and Samsung, betting that demand for artificial intelligence wearables will balloon in the coming years. The New York-based fashion brand, known for affordable eyewear, is also seeking to head off privacy concerns that have weighed on existing producers of the glasses. Warby Parker shoppers will start placing pre-orders on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The Warby Parker glasses are broadly similar to Meta smart glasses already available from Ray-Ban and Oakley maker EssilorLuxottica, which have faced regulatory scrutiny from Norway to Australia. Like the Meta glasses, they will connect to an AI assistant, in this case Google's Gemini, for tasks such as directions and language translation.

The main difference from existing versions on the market is the privacy framework built into the glasses from the outset, according to Warby Parker Co-CEO Neil Blumenthal. Google will not use visuals captured with the glasses to train its AI, and the glasses will bar facial recognition of bystanders. A small white notification light on the front turns on automatically when a user starts recording video. Google says it will embed privacy guardrails to prevent tampering with that light, redact people's faces from video footage before it is sent to Gemini, and ban targeted advertising on the glasses. Shares of Warby Parker have rallied nearly 40% this year, compared with a 10% gain in the S&P 500.

Warby Parker's Co-CEO Neil Blumenthal said that as long as the tools provide utility to customers, the company will be successful. Juston Payne, who leads extended reality products at Google, acknowledged that public skepticism could be a risk to growth and said trust was lost in this area. Payne said Google is trying to raise the bar and change the conversation about the technology. Meta's spokesperson said input from safety experts helped inform the privacy features on its own glasses, which also include a camera notification light. Google and Warby Parker did not say how the privacy measures would be enforced beyond the listed guardrails.

Ray-Ban's Meta glasses still dominate the market, representing 81.3% of AI glasses shipments in the first half of 2026, according to tech research group Omdia. Global AI glasses shipments more than doubled in the first half of 2026 from a year earlier, though growth has slowed since the second half of last year. Luxury group Kering is also poised to release glasses in partnership with Google. One of Britain's biggest pub chains has restricted the use of the frames, Norway's government is planning a temporary ban on AI glasses in certain locations, and Australia is considering barring camera-equipped smart glasses in government workplaces. Calli Schroeder, who leads the AI and human rights program at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said she was happy footage is not automatically fed into AI training.

Schroeder said that still leaves open the concern that a stranger may have footage of a child on their phone, which is concerning however it is phrased. Analysts at TD Cowen wrote in a research note that smart glasses are poised to be an increasingly important driver of Warby Parker's growth outlook. Warby Parker executives said on an earnings call earlier this month that the new wearable technology would add several percentage points to fourth-quarter revenue growth. Google said it wants to rebuild trust, while the articles do not say whether the guardrails will ease concern about widespread surveillance if the glasses become ubiquitous. The articles also do not say how far Warby Parker's glasses will sell or whether the regulatory moves in Norway and Australia will extend further.

stories.Headline: AI spending helps lift UK growth to fastest since early 2024
stories.Summary:
Britain's economy grew 0.7% in the July-to-September quarter of 2026, its fastest quarterly expansion in two-and-a-half years, helped by investment in artificial intelligence. The Office for National Statistics announced the figure on Thursday, and the growth extended a strong first half of the year. Growth had been expected to slow after the Iran war began, so the result defied those predictions. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the quarterly rate, but output in September alone rose 0.2%, beating expectations of no change for the month. Annual growth picked up to 1.9% in the third quarter, the strongest reading since the fourth quarter of 2024.

Monthly GDP has now beaten consensus forecasts for the fifth month in a row and seven times in the last eight months. Rob Wood, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said these figures strengthened the chances of another Bank of England rate hike next month. Growth over the three months to September was the fastest since May, on a rolling basis. Growth so far this year has been the strongest since 2017, excluding the post-pandemic rebound. British growth in the third quarter was the second-fastest among the Group of Seven advanced economies, behind only the United States.

The Office for National Statistics said there was widespread strength in industries that may be related to artificial intelligence. Computer programming, consultancy and related activity made the largest single contribution to growth in the third quarter. Computer manufacturing made the biggest contribution to industrial production, which rose 4.6% in the three months to September. The economy had expanded by 0.6% in the first quarter of 2026, showing resilience in the first half of the year. Business investment, however, grew just 0.4% on the quarter, half of what economists expected, and was the weakest growth since the start of the year.

Scott Gardner, investment strategist at JP Morgan Personal Investing, said the UK economy has been relatively resilient since the conflict started, but that strength will be tested in the months ahead. He said nervousness before the autumn budget and continued uncertainty from the Middle East war are expected to weigh on confidence and activity in coming GDP readings. The Bank of England last week raised its 2026 growth forecast to 1.6%, against the 1.2% forecast by the government's Office for Budget Responsibility after finance minister John Healey's October 28 budget. The central bank attributed some of the strength to spending on AI and a small, temporary boost from Healey's fiscal plan. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Healey welcomed the data.

The data is likely to increase pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates again. The central bank warned last week that inflation will near 5% in 2027, and investors see a 73% chance of a back-to-back hike in December after November's increase. Wood said that with growth and inflation both strong, he expects at least two more hikes from the Monetary Policy Committee, and that today's figures make a December hike more likely. Household gas and electricity bills are still set to rise by about 25% when the energy price cap changes in January. Britain's government has offered limited support to help families absorb the energy price shock.

Some economists expect slower growth in the final quarter of the year as higher energy prices and borrowing costs weigh on activity. There have been recent signs of weakening consumer and business demand, with retail sales volumes falling in September. Consumer confidence also suffered its sharpest month-on-month fall since April 2020 before the budget. The articles do not say how large the fourth-quarter slowdown will be or whether the Bank of England will raise rates in December. They also do not give the outcome of the autumn budget, which Gardner described as a source of nervousness for confidence and activity.

stories.Headline: KAIST Professor Predicts 100 AI Agents in Semiconductor Design
stories.Summary:
The two articles report that Kim Jung-ho, a KAIST professor who first proposed the core concept of HBM, unveiled a research system on November 11, 2026, at the online "TERA AI Agent Day" event. In his keynote, he described a setup in which a single human engineer commands about 100 AI agents to design semiconductors. The system is being developed by KAIST's TERA Lab, which he leads, and the goal is to demonstrate its core functions by the end of 2027. The articles say the system was tested in the design of next-generation HBM and high-bandwidth flash (HBF), and at the event researchers showed the AI producing performance results immediately after being asked.

Under the structure, a human enters only the design goal and the AI splits the work, runs commercial design tools and checks the results. A top-level "super agent" receives the goal in natural language, draws up a work plan, manages memory and access rights, and assigns tasks to specialized agents covering signal, power and thermal analysis before merging their output. Precise calculations such as signal integrity, voltage drop and resonant frequency are left to verified engineering tools, while language models are used only to interpret inputs and choose tools. The engineer keeps approval of critical steps such as tape-out. The articles also say the approach reuses the reasoning ability of existing AI models rather than training new ones, and they describe verification mechanisms intended to catch design errors.

Kim said the industry faces a triple challenge of shorter development cycles, rising design complexity and a shortage of skilled engineers, and he argued for agents that plan their own work and run specialized simulators rather than chatbots that only answer questions. Kim took part in core design and technical verification during HBM development in 2009 and contributed to SK Hynix commercializing the first HBM in December 2013, which is why he is called the "father of HBM." The articles also present TERA Lab's proposed tHBM and tHBF architectures, which place compute chips on top of memory stacks, and a uHBM structure that stacks memory on top of a GPU. The articles frame the work as aimed at industry bottlenecks, though they do not report a timeline beyond the 2027 demonstration target.

stories.Headline: Arctera Helps Companies Bring Business Information into Microsoft Copilot Workflows with Governance Controls in Place
stories.Summary:
Arctera, a business unit of Cloud Software Group, announced on November 12, 2026, new Model Context Protocol connectivity for Microsoft 365 Copilot from its base in San Ramon, California. The connectivity lets organizations bring enterprise information governed through Arctera into supported Copilot workflows. The capability gives employees access to more of their company's information for AI-assisted work while keeping established governance and compliance controls in place. The new connectivity is part of Arctera AI Converge, which uses MCP to link AI models with enterprise information that Arctera governs. The company said the connectivity is available now.

Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI applications with external data sources and tools. Through a custom federated connector, Microsoft 365 Copilot can reach Arctera's MCP server and interact with enterprise information governed through the platform. Organizations keep control over who can access the information, how it can be used, and how long it must be kept. The connectivity supports Arctera's Modern Compliance Intelligence strategy and builds on the Arctera Unified Platform's communications governance, compliance, and eDiscovery capabilities. Arctera's platform can capture data from more than 130 content sources and includes more than 280 AI policies.

Irfan Shuttari, product manager at Arctera, said that connecting enterprise information to Copilot requires preserving the governance controls built into that content. He said that pairing MCP connectivity with years of secure collaboration data managed within Arctera can accelerate regulatory inquiries and legal investigations while maintaining full compliance. Soniya Bopache, SVP and GM at Arctera, said that much of an organization's knowledge sits outside the workflows where employees could use it. She said the Copilot connectivity brings that information into work while preserving the governance controls businesses have established. Bopache added that leaders can get more value from information they already manage and from their AI investments.

The articles present the Arctera announcement as aimed at organizations that hold valuable information spread across systems and want their workforce to get more useful output from AI tools. Arctera is described as helping the biggest companies in the world monitor and control how their information is accessed, used and shared. Arctera was created in 2024 from Veritas Technologies. A separate article from ITWeb, dated November 12, 2026 and written by Joanne Carew for CloudZA in Johannesburg, covers AI governance for businesses. It recalls that in April South Africa's Draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy was officially withdrawn by Communications and Digital Technologies Minister Solly Malatsi because it contained fake, AI-generated academic references.

Jonathan Oaker, founder and CEO of CloudZA, advises that good AI governance starts with understanding the data a business holds and sorting it into categories. He recommends assessing AI tools by where each model gets its data, how it was trained and what access it has to business information. Oaker suggests weighing return on investment for the next six months or year and embracing Open Telemetry from day one. He says a business that cannot fail and handles identifiable data should consult a service provider or partner, and he warns that retrofitting governance later is complex and costly. Failing to consider governance can expose businesses to data breaches, legal liability and reputational damage.

The articles do not say when or how the Arctera connectivity will be adopted by specific customers, nor what results organizations have achieved with it. They also do not give pricing for the Arctera connectivity or detail how supported Copilot experiences are defined. The ITWeb article does not link its governance advice to the Arctera product. Whether Microsoft or other AI providers will expand similar connectivity is not addressed in the articles. The articles leave open how South Africa's AI policy will be revised after its withdrawal.

stories.Headline: Anthropic says a key AI safety alarm has been triggered, days before its IPO
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, in an amended prospectus filed alongside the price range for its record-setting IPO, Anthropic said it has met a key safety threshold. A week earlier, the company had told would-be investors that AI speeding up its own research might "imminently" trigger this alarm. The filing says Anthropic made the determination based on what it expects from future models and its overall rate of progress, not on what it has observed from current models. The threshold sits in the company's Responsible Scaling Policy, its rulebook for adding tougher safety measures as its AI becomes more powerful.

The threshold is triggered when AI is doing enough of Anthropic's research to roughly double how fast its models improve. The policy says that pace would pack two years' worth of AI progress, at its 2018-2024 rate, into a single year. Anthropic set its IPO price range at $70 to $78 per share on Tuesday as it began its roadshow, the round of investor meetings before pricing. That values the company at as much as about $1.4 trillion, counting every share that could exist, and trading could start as soon as Nov. 19, according to reports. Nvidia and Google are each buying $10 billion of Anthropic stock at the IPO price, part of a $26 billion private placement that also includes AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and Taiwan Semiconductor.

Anthropic says crossing the threshold means more safeguards, not a shutdown, and that humans stay in charge. The filing says the company does not expect to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding. It says it is weighing policy changes to keep humans in control, and that AI has already been accelerating its research and development. Anthropic said it is still weighing what crossing the threshold means and will release further reports. The filing also warns that, as Claude speeds up work inside the company, the organization may lose visibility across certain processes in a way that may become difficult for any individual or group of humans to understand and control.

METR, an independent nonprofit that tests AI systems, estimated last week that Anthropic's models have been improving nearly twice as fast since October 2025. In a separate review, METR called Anthropic's August argument that it was still below the threshold "overstated" and said it was "plausible" the line was crossed by mid-July. Constellation Research founder Ray Wang said ahead of a Yahoo Finance live show appearance last month that in all S-1 filings the risks are deliberately overstated. For investors, the filing's risk factors warn that after a catastrophic AI incident, no single insurer, and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate, may have the capacity to cover the damage. Amazon and Google already own big stakes in the company.

The fear behind the threshold is that AI will improve itself faster than people can check it. In 2023, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei joined other AI leaders in warning that the "risk of extinction from AI" should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war. The same filing swapped in "super intelligence" for "AI" in places, citing President Trump's Sept. 29 executive order telling federal agencies to use the term. Mentions of "AI" fell by about a quarter from the Nov. 2 version, by Yahoo Finance's count, though the filing treats the terms as interchangeable. The change came two weeks after Trump criticized the Wall Street Journal on Truth Social for sticking with the phrase "artificial intelligence."

Anthropic's roadshow is now under way, and trading could begin as soon as Nov. 19, according to reports. The company has said it will release further reports on what crossing the safety threshold means for its safeguards. The articles do not say which additional safeguards Anthropic will adopt or when they would take effect. They also do not say which policy changes the company is weighing to keep humans in control, or whether the IPO timeline could shift. More to follow.

stories.Headline: SpaceXSI's Grok Build AI agent exposed sensitive data
stories.Summary:
Security researchers at Claroc found that Grok Build, an AI coding agent from SpaceXSI, was leaking confidential data from thousands of applications built on the platform. The exposure came from insecure default sharing settings, and the researchers reported it to SpaceXSI on November 8, 2026. Claroc's findings were published on November 12, 2026, in reporting by TechGig and Ars Technica. Researchers identified 43,601 addresses ending in grok.me that were visible through passive DNS services. Passive DNS services collect and index domain names seen in DNS traffic, which made these addresses discoverable.

Of those 43,601 addresses, 35,578, or 94.7 per cent, could be accessed without any authentication, according to TechGig. Claroc said the default privacy option for publishing apps was "Anyone with the link," which was pre-selected for users. Ars Technica reported that Grok Build's randomized URLs were structured so the random words sat to the left of grok.me, letting passive DNS searches enumerate them. Claroc said Google's approach places the randomness to the right of the domain, which would have kept the links invisible to such searches. Claroc said that Grok Build's links were set to "Anyone with the link" by default, and users could change the setting to "invited users" or "only you."

Claroc reported that about one in ten apps held sensitive internal business information, and 2 per cent exposed data serious enough for a high or critical severity rating. The exposed material included a hospital employee directory with more than 3,500 names and an intensive care briefing with patient information. A trucking company's recruitment database listing more than 1,000 individuals was also exposed. An employee timesheet's downloadable code contained 18 accounts with plaintext passwords, including administrator credentials. Ars Technica added that a Peruvian construction company's dashboard held 3,784 worker medical exams, and that a Tesla service-center scorecard named 22 technicians.

SpaceXSI itself was among the affected parties, and Claroc found 24 of its apps exposing an onboarding plan, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and advertising proposals. Claroc said SpaceXSI did not respond to its initial notice, so a Claroc official tagged Elon Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer on X. Ars Technica reported that SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending questions about the article. A Cursor representative, which SpaceXSI recently acquired, said that Grok Build apps are "private by default" and that competing coding agents also offer shareable links. Claroc's tests contradicted that statement, showing that Grok Build required users to change the default setting to one of the two more restrictive options.

The problem traces to how Grok Build placed the random portion of its links, which is a design decision that undermined the access protection the randomization was meant to provide. Ars Technica reported that Muse, a Meta agent, had also suspended a link-sharing feature after it was found leaking sensitive data. According to Ars Technica, Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini place their secret randomness in the URL path, so DNS does not expose it. Claroc said it was working to notify other affected app creators, and Asaf Aprozper, Claroc's co-founder and CTO, said he was contacting companies directly. Ars Technica noted that a luxury cruise company's security team began containing the exposure after Claroc shared its findings.

Several questions remain open in the reporting. The Cursor representative did not respond to follow-up questions about whether SpaceXSI intentionally exposed its internal information. Ars Technica reported that SpaceXSI also did not say why it removed the data after Ars asked about it, or whether it planned to notify customers whose information was exposed. The articles do not say how many of the affected organizations will be contacted or what remedies they will receive. Ars Technica advised Grok Build users to choose the "invite others" option unless they intend to make an app widely available.

stories.Headline: European shares log record close on Siemens, CoreWeave-fuelled AI optimism
stories.Summary:
European shares closed at a record on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, just short of their intraday high, as strong forecasts from Siemens Energy and CoreWeave lifted investor confidence in artificial intelligence. The pan-European Stoxx 600 rose 0.72 per cent to 663.05 points, a whisker below the intraday record of 663.41. Germany's DAX also rose 1.2 per cent and hovered near its own all-time high. Siemens Energy led the gains after its shares jumped 10.8 per cent.

The AI equipment maker raised its profit margin expectations for 2027 and said it planned to more than triple its dividend. Peers Schneider Electric and Legrand gained 3 per cent and 2.2 per cent, while the broader tech sector added 2.5 per cent. Chip-related stocks also rose, with Soitec up 11.9 per cent and Aixtron up 8 per cent. Optimism was further boosted by CoreWeave, a neocloud company, which said it expects to become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028.

CoreWeave had been at the centre of AI bubble fears that triggered a global market selloff the previous week. Analysts quoted by Reuters questioned whether the large AI investment would prove profitable across the industry, noting that not all AI companies would succeed. Societe Generale analysts said the rally looked somewhat stretched given political and economic risks, and they saw limited further upside for the index by year-end. Investors also watched interest rates closely after hotter-than-expected US inflation data and hawkish Federal Reserve comments pointed to another rate hike next month.

Sectors less exposed to AI, including retail and food and beverage, lagged on the day. Czech ammunition and arms producer CSG fell 21.6 per cent after cutting its full-year operating margin forecast. A rebound in Brent crude after shipping attacks in the Strait of Hormuz added to inflation concerns in energy-importing Europe. Traders expect at least one quarter-point rate hike by the European Central Bank by February 2027.

stories.Headline: Gray Swan Announces Participation in the NIST Artificial Intelligence Consortium
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, Gray Swan, an AI security company based in Pittsburgh, announced that it is joining the NIST Artificial Intelligence Consortium, which sits within the Department of Commerce's National Institute of Standards and Technology. The consortium is meant to bring together work on new measurement science, aiming to identify techniques and metrics for AI that are proven, scalable, and interoperable. The same day, Vals AI, an independent AI evaluation company based in San Francisco, said it was also taking part in the reconvened consortium. Both companies framed their participation as a way to help the government and industry build better ways to test and compare AI systems.

Gray Swan's CEO and co-founder, Matt Fredrikson, said that AI systems are reaching production faster than testing methods are improving. He said the company's research and its Gray Swan Arena have uncovered thousands of ways that models and agents can be manipulated, and that this evidence should shape how the field measures AI security. Fredrikson said the company intends to bring that research to NIST's work alongside industry and academic partners. Gray Swan noted that it already has a long history of collaboration with NIST through the Arena platform. Through the consortium, the company said it will work with NIST to identify scalable and secure methods for promoting AI adoption.

Vals AI's co-founder and CEO, Rayan Krishnan, said that independent evaluation is essential for measuring AI capabilities, performance, and risks. He said the company looks forward to working with NIST and other members to develop rigorous, reproducible evaluations that reflect real-world uses. Glenn Parham, the company's head of public sector, said policymakers in the United States and elsewhere need confidence in how AI performs, and that independent evaluations give them a common basis for comparison. Vals AI described its work as building benchmarks grounded in real-world tasks, with results cited by frontier AI labs in their model cards.

The consortium supports initiatives set out in the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 and America's AI Action Plan, which was published in 2025. NIST stated that it does not evaluate commercial products under this consortium and does not endorse any product or service used. Both companies pointed readers to the full announcement from the Department of Commerce and NIST for details on the consortium's structure. The articles do not describe specific deliverables, timelines, or outcomes that the consortium will produce.

stories.Headline: CoDE: A Patient Cohort-Based Study of Evidence Coverage and Support in Diagnostic Explanations Generated by Large Language Models
stories.Summary:
AI decision models are a newer category of AI systems built to return a bounded, structured answer rather than free-form text. The application supplies an input and a fixed set of permitted answers, and the model returns a selected label, a probability or a score, usually with a confidence value. One example cited in the coverage scores a support ticket against billing, shipping and returns, selecting billing and giving a probability for each option, so the calling code never has to pull a label out of prose. Several of these models compute their scores in a single pass rather than generating output one token at a time, and many accept new questions and answer options at call time.

The articles describe this as a response to the fact that most business processes exist to make judgments rather than produce content, such as deciding whether a claim needs more evidence or whether an application should be approved, reviewed or denied. In September, TypeSafe AI introduced a model called Jev, which it positions as a fast, intuitive System One model. Vercel reported that Jev became the fastest-adopted model in its AI Gateway's history, reaching more than twice as many paid teams in its first 24 hours as any previous launch. Benchmarks cited by Diplo put Jev's response times at 70 to 500 milliseconds, compared with 3 to 329 seconds for frontier large language models in the same tests. Within weeks, AWS, OpenAI, Liquid AI, Cloudflare and Microsoft had also brought decision models to their platforms.

Coforge's Momentuum blue unit compared four decision architectures across customer support routing and insurance underwriting, and in the underwriting benchmark Jev matched all eight rule-derived business outcomes, outperforming the larger frontier models tested. The more telling finding concerned failures: in one scenario a model approved an application despite missing claims history, and only a downstream control caught the error, so auditing intermediate decisions was what exposed the flaw. Coforge concludes that enterprise AI will increasingly divide work among generative models for language, reasoning models for synthesis, decision models for structured choices and governance layers for oversight. Researchers Edona Elshan, Muhammed-Faith Kaya and Dominik Siemon, writing in Group Decision and Negotiation in 2026, trace this trend from early rule-based systems through to today's collaborative architectures.

The articles also flag limits. jnaapti warns that a wrong answer can still be well formed, that a confidence value is not automatically the probability of being correct, and that thresholds should be tested on an organisation's own labelled data rather than copied between providers. Diplo says most AI rules focus on text, image and code generators, leaving no clear category for embedded engines that output only labels and numbers, and it argues that procurement guidance should distinguish conversational AI from decision AI. The articles expect decision models to sit beside large language models rather than replace them, handling high-volume, low-latency judgments while generative systems take on explanation and open-ended reasoning.

stories.Headline: HeartCore Partners with ONE AI to Bring Physical AI to Existing Industrial Robots in Japan
stories.Summary:
HeartCore Enterprises, Inc., a Tokyo-based IPO consulting company listed on Nasdaq as HTCR, announced on November 12, 2026 that its subsidiary HeartCore Financial signed a non-exclusive business development and sales agency agreement with ONE AI Co., Ltd. in Japan. ONE AI is a Korean developer of CPU-native, on-device physical AI, led by former Intel APAC AI leadership. The partnership will introduce Axis.ONE, a platform meant to add AI capabilities to robots, cameras and industrial PCs that manufacturers already operate. Axis.ONE runs on standard Intel-architecture industrial PCs and edge devices. Its developers say it brings vision and decision-making to existing systems while keeping customer data and models on-site.

The article cites the International Federation of Robotics as saying more than 4.6 million industrial robots operate in factories worldwide. Axis.ONE is intended to upgrade this installed base without replacing robots, controllers or cameras, and without modifying existing robot control systems. ONE AI estimates total cost reductions of up to 90% compared with conventional GPU-based deployments. The platform can operate fully on-premise, including in air-gapped environments. ONE AI reports that per-site learning cycles fell from about 100 days to 10 days in some cases, and from 30 days to one hour in others.

HeartCore will introduce Axis.ONE to Japanese manufacturers, system integrators and industrial operators, coordinate proof-of-concept deployments and pilot programs, and negotiate commercial agreements. ONE AI will provide technical support and demonstration resources. The agreement runs for an initial three years, with automatic one-year renewals unless either party gives notice of non-renewal. HeartCore will earn commissions of 15% of net revenue in the first year, 10% in the second year and 8% in the third year from customers it refers. The parties also intend to explore expansion opportunities with manufacturers in the United States.

HeartCore CEO Sumitaka Kanno said the company believes ONE AI's technology could change how manufacturers use AI, and that Axis.ONE can make installed robots intelligent without replacement. ONE AI CEO In Chan (Colin) Baek said industrial robots should not have to be replaced to become intelligent, and that his team spent more than two decades optimizing AI on Intel silicon. The article identifies manufacturers, energy, public infrastructure, defense and healthcare as potential application areas. The article notes that the performance figures come from ONE AI and have not been independently verified by HeartCore, and that results are not guarantees.

ONE AI was founded in January 2026 and is headquartered in Seoul, Republic of Korea. HeartCore describes itself as guiding Japanese growth companies to U.S. exchange listings through its Go IPO service. The announcement is accompanied by forward-looking statements that cite risks including market acceptance, competition, the early-stage status of ONE AI and regulatory, intellectual property and cybersecurity risks. The filing that the statements reference is HeartCore's Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025.

A separate report dated November 11, 2026 describes a different initiative. Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri announced a partnership with Poste Italiane and telecommunications company TIM to build what it calls Italy's first integrated national Physical AI ecosystem. The effort, named Fincantieri Ontology, is part of the company's 2026–2030 industrial plan, F4. It aims to automate shipyard design and production and to capture technical expertise in digital form. Fincantieri says its industrial workload is valued at about $81 billion (€70 billion) through 2036, supported by 7,000 small and medium-sized suppliers and 18 shipyards worldwide.

Fincantieri CEO Pierroberto Folgiero said that data and artificial intelligence drive the industrial plan, and that the partnership documents and protects the ontology of the company's technical culture. The companies plan four-dimensional design and construction models that give shipyard workers and robotic systems AI-optimized work packages and daily instructions. Fincantieri says the partnership will create a protected computing environment that combines local AI processing with secure cloud infrastructure. The article says about 100,000 people access its facilities daily, and that the partnership aims to transition traditional manufacturing roles toward digitally enabled production.

stories.Headline: Who would be next CEO at Nvidia? Top engineer and CFO favored as candidates
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board is preparing to oust CEO and founder Jensen Huang, according to a Semafor report published November 11, 2026, with a meeting scheduled for Wednesday evening. Some directors reportedly favor naming Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO if Huang is removed. The move follows media reports that Huang had a second extramarital affair. The company's stock fell more than 8 percent in after-hours trading, reaching a 52-week low.

The board's planned action would end a saga in which Huang admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The company's long-tenured board had already announced a probe, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton, into whether Huang may have shared corporate secrets or endangered US national security. Nvidia has tapped an outside search firm to find a permanent successor, Bloomberg reported. One candidate reportedly under consideration is Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who was considered for the Intel CEO job in 2019.

Semafor reported that the board briefed the White House on its planned meeting, according to a senior administration official. Senators Chris Coons and Elizabeth Warren wrote to members of Trump's cabinet asking them to preserve documents related to Nvidia's chip exports to China and to any entities that could divert those chips there. They also asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller to preserve records about Huang and his correspondence with President Trump. In their letter, the senators said reports suggest officials at several agencies knew of concerns about Nvidia's relationship with a company called Megaspeed yet did not act to stop the flow of advanced chips.

Nvidia's spokespeople did not immediately comment. The context is that Nvidia supplies many of the most advanced chips used by major cloud companies and has entered billions of dollars in financing deals supporting the AI buildout, which raises the stakes of its leadership change. The articles do not say whether the board will make a final decision on Wednesday or who will ultimately be named CEO. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Can HMRC look into your AI chat history?
stories.Summary:
From May, HMRC is set to gain new powers to scrutinise the use of large language models in preparing self-assessment tax returns. The change is part of the Budget Bill, which is expected to become law at the end of May, and it would let the tax authority demand computer records from third parties such as AI platforms, as well as personal data from taxpayers themselves. The power would be used to check whether enough tax has been paid, and the articles describe it as an update to existing information powers rather than a blanket inspection of chatbot conversations. Anyone who fails to respond could face a £300 fine, and taxpayers who fail to report inaccuracies could be liable for up to £3,000. HMRC has said it can only request information where it already has a lawful basis to do so.

The articles point out that completing a tax return is a demanding task, which is why millions of self-employed people and higher earners have turned to AI for help. Government concern is that some of these users may be leading themselves into paying too little tax. HMRC can only issue "Schedule 36" notices, demanding information, when it can show a reasonable need. One article notes that the government has said safeguards are in place and private data will not be compromised. Meanwhile, the Budget Bill also gives the tax authority separate powers to recover debts directly from bank accounts from July 2029.

Seb Maley, chief executive of the tax insurance provider Qdos, said HMRC was making sure it isn't left behind as more people and businesses use AI for their tax affairs. Anne Strickland of the Taxpayers' Alliance campaign group warned that demanding private chatbot data would be a deeply intrusive overreach, and argued that the tax authority already has sweeping powers. David Stirling of Mint Wealth advised people to assume their chatbot workings could one day be scrutinised. An HMRC spokesperson said the change reflects how tax information is now stored digitally and that it is not about going through everyone's use of large language models.

The debate comes as the government works to recover an estimated £59.2 billion owed in the 2024/2025 tax year, which the articles present as part of Labour's broader effort on unpaid tax. The articles suggest that the new powers will not automatically give HMRC access to anyone's full chatbot history, but they leave open the possibility that such records could be requested. Critics argue the proposal goes too far in intruding on privacy, while HMRC maintains that its requests will be limited and lawful. The articles do not say how often such requests are expected or how the safeguards will work in practice.

stories.Headline: AIIM summit connects U-M leaders across disciplines to explore AI research opportunities, challenges
stories.Summary:
The AI Institutes at Michigan, known as AIIM, held its second AI Research Summit for Academic Leadership, bringing together deans, department chairs and other leaders from across the University of Michigan. The event was presented with the Office of the Vice President for Research and the Michigan Institute for Data & AI in Science, known as MIDAS, and coordinated with the Office of the Provost. It gave leaders a chance to assess progress, identify barriers and refine the university's long-term approach to AI in research. The summit came one week after U-M released guiding principles for AI use in education.

Participants came from the medical school, engineering, the humanities, the social sciences and the arts, representing units as varied as history, robotics, neurosurgery and sports management. Patricia Hurn, interim vice president for research and innovation, opened by saying AI allows experiments that cannot be done in the physical world, and that realizing this will require greater supercomputing capacity. President Domenico Grasso urged the university to embrace AI deliberately while keeping human judgment and oversight central. Provost Laurie McCauley encouraged leaders to review expectations, consider investments in AI and learn from one another in guiding students.

The program combined short presentations with small-group discussions on three topics: departments' five-year visions for AI research, the challenges they have faced, and changes in their AI culture and daily practices. MIDAS researchers compiled the takeaways, which included calls for flexible, principle-based frameworks that protect foundational learning, verification and human judgment. Participants also asked for equitable access to AI tools and computing resources, coordination across units to share practices and reduce duplicated effort, and a culture of responsible use built on transparency and clear disclosure. Brad Orr, associate vice president for natural sciences and engineering, said the range of disciplines offered a useful chance to exchange ideas and identify shared challenges.

AIIM, launched in 2025, supports Look to Michigan, the university's strategic vision for innovation and societal impact. At the summit it opened a call for submissions for its 2027 Empowering Research with AI Awards, which recognize innovative and responsible uses or evaluations of AI. Researchers on the Ann Arbor, Dearborn and Flint campuses can receive awards of $1,000 to $3,000 per project, with submissions due Jan. 17. Winners will be announced at the AI in Research Symposium hosted by MIDAS on March 16-17. Grasso said the university has an obligation to lead by showing that bold adoption and responsible use of AI go hand in hand.

stories.Headline: Analysis: Is Nvidia too big to fail? Its AI financing web raises the stakes
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board is investigating allegations involving CEO Jensen Huang, and CNBC reports that the company has made hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments to other firms that support the AI boom. The New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital affair with a company executive and a relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China, while The Wall Street Journal reported the board was preparing to oust him. Nvidia's board has expressed confidence in its CEO, and the company did not respond to a request for comment. Nvidia's stock fell 27% from its October 6 peak through Wednesday's close, and it fell a further 8% in after-hours trading that day.

The company's commitments include a plan to buy up to $36 billion in cloud services from smaller AI companies known as neoclouds, which Nvidia disclosed in July. Nvidia also agreed to a $105 billion phased guarantee for a data center project in Ohio planned by OpenAI and SB Energy, subject to certain conditions, and promised to backstop up to $125 billion of a $500 billion credit program by Wall Street firms. Columbia Business School finance professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh estimates the obligations at $400 billion overall. The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are watching how this financing could amplify an AI downturn.

Analysts interviewed by CNBC said a rerun of the 2007-2008 financial crisis is unlikely. Sheila Bair, a former head of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., said Nvidia is not "too big to fail in a bank sense at all," because it is not vulnerable to a sudden loss of confidence and its large equity provides a cushion. She said regulators still need to watch banks' and the wider system's exposure to Nvidia and similar firms, and that "Nvidia going down would be a pretty seismic event." Van Nieuwerburgh said that "there's a lot of equity in the system right now," though he would not call it a safe system.

The concern centers on circular financing, in which larger firms help customers buy their products. Jason Wu, an assistant director at the International Monetary Fund, said that if the value of Nvidia's chips fell, borrowers might be unable to repay debts, and that "both the economy and financial markets are standing on the same leg." The IMF's October Global Financial Stability report warned about leverage among AI firms and investors. The so-called hyperscalers grew from 1% of bond issuance in the $15 trillion investment-grade debt market to 10% in two years. Neocloud stress is visible in CoreWeave's credit-default spreads, which rose 94% from October 1 to November 5, and in an IREN convertible bond that fell 23% from November 3 to November 5.

Nvidia's troubles have so far separated it from other firms, since most neocloud equity prices recovered this week as Nvidia's shares fell, suggesting investors see the problems as specific to the company. AMD, Broadcom, Intel, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI are all building their own AI chips, which could eventually replace Nvidia's products and cap any fallout. Van Nieuwerburgh said central bankers "are clearly very, very, very anxious about this." Nvidia is scheduled to report earnings on Tuesday, and analysts expect its revenue to more than double in the current fiscal year and roughly double again over the following two years, according to LSEG data.
