stories.Headline: Americans growing more comfortable with AI in medicine, but they want providers involved
stories.Summary:
A new Gallup survey of more than 5,000 US adults, published in November 2026, finds that Americans are growing more comfortable with artificial intelligence taking part in medical decisions, but they still want a clinician to have the final say. Among respondents who had seen a healthcare provider within the past year, 56% said they were somewhat or very comfortable with AI making diagnosis and treatment decisions as long as the provider could override them. Only 9% were comfortable with AI deciding without provider review, while 38% were comfortable when AI assisted and the provider made the call. Similar patterns held for AI review of medical imaging (53%) and medication decisions (49%) when a provider could make the final decision.

For people who were uncomfortable with AI working without oversight, the single factor that would most change their view was the ability to request review by a provider, which 48% and 47% said would make them more comfortable with diagnosis and treatment decisions and imaging review, respectively. Fewer than one in three respondents said other factors, such as strong privacy protections, evidence of safety and effectiveness, faster decisions, or lower costs, would ease their concerns. The survey was conducted August 12 to 24, with a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 1.7 percentage points. A separate survey of more than 1,000 licensed primary care physicians found that doctors underestimate patient comfort: 36% of them thought patients would accept AI decisions that a provider could override, compared with 56% of patients.

Use of AI by clinicians is already widespread, according to the reporting. Nine in 10 physicians surveyed said they had used an AI tool or chatbot in the past year for at least one work task, most often gathering medication information (78%), reviewing patient-specific information (53%), writing clinical notes (50%), and writing after-visit summaries (49%), yet only 20% reported receiving any formal training. A study published in JAMA, led by researchers at Harvard Medical School, reported that more than 950,000 US physicians submitted over 270 million queries to the AI-enabled clinical information program OpenEvidence between January 2024 and June 2026, with monthly active users rising from 355 to 703,265. The authors wrote that efforts to evaluate, teach, and integrate AI in clinical medicine should be informed by studies of how it is actually used in practice. The articles do not describe any specific policy or regulatory change that would follow from these findings.

Articles.Title: Americans growing more comfortable with AI in medicine, but they want providers involved

stories.Headline: Implementing AI: How Companies Might Manage — Even Avoid — Employee Burnout
stories.Summary:
A recent survey of nearly 3,900 full-time U.S. workers found that more than 90% of people who use AI daily at work say it makes them more productive. The same research, reported by WebMD, found that the most productive AI users face a burnout risk 4.5 times higher than their peers. The study authors described these employees as the ones delivering the greatest productivity gains while also being the most vulnerable to burnout. The findings raised a question about whether the technology itself or the way companies manage workers is driving that strain. UCLA Anderson's Auyon Siddiq offers a theoretical explanation in a working paper built on game theory.

In his model, employees decide how hard to work, knowing that better technology makes each hour count for more and that pushing harder raises their burnout risk. Workers also know their pay depends partly on how they compare with colleagues. Siddiq suggests the culprit may be less the technology and more how management chooses to measure and reward employees, since AI can make everyone's bar for advancement rise at once. Ranking systems amplify this effect, and Siddiq cites Meta, which in 2025 told teams of 150 or more to place 15% to 20% of employees in its lowest performance category, a group more exposed to layoffs.

Microsoft and Amazon have used similar systems. In Siddiq's model, if AI makes everyone more productive, the bar for moving up the scoreboard rises, so everyone works harder just to keep up. Because everyone pushes equally hard, no one gets ahead, and the group would be better off working less. Limited pay raises, bonuses and promotions can create the same rat race even without forced ranking.

The model also shows that policies such as flexible hours can lead firms to push employees harder, since management may raise the stakes once burnout risk falls. Siddiq also cautions that bigger wellness budgets can signal how hard a company pushes its workers, and that wellness programs do not necessarily slow the rat race. He recommends easing quotas that force a fixed share of employees into low-performer labels, giving more weight to measures such as collaboration, and not raising performance targets when conditions improve. The costs of burnout are substantial, according to a recent estimate that puts the expense for an average U.S. company with 1,000 employees at about $5 million a year, mostly through missed work.

Replacing workers is also very expensive, which gives firms a reason to take the problem seriously. Siddiq's model compares a profit-driven firm with one that also weighs worker well-being, and finds that the profit-driven firm pushes harder and ends up with more burnout even while spending more on prevention. When AI delivers large productivity gains, even the employee-minded firm may spend more on burnout prevention, since easing work intensity becomes costlier. The paper's broader message is that generous wellness benefits do not by themselves end the pressure to compete.

Articles.Title: Implementing AI: How Companies Might Manage — Even Avoid — Employee Burnout

stories.Headline: Grambling State Advances AI-Powered Student Support Through IBM Collaboration
stories.Summary:
Grambling State University is building a Student Digital Assistant meant to make campus information easier to find and to streamline student support. The tool is being developed with IBM and implementation partner Blue Polaris, using IBM watsonx Orchestrate, and is still in development and validation. Phase 1 is expected to go live Dec. 7, ahead of the Spring 2027 semester. The initial version is intended to help students with commonly requested information such as registration, financial aid, housing and other student services.

Content for Phase 1 will continue to be refined through the validation process. Max Ferguson, Chief Experience & Digital Strategy Officer at Grambling State, said the goal is to help students get the information they need and connect with the right resources when they need them. He described the project as more than a technology rollout, framing it as a way to improve the student experience with students in mind. Students are already part of the work: cybersecurity student Terry Douglas Jr. and recent graduates Hollidae Coleman and Elijah Neal are helping validate content by reviewing and structuring information so responses are clear and student-friendly.

Coleman holds a Bachelor of Science in Management and Neal a degree in Criminal Justice. A second phase of engagement is planned with students from the Thomas and Joyce Moorehead College of Business and Entrepreneurship, who will take part in marketing, feedback and ongoing refinement. Ferguson discussed the Student Digital Assistant during IBM TechXchange 2026 in Atlanta, where he spoke with IBM Automation Specialist Shanu Bhargava about Phase 1 and the university's approach to using artificial intelligence to improve access to student information and services. The project builds on the university's wider relationship with IBM.

Through IBM SkillsBuild and related programs, Grambling State students can train in artificial intelligence, cloud computing, cybersecurity and data science and earn digital credentials. The assistant offers a way to apply those skills to practical campus needs. After the anticipated launch, the university plans to keep evaluating the tool, gathering feedback and refining the experience as more capabilities are considered. The university also plans to explore a future case study with IBM on implementation, lessons learned and student impact once the project has progressed and measurable outcomes are available.

Articles.Title: Grambling State Advances AI-Powered Student Support Through IBM Collaboration

stories.Headline: Can AI Agents Help Los Angeles Evacuate Faster During Wildfires?
stories.Summary:
USC researchers are developing an AI framework called EVAC-AI to help Los Angeles residents evacuate faster during wildfires. The effort follows the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires, in which delayed warnings, alerts sent to the wrong neighborhood and clogged evacuation routes exposed weaknesses in the city's evacuation system. According to the article, the city lacks the ability to coordinate fire conditions, traffic and residents' movements in real time. The team aims to shift wildfire management from reacting to evacuations toward anticipating bottlenecks before they become crises.

The project is a four-year effort funded by the National Science Foundation's Focused Interdisciplinary Research in Engineering program. EVAC-AI would integrate fire behavior, transportation networks, emergency response and human mobility into one system. It is designed to support emergency managers, local agencies, residents, vulnerable communities, autonomous vehicle operators and mobility providers. The framework would update road-accessibility information every five minutes at the census tract level, according to the team's plans.

The project is led by Ruolin Li, a USC assistant professor of civil engineering. The research team also includes Yue Zhao, assistant professor of computer science, and Ketan Savla and Costas Synolakis, both professors of civil and environmental engineering. Li said the goal is to approach evacuation as one interconnected system rather than a collection of separate problems. Li also said that factors like fire behavior, transportation networks and human mobility are deeply connected. Zhao noted that evacuation plans fail to address the needs of elderly people, people with disabilities and households without personal vehicles.

The article explains that current fire prediction models forecast fire spread without accounting for the transportation network, while evacuation models may not account for ember-driven spot ignitions that can make roads inaccessible. Los Angeles fires frequently begin in hillside vegetation along the metropolitan border and can rapidly approach densely populated communities. Emergency alerts can prompt entire neighborhoods to leave at once, creating traffic that overwhelms limited mountain and canyon routes. The article also notes that the city's growing network of autonomous vehicles, such as those operated by Waymo, offers another opportunity for the project.

The framework includes an agentic AI system connecting its components, and the team plans a resident-facing app that residents could use to report vehicle access, elderly family members or pets. The researchers will explore staggered, targeted evacuation instructions instead of single mass alerts. They will also explore centrally coordinated dispatching of autonomous vehicles to pick up residents who lack transportation or need accommodations. The article describes these as plans under development, and it does not say when the tools will be deployed.

Articles.Title: Can AI Agents Help Los Angeles Evacuate Faster During Wildfires?

stories.Headline: A Blueprint for Evaluating AI in Public Administration
stories.Summary:
Stanford's Human-Centered AI institute (HAI) has published a policy brief laying out a blueprint for how government agencies can evaluate AI tools used in high-stakes public services. The brief frames the problem against recent incidents, including a June 2026 case in which autonomous AI agents gained unauthorized access to the Australian Medicare statistics portal, which the brief describes as the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website. It also points to California Governor Gavin Newsom's Executive Order N-9-26, which aims to speed up a framework for independent verification organizations that would evaluate AI systems. The brief notes that federal agencies reported 3,611 AI use cases across 56 agencies in 2025, a 69 percent rise over the previous year.

The authors argue that common AI evaluation methods are not sufficient for governments in practice, and that agencies often struggle to carry out effective evaluation even where legal mandates exist. They suggest agencies can draw on "hidden benchmarks," meaning administrative records of past task performance that could be used to train and test AI models for public sector needs, and that releasing such benchmarks could help measure and drive progress. The brief recommends that agencies require third-party evaluations as a condition of procurement, run randomized A/B tests to understand the effects of systems once deployed, and partner with universities and research institutions for independent expertise at lower cost. It also calls for rethinking quality assurance after deployment so that human-AI collaboration is part of oversight.

The brief identifies two categories of risk: safety risk, where tools can be manipulated or agentic systems with access to government data can take unintended actions, and performance risk, where systems may fail to do what they were meant to do or to deliver expected benefits. It is written by Stanford researchers, and the article does not name a single individual author beyond the institute itself. The brief also cites Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who urged frontier AI labs to devote 80 percent of engineering resources to verification and 20 percent to development, a split the brief contrasts with current industry norms. The brief presents itself as a basis for recommendations on how government can shape standards for evaluating increasingly powerful AI in mission-critical areas, and it points to related HAI work on FDA regulation of generative AI medical devices and California's frontier AI transparency requirements.

Articles.Title: A Blueprint for Evaluating AI in Public Administration - Stanford HAI

stories.Headline: RIT students win Microsoft hackathon with AI-powered shopping solution
stories.Summary:
Five Rochester Institute of Technology students won first place at a Microsoft hackathon in New York City for a strategy that helps AI shopping agents make better purchase decisions. The team competed in the LEAD Aspire 2026 event at Microsoft's Times Square office, where students take on a real business challenge for a day. Out of more than 1,000 applications, the RIT team was one of 17 finalists selected. The team members included Denise Reyes Lujan, Emilio Garcia Rabell, Gesem Mejia, Carla Lopez, and Cristian Morataya. They had initially missed the application deadline, but Reyes Lujan contacted an organizer directly through LinkedIn and was able to join.

The challenge was set by Mastercard, which asked students to consider how to build consumer trust in agentic e-commerce, a growing form of online shopping in which AI agents handle purchases. The team built Align Buddy, a tool designed to work alongside Mastercard's existing Agent Pay and Verifiable Intent initiatives. Instead of only checking whether an agent started a transaction, Align Buddy builds a fuller picture of each customer's preferences from past transactions and evaluates proposed purchases before payment is made. For example, if a customer always books nonstop flights, the tool could flag an itinerary with several layovers. The students said this approach could reduce returns and raise customer satisfaction.

Mastercard representatives guided the students through the challenge, and a product manager advised the team that the best ideas were ones the company could easily implement or fit with its current work. The students said that advice helped them stand out. The team received funding for the trip from RIT's Golisano College of Computing and Information Sciences, Kate Gleason College of Engineering, and Student Government. The students credited RIT's required co-op, internship, and capstone projects with preparing them to work with customers and build solutions businesses can adopt. Competitors from Microsoft, Mastercard, EY, and GitHub were also involved in the event.

The team earned a trophy and headphones, but the students said the most valuable outcome was the connections they made with professionals from the sponsoring companies. Mejia said that after the award, representatives shared their contact information and said the team was the kind of people they wanted to hire. Several team members first met through RIT's chapter of the Society of Hispanic Professional Engineers. The article reports the win and the students' own account of the experience, without any figures beyond those given above.

Articles.Title: RIT students win Microsoft hackathon with AI-powered shopping solution

stories.Headline: WIU Cybersecurity Center Director Shares Insights on Cybersecurity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence - Western Illinois University
stories.Summary:
Tahir Khan, Interim Director of the Western Illinois University Cybersecurity Center, gave a presentation titled "Cybersecurity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence" on October 29, 2026, at the invitation of the Macomb Area Chamber of Commerce. The talk was held in recognition of Cybersecurity Awareness Month and drew members of the Macomb business community. It focused on the growing cybersecurity risks tied to artificial intelligence and what those risks mean for businesses and organizations. The session was a public event rather than a regulatory action, so it did not create new requirements. Khan described how artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape, including its growing role in cyberattacks and in everyday business operations.

He identified the main security challenges organizations face in an increasingly AI-driven environment. He also discussed practical strategies businesses can use to reduce cybersecurity threats and AI-related risks. The workshop stressed that proactive measures help organizations protect digital assets, strengthen security practices and respond effectively to new threats. The articles report no specific numbers, dates beyond the event date, or policy changes arising from the session. The presenter was Khan, and the event was organized through the Macomb Area Chamber of Commerce.

According to the university's account, Khan explained the risks and offered guidance without announcing any new program or mandate. The article was published by University Communications at Western Illinois University, which framed the session as part of its continuing effort to share knowledge on digital security. The session sits within the university's broader role in cybersecurity education and awareness, which the article says the WIU Cybersecurity Center advances through engagements like this one. The article does not describe any follow-up sessions, deadlines or next steps. Readers who want more about the center can find it through the university's website.

Articles.Title: WIU Cybersecurity Center Director Shares Insights on Cybersecurity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence - Western Illinois University

stories.Headline: November AI workshops offer hands-on learning
stories.Summary:
Clemson University has announced a new set of AI workshops for November 2026, aimed at students, faculty and staff who want to build their AI skills. The lineup, published on November 11, 2026 by Clemson News, covers evaluating AI-generated information, getting help with everyday questions, and using tools such as ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot. The sessions are organized by several groups on campus, including the Clemson Libraries, the Wilbur O. and Ann Powers College of Business, and an AI office hours program. The announcement says the workshops are meant to give hands-on experience rather than only lectures. Several sessions focus on OpenAI's planned retirement of custom GPTs, which the article says is scheduled for December 11, 2026.

Anyone who has built custom GPTs in ChatGPT Edu can attend a virtual session on moving them to ChatGPT plugins, offered on Tuesday, November 17 and Thursday, November 19, each from noon to 1 p.m. over Zoom. A drop-in virtual AI Office Hours session runs Friday, November 13, from 1 to 2 p.m., where participants can ask practical questions about AI tools and use cases. The article notes that these office hours are led by Clemson AI experts. The library's "Making Sense of AI" series includes three 30-minute Zoom sessions.

The first, on Thursday, November 12, from 11 to 11:30 a.m., covers how to tell which claims need checking and when an answer is useful enough. The second, on Tuesday, November 17, from 11 to 11:30 a.m., explains how AI tools behave when they draw on library collections, the web, or a user's own document. The third, on Wednesday, November 18, from 11 to 11:30 a.m., shows participants how to confirm that a cited source exists and actually supports the claim attached to it. A student-led in-person session, "AI Literacy: A Workshop For Students, By Students," is set for Wednesday, November 18, at noon in 416 Cooper Library and at 6 p.m. in 309 Cooper Library, with pizza provided.

The Copilot 101 Workshop, hosted by Microsoft, is designed for faculty and staff and will be held Monday, November 16, from noon to 1:30 p.m. on Teams. According to the article, the online session will combine practical demonstrations, tips and discussion on using AI for teaching, research, student support and everyday work. The announcement is framed as an invitation rather than a requirement, and it does not describe any penalties or mandates tied to the workshops.

The university's own news office is the source of the schedule, and the article does not name a single person responsible for the program. The timing of the lineup is tied to OpenAI's decision to retire custom GPTs, which leaves users who depend on them with a deadline in December. The article does not describe any further sessions beyond those listed, and it does not say whether the series will be repeated in future months. Readers wanting to register or get more details are directed to the sessions' individual listings in the article.

Articles.Title: November AI workshops offer hands-on learning

stories.Headline: UT San Antonio researchers discuss AI’s promise, challenges at brain health conferences
stories.Summary:
In early October, researchers from The University of Texas at San Antonio presented work on artificial intelligence in brain health at two conferences, the Neurepiomics Conference and the International Stroke Genetics Consortium annual meeting. The presentations covered efforts to adapt imaging tools to different research datasets and ways to improve the accuracy of AI models. The story was published on November 11, 2026, by UT Health San Antonio, which reported on the presentations. Its reporting described AI as opening new possibilities for biomedical research, particularly in analyzing brain scans and expanding participation in studies of cognitive decline.

Ngoc-Huynh Ho, PhD, presented research on a common problem: an AI model may reach high overall accuracy yet perform less reliably for certain populations. Ho's work aims to improve how well such models classify dementia from brain imaging across racial and ethnic groups that are unevenly represented in training data. Ho said the goal was to guide the model to learn the probability of each class efficiently. The article notes that overall accuracy alone cannot show whether a model's predictions will apply to every individual.

Shamsudeen Kutty, PhD, described the Vascular Imaging Biomarker Relationships to Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias project, which develops AI methods to measure cerebral small-vessel disease across MRI datasets from different research centers. He said identifying imaging markers of this disease is time-consuming, and differences in scanners and protocols make a single model hard to apply across institutions. The team trains models on data from several National Institute on Aging Alzheimer's Disease Research Centers and adapts them to new datasets. Examples shown at the conference found that adding five to 10 annotated samples from a new dataset improved detection compared with using none, although errors remained.

Juan B. Gutiérrez, PhD, a mathematics professor, urged researchers to challenge AI outputs, arguing that AI models make mistakes and that an error-free large language model is a mathematical impossibility. He advocated independent verification, including using one AI system to check another, while noting this cannot remove every error. He also urged researchers to read commercial platforms' confidentiality and data-use policies before submitting unpublished findings or code. He said universities must set expectations for accountability and teach students to evaluate evidence rather than accept AI conclusions uncritically. The article concludes that AI-assisted brain health research could widen participation and make imaging analysis more scalable, but scientists must still judge where these tools succeed and fail.

Articles.Title: UT San Antonio researchers discuss AI’s promise, challenges at brain health conferences

stories.Headline: Columbia’s Jeannette Wing to Co-Lead New York’s AI Safety Research Center
stories.Summary:
Columbia University's Jeannette Wing, the institution's executive vice president for research, has been named interim co-director of the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research. New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced the appointments on November 10, and the center is described as a first-of-its-kind statewide effort to advance artificial intelligence security and safety. Wing will lead the center together with Greg Morrisett, who serves as dean and vice provost of Cornell Tech. The announcement was published by Columbia News on November 11, 2026. The center will draw on the expertise of more than 80 AI safety and security researchers at colleges and research institutions across New York.

Those researchers will work from their home institutions rather than relocating. They will use computing resources supplied by Empire AI, the state's public-private research initiative that gives member institutions shared access to supercomputing for AI research. The arrangement pools talent and infrastructure across the state instead of concentrating them in one place. Wing said that as AI systems become more autonomous, researchers need better scientific methods to ensure those systems do no harm. She argued that the field must anticipate new kinds of failures, vulnerabilities, and attacks, and then find ways to prevent, detect, and recover from them.

Her remarks frame the center's work as a forward-looking effort rather than a reaction to any single incident. The articles quote her directly, and her views are presented as the stated purpose of the center. The articles describe the center as an early, statewide step in a rapidly developing field, and they do not say what specific outputs or timelines the center will produce. Because Wing and Morrisett hold interim leadership roles, the articles leave open how the permanent leadership will be chosen. Further details about funding, research agendas, and governance are not reported in the material provided.

Articles.Title: Columbia’s Jeannette Wing to Co-Lead New York’s AI Safety Research Center

stories.Headline: Saint Vincent College approves new artificial intelligence minor - Saint Vincent College
stories.Summary:
Saint Vincent College in Latrobe, Pennsylvania, has approved a new interdisciplinary minor in artificial intelligence, announced on November 11, 2026. The minor was developed by the Computing and Information Systems and Mathematics departments together with the Data Science program in the Herbert W. Boyer School of Natural Sciences, Mathematics and Computing. The program is 18 credits and draws on coursework in computer science, data science, mathematics and ethics. Students will study foundational AI concepts, machine learning, data and knowledge engineering, and the design of AI-related technologies.

The structure is flexible, letting students choose courses across several areas so the minor can complement their main field of study and career goals. The program stresses both the technical basis of AI and the ethical questions raised by its development and use. The college says the minor reflects its aim of preparing graduates to take leadership roles in an AI-driven world rather than simply using emerging tools. Dr. Mary Regina Boland, an assistant professor of data science, said the Boyer School surveyed regional employers beforehand and found a desire for more AI training. She said the minor pairs well with existing majors including computer science, data science, mathematics, cybersecurity and information systems.

Dr. Anthony Serapiglia, chair of the Department of Computing and Information Systems, said AI now touches nearly all professions and that the program is meant to give students a direct technical foundation and practical experience. He emphasized that human responsibility and ethical considerations remain central to the college's approach. Dr. Stephen Jodis, dean of the Boyer School, said the minor draws on faculty from computer science, data science and mathematics, and that its goal is to prepare students to understand, develop and responsibly apply these technologies in their chosen fields. The articles do not give a start date, enrollment figures or course list for the minor.

Articles.Title: Saint Vincent College approves new artificial intelligence minor - Saint Vincent College

stories.Headline: With new Democratic Congress incoming, Pritzker calls for federal AI regulations
stories.Summary:
Governor JB Pritzker has called on the incoming Democratic Congress to adopt a federal framework covering digital privacy, AI safety and data centers, as part of a suggested 200-point national agenda. The plan, announced in Chicago, was reported by Capitol News Illinois and WIFR in November 2026. Pritzker's proposal lists three action points for Congress to take up. It calls for durable federal privacy laws, federal requirements for AI risk assessment, testing and monitoring, and rules requiring data centers to be energy- and water-efficient. Pritzker has said any federal action should build on state leadership rather than override what Illinois and other states have already done.

Illinois joined New York and California in July to become the third state to pass frontier AI regulatory legislation. Pritzker's agenda was written for the Democratic Party and the new Congress. The state law he signed this year, Senate Bill 0315, aims to increase transparency and prevent catastrophic risk. That law defines catastrophic risk as a foreseeable material risk leading to the death or serious injury of more than 50 people, or more than $1 million in property damage from a single incident. The frontier legislation targets the most advanced AI models, those generating more than $500 million in annual revenue.

Illinois also pioneered a mandatory annual third-party audit of frontier AI models under its Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act. State Representative Daniel Didech has argued that a federal catastrophic-risk regulation would be preferable to a patchwork of 50 state laws. Pritzker's agenda is the Democratic governor's proposal, and it is not yet law. Currently, no comprehensive federal regulatory framework exists for AI.

President Donald Trump, who has taken a laissez-faire approach toward AI, signed an executive order in September and created a voluntary, nonbinding White House accord with leaders of OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, XAI and Nvidia. Didech said the federal government is not taking meaningful steps to protect against these harms, so states have had no choice but to fill the gaps. Megan Stokes, state director at the Computer and Communications Industry Association, said conflicting state laws would create a costly compliance landscape that hurts startups and weakens competitiveness. Stokes said her association has pushed for a federal solution partly to keep companies compliant across states with varied rules.

Her group is also concerned about the third-party audit model, because such audits have not been done before. She raised questions about auditor training, protecting industry secrets and whistleblowers, and maintaining independence. Bamshad Mobasher, a DePaul University professor, said regulations also need to protect users from undue surveillance, discrimination and leaked private data. He said Illinois's law focuses largely on bigger companies rather than downstream applications and potential harms.

Volodymyr Kindratenko, a University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign professor, said the technology moves so fast that rules written today may not stay relevant. Stokes said she expects a very active 2027 for AI proposals, discussions and oversight at both federal and state levels. Congress's response to Pritzker's agenda remains uncertain, and the articles do not say whether Trump would sign any such legislation. The articles also do not say which specific provisions Congress would adopt or how the audit concerns would be resolved.

stories.Headline: New Report: The Impact of AI on Student Safety and Learning Needs Strong Guardrails and Support for Educators - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
Texas 2036, a nonpartisan public policy organization, released a report on November 10, 2026, titled "In Ctrl of AI in Schools." The report concludes that artificial intelligence can help or harm Texas students depending on the decisions people make around it. Its findings say AI benefits appear when tools are built with safeguards, when clear guidance governs their use, and when an educator controls how they are used in instruction. The report arrived as AI use in Texas schools is outpacing the rules governing it. Texas lawmakers were beginning to file legislation for the 2027 session when the report was released.

A fall 2025 survey of Texas school and district leaders, conducted by the University of Texas at Austin and the Texas Association of School Administrators, found that 86% said teachers were using AI. The same survey found that 61% reported student use. Only 29% of leaders reported a district policy governing student AI use, and just 20% had one for teachers and staff. The report offers insights for the state's efforts to give schools and teachers the resources they need. Its four priorities call for statewide guidance, student safety, equipped teachers and students prepared for an AI-driven future.

Renzo Soto, deputy director of education and workforce policy at Texas 2036 and the report's author, said that school leaders and teachers must control how AI appears in schools. Soto said the early research does not show that AI is simply good or bad for students. Mary Lynn Pruneda, director of education and workforce policy at Texas 2036, said parents should be able to trust that classroom technology is safe, protects privacy and helps students learn. Pruneda said safety and effectiveness must be the starting point for AI in classrooms, not an afterthought. The report does not advocate putting AI in every classroom or banning it entirely.

The report analyzes mixed evidence on AI and learning, in which some studies find real gains, others find real harms, and many find both. The difference often depends on how tools are designed, how teachers guide their use, and whether students can think critically and independently. Three laws passed in Texas in 2025 established a foundation for responsible AI governance, including requirements affecting public school districts. Those broad standards have yet to be translated into consistent, classroom-specific guidance. The report finds that 42 states have issued statewide AI guidance or model policies for schools, while Texas is among the eight that have not.

Texas 2036's 10th Texas Voter Poll found strong public support for protecting students as AI enters classrooms. Nearly 85% of Texas voters said protecting student data and privacy is extremely or very important if schools use AI. More than three-quarters prioritize safety and quality standards for AI tools, and 71% said teaching students to use AI responsibly and ethically is important. The report's four priorities are establishing statewide guidance, putting student safety first, equipping Texas teachers, and preparing students for an AI-driven future. Building on Texas 2036's recently released legislative agenda, these priorities target responsible AI use in K–12 education.

This report is the first installment of Texas 2036's research on artificial intelligence in K–12 education. A second report will analyze policies, guidance and resources from other states to help Texas build a statewide model policy. That model policy is intended to prioritize student safety and learning. The articles do not say when the second report will be released or whether Texas lawmakers will adopt any of the report's priorities in the 2027 session.

stories.Headline: Putting AI on pause: South Portland schools consider moratorium
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 9, 2026, the South Portland School Board voted 6-1 against a proposed moratorium on student-facing generative AI use for the remainder of the 2026-2027 school year. Only At-Large Board Member Claire Holman, who originally proposed the moratorium, voted in favor of it. The vote came at the board's regular meeting, which included several highly anticipated agenda items. WGME reported the result late that Monday evening, and its story was updated the following morning. The South Portland School Department remains without a specific AI policy after the failed vote.

Official city documents show the moratorium would have paused student-facing generative AI use in classrooms and assignments for students in grades PreK-8 across the South Portland School District. The pause was meant to give the board time to develop an appropriate AI policy. The proposal also stated that the school department would make sure all staff received two hours of AI awareness training and three hours of AI literacy training. After finishing that training, teachers would have been allowed to use only AI tools sanctioned by the South Portland School Department. Exceptions could have covered assistive technologies and centrally approved instructional uses.

Holman, who brought the proposal, told the meeting that nothing in it stops students from learning about AI or stops teachers from generating a whole curriculum with it. She said she knew some audience members were laughing at her. She voiced concern about the consequences of allowing student-facing AI use without a moratorium, asking what happens if kids cannot think, and saying simply that she does not like it. Board Chair Rosemarie DeAngelis said she would not support the moratorium that night, based on what she had heard, and stressed waiting for a more detailed plan on AI use. Superintendent Dr. Angela Atkinson Duina also opposed the proposal, saying she is confident in the judgment and oversight of the district's educators.

Board Vice Chair Tyler Smith and At-Large Board Member Eleni Richardson also spoke against the moratorium, and Richardson said many high school students she has spoken with are not excited about AI use. Student Representative Sarah Lupien said AI has not hurt her own learning, since many of her classes never discuss it, and she trusts her teachers to decide how to use it. Peter Wetzel, a middle school computer science teacher and South Portland resident, said it was his first time hearing of the moratorium and that it would directly affect a curriculum he worked hard to build. Cidney Mayes, who teaches digital literacy to fifth and sixth graders at South Portland Middle School, said AI literacy makes up a significant part of her curriculum and that the moratorium would cost her four weeks of instruction. She called the proposal an overstep and later thanked the board for rejecting it, saying something is wrong if she must justify her curriculum, while a Waldo T. Skillin Elementary School teacher said the board should have asked teachers who actually do this job.

Other speakers were split. One community member warned that using AI in certain ways weakens children's critical thinking, and the mother of a kindergartner at Frank I. Brown Elementary School supported the resolution but urged exceptions for classes that teach AI literacy. Brown School's librarian asked why she should not talk with children about AI when they already raise it with her. South Portland High School student Ian Archibald said some teachers weave AI into their courses, but that the repetition he has noticed has lowered his learning experience. WMTW had reported before the vote that the board would consider the ban over concerns about negative effects on children's cognitive development.

The moratorium was limited to students in grades PreK-8 and would have lasted only through the current school year. Mayes teaches students about what a language learning model is, about bias, about the upsides and downsides of AI, and about its environmental impacts. WGME's coverage tagged the story with topics including cybersecurity, student education, staff training and AI integration. Wetzel and Mayes both said they had not been consulted before the proposal came forward. The board's stated purpose for the pause was to buy time to write a policy, which the district still does not have.

Board members told WGME that the conversation is far from over, even though the ban failed to pass. Officials are now working on a comprehensive plan set to launch in January, which will address AI integration as well as broader cybersecurity issues in the district. DeAngelis tied her opposition to waiting for a more detailed plan addressing AI use. The articles do not say what the January plan will contain, whether it will limit student use, or how teachers will be consulted. They also do not say whether the proposed staff training will go ahead, or whether Holman or anyone else will bring back a new moratorium proposal.

stories.Headline: AI Is Accelerate Cyber Bullying, Which Impacts One In 10 Students Worldwide: UNESCO
stories.Summary:
A new policy brief from UNESCO, titled "Connected and Safe," warns that artificial intelligence is speeding up new forms of technology-facilitated violence against students. The agency says one in three learners worldwide experiences bullying every month, and one in ten faces cyber bullying. The brief describes nudification apps, voice cloning, automated harassment and AI companion apps used for grooming as already appearing in school-based incidents across several regions. UNESCO's director-general, Khaled El-Enany, cited these figures, saying the children affected have their education, health and well-being at risk.

UNESCO is calling on countries to invest in digital safety measures, teacher preparation and mental health support for students, working with technology companies. The brief says that between 2018 and 2022, cyber bullying prevalence rose from 12 to 15 per cent across 44 countries in Europe, Central Asia and North America, among both boys and girls. It notes that some learners face greater exposure, including girls, learners with disabilities, learners of diverse sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, and those marginalised by socio-economic status or geography. The brief also explains that boys are more exposed to physical bullying and violence, while girls are more exposed to psychological bullying, especially cyber and appearance-based bullying. Sexual bullying affects boys and girls at similar rates, although girls are more likely to experience physical sexual violence.

UNESCO argues that responsibility for safer digital environments must be shared by governments, technology companies, platforms and regulators, because schools cannot tackle the issue alone. The agency says safer schools need sustained investment in teacher preparation, mental health and psychosocial support, reporting and response systems, digital safety measures, and coordinated action across education, child protection, health and technology sectors. It also recently began work toward a new global recommendation on young people and digital environments in the age of AI. The stated aim of that work is to ensure these technologies protect children's rights and well-being, strengthen critical thinking and empower young people to shape their future.

stories.Headline: AI Debt Under Pressure: Credit Spreads Widen as Democrats Target AI Regulation - News and Statistics
stories.Summary:
Bond investors have become more cautious about debt tied to the artificial intelligence boom, reflecting worries that a Democrat-controlled Congress will try to slow AI investment and data center expansion. Reuters reported the shift, and the articles place it in the week after the midterm elections. US high-yield credit spreads widened to 348 basis points during last Thursday's stock-market swoon, according to ICE BofA US Corporate Index data. That was the widest level since May 2025, one month after President Donald Trump imposed global tariffs. By Friday, the spreads had narrowed to 342 basis points.

Investment-grade spreads stood at 93 basis points last Thursday, compared with 91 basis points in the previous session. Single-B spreads widened 35 basis points to 367 basis points, which led the deterioration in the high-yield market and marked their highest levels since March. Galaxy Helios Data Center bonds fell to 89.25 cents on the dollar on November 5, lifting yields to 13 per cent. Those bonds carry a B+ rating and were sold by a wholly owned unit of Galaxy Digital in late July at a yield of 9.875 per cent. Many data center bonds sit in the BB and single-B tiers of the junk bond market, and they have faced fresh pressure in recent weeks, especially during the technology selloff.

Democrats plan to introduce a flood of new legislation targeting AI systems and data center development when they take control of Congress in January. Republican President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed calls to write mandatory rules for AI technology. Over the weekend, following a historic midterm loss for his party, he signaled openness to safeguards. The articles do not say what form those safeguards might take or when the president might act.

Larry Holzenthaler, a senior portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds in New York, said markets are definitely anxious and that he would not be surprised by continued volatility in high yield and loans. Ali Hassan, a portfolio manager at Thornburg Investment Management, said appetite is more cautious and discriminating, with scrutiny prompting a review of credits from developers to contractors to suppliers. Peter Yanulis, a multi-asset portfolio manager at Loomis Sayles, warned that a slowdown would have second-order effects on the supply chain, power producers, electrical contractors, equipment and machinery makers, and data center developers. Abiel Reinhart, a senior economist at J.P. Morgan, said any slowdown in data center development could materially slow overall business investment.

Healthy corporate fundamentals continue to support the market, according to analysts and portfolio managers. A deeper reassessment of AI-related risk could still push spreads wider in both high-yield and investment-grade debt, as investors anticipate stricter regulation. Investment in artificial intelligence and its supporting infrastructure has been a major engine of US expansion this year, helping keep growth resilient despite broad uncertainties. Some investors believe a slowdown could be healthy for the credit market and for AI companies, because stricter regulation would mean less bond issuance, which should support prices. Yanulis said the market can now digest a transition period over the next six to 12 months, after the open floodgates of AI supply.

Karen Choi, a portfolio manager at Capital Group, said political and regulatory uncertainty could affect the later years, 2028 to 2030 and beyond. She added that it is unlikely to change capex and issuance numbers for 2027 significantly, because many projects are underway and capital commitments have been made. Investors see little risk of an immediate pullback in borrowing or spending on projects already under construction. Ben Emons, chief investment officer at FedWatch Advisors, argued that AI is not going to slow down, and that a slowdown in Texas would simply pop up in another state. The articles leave open how far spreads will move, what legislation Democrats will actually propose, and how the president's openness to safeguards will play out.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang's Nvidia exit casts shadow over Wall Street’s $500 billion AI financing bet
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's president, chief executive and board member, the company's board said on Thursday. Nvidia has never named a successor to Huang, who had led the chipmaker since it was founded in 1993. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, has been named interim chief executive. Shares in the company initially fell more than 13% after the resignation, before paring those losses. The resignation followed revelations that Huang had two extramarital affairs, one with an employee and another with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a Chinese spy.

In August, Nvidia signed memorandums of understanding with six major financial firms aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure. The firms are Apollo Global Management, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR. The arrangements seek to tap institutional investors and private capital to finance computing infrastructure, including data centers and chip factories. The funding would run through specialized financing vehicles, with Nvidia's AI chips serving as underlying collateral, in structures comparable to real estate or toll road securitizations. The financing arrangements remain preliminary and are subject to final agreements.

Huang's departure raises the question of whether his successor can carry forward a strategy meant to turn GPUs from rapidly depreciating hardware into bankable infrastructure assets. Nvidia's $4.2 trillion market value and industry dominance, with Huang at the front, allowed it to secure those memorandums. The company has been described as the "central bank" of the AI build-out, with Huang seen as the sector's "hypeman" and its chips considered the industry's gold standard. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress following his resignation, according to CNBC's live coverage. Nvidia's board chair is Harvey Jones, who wrote to employees along with Kress.

Sunaina Sinha Haldea, global head of private capital advisory at Raymond James, said a leadership change gives every firm involved a natural moment to pause and review the terms. She said a new chief executive would be wise to leave these partnerships alone in the first months and focus on signing the final agreements. Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said a successor would need to reassure lenders that Nvidia's technology roadmap, customer relationships and strategic vision remain intact. Chanana warned that a leadership shake-up could make Wall Street more cautious, potentially slowing commitments or tightening financing terms. BlackRock and Goldman Sachs declined to comment on the resignation, and the other firms were not immediately available.

Chanana said the bigger risk is a ripple effect across AI financing, given that rising debt, circular financing and uncertain investment returns were already under scrutiny. Haldea said she expects more discipline among investors after the scandal, with lenders asking harder questions about who really carries the risk in these structures. A separate CNBC analysis said Huang's exit raises critical questions about the future of AI. Those affected include lenders and the financial firms party to the memorandums, along with the AI infrastructure deal market more broadly. Analysts said the financing could come under heightened scrutiny in the aftermath of Huang's departure.

Early in November, a Motley Fool podcast recorded on October 30, 2026 discussed a market shift in which investors were questioning how big technology companies would finance AI spending. Alphabet's stock fell about 13% after earnings, even though its Cloud business reported 100% growth. Microsoft's Cloud growth was 48%, and its free cash flow was roughly double analyst estimates. Alphabet took on another $29 billion in debt and issued about $12 billion in new stock in the quarter, with another $28 billion already approved for issuance. Oracle said at its investor day that it would turn free cash flow positive sooner than expected, which investors welcomed.

Analysts disagree on how long the financing strain will last, and the articles give no clear answer. The articles do not say whether Nvidia will name a permanent chief executive, or when the preliminary financing agreements will be finalized. It remains unclear whether the six financial firms will proceed, slow commitments or seek higher pay for the added uncertainty. Huang's testimony before Congress is also not yet scheduled in the articles. Whether the scrutiny spreads into a broader repricing of AI risk, as Chanana suggested, is not settled.

stories.Headline: Your Next Bank Customer Might Not Be Human: Feedzai Helps Banks Spot AI Agents at the Front Door
stories.Summary:
Feedzai, a financial crime prevention company, expanded its Digital Trust solution on November 12, 2026, to help banks detect AI agents accessing customer accounts. The announcement was made from New York and Lisbon, Portugal, through a PR Newswire release. The expansion adds stronger device persistence, a fraud score built on Feedzai's network view and shared intelligence, and cryptographic device binding. These additions are described as creating a triangle of trust between the customer, their device and the bank. Feedzai says the same pillars also help banks remove unnecessary step-ups, cut authentication costs and strengthen protection against MFA bypass.

The release says the solution combines endpoint, device, behavioral and network signals to assess risk before login and throughout the customer journey. It identifies agents by combining the signals they declare about themselves with device fingerprinting and behavioral signals that reveal automated activity. Once an agent is recognized, banks can trust returning user-agent relationships and avoid challenging them again where their policies allow. Cryptographic device binding lets a trusted device act as a possession factor, reducing reliance on SMS one-time passcodes. The release reports 44% more fraud detected in the highest-risk 0.1% of sessions, 6,000 fewer unnecessary authentication challenges per million logins, and 41% fewer SMS one-time passcodes.

Feedzai's Pedro Barata, Chief Product Officer, said that personal and malicious agents can look very similar and that the advancements help banks tell them apart. Barata said the tools block unwanted agents and trust the ones customers choose to use. Vatsal Sharma, Director Analyst on the Banking team at Gartner, said 95% of banks use MFA, with SMS one-time passwords the most commonly cited method by Gartner clients. Sharma said social engineering, SIM swapping and phishing can bypass such MFA, creating a false sense of security. The release states that a successful login does not mean a session can be trusted, because AI agents can sign in with valid credentials.

Banks, their customers and the businesses using AI agents to access accounts are the groups most directly affected by these measures. Feedzai's release describes its own customers as the world's top banks, payment networks and acquirers, which it says safeguard more than one billion consumers and $19 trillion in payment volume. A separate PYMNTS report from November 9, 2026, said banks are weighing how much access AI agents should have to customers' online banking accounts. It also reported that in a Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas survey of 70 bankers, 11.4% said restrictions had been taken and 22.9% planned restrictions within six months.

PYMNTS also reported in October that major U.S. banks were detecting and deleting unauthorized third-party AI agents acting within customer accounts. According to a separate PYMNTS report from October, JPMorganChase, Citigroup, Bank of America and Charles Schwab all said AI agents would not be allowed to move customer money. The Dallas Fed survey was conducted between October 27 and November 4 among bankers in its Eleventh Federal Reserve District, and 27.1% of respondents did not know whether their institution had restricted AI-agent activity. The PYMNTS article says the results are a regional snapshot rather than a measure of the whole U.S. banking industry.

Feedzai says it will continue to expand its agentic detection capabilities in the coming months. The articles do not say how banks will set their policies on which agent activity is allowed or how customer consent will be handled beyond the banks' own control. They also do not say how many banks have adopted the Feedzai tools or how the 38.6% of surveyed bankers with no planned restrictions will respond. The articles leave open whether the restrictions in the Dallas Fed survey will spread to more institutions.

stories.Headline: Hackers stole AI credentials to get $740,000 in free compute; Railway picked up the bill
stories.Summary:
Hackers exploited Railway, a cloud hosting provider, in an attack that began on October 20 and lasted nearly 26 hours. They first exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway's build infrastructure, evading filesystem isolation protections to obtain an internal credential. Using that credential, they accessed stored build histories and retrieved a copy of Railway's internal source code. They then used a misconfigured trust relationship to reach more of the infrastructure and obtain credentials that decrypt customer environment variables. Railway disclosed the incident on October 22 and posted a follow-up report the week of November 11.

The attackers were fully evicted on October 21, after they had decrypted a subset of roughly 100,000 customer variables, or at most 1.85 percent of workspaces. They generated about $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges, with customers reporting that their keys answered coding questions and performed training-data tasks they never ran. The breach also exposed linked-account tokens belonging to more than 1,850 users, including GitHub and OAuth tokens that Railway reset. Railway worked with GitHub, GitLab, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, SpaceXSI, Stripe and others to revoke potentially compromised keys. Customers were advised to revoke and reapply sensitive environment variables stored on Railway before October 21.

Railway is working to reimburse customers, including for charges that providers decline to refund. The company said it shut down potentially compromised internal tooling and rolled all keys after validating that intruders had been shut out. It moved to a new generation of infrastructure, rebuilt the tooling used to run its infrastructure, and added functionality to mass revoke app permissions after suspicious activity. Railway also said it is moving to short-lived credentials and logging every decryption. The company described the incident as a contest of agent speed, in which both attackers and defenders worked in parallel.

David Shipley of Beauceron Security said AI credentials are becoming the new credit card numbers, and that so-called LLMjacking is expected to displace cryptojacking. Frank Dickson of Dickson Research called Railway's report remarkably candid, noting that it owns its configuration mistake and admits it cannot be sure it found every account the attacker created. Dickson said stolen keys let thieves get cost-free compute while the key owners pay the bill. Customers of Railway, he advised, should treat every stored secret as stolen until rotated. The affected parties are Railway's customers, the 1,850-plus users with linked accounts, and the AI providers whose keys were misused.

AI credentials are cheap to harvest at scale, and attackers can resell access through so-called AI routers that provide models users otherwise could not afford. Such access is valuable for distillation, which transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller one to cut costs. Dickson said training on another model's answers takes millions of questions, and stolen keys spread those questions across thousands of real customers. An investigation by Wiz found that stolen keys were tested within 30 minutes of theft, then flooded with traffic four to seven days later. Wiz also found that a key restricted to a narrow set of model profiles left most of the thief's traffic throttled.

Railway said it cannot yet share the specific details and scale of the exploits because the investigation is ongoing. Dickson advised customers to check AI provider bills and usage logs, rotate cloud, database and payment credentials, and set hard spending caps on every AI key. Customers were also advised to remove public network access to databases, check GitHub audit logs and Dockerhub registry logs, and review all app access. The articles do not say whether Railway has found every account the attacker created, nor whether all reimbursements will be paid. They also leave open whether providers will refund the disputed charges they have declined to reverse.

stories.Headline: TSMC October revenue hits record $17.81 billion
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, known as TSMC, reported its highest-ever monthly revenue for October, reaching about $17.81 billion. The figure was up 59.7 per cent from a year earlier and rose 14.7 per cent from September. The world's largest contract chipmaker posted consolidated revenue of NT 586.89 billion for the month. October's total beat the company's previous monthly record of $15.63 billion, set in August.

Revenue for January through October totaled $140 billion, a 43.3 per cent increase over the same stretch last year. The company credited the growth to strong demand for advanced semiconductors, particularly chips used in artificial intelligence infrastructure. Its 2-nanometre technology has entered commercial production and is contributing to sales. High-performance computing rose 22 per cent from the previous quarter and now makes up 68 per cent of total revenue, while the 2nm process accounted for 8 per cent of wafer revenue in the third quarter.

TSMC also raised its full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast to about 44 per cent in US dollar terms, up from an earlier projection of slightly above 40 per cent. The company attributed the revision to robust demand for its advanced manufacturing processes during its October earnings conference. For the fourth quarter, it expects consolidated revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion. The company's shares closed 2.24 per cent higher on the Taiwan Stock Exchange on November 10.

The results come as the chipmaker's customers face their own scrutiny. TSMC manufactures chips for several technology companies, including NVIDIA, whose shares fell 4.3 per cent on November 9, wiping out about $190 billion in market value according to Reuters. That drop followed reports of an investigation involving NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with an accused Chinese spy, as well as a proposed shareholder lawsuit. The articles do not say how these developments will affect TSMC's future orders.

stories.Headline: Arkansas governor embraces Trump, calls for AI guardrails in new book
stories.Summary:
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders released a new book on Tuesday in which she praises President Donald Trump's leadership. The book came out a week after Republicans suffered heavy losses in a midterm that was widely seen as a rebuke of Trump by voters. Sanders, who won reelection last week and is considered a potential 2028 presidential hopeful, also distanced herself from the president by calling for "commonsense" guardrails on artificial intelligence. The book is titled "Unapologetic: Clarity and Conviction in a World Gone Crazy," and it covers her election and first term as Arkansas governor. In it she also writes about her family and her Christian faith, regularly quoting the Bible and authors such as C.S. Lewis.

The book arrives as Republicans grapple with an election in which they lost control of the U.S. House, the Senate and a majority of governorships. Sanders was first elected in 2022 and won a second term by double digits this year. Even so, Republicans lost the supermajority in the state House that is needed to pass most budget bills without Democratic support. On artificial intelligence, Sanders highlights her opposition to a provision in the One Big Beautiful Bill tax and spending cut law, signed last year, that would have prevented states from regulating the technology. The book also covers her stalled plan for a 3,000-bed prison in Franklin County, her 2022 thyroid cancer diagnosis, and her 2023 State of the Union rebuttal.

Sanders says in the book that she decided to run for governor with Trump's leadership style in mind, hoping to bring bold, new leadership to Arkansas. She writes that she loves Arkansas but was not blind to the problems the state faced. On artificial intelligence, she writes that Trump is right that the United States must win the AI race against China to survive. She adds that the race cannot become a race to the bottom that enriches billionaires in Silicon Valley and leaves the rest of America behind. She also wrote that conservatives should be skeptical of Big Tech when it comes to AI.

Trump has dismissed the calls for more guardrails around artificial intelligence, which is where Sanders parts ways with him. The provision that would have blocked state regulation of AI was stripped from the legislation after Sanders and other Republicans objected. On the prison plan, Sanders faced resistance from locals, from members of the Board of Corrections, and from lawmakers of both parties. She expresses frustration at opposition from her own party and labels those opponents, along with Democrats, the "coalition of the unwilling." She writes that she expected to fight the left over making communities safer, but had no idea some of the fiercest opposition would come from within her own party.

Sanders served as White House press secretary during Trump's first term and touted his endorsement when she first ran for governor. She has signed into law measures limiting youths' access to social media. She was diagnosed with thyroid cancer in 2022, just a couple of months before she was elected governor, and returned to the campaign trail after surgery and being declared cancer-free. Doctors had warned her that some patients suffer damage to their vocal chords or changes to their voice, which she says could have derailed her career, though the damage did not occur. Shortly after taking office in 2023, she hesitated before accepting an invitation to deliver the Republican response to President Joe Biden's State of the Union address.

Sanders put the Franklin County prison project on hold after the resistance she met. The articles do not say whether the project will resume or what will become of it. Her speech painted a bleak picture of life under Biden, but she says it only reached that form after she and First Gentleman Bryan Sanders revised a first draft that was too dark and heavy on policy. She says she and the unnamed speechwriter agreed to part ways after she rewrote the speech. The articles do not say what Sanders will do next, and they offer no announcement about a 2028 run beyond describing her as a potential hopeful.

stories.Headline: Banks seek to rein in soaring AI agent costs, McKinsey says - CNA
stories.Summary:
Banks around the world are trying to curb the rising cost of AI agents, according to McKinsey's Global Banking Annual Review published on November 10, 2026. The consultancy warns that spending on the tokens that power these agents could reach as much as 20 percent of total labor costs. Banks have begun shifting responsibility for AI spending to new teams, which some institutions call AI FinOps. Early efforts to control expenses relied on routing employees to different AI models depending on how complex their queries were.

Those earlier methods do not work well once AI agents are active, because the agents communicate with one another and their token usage adds up quickly. As a result, banks are becoming more selective about where they deploy agentic AI, concentrating on areas with the strongest expected returns. Productivity savings are comparatively easy to measure, so banks are increasingly weighing AI-driven revenue growth when deciding whether higher spending is justified. Most banks currently block external AI agents from authorizing transactions within their systems, which has kept the effect on profits limited so far.

Vik Sohoni, a senior partner at McKinsey and one of the report's authors, explained the problem in an interview with Reuters. He said the model-routing systems banks first used are ineffective for agent-driven workloads. The report also finds that customers are adopting AI faster than they adopted earlier technologies. McKinsey expects AI agents to become widely used within three years, compared with the five to ten years it took mobile internet to reach broad adoption.

A McKinsey survey of 46,000 retail banking customers worldwide found that most already use AI to compare banking services, find higher-yield savings accounts, and refinance or consolidate debt. Of those who use AI, 72 percent said they would let a banking agent carry out one financial task, although they would cap autonomous approvals at $500. Meta's Muse agent was downloaded 5 million times in the United States during its first 22 days after launch. The report notes that AI agents could help banks grow revenue and cut costs, but they could also squeeze profits by moving deposits from non-interest-bearing accounts into higher-yielding ones.

stories.Headline: Practical workshops on Artificial Intelligence Applied to Legal Research begin today - Universitat de València
stories.Summary:
The Regulation Research Group at the University of Valencia began a series of practical workshops on artificial intelligence applied to legal research today, 9 November 2026. The workshops are taught by Andrés Marzal Varó of the Universitat Jaume I. The programme runs on 9, 16 and 23 November 2026, with a final session on 14 December 2026, each from 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. In-person sessions are held in Room 3P12 of Administrative Law at the Faculty of Law of the University of Valencia, with online attendance also available. The course consists of four highly practical sessions in which participants work directly on their laptops to apply AI tools rigorously to legal research tasks.

The theoretical component builds a conceptual framework covering how generative AI systems learn, why they are not deterministic, what hallucinations are and how to mitigate them. It also covers what an AI agent is and how AI systems interact with the internet, databases and personal documents. Participants practise searching, summarising, organising, analysing, comparing, verifying and arguing as part of everyday academic research. Each session ends with a tangible output, including a configured AI assistant for research, a workflow for case-law summaries, an AI-assisted thematic research wiki and monitoring tools. To take part fully, attendees must hold an active Claude Pro subscription during November, which currently costs about €20 for one month and is separate from the free course.

The articles identify the Regulation Research Group, which organises the workshops, and Andrés Marzal Varó, who teaches them, as responsible for the programme. The group presents the course as a response to artificial intelligence becoming part of the work of anyone conducting legal research. The articles state that its importance is likely to increase in the short and medium term. Marzal Varó is described as teaching from the Universitat Jaume I. The articles do not give any further statement from either of them about the course.

The articles present the workshops as aimed at those who conduct legal research, including academics whose everyday work involves searching, summarising and verifying material. Participants are affected by the subscription requirement, since they must pay for a Claude Pro subscription that is not part of the course. The articles note that participants may cancel the subscription once the training period has ended. No other groups, reactions or objections are reported in the articles.

The workshops are listed on the University of Valencia website under the Regulation Research Group's training and teaching activities. The announcement was published on the university site on 9 November 2026, and an earlier version of the same item appeared that day. The articles also list other recent items from the group, including an international workshop on the proposed forestry law of the Valencian Community and specific postgraduate degrees for 2026/2027. The articles give no earlier history of the course itself.

The articles state the schedule of the remaining sessions but do not describe their content in detail beyond the general outline. They do not say how many participants may enrol or whether registration is still open. They also do not state how the online attendance link will be managed, nor whether the course will be repeated. The articles leave unstated whether the Claude Pro subscription cost may change during November.
