Background from the article includes the planned Nasdaq listing of SB Energy, backed by roughly 8.8 GW of contracted AI data center capacity and an estimated US$430b lease revenue backlog. It also mentions a planned multi-gigawatt AI data center build-out in France, including an initial €45b investment to deliver 3.1 GW of capacity by 2031.

The article says higher funding costs or further delays in key exits such as OpenAI and SB Energy could weaken the case. The article does not say when the Malaysia projects will begin or when the SB Energy Nasdaq listing will take place. It does not say whether the Malaysia deal will change the company's reported results. The article gives no further announcements or decisions on these matters.

Articles.Title: SoftBank Group (TSE:9984) Lands Malaysia AI Deal, But Is The Valuation Opportunity Real

stories.Headline: AI has made it ‘close to impossible’ to assess university coursework, regulator says
stories.Summary:
The Office for Students, England's higher education regulator, has concluded that artificial intelligence has made it close to impossible to assess university coursework fairly. Its investigation, published on 11 November 2026, found that lecturers are struggling to grade essays, dissertations and open book exams because AI use is widespread and often goes undetected. The regulator is urging universities to return to traditional exams and in-person presentations as a way to grade students. It warned that the credibility of degrees in England is under threat.

The regulator said institutions that fail to design valid and reliable ways of measuring students' knowledge and skills to counter AI could breach their conditions of registration. Such failures could lead to sanctions being imposed on the institutions. Josh Fleming, the OfS director of strategy and delivery, described AI in higher education as a generational risk that threatens both learning and the ability to assess students. He said the sector needs far greater use of AI-free assessment. The regulator said it will keep working with universities and colleges to capture AI's benefits while managing its risks.

The findings come from a report by the OfS and Advance HE, a charity that promotes university governance and teaching, which interviewed more than 300 students and staff at 127 universities and colleges this year. Many institutions have already changed how they assess students, using more in-person written exams, oral examinations known as vivas, and process-based assessments in which students explain how they researched and produced their work. The report also cited students who said peers completed assessments with AI in a few minutes and still received grades similar to those who did not use it. Academics described receiving large numbers of near-identical submissions that cited the same literature and shared a style. A Department for Education spokesperson said universities should take the issue seriously and that the OfS should enforce existing standards and make its framework on AI explicit, strong and durable.

Articles.Title: AI has made it ‘close to impossible’ to assess university coursework, regulator says

stories.Headline: West Virginia lawmaker seeks to strengthen state police investigations into AI-generated crimes involving children
stories.Summary:
Sen. Vince Deeds, a Republican from Greenbrier County, said he will introduce legislation in January to expand the West Virginia State Police's ability to investigate tips about the production, possession and financial extortion of child sexual abuse material. The announcement came during an interim meeting of the Joint Judiciary Committee in Charleston on a Tuesday, as reported on November 11, 2026. Deeds described the state police as the front line in these cases and said the agency needs additional resources to keep up. He framed the bill as a way to supplement law enforcement work through legislation. Sgt.

Rachel Blankenship, director of the State Police Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force, told lawmakers that tips have grown faster than the agency's capacity to respond. So far this year the task force has received just under 2,300 tips from internet service providers and child welfare agencies, handled by 15 troopers and 50 affiliates in counties and cities. She also reported more than 1,700 screened-out child protective services referrals this year, up from 1,382 last year, meaning more tips are being routed to agencies that coordinate with her task force. Blankenship said the main focus of her testimony was the need to address AI-generated child sexual abuse material through law. She noted that West Virginia defined "computer-generated pornography" in its sexually explicit conduct statute in 2025.

Blankenship described a pattern in which offenders take existing photos of people, feed them into AI platforms and generate abusive images. According to her, Meta and Google have been reliable in reporting, but newer messaging providers that emphasize anonymity have become a hotbed for self-produced material by teenagers, along with financial sextortion and sadistic online exploitation. Deeds said lawmakers have had to update the criminal code repeatedly over the past decade as the crimes changed, and he said artificial intelligence is now being used to alter images and extort children who may feel unable to report. Separately, Attorney General JB McCuskey announced that his office is seeking legal action against Snapchat under the West Virginia Consumer Credit and Protection Act, citing the rise of online exploitation.

Articles.Title: West Virginia lawmaker seeks to strengthen state police investigations into AI-generated crimes involving children - WBOY.com

stories.Headline: Litera Brings Document Comparison and Firm AI Search to Microsoft Copilot for Legal - LawSites
stories.Summary:
Litera announced on November 10, 2026, in Chicago, that its Litera Compare and Firm AI Search tools are now available inside Microsoft Copilot for legal through plugins. The announcement describes Litera as a Legal AI platform provider that unifies the practice and business of law. Litera also said it has adopted Microsoft 365 E7, the Frontier Suite, which the company says gives it access to the most advanced tier of Microsoft's enterprise AI stack. The company frames the integration as a follow-on to its recent announcement as a Microsoft Copilot for legal launch partner. The articles describe the launch as bringing 30 years of deterministic document comparison accuracy into the environment where lawyers work.

Through the plugins, lawyers can ask Copilot in plain language to compare documents, and Copilot calls Litera's comparison engine to generate a legal-grade redline. Litera Compare works across Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF files, and the company says its proprietary algorithm is more accurate than general-purpose LLMs. Firm AI Search connects matter databases, CRM platforms, expertise profiles and experience records into one conversational interface. Its answers are cited and respect ethical walls and access permissions. A sample query asks which firm lawyers have handled cross-border M&A work for pharmaceutical companies in Germany, and the search draws on Litera Foundation, matter systems and expertise databases.

Joey Benedek, Senior Vice President of Product Management at Litera, said law firms and corporate legal departments are increasingly making Copilot their productivity standard. Benedek said the integration brings legal intelligence into that environment and that Compare delivers the deterministic accuracy high-stakes legal work demands. Carina Negreanu, Partner Director, Science & Verticals at Microsoft, said Copilot is designed to be the AI layer where legal professionals work. Negreanu said Litera's integration is a strong example of how partners with deep industry expertise can extend Copilot's value for legal professionals. The articles identify Litera's own leaders and Microsoft's representative as the sources of these statements.

Law firms and corporate legal departments are the groups the articles name as the users who depend on these capabilities. Benedek said the E7 adoption is meant to speed how quickly new capabilities reach firms and in-house teams. The articles say Litera serves more than 15,000 global customers and over 1 million daily users, including 99% of the Am Law 100. Litera is integrated directly into Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace across devices, according to the company. The articles present these figures as Litera's own description of its reach and do not report any independent assessment of the tools' performance.

Litera's own description places the company's roots in 30 years of legal expertise, and the articles say it combines legal technology with Lito, its award-winning Legal AI agent. The articles report that Litera offers AI solutions spanning legal drafting, document comparison, contract review, knowledge management and business development. The articles were published by LawSites on November 11, 2026, with author Robert Ambrogi. Press contacts listed in the release are Jared Albert of Litera and Tracy Wemett of BroadPR. The articles do not describe any pricing, availability dates beyond the announcement, or customer deployments.

Articles.Title: Litera Brings Document Comparison and Firm AI Search to Microsoft Copilot for Legal - LawSites

stories.Headline: Most large firms plan higher open-weight AI use to cap bills, study shows
stories.Summary:
Nearly six in ten senior executives at large companies plan to increase their use of cheaper open-weight AI models over the next year, according to a study by Capgemini released on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The survey found that the shift is driven by AI bills overshooting budgets. Fifty-nine percent of the surveyed executives said their AI spending over the past year had been significantly above their expectations or budgets, by 24 percent on average. Fifty-three percent said they were worried about AI costs, up from 45 percent last year. Capgemini said open-weight models handled 72 percent of traffic on OpenRouter, a multi-AI provider, in September, yet accounted for just 27 percent of AI spending.

The consulting firm reported that open-weight tokens were on average 87 percent cheaper than closed ones. Open-weight models, such as those from DeepSeek or Mistral, can be downloaded and run anywhere, while closed options like Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini are only accessible from the cloud. Closed models still have a place, since half the respondents said they would keep them where the complexity of a task justified the extra cost. The study was conducted by Capgemini, an IT consulting firm that helps companies embed AI into their existing platforms. It surveyed 500 executives at enterprises with annual revenue above $1 billion across 10 countries.

The article presents the findings as the company's own research rather than attributing a policy or requirement to any single party. The trend echoes moves by other large players. SAP's finance chief said last month that the company was replacing some of its costliest AI models with cheaper ones where performance held up. Anthropic, which launched its IPO roadshow this week, also warned in its prospectus that customers may shift to cheaper options, including open-weight models.

Articles.Title: Most large firms plan higher open-weight AI use to cap bills, study shows

stories.Headline: Validating GPU Platforms with Runtime AI Inventory via the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's developer blog published a post on November 11, 2026, describing how its AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) now includes a qualified AI bill of materials component built on the open source k8s-aibom project. The integration tracks AI workloads running on Kubernetes, and it was announced as part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform. AICR is an open source modular component of that platform, and k8s-aibom is an open source project created by Google. Two stock recipes, h100-gke-cos-inference and h100-gke-cos-inference-dynamo, select k8s-aibom by default. Other GKE recipes can opt in during generation using the --runtime-inventory flag, and recipes that select it can opt out with --runtime-inventory disabled.

AICR generates version-locked recipes and reproducible deployment bundles, with checksums and optional signing through aicr bundle --attest. The integration was validated with AICR v1.2.0, which pins k8s-aibom 1.6.2, and the k8s-aibom controller emits CycloneDX 1.6 AIBOM records for supported workloads. During steady-state observation, the tested setup showed about four API-server requests per minute, 2.2 millicores average CPU, and a 28 to 34 MiB controller memory working set. The article names NVIDIA as the author of the AICR component and Google as the creator of k8s-aibom, and it describes the two projects as addressing opposite sides of the same problem. AICR works at the runtime deployment layer, covering drivers, operators, kernels, and Kubernetes components, while k8s-aibom watches workload and pod APIs higher in the stack.

The authors state that neither view is sufficient for AI governance on its own. The article describes the work as aimed at platform teams and application teams that deploy AI workloads with tools such as NVIDIA Dynamo, Kubeflow, or Slurm. The stated audience includes teams that need to find unregistered or shadow AI workloads, identify models and inference runtimes, track external AI APIs and vector databases, detect drift in AI dependencies, and support security reviews and compliance audits. Mutable image tags such as :latest are described as a risk, because two nodes can run different code under identical tags. The article also notes that k8s-aibom inventory is opt-in per namespace, and that no sink and no secret access are configured by default.

Organizations running GKE clusters with H100 GPU nodes are the affected group the article describes. Background given in the article is limited to the motivation: application teams update AI workloads independently of platform recipes, so a reproducible deployment bundle alone cannot establish which workload artifacts run on each node. The article explains that AICR records qualified deployment intent and evaluates it against a cluster at a point in time, while k8s-aibom records what it observed and how confidently it determined each attribute. It also states that the pairing is meant to close a gap between the platform configuration and the workloads actually running.

The article leaves open how the integration will perform beyond the tested configuration, and it does not say when AICR or k8s-aibom will ship further updates. It notes that Helmfile, Terraform, and Fleet require a documented manual CRD update in some transitions, and that AIBOM records can appear before pods are running. The article ends with links to the AICR and k8s-aibom repositories as next steps. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Validating GPU Platforms with Runtime AI Inventory via the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory | NVIDIA Technical Blog

stories.Headline: Law in the age of AI: Law Faculty’s International Research Conference
stories.Summary:
The Law Faculty of the University of Colombo will hold its annual International Research Conference on 13 and 14 November 2026, under the theme "Law in the Age of Artificial Intelligence (AI): Advancing Equality, Sustainability and Innovation." The conference is designed to bring together legal experts, academics, researchers and practitioners from Sri Lanka and abroad. Its purpose is to examine the legal challenges and opportunities that arise as AI becomes more widespread. Organisers say the event will focus on how the law can respond to these developments in a fair and forward-looking way.

The programme includes thematic sessions on commercial law, private and comparative law, and public and international law, each viewed through the lens of AI. Participants are expected to take part in scholarly discussion, interdisciplinary research and new legal approaches to the problems AI poses. The aim is to encourage dialogue across disciplines rather than within a single field of law. The event is intended to produce ideas that address how AI affects equality, sustainability and innovation.

Justice Rohantha Abeysooriya, President's Counsel and President of the Court of Appeal, will attend as Chief Guest. The University's Vice Chancellor, Prof Indika Karunathilake, will be Guest of Honour. Prof M. Sakthivel, Dean of Research at the Tamil Nadu National Law University in India, will deliver the keynote address. The conference is being steered by Conference Chair Dr Udapadie Liyanage, working under the guidance of the Faculty's Dean, Prof Sampath Punchihewa.

The conference is an annual event, and this year's edition is set to concentrate on AI, a subject that the articles describe as producing emerging legal challenges. The articles do not report any specific outcomes, recommendations or follow-up measures from the gathering. They also do not say what material will be published afterward. Further details about the sessions and proceedings are not available in the reporting.

Articles.Title: Law in the age of AI: Law Faculty’s International Research Conference

stories.Headline: Pactum: Procurement’s Execution Layer for the Agentic AI Age
stories.Summary:
Pactum, a procurement technology company, has been developing AI agents that carry out procurement tasks themselves rather than only supporting human staff, according to an interview published on November 12, 2026 by Procurement Magazine. The interview features Paige Wei-Cox, the company's Chief Product Officer, who has more than 25 years of enterprise technology experience, including two decades at SAP where she led SAP Business Network. The company started by letting enterprises negotiate with thousands of suppliers at scale, and it has since widened its aim toward a connected AI layer for indirect procurement. That layer rests on four capabilities: Intake, Alignment, Negotiation and Sourcing.

The newly launched Intake Agent applies procurement policies and category strategies to purchasing requests, decides how goods or services should be bought, and prepares aligned, compliant requisitions. The Alignment capability checks requests against relevant policies and contracts, and Pactum's work with AstraZeneca is cited as an example. There, the Alignment Agent has reportedly cut requisition and contract reviews from days to less than a minute, with 100% requisition coverage. Negotiation lets AI agents engage suppliers at a scale that would be hard for human teams to match, aiming for the best overall commercial outcome rather than only the lowest price. Sourcing extends these activities so that commercial intelligence can be turned into action.

Wei-Cox argues that the main challenge is not proving that AI can perform a task but establishing the trust, governance and operational reliability needed to delegate meaningful work at scale. Enterprises must decide which tasks agents can perform independently, where human approval is required and when decisions should be escalated. She contends that human control need not mean reviewing every action, since policies, commercial objectives and escalation thresholds can set the boundaries within which agents operate. Pactum is designed to work alongside established platforms, with integrations involving Coupa, SAP Ariba and Microsoft Teams. The company also lets suppliers negotiate over email, avoiding the need to register on another portal.

The article presents this as part of a broader move in enterprise software from supporting human decisions toward carrying out defined work autonomously. Wei-Cox says the company hopes to help enterprises manage more spend, improve compliance and secure stronger commercial outcomes without scaling operational effort at the same rate. As the connected AI workforce develops, she believes the focus will increasingly shift from what AI can recommend to the work organisations can confidently hand over to it. The article is a premium interview and does not report any regulatory requirement, deadline or formal change beyond the product launch described.

Articles.Title: Pactum: Procurement’s Execution Layer for the Agentic AI Age

stories.Headline: Energy crisis and AI rise reshape economic decisions, CBC Governor says
stories.Summary:
The Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus and member of the ECB Governing Council, Christodoulos Patsalides, said on Wednesday, 11 November 2026, that the energy crisis and the rise of artificial intelligence are reshaping economic decisions. He made the remarks in his opening speech at an MNI Connect Video Conference with economists, investors and financial market participants. He called for readiness to adjust assessments as the evidence evolves. Patsalides focused on the persistence of the energy shock and the growth of AI, which he said shape today's economic landscape. He said the blockade at the Strait of Hormuz had altered the course of history through the energy inflation channel.

Patsalides said supply shocks differ in magnitude, duration, systemic interactions and the political landscape in which they unfold. He said the ECB Governing Council must understand how the energy shock spreads through the economy and act to meet its 2% inflation target in the medium term. He said policy credibility depends on disciplined use of a robust, data-based analytical framework. He stressed a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach as essential under heightened uncertainty. At the October meeting, the Council kept key interest rates unchanged because inflation expectations remained well anchored and monetary transmission remained effective.

Patsalides said the ECB estimates that around 90% of the rise in energy inflation reflects adverse energy-supply developments linked to the Middle East conflict, rather than excessive domestic demand. He warned that this should not lead to complacency, and that monetary policy must keep inflation stabilising at the medium-term target. He said a key question is how far higher energy prices are becoming embedded in broader inflation dynamics. He noted slight upward pressure in food-price and services inflation, while core inflation remained unchanged. He said crude prices had recently retreated substantially, though their forward path requires ongoing observation.

Patsalides said that, although long-term inflation expectations are firmly anchored, short-term inflation expectations remain persistently higher and require heightened vigilance. He described AI as disrupting lives and being here to stay, and said both energy and AI are global and disruptive, with implications for growth, inflation, financing conditions and financial stability. He said AI has become a significant contributor to euro area growth through spending on AI adoption and European firms' participation in the global AI supply chain. He cited research suggesting AI-related investment could reach as much as $9 trillion between 2025 and 2032. He said technology and hardware firms issued around $350 billion in bonds this year, roughly double the amount issued a year earlier.

Patsalides said that, with capital expenditure rising faster than cash generation, financing is increasingly pursued through bond markets, private credit and interlinked circular funding arrangements, which make underlying risks harder to assess. He said total outstanding hyperscaler bonds stand at around $570 billion, of which €39 billion has been issued in euros. He said European investors participate in euro-denominated issues, mainly by allocating less to US Treasury bonds. He said increased supply, credit risk and uncertainty are widening credit spreads in both the debt and CDS markets, although investor absorption has been smooth so far. He added that there is little evidence AI financing has materially crowded out funding for other sectors.

Patsalides concluded that the energy crisis erodes purchasing power and constrains production, while AI promises higher productivity and growth. He said both call for rigorous examination of evidence and careful assessment of uncertainty. For energy, he said, this means further study of the granular networks of price dynamics. For AI, he said, it means greater visibility into opaque funding structures and closer scrutiny of the assumptions behind projections. He said sound policy must look beneath aggregate developments and identify how disruption spreads through the economy.

Articles.Title: Energy crisis and AI rise reshape economic decisions, CBC Governor says

stories.Headline: The AI Debt Bill Is Coming Due, But Biotech Has Revenue to Show for the Boom
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4% on November 5, 2026, its worst session since 2020, after the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped more than 12%. The sell-off followed Democratic midterm wins in key data-center states, which raised the odds of tougher AI regulation. The article describes the pressure as falling on the AI buildout itself, including its debt, permits, power and politics. Companies that buy compute rather than build data centers carry none of that financing risk. Tempus AI and Recursion Pharmaceuticals are the biotech examples the article offers for that role.

Debt is the weak point in the builder story, according to Ross Givens, market strategist at Traders Agency. Neoclouds such as CoreWeave carry expensive borrowing, and hyperscalers are issuing stock and bonds to fund capital expenditures on AI capacity. Givens argues that as compute costs fall, builders could be left servicing heavy debt against shrinking prices. He compares the shift to Netflix replacing the trip to Blockbuster, noting that the winner did not build the pipes. The article says money is moving from the companies making AI to the ones using it.

Givens is quoted as saying he is not calling the end of AI, and the article notes that drug developers hold large datasets that AI helps them use to test and design treatments faster. Tempus AI, which tests tumors and builds a library of results, is described as earning revenue from both doctors and drug companies. Recursion Pharmaceuticals is described as the earlier, riskier position, with robots running cell experiments while AI selects compounds. The article says Givens treats $3 to $4 as the band where Recursion's idea stays in play, and that its shares could lose most of their value on a failed trial.

Tempus AI reported third-quarter revenue of $411.5 million, up 23%, with adjusted EBITDA of $25.6 million and raised full-year guidance above $1.60 billion. Recursion's runway was extended after an October offering of 61.54 million shares at $3.25 raised roughly $187.2 million. The iShares Biotechnology ETF, which holds 248 companies led by Gilead Sciences, Amgen and Vertex, is presented as a broader way to hold biotech without single-trial risk. The article says it set a record closing high above $221 in early November before falling a few percentage points in the sell-off.

The article's background is that many railroad builders went bankrupt under debt while grain traders profited from the rails, and that dot-com fiber builders failed while Alphabet, Amazon and Meta turned bandwidth into empires. It notes that the 10-year Treasury yield is near 4.9% with a December rate hike back on the table, which the article says pressures unprofitable, long-dated stocks most. Givens is described as walking through entries, stops and chart setups weekly through his Black Ops Trading Club. The article states that AI adoption must keep spreading for biotech to remain a leadership group.

The article leaves open whether biotech will keep attracting capital on days when chip stocks fall, and whether the rotation has lasting strength or was a single week of fear. It does not say how the debt-funded builders will fare as compute costs fall, or what tougher AI regulation would look like. It also leaves open whether Recursion's cash runway will hold through its trials, and how the new Tempus collaborations will affect its results. The articles give no further timetable beyond the December 1 date in MarketBeat's stock preview.

Articles.Title: The AI Debt Bill Is Coming Due, But Biotech Has Revenue to Show for the Boom

stories.Headline: 'A Massive Mistake': Tech, AI and Crypto Founders React to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Exit
stories.Summary:
Nvidia confirmed on Thursday that co-founder Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and board member after 33 years at the company. The board named longtime finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO, and Nvidia shares fell 14% at the opening bell. The resignation followed reports of two extramarital affairs, one involving a businesswoman that U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected of links to China. Huang acknowledged in a message to employees on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised, and an independent investigation remains underway.

Nvidia said it is searching for a permanent CEO from inside and outside the company, with Kress running the business in the meantime. The company's next scheduled earnings report is set for November 17, its first major financial update since Huang's departure. Nvidia agreed in September to acquire open-source AI repository Hugging Face for roughly $12.9 billion, subject to regulatory clearance. That deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027. Shares fell 14% at Thursday's opening bell, wiping out more than $500 billion from U.S. stocks in a single minute.

Nvidia has now dropped to third place in market value. Binance co-founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao said it was a mistake for Nvidia to let Huang resign. Bitcoin entrepreneur Dan Held agreed, arguing that Huang's personal problems should be weighed against the company he built. Erik Voorhees, founder of ShapeShift and the privacy-focused AI platform Venice, questioned the evidence that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy.

North Dakota Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer had called for Huang's exit, warning of blackmail risk and saying the internal investigation was insufficient. President Donald Trump said Huang was "definitely suffering" and would "be in good shape." Epic Games founder and CEO Tim Sweeney called it a sad day for Nvidia, developers, America and all humanity. Perplexity AI CEO Aravind Srinivas thanked Huang for 33 years of bold leadership.

Peter Steinberger, creator of the open-source OpenClaw agent and now at OpenAI, said the ouster felt rushed and not right. Developers concerned about open-weight models feared an Nvidia without Huang might be less willing to confront firms keeping advanced models proprietary. Elon Musk replied to a user asking him to hire Huang that it would be an honor. Huang co-founded Nvidia and led it through its growth into one of the most valuable companies in the world.

In July, Nvidia joined Microsoft, IBM, Hugging Face and dozens of other organizations to launch the Open Secure AI Alliance, which works on open AI security tools and standards. Nvidia also backed a letter defending open weights against broad restrictions. Jun Song, an open-source AI advocate, alleged that OpenAI and Anthropic had spent millions lobbying Congress to restrict open weights. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said his company had never advocated such a ban, while OpenAI later signed the pro-open-weight letter.

Articles.Title: 'A Massive Mistake': Tech, AI and Crypto Founders React to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Exit

stories.Headline: Dentons conference examines employment law changes and workplace AI
stories.Summary:
The Dentons Elevate Scotland conference, held in Glasgow, examined the sweeping changes in the Employment Rights Act 2025 and the effect of artificial intelligence on the workplace. The event was designed to help in-house lawyers and human resource professionals keep pace with developments driven by legislation and technology. Alison Weatherhead, partner and head of employment and pensions at Dentons, led a session on the Act that covered trade union access and unfair dismissal. She said Dentons has a practical toolkit and other resources to help companies work through the changes.

Weatherhead explained that trade unions can request formal physical or digital access to a workplace, and that businesses with 21 or more workers are now within scope. Employers may refuse such a request, but the Act creates a statutory presumption that access should be granted. Timing is tight, with 15 working days to respond to a request and 25 working days to negotiate terms. She also warned that penalties can rise quickly, with fines of up to £75,000 for a first breach of an agreement, £150,000 for a second, and £500,000 for any further breaches.

Other sessions covered building a personal brand, time management, competition law in the workplace, and the EU Pay Transparency Directive. Sarah Jackman, counsel at Dentons, spoke with regulatory colleague Katy MacAskill about the Financial Conduct Authority's guidance on non-financial misconduct. Jackman said the guidance marks a new era for employers, who must consider exits, investigations, references, conduct in private lives and manager accountability. Weatherhead chaired a panel on AI in employment that included Elouisa Crichton, Rowena Rix and Nicola Hamilton of Edrington.

The panel explored how organisations are moving from AI experimentation to practical implementation. Rix argued that AI should be built into actual workflows rather than merely made available, and that governance should not become a department of no. Crichton examined how AI affecting people and employment decisions raises questions of fairness, discrimination, transparency, privacy, accountability and where human judgement must sit. She stressed that trust and engagement are vital and that organisational messaging should not drift away from lived experience. The article does not report any further steps or outcomes from the conference.

Articles.Title: Dentons conference examines employment law changes and workplace AI

stories.Headline: Armanino builds an AI App Factory on Microsoft Foundry, cutting production time 89%
stories.Summary:
Armanino, an accounting, consulting, and technology firm in San Ramon, California, built an AI App Factory on Microsoft Foundry and GitHub Copilot, according to a Microsoft customer story dated November 11, 2026. The firm set out to grow by meeting rising customer demand for AI solutions without proportionally increasing its resources. Its production time for new AI applications fell by 89 percent. Consultants now turn a two-hour client session into finished requirements in 30 minutes. The firm also builds solutions it once found too costly to attempt.

The App Factory is a standardized four-phase delivery pipeline covering discovery, design, engineering, and launch, running end to end on one Microsoft stack. Discovery uses Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot, and design uses Microsoft Copilot Studio to build a client-facing agent prototype. Engineering runs on GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and Azure DevOps, while launch adds automated test coverage through Playwright. Foundry serves as the landing zone for all factory output, carrying model orchestration, prompt management, evaluation pipelines, and production deployment. Armanino also moved from Claude and ChatGPT to GitHub Copilot for engineering, with the back end now entirely Microsoft.

Carmel Wynkoop, Partner, Artificial Intelligence Solutions at Armanino, said the firm had to reengineer its delivery workflows to be AI-native rather than simply adopt AI tools. Drew Armanino, Lead, Artificial Intelligence Solutions, said the firm's small core developer team had to produce output for a large business, and that constraint became the catalyst. Talbot Harty, Artificial Intelligence Delivery and Product Lead, said that after switching tooling to GitHub the team revved an enterprise application update in four hours. The article does not name a separate party responsible for the story beyond Armanino and Microsoft's own customer-story format.

Armanino's clients, many of which already operate in the Microsoft ecosystem, are affected by the change in how solutions are delivered and governed. Casey Williams, Director, Dynamics 365 Finance & Supply Chain at Armanino, said Requirements Miner has let the firm expedite FitGap reviews and bring in milestones sooner. Chris Hood, Director, Sales at Armanino, said the tool halves the time for discovery-to-solution discussions and product demonstrations. Drew Armanino said the firm's ability to engineer solutions has increased tenfold, and that many current projects would not have been attempted before because they were time and cost prohibitive. Wynkoop said the most consistent client reaction is surprise at seeing a working prototype instead of a strategy deck.

Before the factory, Armanino ran Claude for intake to functional spec and ChatGPT for use case intake, with standalone services in between that consumed engineering time on handoffs. Each new build restarted from zero on identity, security, deployment, and monitoring, and the firm's growth ambitions were limited by its developer headcount. The firm's Cloud Sync service, an Azure-native integration and analytics offering used by multiple customers, runs on Azure Functions, Azure SQL Database, Azure API Management, Azure App Service, and Microsoft Entra ID. The App Factory has produced a technical accounting memo drafter for ASC 606 revenue recognition analysis, Requirements Miner, a request-for-proposal generator, and an agentic application that replaced the marketing department's tooling. Armanino's listed industry is accounting and tax services, and it has 1,000 to 9,999 employees.

The article says Armanino is adding Microsoft Fabric as the governed data layer beneath the App Factory. It also says the factory pattern is moving into healthcare and adjacent industries, and that each shipped application is being productized for resale to mid-market clients. The articles do not give a timeline for either effort, the number of clients that have deployed factory-built applications, or the commercial terms of any resale. They also do not report how the 89 percent and 90 percent figures were measured beyond the firm's own statements.

Articles.Title: Armanino builds an AI App Factory on Microsoft Foundry, cutting production time 89%

stories.Headline: SEA AI funding rises 121 percent to $4.2 billion in 9M 2026 - Tracxn
stories.Summary:
Southeast Asian artificial intelligence companies raised $4.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026, according to a statement from Tracxn released on Thursday, November 12, 2026. That total is up 121 percent from $1.9 billion in the same period of 2025 and 453 percent above the $768 million raised in the first nine months of 2024. The funding came across 28 rounds, which is down 12 percent from 32 a year earlier. The firm said the total was concentrated in a small number of very large rounds, with the ten largest accounting for 98 percent of all funding.

The single biggest deal was Kling AI's $2.8 billion Series D in July 2026, backed by BlueFive Capital, CPE and Guofang Capital among others, which alone equaled 66 percent of the total. Sharpa followed with a $670 million Series D in August 2026, backed by Alibaba, Meituan and Tencent among others, and Zelostech raised a $300 million Series C in February 2026. The average round rose to $152 million from $60 million in the first nine months of 2025. Late stage companies took $3.8 billion, or 89 percent of the total, while early stage funding fell 25 percent to $444 million and seed funding rose 28 percent to $33.8 million.

Tracxn's figures show the enterprise applications segment raised $3.1 billion, about 16 times the amount it drew a year earlier, and Singapore-based companies accounted for essentially all of the capital. The number of investors backing the sector fell to 56 from 69, and 39 of them were investing in Southeast Asian AI for the first time. Exits were limited to one acquisition and one public listing, with MiniMax listing in January 2026 at a market capitalization of $6.5 billion and Manus being acquired by US-based Meta in April 2026 for an undisclosed sum. No new unicorns emerged during the period, the same as in the first nine months of 2025.

Articles.Title: SEA AI funding rises 121 percent to $4.2 billion in 9M 2026 - Tracxn

stories.Headline: Chinese banks have been using artificial intelligence (AI) for their work in earnest, from simple ta..
stories.Summary:
Chinese banks have been putting artificial intelligence to work in earnest, moving from simple task automation toward systems that accelerate research and handle complex jobs. According to a report by the Chinese outlet Caixin on the 11th, Jiangsu Bank replaced 1.2 million cumulative business hours through AI-related applications. Shanghai Pudong Development Bank handled a workload equivalent to more than 2,500 internal digital workers per year. The Bank of China's AI system has reached the ability to identify 305 types of documents across 3,800 business scenarios. Overall, the strongest results so far come in tasks that involve repetitive, regular, large-scale information processing.

Those tasks include document processing, customer response, payment fraud detection, and preliminary credit ratings. Jiangsu Bank cut the time needed for credit approval for small and medium-sized enterprises by 30 percent after introducing AI. Investment research is still being tested, since AI can shorten basic work such as collecting information, analyzing financial statements, selecting items, and drafting reports. However, the article says this does not mean AI can make reliable investment decisions. Reports generated by AI serve as reference material or a starting point, and they are hard to apply to external publications or decisions carrying large financial risk.

When information is incomplete or conflicting, humans still interpret results, verify evidence, and make the final call. The next step is expected to be "AI agents" that carry out several connected tasks. Jungshin Securities has developed its own AI for exchange-traded fund screening, stock analysis, and financial statement analysis. Major institutions such as the China Commercial Bank and the China International Finance Corporation have introduced financial AI solutions, including Kimi from the startup Moonshot.

The article notes that the reliability of such agents depends on the quality and currency of the information available to them. Financial institutions must therefore supply accurate, up-to-date data and define the access rights and scope of their AI agents. Cost and integration remain obstacles, and the article describes them in detail. An official at Tencent's Workbuddy platform said self-built AI projects alone cost millions to tens of millions of yuan, roughly tens of billions of won, with maintenance costs on top.

Self-built systems also take about three months to update, while Software as a Service can be updated in two days, though it brings security and data risks. Fragmented data and a gap between business and technology staff also limit what AI can do. Cybersecurity is another concern, as the Bank for International Settlements estimated that simple cyberattack costs fell from $50 to $100 per case and sophisticated attacks from $5,000 to $10,000. Fan Yuan, chairman of the cybersecurity company Anheng Information, argued that the financial industry should review its security governance for the AI era.

Articles.Title: Chinese banks have been using artificial intelligence (AI) for their work in earnest, from simple ta..

stories.Headline: Voluntary buyouts: Big Tech pays staff to walk away as the AI bill comes due
stories.Summary:
On October 26, Microsoft opened a Voluntary Exit Offer to about 60,000 employees, roughly 27% of its global workforce. Google later extended its voluntary exit programme to staff in Canada, France, Germany, Japan and Switzerland. Meta is finalising a voluntary departure scheme in France that could see up to a third of its roughly 300 French staff leave. On November 4, Canva told 1,271 employees, or 22% of its workforce, that their jobs would end, change or move. Canva's package is not strictly voluntary, but it has drawn wide attention.

A voluntary buyout is an offer of money and benefits to employees who agree to resign, and unlike a layoff, nobody is forced out. Microsoft's October offer covers participating teams in the US, UK, Canada and India at internal level 70 and below, with no age or tenure test. Employees must decide by early December and leave on December 31. Canva's departing staff receive at least six months' salary, 12 months of continued healthcare where provided, and a chance to apply for a USD 10,000 grant. Google's Swiss staff received one month's salary per year of service, capped at 12 months.

Microsoft, Google, Meta and Canva have not framed these exits solely as cost cutting, and the articles do not give a direct statement on their motives beyond what follows. Meta's chief people officer, Janelle Gale, told staff the April cuts were meant to run the company more efficiently and offset its other investments. Canva tied its slower growth directly to AI computing costs. Microsoft's chief people officer, Amy Coleman, said the turnout for its spring scheme reduced the size of the July layoffs, when the company cut 4,800 jobs.

Supporters say buyouts let people leave on their own terms with real support, and about 30% of those eligible for Microsoft's spring scheme accepted. Critics argue that buyouts may not guarantee the right people leave, since Microsoft's spring scheme targeted long-serving staff who hold knowledge about systems the company still depends on. Employees who decline offers may wonder whether they are next, given Google's record of following voluntary offers with layoffs in at least one division. Alphabet's workforce grew to 204,757 at the end of September from 194,668 in March.

Alphabet expects to spend between USD 195 billion and USD 205 billion on capital expenditure in 2026, more than double its 2025 figure of USD 91.4 billion. Meta has narrowed its 2026 range to between USD 135 billion and USD 145 billion, and Microsoft expects about USD 170 billion for the fiscal year to June 2027. Canva cut its 2026 revenue growth forecast from 30% to 20% in August, and investors Blackbird and Airtree later marked its value down from USD 42 billion to USD 34.9 billion. The articles leave open whether the buyouts will meaningfully reduce headcount or payroll costs against these capital budgets.

Articles.Title: Voluntary buyouts: Big Tech pays staff to walk away as the AI bill comes due

stories.Headline: Kenosha County man faces 12 felony counts under new Wisconsin AI law
stories.Summary:
A Kenosha County man, Tristan Preuss, 23, faces 12 felony counts after allegedly using AI to manipulate photos of his ex-girlfriend to make her appear nude and posting them online. According to a criminal complaint, he created four fake social media accounts posing as her, beginning in August 2025. The charges are brought under Act 34, a Wisconsin law passed last October that makes it a crime to post a synthetic intimate representation of an identifiable person. Authorities described this as one of the first times the charge has been prosecuted in the state. Preuss is expected in court on Dec. 2 for an initial appearance.

The complaint alleges that in some of the posts, Preuss demanded money in exchange for the images, directing payment to a phone number that belonged to him. When police questioned him, he reportedly said he had no ill intent, that the images were for his own satisfaction, and that he was sorry. He also told police he did not know the conduct was illegal, a claim tied to how new these charges are. Local attorney Jonathan LaVoy, of Kim and LaVoy S.C., said the public distribution of the photos is a key factor in the case. The evidence against Preuss appears fairly strong, LaVoy said, though the statute itself may face legal challenges on appeal.

LaVoy also described the broader issue, saying AI brings both benefits and harms and that the law is trying to catch up with the technology. The article notes that the case is one of the early tests of this new Wisconsin statute and that its legal footing could be examined by the state's appellate courts. The information came from the Kenosha County criminal complaint, the state court records system, and LaVoy. The story also notes that portions of the article were produced with AI assistance and reviewed by a FOX6 journalist and an editor before publication.

Articles.Title: Kenosha County man faces 12 felony counts under new Wisconsin AI law

stories.Headline: EU Unveils DFA Bill to Regulate AI-Driven Personalized Pricing and Purchase Nudges [Global AI Briefing]
stories.Summary:
The European Commission formally adopted and unveiled the Digital Fairness Act bill on November 11, 2026, local time, aiming to rein in online companies that use artificial intelligence to steer consumers toward purchases or charge different prices to different people. The article notes that AI now analyzes consumer preferences and purchasing power to recommend products and ads, and can even buy on a shopper's behalf. The EU wants new consumer-protection rules for this digital marketplace. The bill has not yet become law, since it must still be deliberated and approved by the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union. It is meant to sit alongside the Digital Services Act and the Digital Network Act, giving the EU a three-pillar framework for AI and digital industries.

The bill would target practices that pressure consumers into buying, such as labeling an item as the "last one" when stock is not low or showing a fake sale countdown. Subscription services that are easy to join but hard to cancel would also be regulated. For AI-driven personalized advertising and pricing, the bill would bar companies from using sensitive personal information to exploit consumer vulnerabilities and would require more transparency about how prices are set when they vary with demand. Rules could also reach gaming and content businesses, including repeated payment prompts aimed at minors and influencer promotions not clearly marked as advertising. The article says the law would extend consumer protection beyond false advertising and data leaks to cover how AI influences buying decisions, including guaranteeing freedom of choice when AI agents buy for consumers.

The European Commission is the body that unveiled the bill, and the article reports its aims in its own words without attributing new quotes to officials. Its stated core aim is to stop online platforms and e-commerce companies from misleading consumers and to strengthen consumer rights in the digital environment. The article also cites experts who advise South Korean platforms, gaming firms, and e-commerce companies operating in Europe to review their recommendations, personalized advertising, and subscription-cancellation procedures. It adds that calls are growing to review consumer-protection principles in South Korea's own market, where AI-powered pricing and purchasing-agent services are spreading. The report is a translated Korean news piece and does not indicate a timetable for the bill's passage.

Articles.Title: EU Unveils DFA Bill to Regulate AI-Driven Personalized Pricing and Purchase Nudges [Global AI Briefing]

stories.Headline: How CUBE Is Transforming Global Regulatory Compliance with AI
stories.Summary:
CUBE, a regulatory technology company, is extending its AI software by placing its regulatory intelligence directly inside the platforms businesses already use. Its Powered By technology lets software providers access CUBE's regulatory data and AI agents without having to collect, organise or maintain the underlying information themselves. The latest example is Thomson Reuters, which has integrated CUBE's technology into CoCounsel Legal. The article says the integration gives corporate legal teams and international law firms access to regulatory information across more than 150 countries and could reach up to one million legal professionals.

Through this integration, CoCounsel Legal users can research laws, rules, guidance and regulatory developments alongside Westlaw, Practical Law and Reuters content. CUBE has also published internal benchmark findings comparing its regulatory intelligence agents with two leading AI models. The evaluation, conducted in August 2026, involved 13 regulatory queries covering the UK, Spain and the UAE. According to CUBE, its agents identified three to four times more essential regulatory material than the competing models, and six to 17 times more regulatory guidance, codes and supervisory material, depending on the model. The article notes these results come from CUBE's own evaluation rather than independent testing.

Ben Richmond, Founder and CEO of CUBE, said the company aims to be the regulatory data infrastructure that the world can trust and that delivering regulatory intelligence at the point of need is the future of the industry. Thomson Reuters said its subject matter experts assessed how CUBE's content would complement its existing resources before the integration. Its representatives said that global coverage and quality were both essential to them and that CUBE met both requirements. The article also says CUBE has spent 15 years building a database covering more than 12,000 issuing bodies across 750 jurisdictions, validated by 250 subject matter experts and processing more than ten million data points each year. CUBE adds that 24 of the world's 29 Global Systemically Important Banks already use its regulatory intelligence.

Articles.Title: How CUBE Is Transforming Global Regulatory Compliance with AI

stories.Headline: US-Canadian AI-powered law firm start-up Blackletter raises $6m in seed funding round
stories.Summary:
US-Canadian legal technology start-up Blackletter has raised $6m in a seed funding round, according to The Global Legal Post, which reported the news on 11 November 2026. The round was led by early-stage investor Lerer Hippeau, with legal funding specialists Seven Stars taking part alongside Maple VC, Garage Capital and Ripple Ventures. Several AI founders also joined the round, including Aidan Gomez, Ivan Zhang and Nick Frosst of Cohere, Jae Lee of Twelve Labs and Sara Hooker of Adaption Labs. The firm says it will use the money to expand its platform and to grow its bench of lawyers and engineers.

Blackletter describes itself as a firm that pairs experienced lawyers with its own AI software to deliver legal work faster and at lower cost. Its current practice areas are corporate, commercial, financing, M&A and employment. The firm has built a proprietary platform, Blackletter OS, which stores knowledge about each client and manages legal matters from start to finish. It charges fixed fees instead of traditional hourly rates, and says AI reduces the time its lawyers spend on each case.

Jonathan Rosenbluth, the firm's co-founder and CEO, argued that the traditional law firm model is built to benefit the firm and its senior partners rather than clients or many of its lawyers. He said Blackletter was designed the other way around, so that its technology and structure let it act as a strategic partner to clients. Graham Brown, managing partner at Lerer Hippeau, said the legal industry is ready for structural change and praised the team's mix of AI experience and expertise in scaling legal operations. Since emerging from stealth mode in June, the firm says it has signed more than 75 early-stage and growth-stage companies and investors as clients, including Ada, Antidote, Fanatics Betting & Gaming and Twelve Labs.

The New York and Toronto-based firm was co-founded by Rosenbluth, Avi Brudner and David Stewart. The article notes that Rosenbluth and Stewart previously worked together at software developer Oumi for eight months before starting Blackletter. The report places the round within a wave of investment in legal technology this year, pointing to Athena, a US AI-powered hybrid corporate law firm that secured $2.5m in pre-seed funding the previous week. The article does not say what further funding or growth milestones Blackletter expects to reach.

Articles.Title: US-Canadian AI-powered law firm start-up Blackletter raises $6m in seed funding round

stories.Headline: Bill Gates Says Next Four Years Are Critical for AI Safety, Calls for Urgent Regulation
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates warned that the next four years will be a critical window for ensuring artificial intelligence safety, according to a report published on November 11, 2026, by Bloomingbit. The report cited Cointelegraph, which said Gates made the comments that day. Gates pointed to rising risks, including cyberattacks, bioterrorism and threats to critical infrastructure. He described these as major risk factors that grow as AI technology advances. Gates said AI could surpass human intelligence by 2030, and that it may replace human jobs across a range of industries.

He called for swift regulation of AI to address these threats. He also urged cooperation between the United States and China to respond to them. The articles do not describe any specific rule, law or deadline that has been proposed. Gates, a co-founder of Microsoft, is the person who made these remarks, and the articles present them as his own warning rather than a formal government position.

The Bloomingbit piece was written by reporter JH Kim and includes an AI-generated summary that the outlet says is for reference only. Its tags link the story to AI safety and crypto regulation. The articles do not say whether any government or company has responded to Gates's call. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Bill Gates Says Next Four Years Are Critical for AI Safety, Calls for Urgent Regulation

stories.Headline: AI in Corporate Law and M&A: Where Technology Meets Judgment - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
On November 11, 2026, The National Law Review published a commentary by Michael Weis of Weis & Burney titled "AI in Corporate Law and M&A: Where Technology Meets Judgment." The article is an opinion piece, and the author says it does not necessarily reflect the position of the publication. Weis writes that he is frequently asked about artificial intelligence, including its impact on legal practice and on mergers and acquisitions. He says the broader question of AI's impact on business is too wide for one article, so he focuses on the first two questions. The piece is dated Wednesday, November 11, 2026.

Weis compares AI in legal work to medical symptom-checking websites, which can suggest possible diagnoses but do not replace a physician. He argues that AI can help attorneys with routine matters, document review, legal research, identifying relevant forms or precedents, and researching jurisdictional requirements. He notes that lawyers have long relied on form files, case research services, treatises and written analyses, and that AI lets these resources be accessed and analyzed faster. He says experienced counsel must still know what questions to ask, what information matters, what authority applies, and how the law applies to a client's facts. He stresses that AI is a valuable tool but not a substitute for legal judgment.

The article lists areas where AI is relevant to evaluating a business in an M&A transaction: accounting and financial analysis, valuation, operations, human resources and employee benefits, intellectual property, tax, technology and cybersecurity, and market analysis. Weis says buyers can use a target's AI use to assess operations, competitive position, efficiency and future prospects, while sellers can position their business with the same considerations in mind. He argues that a company's AI readiness can affect its value, since effective use may bring efficiency, productivity, better customer service and growth. He adds that a company that has fallen behind may face investment needs or competitive challenges that buyers must weigh. He suggests diligence should ask how technology is used, whether it fits the business, and what infrastructure and expertise support it.

Weis points to heavy investment in AI infrastructure, which he says is creating demand across many industries, including data center construction, real estate, energy, equipment, logistics, chips and networking. He identifies environmental, infrastructure and community concerns, particularly around data center development and energy consumption, as legitimate issues. He says these competing interests must be balanced, and that the balance will influence investment and development decisions. The article does not name specific companies or transactions, and it does not give figures on investment amounts or energy use. Weis writes from his position as a practitioner, and his observations are presented as opinion rather than as findings from a study.

Weis describes the impact of AI on business and transactions as still evolving, and he calls the challenge for corporate lawyers one of using AI while preserving professional judgment and client-specific analysis. For buyers and sellers, he says technology strategy can affect operational performance, competitive position, risk and business value. He concludes that AI is unlikely to be a discrete issue addressed once and set aside, and that it is becoming part of the broader environment in which companies operate. The article offers no new deadlines, regulatory changes or pending decisions. It also leaves open how buyers should price AI readiness in a deal, and how the balance between data center development and community or environmental concerns will be struck.

Articles.Title: AI in Corporate Law and M&A: Where Technology Meets Judgment - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: CoreWeave targets 2028 profitability as AI demand surges
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that it expects to become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028. The AI cloud company made the statement as it sought to reassure investors that strong demand and customer commitments can support its debt-fuelled expansion. Shares of the Nvidia-backed company rose about 5 per cent in extended trading after the announcement. The stock had crashed more than 40 per cent in the past month as the firm became the focal point of growing AI bubble fears. Investors were also worried about heavy borrowing for data centres amid rising interest rates and the pace of returns on massive investments.

CoreWeave said it would not tap unsecured debt markets at current yields and had enough cash flow from existing customer commitments to repay current debt and additional borrowing. The company had about US$46.9 billion in total debt as of the end of September, and it expects to raise less than US$5 billion in additional capital through 2027. Its CEO Mike Intrator said the company had US$9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits that will flow in over the next three months. CoreWeave's revenue backlog stood at US$132.5 billion at September-end, up from US$104 billion at the end of June. Its quarterly capital spending rose to US$14.5 billion from US$9.4 billion in the prior quarter.

Intrator said in a statement that customer contracts come first and investment follows, so lenders have something concrete to lend against. He added that customers typically help fund the buildout. CoreWeave said it does not see any material risks to its data-centre buildout from a potential shift in the regulatory landscape after the Democrats' sweeping win in the US midterms. Intrator told Reuters that he expects more scrutiny on how data centres are built and how resources are used. He said he does not think this will materially change how the company builds its infrastructure or distort the costs of the buildout.

Intrator said there will be a pacing issue, as companies need to be more transparent and work through the process with communities, which he expects to be prevalent across the industry. He also said CoreWeave will not ramp up its international expansion plans because of the election results, noting the strategy has been worked on for a year and a half. Public backlash has been growing in the US around data centres' impact on local resources, including water and power. Among CoreWeave's customers are Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic. Earlier on the same day, Anthropic kicked off a roadshow for its share sale at a lower target valuation than earlier estimates.

CoreWeave has never turned a profit, according to data compiled by LSEG, and its shares had also been hit by a broader crisis of confidence in the AI trade. Recent earnings reports from hyperscalers hinted at delays in data-centre projects and a slower ramp in spending. The company said it is largely sold out of capacity through the next year, with about ten times as much demand as available capacity. Its third-quarter revenue surged nearly 170 per cent to US$3.66 billion, beating estimates of US$3.55 billion. Its per-share loss of 95 cents was smaller than the US$1.16 loss analysts had estimated, according to LSEG.

CoreWeave now expects 2026 revenue of between US$13 billion and US$13.3 billion, up from the earlier range of US$12.4 billion to US$13.2 billion. It also raised the lower end of its annual spending target by US$2 billion, now projecting spending of US$37 billion to US$39 billion. The articles do not say when the company will report its results for the coming quarters. They also do not say how the regulatory environment will develop after the midterm elections. Whether the company's expected 2028 profitability will be achieved is not addressed beyond its own projection.

stories.Headline: AI Drives Surge in New Businesses. Why the Boom Isn’t Creating Jobs.
stories.Summary:
Barron's reported on November 12, 2026, that a surge in new businesses is being driven partly by artificial intelligence, but that this boom is not producing as many jobs as earlier ones did. The article notes that the number of new firms opening for business continues to trend upward. It adds that employers have averaged 86,000 jobs added per month this year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The piece is written by Megan Leonhardt and carries Dow Jones copyright.

Euronews reported on November 10, 2026, that Denmark is putting another 500 million Danish kroner, about €67 million, into Gefion, its AI supercomputer. The announcement, made on a Tuesday by the Export and Investment Fund of Denmark, says the money will support the machine's infrastructure and operations at the Danish Centre for AI Innovation, which runs it. The funding adds to an earlier 700 million kroner, about €93.8 million, from the state investment fund and the Novo Nordisk Foundation. Gefion launched in 2024 with 1,528 Nvidia chips and is now nearing full capacity. The article does not say how the new money will be spent or when the extra capacity will become available.

Denmark's minister for business and competitiveness, Martin Lidegaard, said in a statement that greater computing access would let Danish companies and researchers turn ideas into new solutions, companies and jobs, and would keep ownership of future technology from passing to others. Another goal, the article says, is to help public institutions and businesses use AI while keeping sensitive data under their control. Netcompany, a Danish technology firm that builds public-sector IT systems, is joining the centre's investors and will supply software for access management, monitoring and security. Christina Egelund, Denmark's minister for research, education and digitalisation, argued that Europe must do more on its own and that Denmark should help secure European technological independence.

The Euronews piece places the announcement within a wider European effort to control the infrastructure behind AI. It cites the United Kingdom's 225 million pound investment in an AI research supercomputer in 2023, and Finland's LUMI supercomputer, funded by the European Union and participating countries at a lifetime cost above €200 million. In July, the European Commission opened a call for up to seven AI gigafactories, large data centres backed by up to €10 billion in EU and national funding. The Barron's article, by contrast, focuses on the American business boom and offers no comparison to these European investments.

stories.Headline: Nvidia spy scandal revives push to write China chip export limits into the defense bill
stories.Summary:
Reports that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman U.S. officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence have given Washington's chip hawks a fresh argument, and they are pressing it in this year's defense bill. Lawmakers and advocates told Reuters that Congress is now more likely to pass limits on China's access to AI chips, with three measures possibly headed into the National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal 2027. On Monday, Nov. 9, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he strongly supports chip restrictions in the final bill, after a classified briefing for congressional leaders. The woman is Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's big Southeast Asian customers, and she has not been charged. Huang has admitted being unfaithful to his wife, and Nvidia's board has opened an investigation into whether he was targeted by foreign intelligence.

The three measures already sit in the Senate's manager's package for the defense bill, after the House Foreign Affairs Committee advanced all of them earlier this year. The AI Overwatch Act would treat AI chip sales to adversary nations much like arms sales: Commerce would have to notify two congressional committees at least 30 days before licensing chips such as Nvidia's H200, and Congress could block a sale by joint resolution. Blackwell-class chips would face mandatory denial, and the House text would end existing licenses for covered exports. The Chip Security Act would require companies to track their chips to fight smuggling, and its House version passed committee unanimously.

The MATCH Act would push U.S. allies to restrict more chipmaking equipment sales to China. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks said in a joint statement that Huang's relationship with a suspected spy makes the national security concerns even more urgent, and they urged Congress to pass the AI Overwatch Act. Nvidia declined to comment and says it follows export laws, while its board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. China's foreign ministry calls the spying allegation unsubstantiated.

The White House did not comment on the bills, though The Information reported that its officials shared feedback with congressional staff in late October. President Donald Trump has backed Huang, calling him an amazing guy and saying Huang told him he had no idea the woman was a spy. Congress has been here before: a similar Senate provision, the GAIN AI Act, was dropped from last year's final defense bill after lobbying by the White House and Nvidia. A former congressional staffer told Reuters that Nvidia is the biggest opponent of the Chip Security and AI Overwatch Acts, and an industry group that counts Nvidia as a member also opposes them.

If the provisions are dropped again, they would return to a Congress run by Democrats from Jan. 3, with chip hawks such as Chris Coons and Warren in line for key chairmanships. Nvidia's licensed H200 sales to China were under 1% of data center revenue last quarter, so a congressional veto would mainly cap future sales. Huang was asked to give House Republican chairmen a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18, and Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Nov. 17. Nvidia shares fell about 5% on Monday, more than 20% below their peak a month earlier.

stories.Headline: Helsing Unveils AI Targeting Software as Europe’s Answer to Palantir’s Maven
stories.Summary:
Helsing, a Munich-based defense company, is presenting new AI targeting software in Berlin on Wednesday, 11 November, and pitching it as a European alternative to American suppliers. The company has not publicly named the product ahead of the event. Its invitation said it was crucial to conduct precise reconnaissance, make sound decisions under uncertainty, and act on the battlefield with autonomy and without dependencies, from Europe and for Europe. The presentation comes as Germany's armed forces have set aside Palantir's Maven Smart System for now.

The Bundeswehr plans to field its own AI targeting system from 2027, with full rollout in 2028. Helsing is positioning its software to fill that gap. Its earlier products include the HX-2 strike drone, supplied to Ukraine, the CA-1 Europa uncrewed combat aircraft, and the Altra software that combines sensor data for reconnaissance and strike missions. Earlier this month, the company handed Germany the source code for its future combat drone software, giving the state direct control over a key piece of military code.

Palantir, which builds Maven, rejects the idea that customers could be cut off. The company says buyers keep full operational control of the software and that it has no remote kill switch. European concern about dependence on Washington has nonetheless grown, with President Donald Trump repeatedly threatening to pull the United States out of NATO. Last month, speed limits on Ukraine's Starlink terminals hampered Kyiv's efforts to intercept Russian drones, and in June the Trump administration moved to block non-US residents from Anthropic's most advanced models before lifting the restriction later that month.

The war in Ukraine has made AI decision tools a practical requirement, since drones, satellites and ground sensors produce more data than analysts can sort in time. Maven already runs inside NATO structures and several national forces, so any newcomer must prove itself in exercises and fit into existing command systems. Helsing's advantage is that it already supplies combat drones to the Bundeswehr, which gives it an existing foothold. Helsing has not said how its targeting software will be tested or when German forces might adopt it.

stories.Headline: Microsoft Researchers Show AI Agents Can Be Backdoored by Editing Fewer Than 10 Neurons
stories.Summary:
Microsoft researchers have shown that an AI model can be given a hidden backdoor by editing fewer than 10 of its rarely used neurons, without retraining the model. When a chosen trigger appears, the model outputs an attacker's command, which an agent using that model would run with the agent's own permissions. The attacker must be able to change the model's weights, and the researchers published the research this week. Microsoft says it has not seen any threat actors use the technique. The company has also published guidance on defending against it.

The method, which the researchers call Lazarus, edits neurons that rarely fire and barely affect the model's answers. Each edited neuron is set to fire only when a trigger string appears, either in a user's request or later in a tool's output. Each edited neuron forces one token of the command into the output, so a command needs about one neuron per token. The new settings are calculated directly and can then be tuned with a few hundred training steps on those neurons alone, leaving the rest of the model file and code unchanged. Microsoft describes the trigger as potentially as mundane as a date change, such as the clock passing midnight into 2027.

In a walkthrough posted on X, a backdoored Nemotron-Terminal-8B model with 10 edited neurons worked normally for three turns while fixing a Node.js server. When the server returned a connection error, the model output a command to download and run a remote script, which ran as root inside the test container. On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the team edited and tuned seven of the more than 12,000 neurons in the model's last feed-forward layer, using 23 example sessions. The edited model output the command in at least 98.8% of test sessions containing the trigger and in none of the trigger-free sessions checked. With the tuned version, success rates on Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT ranged from 51% to 99.5%, and the Qwen model used six neurons.

Anyone who can change a model's checkpoint, the file that stores its weights, before deployment could plant the backdoor, including an insider, an attacker with a stolen account or access to a build pipeline, or whoever publishes a modified model on a public hub. Planting it does not require the computing power of full training. The researchers credit Claude Code, running the Opus 4.5 model, with finding the core idea and say coding agents can make such attacks easier to build. Microsoft's blog describes the work as starting in March as a quick experiment that became a months-long study. Earlier, in an October 6 proof of concept, ProjectDiscovery researchers fine-tuned an open Qwen model to react to a trigger phrase, whereas Lazarus edits a few neurons directly.

Microsoft says Foundry customers are protected from these attacks for models from trusted labs, because models are tied to their original publishers and run inside separately scanned containers. The remaining risk, the company says, is that a trusted provider is itself compromised. Microsoft is working with internal AI security teams to turn its detection techniques into a red-teaming harness and is exploring weight scanning with frontier agents as an additional signal for open-weight models. It also plans to have models signed with verifiable provenance and tamper-proof audits. The researchers say reliable detection requires comparing a checkpoint with its original weights, and that no scan can prove a model is safe.
