stories.Headline: Jensen jeopardy will disrupt the AI industry
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's position is under threat after an admission that he had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company whom US intelligence concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. The reporting in Wired is dated November 9, 2026, and the Financial Times article carrying the same headline is dated November 12, 2026. The Financial Times piece itself is a paywalled page that gives only its headline and subscription offers, so it contributes no further facts. Wired reports that the scrutiny began over the last few days, after the admission became public. Huang had previously been a close confidant of President Donald Trump and a prominent voice in US-China relations.

Nvidia's board of directors said it would launch an investigation into the incident, and the company said Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. According to a corporate filing, Huang earned $36 million last year and owned about 3.5 percent of Nvidia as of March. The same filing noted that Huang is an at-will employee who can be let go at any time without severance. Wired reports that how the investigation turns out, and what it means for Huang's future at the company, remains unclear. Nvidia, which Huang cofounded in 1993, controls 90 percent of the market for chips used in training frontier AI models.

Nvidia's board is the body responsible for the investigation, and Wired reports that the company said Huang supports it. Harvard Business School professor David Yoffie, who tracks the chip industry, says Huang is the person who decides who gets the chips and who does not. Yoffie also says the board's investigation will most likely focus on whether Huang violated any company policies. Wired notes that Nvidia did not immediately respond to its request for comment. The article does not report any statement from Huang himself beyond the company's account that he supports the review.

Wired reports that Nvidia has invested billions in companies buying its chips, including OpenAI and Anthropic, and that Huang has the power to determine which areas of AI get a boost. Nvidia has roughly 60,000 staff, and according to current and former employees, Huang closely manages even small details and responds to emails from any of them. Nvidia has no other executive close to Huang's prominence and no apparent potential successor, according to Yoffie. Ryan Fedasiuk of the Foundation for American Innovation says Huang has become load-bearing for the entire US AI industry. Nvidia shares fell more than 4 percent on Monday, even as broader stock market indices rose.

Wired reports that Huang has been outspoken against calls for more aggressive technology export controls on China, which makes the affair especially damning for his credibility. The first Trump administration and the Biden administration both imposed export controls designed to limit China's access to Nvidia's chips and the technology needed to mint advanced semiconductors. In his second term, Trump loosened these controls, giving China access to older generations of Nvidia chips. Sam Bresnick of Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology says the scandal is likely to accelerate efforts to crack down on chip exports. The Financial Times article offers no facts beyond its headline and subscription offers.

Wired reports that the FBI could investigate whether laws were broken and that Congress may examine whether the affair influenced US policy on selling chips to China. Fedasiuk says the scandal raises questions about whether China may have gained sensitive information about US AI companies and the government's strategy on China. Bresnick expects more scrutiny from the Commerce Department over what chips are being sent to China. The article does not say whether the FBI or Congress has opened any such inquiry. It also does not say what the investigation will find or how it will affect Huang's future at Nvidia.

stories.Headline: Google unveils Gemini Robotics 2.5 with 96% success rate in tasks
stories.Summary:
Google has launched Gemini Robotics 2.5, an AI model meant to improve how quickly and precisely robots learn and perform tasks. The company announced the model, which it calls its most capable vision-language-action model to date, on November 10, 2026. Google DeepMind's Carolina Parada, who leads the company's robotics work, introduced it in a post on the company's website. Its tests were run with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz, where humanoid robots sorted automotive parts successfully. The announcement came in reports published on November 9 and 12, 2026.

The model increases the number of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it learns them. Google tested Gemini Robotics 2.5 across more than 200 distinct tasks, such as serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box and pipetting a liquid. Compared with previous baselines, it achieves a 30% to 100% higher success rate depending on the task, while completing tasks 20% to 30% faster. The model natively works with several robot types, including Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid with a five-finger, 22 degree-of-freedom SharpaWave hand, and the Franka Duo platform with two-fingered grippers. Gemini Robotics 2.5 is rolling out to Google's robotics partners.

Google is responsible for the model, and Carolina Parada described it as a step toward robots that can work in less structured settings. The company said the model improves dexterity, reliability and safety, helping robots leave the lab for everyday environments. Google also said Gemini 4 Argon, its frontier model, helped accelerate the robotics research behind the release. The company framed the work as progress toward physical artificial general intelligence. Google also said it is releasing the ASIMOV-Jailbreak benchmark as an open-source tool for testing robots against unsafe instructions.

Apptronik's co-founder and CEO, Jeff Cardenas, said the models improved dramatically in just a few weeks of post-training. He said they carried over to Mercedes-Benz production with very little drop-off. The pilot ran on active automotive production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. Factory technicians are affected because the robots take over repetitive kitting work, freeing them to focus on complex build tasks. Monotonous parts sorting is the work the robots were built to relieve, and the companies said it can help keep assembly lines moving.

Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz tested the model in a proof-of-concept on the production lines. In that pilot, Apollo 2 autonomously sorted metal automotive brackets from bulk bins into trays in the order each vehicle needed. The system pairs Gemini Robotics ER, which tracks the workflow, with the Gemini Robotics 2.5 actions model, which controls the hands and arms. Google said its safety features let robots steer around hazards in real time, improving safe task completion by 33% around obstacles and 43% around nearby people. The company reported that its Argon model achieved 99.5% jailbreak resistance, compared with 82% for its previous baseline.

Google presented the release as an advance in dexterity, reliability and safety for robots working alongside people. The company described earlier work, including Gemini Robotics 2 in July 2026, which brought whole-body intelligence to robots. The Gemini Robotics 1.5 model, introduced in September 2025, brought AI agents into the physical world. The first Gemini Robotics model appeared in March 2025 and brought AI into the physical world. Google's releases in this line have built on one another over roughly two years.

Google has not said when Gemini Robotics 2.5 will be generally available beyond its robotics partners. The articles also do not say how many factories or robot fleets will adopt the model. They give no detail on the outcome of the ASIMOV-Jailbreak benchmark beyond Argon's score. Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz have described the pilot as promising progress toward widespread industrial use, but the articles do not say when that might happen.

stories.Headline: Nitrogen Brings Its AI-Powered Advisor Platform to Claude and ChatGPT, Expands Nucleus Capabilities
stories.Summary:
The headline says Nitrogen is bringing its advisor platform to Claude and ChatGPT and expanding its Nucleus capabilities, but the two articles supplied never mention Nitrogen or Nucleus. What they cover is the arrival of personal finance features in Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT, so this account sticks to that. Anthropic introduced Personal Finance as a dedicated feature within Claude on November 5, 2026, and OpenAI had introduced its Finances feature in ChatGPT on May 15, 2026. Both tools let users link bank accounts through Plaid and review spending, investments and savings goals through a conversational interface. Both reportedly give a read-only view of linked accounts, so neither chatbot can move money or change account details.

Claude Personal Finance connects supported bank accounts, credit cards, loans and investment accounts through Plaid, and it began rolling out in beta to Pro, Max and Ultra subscribers in the United States. It works across Claude's web, desktop and mobile applications, though access is being introduced gradually. Anthropic says Claude can see bank names, account names, account types, the last four digits of an account number, balances, credit limits and transaction history. Mint reports that history as up to 2 years, while iTech Post puts it at 24 months. Compatible institutions mentioned include Bank of America, Capital One and Chase, and Claude can build dashboards and flag unusual charges, duplicate transactions and rising bills.

Anthropic is the company behind Claude Personal Finance, and it says conversations inside the Personal Finance hub are not used to train its models by default. The company also says removing a bank account means Claude can no longer use that previously shared financial data. Anthropic has also stated that Claude Personal Finance carries no advertisements or product suggestions, and the company does not offer its own credit cards, loans or savings accounts. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, applies the user's existing ChatGPT data controls to conversations about connected financial accounts. OpenAI says financial account data is removed from its systems within 30 days of a user disconnecting the account.

The Mint article notes that ChatGPT's data controls leave model improvement switched on by default, so users must open Settings and turn off the option called Improve the model for everyone. iTech Post adds that Anthropic's no-training promise covers only the Personal Finance hub, while conversations outside it remain under the user's regular privacy settings. Mint says neither tool is meant to replace a professional financial advisor, and iTech Post says they are not substitutes for banking applications either. iTech Post warns that AI responses can contain errors and that balances may not reflect the latest transactions. Users are advised to check figures against official statements and to consult qualified professionals for important decisions.

On the background, Mint says OpenAI began testing advertisements on selected lower-priced ChatGPT plans in January 2026, while no clear advertising policy has been given for the Finances feature. OpenAI's feature has grown since its May launch, and it now includes weekly financial insights, credit monitoring, stock watchlists, voice support and manual account entry. iTech Post says ChatGPT can reach balances, transactions, investments, liabilities and subscriptions, and can help with expense organization, budgeting and savings planning. Mint describes Anthropic's approach as a deliberate disconnect from promoting finance products. The Mint piece was published on November 9, 2026, and the iTech Post piece followed a day later.

Looking ahead, Mint reports that OpenAI is aiming to widen ChatGPT's financial abilities through a tie-up with Intuit. The partnership is expected to bring more help with credit card applications and tax questions, among other services. Anthropic, for its part, is aiming to partner with banks, wealth managers and other financial services firms to improve Claude Personal Finance. Mint says both tools currently offer more or less the same tracking options, and that Claude's default privacy stance may appeal to users wary of how their financial data is used. The articles leave open when Claude's rollout will reach all eligible users, and neither mentions Nitrogen or Nucleus.

stories.Headline: Nvidia Leadership Scandal Drags on U.S. Stock Futures, Pressures AI Trade
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board opened an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang, who remains in his post for now, according to a Yahoo Finance segment published on November 9, 2026. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence concluded a woman close to Huang was feeding information to Beijing. She was a top executive at Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia. In a letter to employees, Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife and supported the board's investigation. The board said it had no reason to believe that secrets were compromised.

Nvidia shares fell about 5 percent on the day, and the stock sat more than 20 percent below its peak from about a month earlier. The rest of the chip sector rose that day, but the reports reached beyond one executive. Huang has largely shaped America's AI policy toward China, arguing that cutting Chinese firms off from American chips leaves them dependent on U.S. technology. Less than three weeks before the reports, in Berlin, he said he believed the U.S. government would encourage Nvidia to compete around the world.

Huawei is the example Huang's critics and supporters both cite, since Washington cut it off in 2019 over national security concerns. Four years later it shocked the industry with a phone running an advanced chip made in China. The analysis holds that Huang may still be right but has lost the standing to make his case. Hawks in Washington are now likely to win tighter controls, possibly including older chips and cloud access in Southeast Asia.

Deirdre Bosa interviewed Bret Taylor, chairman of OpenAI's board, and Clay Bavor, co-founders of Sierra, which builds AI agents for customer service. Taylor said the Nvidia board's matter was above his pay grade and best left to that board. Bavor said that concentrated power at the top of companies is the flip side of exceptionally strong leadership. Taylor said there is a lot of risk in the AI economy, including data center buildout, chips, and manufacturing, while calling himself bullish on the technology.

Sierra works with established firms, including Santander, founded in 1857, ADT, and Rocket Mortgage, which the interview described as the largest mortgage originator in the country. Bavor said Sierra's clients use its agents to drive revenue growth as well as cut service costs. Taylor argued that new technologies like the web and mobile phones tend to create fertile ground for startups, and that established companies' strengths can become weaknesses. The interview did not say how the Nvidia investigation will conclude or whether Huang will remain CEO.

Two administration officials told Semafor that multiple US Justice Department probes could sweep up Nvidia, as fallout from former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation continues to spread through Washington. One inquiry is an antitrust investigation focused specifically on the chipmaker, according to those officials. Two other probes center on the tech companies Megaspeed and Supermicro. The article was published on November 12, 2026.

The Megaspeed and Supermicro inquiries reportedly focus on the involvement of Alice Huang, whom the article describes as an alleged Chinese spy. The article says Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair with her before he resigned. Nothing in the reporting indicates that the Justice Department intends to bring criminal charges against Nvidia or against Jensen Huang at this time. Semafor's account of the probes rests on the two officials, and the article does not describe any formal public filing or announcement by the department.

Nvidia and the Justice Department declined to comment to Semafor. Megaspeed and Supermicro did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The article does not say whether the probes have produced any findings, subpoenas, or next steps. Its details come entirely from officials speaking to the reporter, and the piece leaves open how the investigations will unfold.

stories.Headline: GIGABYTE Expands Its Local AI Portfolio with the Launch of AI TOP AERO Powered by NVIDIA RTX SPARK™
stories.Summary:
GIGABYTE announced on November 10, 2026, the launch of AI TOP AERO, a new AI desktop powered by the NVIDIA RTX Spark platform, positioned as a Personal AI Studio. The desktop combines an NVIDIA Blackwell architecture GPU, up to 128GB of unified system memory and GIGABYTE's cooling and compact chassis design. The launch expands GIGABYTE's AI PC lineup, which it says brings local AI development, content creation and gaming to personal workspaces. The company's press release was distributed through PR Newswire from Taipei. GIGABYTE says the product launches on November 10, 2026, and regional configurations, pricing and availability will be set by local GIGABYTE announcements.

The AI TOP AERO uses the NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X Superchip, which integrates a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU with an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU. Configurations offer up to 128GB of LPDDR5x unified system memory and up to a 4TB PCIe Gen5 SSD for local models and creative assets. The compact chassis measures approximately one liter, and GIGABYTE integrates its cooling design to provide thermal headroom for sustained AI and creative workloads. Connectivity includes USB Type-C, 10GbE Ethernet and Wi-Fi 7 for peripherals, data transfers and network access. The desktop also supports NVIDIA PAIR (Personal AI Router), which distributes inference tasks across devices on a local network.

GIGABYTE is the company that announced AI TOP AERO, drawing on its hardware design and system integration experience. Nvidia supplies the RTX Spark platform, which the company describes as unifying NVIDIA AI, RTX graphics and unified memory in one slim Windows PC. Nvidia's Asia-Pacific director of technical marketing, Jeff Yen, spoke about the broader RTX Spark product line at a press event in Seoul on November 6. He acknowledged that RTX Spark laptops are priced at the high end of the market and cannot be considered affordable, though he said they draw demand mainly from early adopters and developers. GIGABYTE's release describes the desktop as an addition to its own lineup of AI PCs.

Developers, creators and AI users are the groups the articles identify as the intended audience for AI TOP AERO. The GIGABYTE release says users seeking local computing options want to run models, process data and test applications on their own devices for reasons of data privacy, responsiveness and usage costs. Nvidia said demand for RTX Spark has been concentrated among companies developing AI-based services and applications, and that initial supplies are limited, leaving many customers waiting. Yen said some consumers may find conventional laptops with x86 CPUs and discrete GPUs more reasonable because of the price difference, and he said there is ample room for both markets to coexist. RTX Spark laptops start at approximately 4.7 million won and reach as high as 10 million won depending on specifications.

The articles give some background on the market shift toward local AI. The GIGABYTE release says generative AI has expanded beyond conversational assistants into AI agents, content generation and workflow automation, which has increased user interest in personal AI computing. Nvidia's Yen said running 61 million tokens through the Claude Sonnet 5.5 model in the cloud costs $1,200 per month, while running the same workload on RTX Spark requires only $20 in electricity costs. Nvidia also introduced Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B, an on-device model optimized for RTX Spark, which was trained on high-performance systems and then quantized to 2-bit precision. Nvidia says the model delivers performance comparable to frontier AI models while significantly reducing memory consumption.

The articles do not say how many AI TOP AERO units will be produced, what they will cost in any region, or when they will reach customers outside the launch announcement. They also do not state how long Nvidia's supply constraints will last or whether demand will continue to grow. The GIGABYTE release points readers to local GIGABYTE announcements for regional configurations and pricing, but no such announcements are included in the articles. Whether the desktop's sustained performance matches its claims in practice is not addressed by the articles.

stories.Headline: Alphabet vs. Broadcom: the best AI stocks for risk and reward
stories.Summary:
Alphabet and Broadcom were compared as AI stock options in an Investing.com piece published on November 12, 2026, while Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO that day. The article named Alphabet Class A (GOOGL) the best risk-adjusted AI pick, priced at $298.38 as of November 12, 2026. It described Alphabet as offering AI exposure without depending entirely on Nvidia's chip ecosystem. Broadcom (AVGO) was called the stronger direct Nvidia alternative, rising 4.69% to $361.42 that day. The article's broader framing was that Alphabet offers resilience and valuation while Broadcom offers higher AI-infrastructure sensitivity and risk.

Alphabet's revenue reached $402.84 billion in fiscal 2025, up from $307.39 billion in fiscal 2023, driven by advertising, cloud and AI products. Its trailing P/E was 15.4 times as of September 30, 2026, against Broadcom's 45.2 times, and fair-value upside was 9.1% for Alphabet and 16.2% for Broadcom. Alphabet holds more cash than debt, according to Pro Tips, and its liquid assets exceed short-term obligations. The article warned that AI infrastructure spending could exceed $10 trillion, with neocloud financing remaining vulnerable, as reported on October 15, 2026. Broadcom's latest earnings beat was only 3.43% as of September 2, 2026, and its moderate debt leaves less margin for disappointment.

The article was generated with the support of AI and reviewed by an editor, according to its own disclaimer. Its recommendations were framed as the publication's view: choose GOOGL for resilience and valuation, choose AVGO for higher AI-infrastructure sensitivity and risk. The article advised against treating Nvidia as automatically cheap, citing challenges involving leadership, financing structures, regulation and sector concentration. Yahoo Finance noted that it is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser, and that a Coinbase link on the page pays it for certain activity. Prices shown on the page were stated to be informational only.

Alphabet fell 15.33% over the month to November 12, 2026, after its October 28 earnings release showed EPS of $2.12 against $3.02 expected, a 29.80% miss. Analyst EPS estimates for Alphabet were revised down 4.79% over the 30 days to November 12, 2026. The article identified execution as the key risk for Alphabet, especially if AI changes search economics faster than monetization improves. Broadcom's shares were described as benefiting from custom AI chips and networking. Nvidia's leadership change was reported as a separate headline on the same page.

A separate Stocktwits article, published November 9, 2026, reported that JPMorgan named Meta Platforms and Amazon its preferred internet stocks on Monday, lifting their shares more than 5% each. Analyst Doug Anmuth added Meta to the firm's Analyst Focus List in place of Alphabet, while keeping an Overweight rating on Alphabet. Meta's third-quarter advertising revenue rose 26% year over year to $63.1 billion, and JPMorgan expects its Family of Apps ad revenue to overtake Google Search from the fourth quarter. Amazon's third-quarter AWS revenue jumped 39% to $46 billion, and JPMorgan expects AWS growth above 40% in 2027 and 2028. Google Search revenue growth slowed to 12% in the third quarter, while Google Cloud revenue surged 103% to $30.7 billion, and the firm warned that AI search monetization could take time.

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was bullish for Meta and Alphabet and neutral for Amazon, according to the same article. So far this year, Meta shares had declined about 1%, Alphabet shares had fallen more than 7%, and Amazon shares had gained nearly 20%. The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS), which holds all three stocks, had risen more than 7% over the same period. The Stocktwits piece noted that higher computing costs and infrastructure spending may pressure cash flow for Alphabet. Its own sentiment figures and price moves are the only market data the article provides on these companies.

The articles do not say how the Nvidia leadership change will affect Alphabet, Broadcom or the other stocks they cover. Neither article states whether Alphabet's earnings estimates will be revised again or when AI search monetization will improve. The Investing.com article does not predict where Broadcom's shares will trade after November 12, 2026. The Stocktwits article does not say whether JPMorgan's Overweight rating on Alphabet will change. Neither piece reports how AWS or Meta results will compare with the 2027 and 2028 forecasts over time.

stories.Headline: ST Unveils Industrial MCU With AI Accelerator
stories.Summary:
STMicroelectronics unveiled the STM32H7P industrial microcontroller on November 10, 2026, featuring hardware accelerators for digital signal processing and artificial intelligence workloads. The new chip combines a 520MHz Arm Cortex-M7 processor with a dedicated hardware signal processor and a neural processing unit. Its hardware signal processor accelerates computations that analyze frequency components in signals such as motor vibrations and electrical currents. The neural processing unit delivers AI computing performance of up to 85 giga operations per second. Meanwhile, on the same week, Knewbots and the Beijing Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center jointly unveiled a full-stack industrial embodied AI platform for logistics at CeMAT ASIA 2026.

The STM32H7P is designed for industrial equipment, supporting applications including digital power, motor control and condition monitoring. ST said the signal processor can reduce processing time by up to 80% compared with conventional CPU-based software processing. The MCU supports up to 2MB of embedded flash memory and integrates analog-to-digital converters, digital-to-analog converters and timers. It is designed to operate at temperatures of up to 125 degrees Celsius. The logistics platform runs on a single-brain, multi-machine architecture that integrates various robot forms to bridge the gap between warehousing and the production line.

ST is the company behind the STM32H7P, and it is currently supplying samples to original equipment manufacturers. On the logistics side, Knewbots is a subsidiary of ThunderSoft, and the platform combines Beijing Humanoid's general platform, called Huisikaiwu, with Xiaowu's industrial platform. The two companies signed a strategic partnership in January 2026. The articles do not give a named executive quoted on either announcement, so their own descriptions of the products are the only statements provided.

ST said AI inference for arc fault detection in solar power systems runs 40 times faster than conventional software-based processing. Pricing for the LQFP100 package with 1MB of flash memory starts at $4.43 per unit for orders of 10,000 units. The logistics platform targets industries including automotive, smart logistics, semiconductors, and 3C electronics and home appliances. It addresses labor-intensive bottlenecks such as end-of-line material delivery, shelf-to-station transfers, unsorted picking and automated loading.

The two companies have repeatedly demonstrated their heterogeneous robot cluster collaboration at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, the World Humanoid Robot Games and the World Robot Conference. Beijing Humanoid's Tianyi series handled precision tasks such as valve core assembly and screw picking during the CeMAT ASIA demonstration. An FMR forklift managed heavy-duty pallet transport, while under-ride AMRs shuttled racks and totes between storage zones and workstations. The companies plan to deliver lightweight, mass-producible robotic cluster solutions for automotive manufacturing, high-end equipment and smart factories.

STMicroelectronics plans mass production of the STM32H7P to begin in January 2027, and the articles give no further detail on volumes. The articles do not say when the logistics platform will reach commercial deployment or how many units the companies plan to produce. Neither article states what share of the market either product will address. The articles also leave open how the two announcements relate to each other, since they describe unrelated products from different companies.

stories.Headline: Abu Dhabi data centre leaders unite to meet soaring AI demand
stories.Summary:
Abu Dhabi's push to become a regional artificial intelligence hub is pushing government, hyperscalers and data centre operators toward closer collaboration, as demand for computing power accelerates across the UAE. The topic is set to dominate Data Center World Middle East, which makes its regional debut in Abu Dhabi on 17 and 18 November, bringing together technology companies, infrastructure operators and policymakers. According to JLL, Abu Dhabi already has the Middle East's largest data centre market, with 374MW of IT capacity. The emirate's Department of Energy expects AI infrastructure to need about 2GW of power in its initial phase, rising to 5GW over time, supported by AED250 billion of planned energy and water investment between 2025 and 2035.

Industry leaders argue that meeting these goals requires a coordinated approach rather than isolated projects. Mehdi Paryavi, chairman and chief executive of the International Data Center Authority, said the biggest gap for Gulf data centres is the lack of coordination at scale, and that the region needs adaptable standards, a skilled workforce, long-term planning, reliable energy and greater stability. He added that developers must work with governments, utilities and industry partners to build an ecosystem that supports sustainable, large-scale AI infrastructure. Morten Tidemand, senior director of operations at Khazna Data Centers, which runs 30 data centres with 673MW of capacity, said operational readiness cannot begin at handover, since higher densities require new cooling strategies, maintenance routines and emergency procedures well in advance. He also said staff must understand how increasingly complex systems interact.

The conference will feature speakers from AWS, Google, Microsoft and Oracle, along with representatives from the UAE Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure and the Ministry of Investment. Sessions will cover topics including liquid cooling and managing mixed-density data halls. Tara Gibb, senior event director for Data Center World, said Abu Dhabi has made its commitments and that turning them into capacity that runs reliably at 50°C depends on everyone working from the same plan. The articles do not describe any outcomes from the event, which has not yet taken place at the time of reporting.

stories.Headline: Silicon Valley's herd mentality in cozying up to Trump backfired as Democrats may seek retribution, China closes the AI gap, and anti-Big Tech sentiment grows (Nick Clegg/The Atlantic)
stories.Summary:
Silicon Valley's tech leaders moved to align themselves with Donald Trump in the period after he won reelection in 2024, and Nick Clegg, a former deputy prime minister of the United Kingdom and former president of global affairs at Meta, argues in The Atlantic that the move has backfired. The article was published on November 11, 2026, after MAGA suffered significant losses in the midterm elections. Clegg frames his piece as a critique of a herd mentality in the Valley rather than of individual leaders, and he says the approach has been a near-total failure measured against its own stated goals. The article notes that the tech leaders gave three main reasons at the time, including helping the United States win its AI competition with China.

Clegg writes that over the past 18 months China has been closing the gap with the United States on model performance and chip development, and in some respects has outpaced America. He says public attitudes toward AI in the U.S. are now more negative than under President Biden and worse than almost anywhere else on the planet. The Trump administration has helped some tech firms in their fights with European Union enforcement decisions, Clegg acknowledges, with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick named as an ally. Yet anti-Big Tech sentiment is higher in many parts of the world, and economies including Canada, India, Germany and Brazil are seeking to depend less on what Silicon Valley produces.

Clegg points to several reasons he believes the miscalculation occurred, and he attributes them to the leaders themselves rather than to outside forces. He describes a fear of missing out after Elon Musk spent Election Night 2024 at Mar-a-Lago, which pushed others to follow. He also describes a desire for payback against traditional media, academia and cultural elites, along with what he calls a misunderstanding of politics among wealthy people who assume it is easy. Clegg further says that tech leaders read Trump's narrow popular-vote win as a mandate and assumed the political pendulum would never swing back. He identifies venture capitalists such as Marc Andreessen and David Sacks as influential in the culture wars and in pro-crypto campaigns in the 2024 cycle.

Clegg cites the background of the Biden administration's clumsy treatment of tech leaders and a conservative sense of being unwelcome in the Valley's liberal milieu. He also draws a comparison to Brexit, where a narrow referendum majority was used to justify a hard-line approach, and he notes that a significant majority of Britons now consider it a mistake. He writes that many U.S. voters dislike the cliquishness and extremism of the second Trump administration and see the government's close relationship with the Valley as part of the problem. Clegg says he announced his departure from Meta a few days before Trump's 2025 inauguration. He also says he now works in venture capital himself.

Clegg warns that Democrats now have every incentive to make life uncomfortable for Trump-supporting tech leaders, which he says could lead to a cycle of retribution that would harm Silicon Valley, innovation and Democrats too. He urges major technology companies to stay out of party politics and to maintain open, productive relationships with whoever holds power. He concludes that tech leaders should stop picking political winners and losers. The article does not describe any further scheduled steps or formal responses from the leaders named.

stories.Headline: Oura to acquire AI-native primary care startup Counsel Health for $625M
stories.Summary:
Oura, the smart ring maker and health intelligence platform, has agreed to acquire the artificial intelligence health company Counsel Health. The deal was announced on November 10, 2026, in a news release issued on a Tuesday. It is an all-cash transaction worth $625 million, according to reporting on the announcement. Counsel runs a primary care platform built around AI, which pairs conversational medical AI with access to licensed, board-certified physicians. The deal follows Oura's recent postponement of its initial public offering.

Under the agreement, Oura will pay $625 million in cash, and the acquisition is expected to close before the end of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions and purchase price adjustments. Approximately 70 Counsel employees will join Oura after the transaction. Counsel co-founder and CEO Dr. Muthu Alagappan will become Oura's chief clinical AI officer. Counsel currently has approximately 50 on-demand physicians supporting its services, and it will keep serving enterprise partners, including health plans, healthcare systems, employers and consumer health organizations. The companies plan to build their combined platform across three areas, preventive care, acute care, and specialty and chronic care, the last covering reproductive health, aging and cardiometabolic conditions.

Oura chief executive Tom Hale said members can now act on what they learn about their physiology, with services ranging from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care and referrals. He described the goal as a new model of care that is more immediate, personalized and proactive. Hale called the deal a major step toward the promise of a 24-7 doctor in your pocket. The company's release said Counsel was founded and built by physicians and AI researchers, and that it combines medical AI with in-house physicians. Oura said members can start from an Oura insight or chat directly with Counsel's medical AI, and conversations can escalate to a board-certified Counsel physician within minutes.

Alagappan explained, in the acquisition announcement, that the partnership is meant to connect continuous health information with clinical expertise. Counsel has stressed that wearable data gives physicians extra context about patients' health patterns between appointments. Oura members are the people most directly affected, since they could gain a closer link between personal health monitoring and medical help. Counsel's enterprise customers are also affected, because those services will remain available to organizations whose members do not own an Oura Ring. The articles caution that wearable measurements do not independently establish medical diagnoses, and that clinical assessments and laboratory testing may still be needed depending on a patient's condition.

The deal builds on an existing partnership that brought Counsel's medical AI service into the Oura app in June 2026, as TechCrunch reported. The Verge reported on November 10 that the acquisition follows that earlier integration of the chatbot. Oura disclosed preliminary fiscal 2026 revenue of approximately $1.75 billion, a 92% increase over the previous fiscal year, along with fourth-quarter revenue of $533 million. That quarter ended September 30, 2026, and revenue rose 153% year over year, with adjusted EBITDA of $87 million, a 16% margin. Oura has more than six million members and was valued at approximately $11 billion after a late-stage funding round in 2025.

The IPO had been scheduled for the final week of September but was postponed despite strong demand, citing market uncertainty. Hale said at the time that the company has the luxury of choosing its moment and aims to deliver an extraordinary IPO for employees and investors. After the deal closes, Counsel's roughly 70 employees will join Oura, and Alagappan will take his new role. The companies are expected to share more as the acquisition progresses and their platforms are integrated. The articles leave open the full availability and pricing of future healthcare features, and they give no new date for the IPO.

stories.Headline: 1 Stock-Split AI Stock to Buy Before It Soars 328%, According to a Wall Street Analyst
stories.Summary:
Sandisk, the memory chip maker, announced an 8-for-1 stock split that takes effect on November 19, 2026. The split follows a share price that has more than tripled this year after a 559% gain last year, driven by a memory chip supply shortage tied to the AI boom. Its share price was $885 when the Motley Fool article was published on November 11, 2026, and the company had traded at $1,330 when the split was announced on October 29. Splits, according to the article, are often seen as signs of quality businesses because they usually come only after sustained price gains.

Bank of America research cited in the article found that stocks rose an average of 25.4% in the 12 months after a split announcement from 1980 to 2023, compared with 11.9% for the S&P 500 over the same periods. Applying that average to the October 29 price of $1,330 would put Sandisk at $1,667, about 98% above its current price. Wall Street's median target of $2,100 per share, drawn from 34 analysts, implies about 150% upside, and Ben Reitzes of Melius Research has a $3,600 target. The article also notes that Sandisk plans to begin sampling a product called high-bandwidth flash next year.

Sandisk reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $11 billion, up 378%, and non-GAAP earnings of $49.51 per diluted share, up 40-fold from a year earlier. The company has signed long-term supply agreements with at least eight customers covering about two-thirds of expected NAND flash production in fiscal 2028. Goldman Sachs analysts estimate high-bandwidth flash could cut inference costs by 30% and create a market worth $40 billion to $150 billion by 2030. The article's author, Trevor Jennewine, says the company's pricing power reflects the current shortage rather than a durable competitive advantage.

The bear case in the article rests on the cyclical nature of the memory industry, where NAND prices dropped 70% during the last downturn. Every major chipmaker is expanding capacity, which the article says would likely lead to a supply glut and falling prices. Sandisk held an 11% NAND flash market share in the June quarter, placing it sixth behind Samsung (28%), SK Hynix (19%), Micron (15%), Kioxia (14%) and YMTC (14%), according to Counterpoint Research. The author says Sandisk trades at 6.7 times earnings, and that earnings will decline when the next downturn arrives.

Trevor Jennewine concludes that patient investors might buy a small position while accepting volatility, but he prefers market leaders with durable competitive edges, which he says Sandisk does not have. A separate Live Trading News piece dated November 9, 2026, by Shayne Heffernan, reports that the broader market fell sharply on November 5 after Democrats won both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterms. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% that day and the PHLX Semiconductor index fell 12.25%, with Nvidia down 9.26%. Heffernan describes the sell-off as an overreaction concentrated in AI hardware stocks, which he attributes to worries about data-center moratoriums.

Heffernan cites the Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act, introduced by Senator Bernie Sanders on March 25, 2026, and by Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on June 24, which would halt construction of AI data centers until Congress legislates. Neither bill has moved past committee, and New York enacted a state pause in July. Heffernan expects the bill will not become law within two years, since overriding a presidential veto would require two-thirds of each chamber. He also notes that Goldman Sachs estimated Democratic state and local wins could bring short-term moratoriums affecting about 45% of planned US data-center capacity expansion.

Siemens has raised its growth goals after a surge in orders tied to the global artificial intelligence boom, according to the company's latest report. The only article on the topic covers Thailand's economy, not Siemens.

The one piece of relevant reporting describes an investment wave linked to the AI boom in Thailand. Board of Investment applications in the digital sector reached THB 1.12 trillion in the same period, already above the THB 746 billion recorded for all of 2025. It argues that the gains are narrowly based, with data centers importing much of their high-value equipment and creating relatively few direct jobs. The authors recommend supplier development, wider access to cloud and AI services, and energy reforms to broaden the benefits. The articles do not say how any of this connects to Siemens' results. stories.Headline: Samsung lifts Chungcheong chip plan to $98B as HBM race heats up
stories.Summary:
Samsung has raised its planned chip investment in Chungcheong to $98 billion, a move that comes as competition in high-bandwidth memory intensifies. The articles provided do not give the date or the full details of that announcement, so the account below draws on what they do report about the equipment market around HBM. High-bandwidth memory differs from conventional DRAM because it requires thinning dies, connecting them through through-silicon vias, stacking, bonding, and inspecting them. Each added step creates equipment demand and potential yield losses, which the articles identify as a second source of spending beyond simple capacity growth. Applied Materials agreed on October 26, 2026, to raise its stake in BE Semiconductor Industries to approximately 20 percent of outstanding shares, subject to regulatory requirements.

Lam Research reported September-quarter 2026 revenue of $8.22 billion, up 54.4 percent year over year, with a GAAP operating margin of 40.0 percent. Camtek reported September-quarter revenue of about $161 million, up 28 percent, and projected revenue above $800 million for 2027. The articles name Samsung, SK hynix and Micron as companies investing in HBM capacity, and they attribute the equipment demand to those memory makers. TOWA reported orders of ¥32.97 billion for July through September 2026, up 125.8 percent from the same period of 2025, while its quarterly sales rose 14.1 percent to ¥17.53 billion. TOWA also raised its fiscal-year revenue forecast to ¥71 billion from ¥64 billion and its operating profit forecast to ¥13.15 billion from ¥10.24 billion.

Wonik IPS, based in Pyeongtaek, reported preliminary third-quarter 2026 revenue of about ₩337.8 billion, up 25.8 percent, with operating profit near ₩66.7 billion. The articles do not include a direct statement from Samsung about the $98 billion Chungcheong plan. Analysts and equipment makers are quoted only indirectly through their financial results, and the articles attribute TOWA's growth to AI and data center investment, including HBM, though TOWA also serves other packaging applications. Equipment suppliers such as Lam, KLA, Applied Materials and Camtek stand to benefit, while memory manufacturers carry the capital commitments. The articles do not describe any other specific group affected by the expansion.

The articles describe an AI investment cycle that has been measured mostly through the revenue of Nvidia, Micron, SK hynix and other processor and memory suppliers. The writer, Dr. Robert Castellano, argues that HBM is creating a second opportunity in equipment makers, extending from wafer fabrication into advanced packaging. The articles frame this as a question of whether the spending is a cyclical increase or a more sustained expansion, and they note that the strength has spread beyond the largest U.S. equipment companies. The articles do not say whether Samsung's Chungcheong investment has a start date, a completion schedule, or specific capacity targets. They also leave open whether Applied's BESI stake will receive regulatory approval, and whether the order growth reported by TOWA will convert into sustained shipments.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Joins AFT and UFT's Binding AI Safety Standard
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has signed a legally binding agreement with the American Federation of Teachers and the United Federation of Teachers to establish safety, transparency and privacy protections for its AI products used in K-12 education. The agreement was announced Tuesday, November 10, 2026, by the two unions, and it puts their AI Safety and Privacy Standard for Schools into practice. It automatically covers school districts already using Anthropic's Claude for Teachers. The agreement's 10 provisions address how AI companies handle sensitive school data, communicate with customers and account for risks associated with their technology. Anthropic is the latest company to adopt the standard, following Microsoft, which partnered with the unions in September.

Under the agreement, districts can incorporate the protections into their contracts, which gives them legal recourse if a company fails to meet its obligations. Once incorporated, the provisions become enforceable, allowing a district to seek damages or termination of the agreement for material violations that remain unresolved. Companies generally cannot use student or educator information to develop or refine AI models, apart from a limited security and safety exception, and cannot sell that data or use it to target advertisements. The restrictions cover prompts, uploaded files and generated responses, and they also apply to previously collected data even after the agreement expires. The standard requires human review of high-risk decisions involving AI, prohibits AI companions within its scope, and requires notification of confirmed or reasonably suspected data breaches within 72 hours.

Anthropic and the unions describe the agreement as a major step for AI safety in classrooms, and Anthropic's head of beneficial deployments, Elizabeth Kelly, said it builds trust with teachers, students and school systems. AFT President Randi Weingarten called it a legally binding contract that ensures algorithms can never replace human judgment, relationships or responsibility. UFT President Michael Mulgrew said the agreement continues the unions' work to keep students and their families safe and said he was heartened that Anthropic sees the value of student privacy. Microsoft committed to making the protections available to U.S. school districts beginning November 1. Parent advocates and a policy group offered differing views: psychotherapist Nicole Runyon called it a positive step, while Michael Marinaccio of the Center for Responsible Technology said such agreements are too little, too late.

The unions have argued that existing federal student privacy law, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, was not written specifically to address generative AI. Mulgrew said that ideally the federal government would step in, but since it has not, teachers unions are working to hold AI companies accountable. Claude for Teachers was released July 14 and gives teachers premium Claude tools for free. Anthropic contributed $500,000 to the AFT's National Academy for AI Instruction in July 2025, alongside $10 million from OpenAI and $12.5 million from Microsoft. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services recommended in August that districts evaluate products based on demonstrated educational benefits, but those recommendations are advisory rather than binding.

The agreement applies only to Claude for Teachers, which is designed for educators rather than students, so provisions governing students' direct use of AI do not apply. Student information entered by teachers remains protected, and any future Anthropic educational product offered directly to K-12 students would need to meet the standard. The articles do not say how or whether the protections will be enforced in practice. Anthropic, the AFT and the UFT did not respond to requests for comment from the Daily Caller News Foundation. The articles also do not say whether Anthropic plans to offer student-facing products, and they leave open how the standard will work for districts that do not adopt it.

stories.Summary:
Fibocom, a Chinese wireless communication module company, showcased its connectivity, AI and robotics technologies at electronica 2026 in Munich, Germany, with a press release dated November 12, 2026. The company offers OEMs options ranging from wireless modules and PCBA designs to application-specific algorithms and system integration support. Its robotic mower portfolio covers three sensing and navigation architectures, which the company presented as options for different design needs. Fibocom's exhibits also included an AI companion solution and board-level wireless products for broadband, portable and IoT applications. The company's showcase framed these products as ways for manufacturers to build devices across consumer, industrial and connectivity markets.

The first robotic mower architecture is a lightweight monocular-vision solution without LiDAR or RTK, designed for cost-optimized products. The second combines monocular vision with 3D LiDAR for complex, obstacle-rich gardens, while the third pairs stereo vision with RTK for depth perception and high-precision positioning across larger lawns. Beyond sensor selection, Fibocom provides core hardware, proprietary perception and navigation algorithms, and system integration support to help manufacturers build on existing solution architectures. The AI companion solution combines the MagiCore core unit, AI Cloud, app, IP Agent customization, and connectivity and AI token services. Fibocom also supports complete device customization and delivery, and its 5G CPE and outdoor unit PCBA solutions are shown alongside MiFi and Dongle designs.

Fibocom states that its robotic mower and AI companion offerings rely on its own hardware, algorithms and services. The company says it is China's first wireless communication module company listed on both the A-share and H-share markets, founded in 1999. Fibocom describes wireless communication and artificial intelligence as its core technologies, providing integrated hardware and software solutions for industry applications. Its one-stop solutions include cellular communication, AI, automotive and GNSS modules, along with AI toolchains, AI Agent, global connectivity and cloud services. The company says these products support digital intelligence upgrades in robotics, consumer electronics, low-altitude economy, intelligent transportation, smart retail and smart energy.

The press release presents these offerings as serving OEMs and device makers that want to accelerate product development. The press release names customers and applications that Fibocom says are affected by its products. A zodiac-themed AI companion toy called AiMOON, developed by a customer using MagiCore, demonstrates integration into character-based consumer products. Customer devices on display cover applications in asset tracking, industrial monitoring and remote health monitoring. An AI smart pet collar combines Fibocom cellular connectivity with pet tracking, activity monitoring and AI-based pet vocalization recognition.

The robotics showcase also featured development kits and stereo camera hardware from D-Robotics. Fibocom's component portfolio includes LE270 and LE271 LTE Cat.1 bis modules, the low-power IoT module MQ771, and the MGB GNSS series. A separate BusinessKorea article, dated November 11, 2026, reports that Doosan Corp. also participated in electronica 2026, held in Munich, Germany, from November 10 to 13. Doosan Corp. showed electronic materials for AI data centers, semiconductor packaging, automotive electronics, and 5G and 6G communications.

Its centerpiece was high-end copper clad laminate for AI accelerators and optical modules, which the company says has low dielectric constant and low dielectric loss properties. Doosan also introduced Patterned Flat Cable for electric vehicle battery systems, which it says can reduce weight and volume by more than 80% compared with conventional wiring harnesses. The company said it can produce 2.5-meter PFC through a roll-to-roll process it developed for the first time in the world. The Doosan article says the company has led the localization of CCL since 1974 and now supplies global AI semiconductor companies. To meet rising demand, Doosan is expanding domestic production lines and building new production bases in Thailand and China.

An official said the company will reflect market trends and customer requirements from the exhibition in product development. The article describes Doosan's European participation as an opportunity to establish its position in the European market. The Fibocom release does not state any follow-up plans beyond offering integration support and customized development for its customers. stories.Headline: AI-assisted reverse engineering challenges proprietary software
stories.Summary:
AI-assisted reverse engineering is making it easier for developers to inspect software and infer how it works, and industry experts say this trend poses new challenges for proprietary software and intellectual property protection. Nishant Tiwari, a software engineer at PayPal and a tech content creator with over 2.8 million Instagram followers, used an AI-assisted workflow to inspect Uber's web application and examine its pricing. His analysis of Uber's client-side code identified scripts that appeared to access battery status and other device information, including browser and hardware attributes. He tested the same ride across four phones, three Android devices and an iPhone, repeating the experiment five to six times, and found a correlation between battery levels and fares. Tools such as Reverse Engineering Anything (REA), an open-source GitHub project created by GitHub user morluto, enabled these findings by connecting AI agents to reverse-engineering tools.

The project has over 447,000 stars on GitHub, up from about 10,000 in early October, and ranks among the platform's top five most-starred repositories. Reverse engineering involves examining a finished software product to understand how it works, such as inspecting a compiled binary, using a debugger, or analysing how an application responds to different inputs. Security researcher Himanshu Anand said the process traditionally required considerable technical expertise, including interpreting assembly instructions. He said large language models have lowered that barrier and estimated that a task that previously took a month could now take "one or two hours" with AI assistance. For enterprises, the question is how much of a product's functionality customers can reconstruct from the code and behaviour available to them.

AI-assisted analysis can help recreate individual features, particularly when their behaviour is visible through a client application, but reconstructing an entire product is limited when core processing happens on remote servers. Anand pointed to services such as Gmail, where users can only conduct black-box testing, which he described as "very limited." Abhishek Agarwal, President of Judge India and Global Delivery at The Judge Group, said AI can help developers identify relevant functions and reduce time spent on false leads, but much of a product's behaviour may depend on a private service. He noted that a recreated feature may also lack the original product's updates and support, which customers pay for alongside the software. Agarwal suggested comparing conventional reverse engineering with AI-assisted analysis under similar conditions, with two engineering teams given the same access and assessed for reliability and human effort.

Bharadwaj Jaishankar-Bharadwaj, Partner at CMS INDUSLAW, said copyright protects software code as a literary work and that there is no copyright in an idea, only in its expression. Shantanu Sahay, Partner in Litigation at Anand & Anand, said recreating a feature does not automatically infringe copyright, since the legal question depends on what has been copied and whether those elements are protected. Anand dismissed concerns that AI tools will end proprietary software, comparing it to saying Microsoft is dead because of open source. Under Section 52(1)(ac) of India's Copyright Act, the observation, study, or testing of a computer program is permitted to determine its underlying ideas and principles while performing acts necessary for the functions for which it was supplied. Section 52(1)(ab) covers acts necessary to obtain information essential for interoperability of an independently created program, subject to conditions including lawful possession and the information not being otherwise readily available.

These provisions do not give a blanket permission to copy or commercially reproduce software, and Sahay noted that licence and non-disclosure agreements can also restrict decompilation. Agarwal said companies should treat client applications and binaries as inspectable rather than relying on unpublished source code. Obfuscation and anti-tampering measures can make analysis harder but may only delay it. He recommended moving core business logic away from distributed clients where practical, removing secrets from software builds, tightening API boundaries, monitoring for repeated probing, and reviewing binaries, packages, and front ends at each release. He also advised changing the design assumption to consider what happens when an AI agent can inspect a product repeatedly and cheaply.

stories.Headline: Investors worry the AI trade needs Nvidia's Huang and its largesse
stories.Summary:
Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy linked to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, pitched a multimillion-dollar AI infrastructure project to investors, according to a Financial Times report. The pitch claimed she could secure Nvidia's advanced chips and cited Chinese technology giant Alibaba as a prospective client. Huang and her business partner Kang Wei sought investment in early 2025 for a Southeast Asian data-centre project. The proposal was estimated to be worth hundreds of millions of dollars, according to the FT, which cited two investors who were approached. During the pitch, the pair said they had no problem securing Nvidia graphics processing units.

The proposed project raises questions about how advanced Nvidia chips could reach Chinese businesses through infrastructure located outside mainland China. US export controls restrict Chinese companies from owning certain advanced AI chips. Chinese businesses can, however, lease computing capacity from overseas data centres, subject to applicable restrictions. Documents reviewed by the FT showed that Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company, through subsidiaries in 2024. People familiar with the company described Alibaba as Megaspeed's anchor customer and largest client.

Alice Huang is a former executive at Megaspeed, and allegations say she was recruited by Chinese intelligence to build a relationship with Jensen Huang. The allegations say she was meant to influence his position on US restrictions on advanced chip exports to China. The allegations have not been independently established. Beijing has rejected the espionage claims, while Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing related to chip smuggling. Jensen Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair and apologized to his wife and family.

US intelligence officials reportedly believe Alice Huang was connected to a Chinese espionage effort targeting Jensen Huang. The alleged aim was to gather information about the Nvidia chief and sway his efforts to persuade Washington to ease AI chip export restrictions. Nvidia's independent directors have launched an investigation into whether he was targeted in a foreign intelligence operation. The company has said it has no reason to believe its national security interests or confidential information were compromised. The allegations have renewed attention to Nvidia's business dealings in China and the security of its global AI chip supply chain.

The FT report and the allegations leave open whether the proposed data-centre project was ever funded or built. They also leave open the outcome of Nvidia's investigation into whether Jensen Huang was targeted. Whether Alibaba's ties to Megaspeed breach any restrictions has not been addressed in the articles. The articles do not say whether Washington will change its chip export policy.

stories.Headline: Carrier delivers consistent, human-centered employee support with Microsoft 365 Copilot
stories.Summary:
Carrier Global Corporation, a global leader in intelligent climate and energy solutions, built an AI agent called Here for You to help its more than 200 Global People Services advisors deliver consistent human resources support. The story was published by Microsoft on November 11, 2026. Advisors supporting employees across Asia, Europe, and the Americas had detailed HR procedures but no shared model for responses. Carrier built the agent with Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Copilot Studio, grounding it in SharePoint content. Here for You has since become one of Carrier's most actively used agents.

The agent gives advisors on-demand guidance for requests, structured replies, tone checks, and relevant process information. Advisors receive requests in ServiceNow, open Here for You in Microsoft 365, enter details or a draft, and then review and adapt the output before returning it through ServiceNow. Carrier is working toward merging Here for You directly into ServiceNow, but that integration is not yet complete. Advisors remain accountable for interactions, and Carrier has applied internal privacy, security, access, and Copilot Studio governance controls. The model defines four stages: connecting personally, confirming the need, owning the resolution, and closing with clarity.

Magda Warda, Executive Director of Global People Services at Carrier, said the agent provides greater response time, accuracy, and clarity without replacing human interaction. Cheryl Rearick, Vice President of Talent and Employee Experience, said the goal is to turn support into moments of connection by pairing technology with empathy. Shraddha Lama, Manager of Global People Services, described Copilot as a force multiplier that gives advisors contextual guidance in seconds. Warda said that trust accelerated the project, and that Copilot Studio let the team quickly turn trusted knowledge into a solution.

Employees in Asia, Europe, and the Americas are affected by the change in how advisors respond to their requests. Advisors supporting employees in Japan and China described clearer local-language responses. Advisors who once asked managers to review messages can now respond on their own. The agent creates consistency without forcing every advisor into an identical voice. Carrier's digital and AI teams identified Here for You as one of its most actively used agents across the business.

Before this work, advisors often asked managers to review unclear or sensitive responses, which risked inconsistent experiences and repeat follow-ups within service-level deadlines. Carrier had Microsoft 365 Copilot available across the company, and advisors worked between Microsoft 365 and ServiceNow. Carrier describes itself as a company with more than 10,000 employees, based in the United States, in the industrials and manufacturing sector. Microsoft's article notes the company's goal is to be more tech and more human as routine HR transactions become automated. Global People Services measures success by whether customer satisfaction is rising and whether employees feel better treated.

The articles do not say how many interactions the agent has handled or how satisfaction has changed. Carrier is still working on the ServiceNow integration, and the timing of its completion is not stated. Warda said Carrier continues exploring AI across the business, but the articles give no further plans. The articles also do not describe any results beyond the advisor feedback and usage described.

stories.Headline: ByteDance Is Reportedly Working On Its Own AI Agent
stories.Summary:
ByteDance is reportedly preparing its own AI agent, according to a Bloomberg report relayed by Engadget on November 11, 2026. The Chinese company is said to be readying an AI assistant that could be revealed in the coming weeks. It is meant to compete with Meta's Muse agent and to serve a similar role. The report does not say what ByteDance will call the agent or how it will work.

Muse has already drawn more than 10 million users, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has predicted that it could generate more revenue per user than the company's existing family of apps. Quartz reports that Meta launched Muse in early September and that 10 million people in the U.S. downloaded it within 40 days. Buying was the most popular task, with purchases averaging more than $200. Muse is also expected to play a big part in Meta's AI glasses, and the company has previewed a standalone charm for it. It is unclear whether ByteDance plans to put its own agent into hardware.

On the ByteDance side, Bloomberg reported that cofounder Zhang Yiming recently told employees it would likely take until at least 2029 or 2030 for the company's AI efforts to catch up with the frontier companies. ByteDance has mostly been known in AI for its video generator, Seedance, whose clips went viral on social media earlier this year and drew legal scrutiny from US-based studios. ByteDance did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Engadget. Meta's chief executive has said the company would take a commission on purchases made through Muse.

An agent from the TikTok maker would likely raise fresh concerns about data privacy and how much access personal agents should get. Quartz notes that OpenAI followed Meta with its own always-on agent, Dots, a few weeks after Muse launched. Agentic web traffic roughly tripled from August to September, most of it heading to e-commerce sites, and retailers responded in different ways. Amazon blocked Muse almost immediately, while Walmart announced a system giving each agent its own profile with approval or spending limits, and JPMorgan said it would not let outside agents into customer accounts. Economist Lindsay Owens has argued that AI shopping agents should be held to a fiduciary-style standard, legally bound to work for the shopper, though no such rule is in place.

stories.Headline: Software Transparency Is Changing: Allan Friedman on SBOM, AI BOMs and What Comes Next
stories.Summary:
Allan Friedman, a cybersecurity policy expert who helped drive early government and industry work on the Software Bill of Materials, discussed the evolution of software transparency on the SecurityWeek Podcast, hosted by Brian Schleifer. The conversation covered SBOMs, AI Bills of Materials, vulnerability management and the Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange. Friedman described software as assembled rather than written, noting that what it is assembled from is more software. The interview was reported in articles published on November 10 and November 11, 2026.

Friedman said producing an SBOM is not the end goal, since the real value lies in what organizations and their suppliers do with the information. He argued that a supplier able to generate an accurate SBOM shows an early sign of supply chain maturity. During a Log4j-style vulnerability or a malicious update, that capability lets suppliers determine exposure quickly and shortens response time for customers. He also said SBOM data should feed vulnerability management, asset management, procurement and continuous risk management instead of sitting as a static document.

Friedman identified the Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange as a companion to the SBOM, providing a machine-processable way to say whether a vulnerability actually affects a product. He said this helps separate the presence of a vulnerable component from an exploitable condition, which matters as security teams face growing volumes of vulnerability data. He also described the emergence of AI BOMs, which would document the model, its supporting data, external data sources and the infrastructure used to operate the system. Friedman argued that transparency should favour defenders, because attackers can already identify components through reverse engineering while defenders need visibility across thousands of systems.

Friedman suggested that the different transparency mechanisms, including cryptographic and hardware bills of materials, could eventually converge, which he jokingly called an "omnibomb." The articles note that interoperability remains a challenge, since two quality SBOM tools analyzing the same software may produce different dependency graphs. Friedman pointed to continuing work among governments, cybersecurity agencies, industry and the open source community to define expectations for the SBOM ecosystem. The articles state that the stated goal is continuous software transparency that supports rapid risk decisions.

stories.Headline: North Carolina artificial intelligence experts weigh in on our AI anxieties
stories.Summary:
The North Carolina Department of Information Technology, known as NCDIT, is seeking artificial intelligence vendors to help integrate and implement generative AI within state government agencies, according to a Spectrum News report published November 9, 2026. The state is exploring how AI could play a larger role in everything from online state services to the tools government employees use behind the scenes. Proposals from potential vendors are due November 30. The effort is meant to give agencies a simpler route to AI tools that are secure and trusted, while providing employee training and security safeguards.

The plan is built around protecting personal information, making sure people can understand how the state reaches its decisions, and keeping humans accountable when something goes wrong. State Director of Cybersecurity Laura Rodgers described AI as a tool rather than a replacement for existing services, and she said the state's approach differs from some industry practices where workers are pressed to use AI or face dismissal. NCDIT Secretary and State Chief Information Officer Nate Denny said in a statement that the aim is to deliver government services to residents better and faster and to free employees to spend more time serving the public. Rodgers argued that the deliberate, guardrails-first approach should make residents feel safe, though she said public trust will remain critical.

A separate WUNC News broadcast from November 11, 2026, approached public worry about AI from another angle. Host Jeff Tiberii, who co-hosts the station's "Due South" program, convened a panel to separate fearmongering from real anxieties and to discuss how AI is shaping society and individuals. The guests were Lee Rainie, director of the Imagining the Digital Future Center at Elon University, Emmy Martin, a technology reporter for the New York Times and a UNC alumna, and Saif Khairat, chief AI officer and vice provost for AI at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, who is also a professor in the School of Nursing. The program, which runs about 50 minutes, was published with a description noting that headlines about AI tend to frighten audiences. Taken together, the two reports show state officials promoting cautious adoption while public discussion focuses on separating real risks from exaggerated fears.

OpenAI reported that its quarterly revenue rose about 50 percent to $10 billion in the third quarter, according to the Wall Street Journal, which reported the figures on Tuesday. Documents the newspaper viewed showed the company telling investors that its adjusted operating margin improved to -109 percent from -150 percent in the prior quarter. Its operating losses, however, widened to $10.9 billion from $10.1 billion.

The disclosure matters because investors are watching the finances of AI startups closely as they weigh profitability concerns against enthusiasm for the sector. Rival Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is preparing an initial public offering that could value the startup at about $1.4 trillion. Anthropic has started a roadshow for the share sale, which is expected to set a benchmark for the industry. The Reuters report noted that the OpenAI figures underscore strong investor appetite for AI companies despite these concerns.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on the report. The Wall Street Journal was the source of the financial details, which were drawn from documents it viewed. Reuters carried the story and reported that the company had not yet replied when it published. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Meta AI Cheat Sheet: Features, Pricing, and How to Use It
stories.Summary:
Meta has launched Muse Ember, a small AI model designed for large-scale, repetitive tasks run by AI agents, announced on November 9, 2026. The model targets businesses and developers who want to automate coding, document processing, data extraction and other routine workflows at a lower cost. Ember is the smallest of Meta's Muse models and is built for agentic workflows that execute several smaller tasks, such as coding subtasks and tool calls. It was trained with Muse Wonder Full, which Meta says is the first of its kind it has released, a development confirmed by Meta Superintelligence Labs lead Alexandr Wang. Meta's Muse family also includes Muse Spark, Muse Image and Muse Wonder, and Ember is positioned as part of that family rather than as a replacement for it.

Ember is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. It natively supports text, images, audio and video, and has a context window of 1 million tokens with up to 512,000 output tokens. That capacity lets it handle large documents, screenshots, charts, meeting recordings and videos without switching models. Meta describes the division of labor between its models with the line "Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume," meaning larger models handle complex planning while Ember handles repetitive execution. The company says Ember works alongside bigger models rather than replacing them, and it is available through developer services.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Ember delivers more intelligence per dollar than rivals such as Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna. Meta reported benchmark results on November 9, 2026, alongside Artificial Analysis, showing Ember scoring 40.9% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, ahead of Claude Haiku 5.5 at 39.2% and GPT-6 Luna at 16.4%. On the Artificial Analysis Index, Ember and Claude Haiku 5.5 each scored 36, while GPT-6 Luna scored 28. Ember did not lead every benchmark, as Claude Haiku 5.5 scored higher on FrontierCode 2.0-AA. Developers and businesses running high-volume automated workflows are the groups the model is aimed at.

Meta's broader consumer assistant, Meta AI, is free for everyday use and is available across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, Threads, web, iOS, Android and compatible smart glasses. Meta AI is powered by the Muse model family, with Muse Spark handling conversation and reasoning. Meta One Core costs $7.99 per month and Meta One Premium costs $19.99 per month in the US, offering expanded creative-tool access. Meta says AI interactions can be used to personalize content and ads in supported regions, with sensitive topics such as health and political views excluded from ad personalization. Users can review these controls through Meta's Privacy Center and can use Incognito Chat.
