stories.Headline: Op-ed: When local government adopts AI, who is accountable?
stories.Summary:
Vista Irrigation District's board adopted an artificial intelligence policy on September 9, according to an October 14 report in The Coast News, while noting that the district had not yet used AI in its operations. The district's director of administration, Shallako Goodrick, said that employees might still use freely available writing tools. She named confidentiality, discrimination, staff training, and vendor use among the agency's main concerns. The article presents the policy as a sensible first step toward governing AI before it is widely deployed.

The op-ed argues that a policy alone does not show that AI is being used responsibly. Its central question is whether employees can spot an error, challenge it, and stay accountable for decisions made on the public's behalf. The author, Glenn Broder, uses the example of an employee relying on an AI summary of a customer complaint that misses an applicable rule, with a supervisor approving the draft because it sounds reasonable. In that case, he says, responsibility rests with the employee and the agency, not the software. Oversight, he adds, must mean more than clicking approve.

Broder recommends five steps for local agencies. They should define where AI is allowed and where it is not, with stronger independent review for higher-stakes decisions such as service, payment, or eligibility. They should protect confidential information and write vendor contracts that spell out what data is processed, where it goes, and who can access it. Staff should be trained to test AI output by checking claims against evidence, and they need a clear path to escalate when evidence is missing. Finally, agencies should publicly explain how AI is used, which decisions stay human, and how errors are corrected.

Broder also notes that AI may reach agency services through third-party vendors even when an agency never buys an AI system itself. He draws a firm line between adopting a policy and proving it works, since proof requires evidence that training is effective, vendors comply, and errors are caught before they reach residents. He credits Vista Irrigation District for acting before deployment, and he urges North County agencies to make their oversight visible and verifiable. His closing principle is that AI should assist public servants and never excuse them from exercising public judgment. The articles do not describe any specific incident or further schedule of action beyond this.

stories.Headline: Cribl acquires Tero to accelerate AI-native observability
stories.Summary:
Cribl, a San Francisco-based AI platform for telemetry, acquired Tero, a developer of intelligence tools for observability data, to expand its AI-native observability capabilities. The acquisition was disclosed during the KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 week and was reported on November 10 and November 11, 2026. Tero's three co-founders, chief executive Ben Johnson, CTO Adam Cohen and COO Nihar Singhal, will join Cribl with their engineering team. The deal is Cribl's third acquisition in four months, following its purchase of CardinalOps in July and the addition of Radiant Security's AI SOC technology in August. Tero's technology helps organisations find information that adds little value to their observability operations, without changing their existing workflows.

The Tero team will focus on four areas at Cribl: host monitoring, application performance monitoring, federated observability and AI-native observability. These capabilities will be built on Cribl's existing open platform, which lets customers collect, route and refine telemetry data. Johnson will take the role of VP of observability and help lead the company's product strategy in the sector. Cribl said Tero brings observability market expertise, established customer and partner relationships, and engineering experience that will accelerate product development. The deal also supports Cribl's strategy of bringing observability and security products together on a shared telemetry platform.

Cribl's co-founder and CEO, Clint Sharp, said the company's customers already trust the platform with their data and that Johnson has spent a decade on the problem of helping engineers control their data. Sharp said Johnson and his team will help Cribl build observability directly on that platform for engineers and the AI agents working alongside them. Johnson, who is now Cribl's VP of observability, said Tero was started to help engineers understand their telemetry rather than simply collect more of it. He said the team could either compete with Cribl or build the product together with it. Johnson previously co-founded Timber, the company behind the open source Vector data pipeline, which Datadog acquired in 2021.

The acquisition affects engineering teams that must manage large volumes of telemetry data across their observability tools, since Tero's technology shows where low-value data is accumulating. Cribl's platform is used by organisations for IT and security telemetry, and it supports the company's own SIEM, observability and AI SOC products. Cribl, which was founded in 2018, also provides a control plane for routing and governing AI traffic, protecting sensitive information and monitoring AI usage, costs, performance and risk. Its platform is designed to let IT and security teams decide how they manage and send data without paying to store the same information multiple times. Customers and partners of Tero are also affected, as Cribl said the acquisition brings established relationships with them.

Tero had been developing its technology as a standalone intelligence layer for observability data before the acquisition, and its co-founders had built it to identify and rectify low-value telemetry across various observability tools. Cribl's earlier acquisitions included CardinalOps in July and Radiant Security's AI SOC technology in August, which the company completed before buying Tero. Johnson's earlier company, Timber, had developed telemetry infrastructure that Datadog bought in 2021. Cribl's platform has been used by customers and AI agents to collect, route and refine data, and the company has offered this platform as the base for its observability roadmap. The articles describe these earlier moves as part of the company's wider push into observability and security.

The articles do not state the price of the acquisition or the terms of the deal. They also do not say when the new observability products built with Tero's team will be released, or how the Tero technology will be integrated with Cribl's existing offerings. The articles give no details on whether Tero's existing customers will continue to be supported as separate products. They also leave open how Cribl's observability roadmap will change once the Tero team begins work and whether further acquisitions are planned.

stories.Headline: Adobe Firefly AI Assistant Can Now Take On Recurring Tasks For You
stories.Summary:
Adobe announced a significant expansion of the agentic capabilities in its Creative Cloud suite at its Max conference in Miami, with the news landing on November 10, 2026. An updated version of its Firefly AI Assistant can now carry out multi-step tasks. Engadget framed the move as Adobe taking a page from Anthropic and OpenAI by dipping its toes into proactive agents. The company has already brought Firefly and other generative AI features to much of the suite, including Photoshop, Premiere and Illustrator.

The updated assistant comes with a new planning mode, which lets users review and edit the agent's proposed workflow before approving it to move forward. Users can also pick a specific model to orchestrate the tasks, or leave that choice to Adobe's software. There is finer control over customization too, so users can define colors and brand guidelines that apply across the projects the assistant takes on. Adobe is also previewing new always-on agents built to handle recurring tasks.

In a preview shared with Engadget, a user prompted the assistant to sort through footage as it was uploaded to a project. The assistant offered to organize the raw files, apply LUTs automatically, clean up audio and back up the files, and the user approved this in the planning mode. The user then asked the assistant to prepare a social media promotion campaign for the project. Adobe is also bringing a new agent to the Premiere mobile app, which debuted on iOS last year and later arrived on Android.

The Premiere mobile agent is designed to help users make edits using natural language, and it is launching first in private preview before a broader rollout. Adobe is also testing a new set of MCP connections that give a user's chosen chatbot local access to Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere and After Effects. With that access, the chatbot could do things like edit layers for the user. Zorana Gee, the company's senior director of agentic product, was shown demoing how entrepreneurs could use the assistant to create social posts for their small businesses.

Engadget's writer wondered whether Adobe's end goal was to eventually bypass the creatives who have long been its customers, noting that far fewer people are skilled with Photoshop and Premiere than might want to use their capabilities. Gee answered that Adobe is ultimately a creative company serving creatives, and that it will meet people wherever they are on that continuum, with the aim of letting anybody hone their craft. The writer also asked about Artcraft, a free Adobe alternative made possible by the growing sophistication of coding models from Anthropic and OpenAI. Gee said she felt the professionalism, security and reliability of Adobe's products would keep users invested in its ecosystem.

Separately, the Verge reported that Disney and Adobe signed a multiyear partnership, also announced at the Max conference, to develop proprietary artist-led generative AI models for Disney's production pipeline. Under the deal, Adobe will give Disney early access to its latest technologies for everything from theme parks and the cruise line to ESPN content. Through Adobe Firefly Foundry, Disney will work directly with Adobe on models tailored to its properties, trained on character attributes, environments and visual styles. Adobe said Disney's Imagineering R&D division already uses the Firefly platform for theme park development, and the new work will also expand creative workflows at Walt Disney Studios.

The Verge noted this is the latest example of Disney embracing generative AI, following a previous deal with OpenAI and involvement with Character.AI's bankruptcy. Bloomberg reported last week that Disney is preparing to lay off thousands of staffers and is targeting 20 percent annual cost savings. That would be its fourth round of job cuts in 2026. Adobe said the collaboration will also explore emerging technologies, including responsibly developed AI, and will look at how AI can enhance engagement with sports fans.

stories.Headline: Picus Security Launches Production-Safe Agentic Pentesting for Autonomous Testing and Defense
stories.Summary:
Picus Security, an autonomous exposure validation company, announced on November 12, 2026 a new product called Picus Autonomous Penetration Testing. The capability puts AI agents on the offensive, letting them think like attackers, chain real exploits toward an organization's most valuable assets, and show what a breach would look like under governance the agent cannot override. The company said the launch rebuilds its automated penetration testing for this agentic era, drawing on five years of enterprise deployments and thousands of automated pentests. Picus also framed the release as a response to AI models that find and weaponize vulnerabilities quickly.

The article says the pace of threats has changed sharply, with 36,971 CVEs published in the third quarter of 2026, more than three times the prior year. Against that pace, it argues, a pentest run once a month leaves an organization untested for the other 29 days, and most organizations test only once a year. The product's engine reads the live environment, picks the next technique and target, links findings into attack paths, and attempts exploits, while the business approves scope and techniques beforehand and hard-deny rules block destructive actions. A single click stops all activity, every action is logged for audit, and teams choose a Cautious, Standard, or Elevated setting plus either fully agentic execution or a deterministic, pre-tested technique library.

Results arrive as attack paths backed by evidence, and findings from three Picus products feed one shared, prioritized backlog. Volkan Erturk, co-founder and CTO of Picus Security, said that every security leader now faces an attacker who never sleeps and that the only credible answer is continuous testing at machine speed. He argued that running such a system in a real enterprise takes more than AI, requiring years of learning about what an autonomous system may and may not do in production. He said the company built the agentic engine on those rules so it can be bold in its reasoning and disciplined in its actions.

The article notes that the full-agentic mode is available through an early access program, while the platform itself is available today to Picus customers. Picus, which is headquartered in San Francisco and pioneered Breach and Attack Simulation in 2013, describes its platform as validating exposures and controls in one loop. The article lists several industry recognitions the company has received, including a Gartner Peer Insights Customers' Choice designation and a Frost Radar 2026 Innovation Leader rating. stories.Headline: Cloud native developer population hits 21.2 million globally
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Native Computing Foundation and the research firm SlashData published a new report showing that the global cloud native developer population reached 21.2 million in the third quarter of 2026. TechGig covered the findings on November 11, 2026, while The New Stack ran its own piece the day before, on November 10, 2026. That figure represents roughly 41 per cent of all developers worldwide, according to the report. The report also found that 75 per cent of cloud native developers now use AI coding tools. The New Stack headlined its coverage with that statistic and brought in Jonathan Bryce to explain the reasons behind it.

The 21.2 million total compares with 15.6 million a year earlier and 19.9 million in the first quarter of 2026. On AI use, 75 per cent of cloud native developers use AI coding tools, against 55 per cent of non-cloud native developers. Meanwhile, 67 per cent of cloud native developers are integrating AI into their services, while only 38 per cent of their non-cloud native counterparts do the same. Among developers who integrate AI into their services, 49 per cent reported having agentic systems in production. In North America, 21 per cent of cloud native developers use AI to draft code before reviewing it, while 12 per cent use autonomous agents for coding tasks.

The report comes from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData, and Liam Bollmann-Dodd, a principal market research consultant at SlashData, commented on its meaning. He stated that cloud native maturity is becoming an important indicator of how actively developers engage with AI. The New Stack presented the findings alongside an explanation from Jonathan Bryce of why so many cloud native developers ship code with AI. The portion of that article available here does not include Bryce's explanation itself, only its headline framing. TechGig, for its part, summarized the report's findings in a short piece under its Software and DevOps section.

The report found that platform engineering is becoming standard practice, with 93 per cent of developers now working at organisations that use some form of DevOps standardisation or internal developer platform. That share has risen from 77 per cent in the third quarter of 2025, a gain of 16 percentage points. Developers who have not yet added AI functionality named cost, data privacy, and security as their primary concerns. Backend developers show specific patterns of technology use, with 40 per cent using API gateways and 30 per cent using microservices. A further 21 per cent of backend developers use observability tools, and 19 per cent use Kubernetes.

The articles give a little history for the numbers. The cloud native developer population stood at 15.6 million a year before the latest measurement, so the figure has grown substantially over twelve months. It had already reached 19.9 million in the first quarter of 2026, which means roughly 1.3 million developers were added between the first and third quarters. The share of developers working in organisations with DevOps standardisation or internal platforms was 77 per cent in the third quarter of 2025. The report's authors, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData, describe the growth as significant compared with the previous year.

The articles do not say when the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData will publish their next report or what the figures will show. The New Stack's page is tagged to KubeCon and CloudNativeCon North America 2026, but the portion provided gives no further detail on that event. Bryce's full reasoning for the high rate of AI coding tool use among cloud native developers is not included in the text available. The articles also do not say how many developers were surveyed or how the global totals were calculated. Nor do they explain how the concerns about cost, data privacy, and security might be addressed for developers who have not yet adopted AI functionality.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA scrutiny, US selloff challenge India's AI cloud boom
stories.Summary:
A selloff in US-listed neocloud companies and growing scrutiny of NVIDIA have raised questions about the financing model behind the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom. Investors have been selling shares of US neocloud companies since September, with CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN seeing sharp corrections. The selling intensified through October and into November, as concerns mounted over the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending and the debt these companies have taken on. These developments could affect India's GPU cloud providers, which face questions about debt exposure, customer commitments and GPU depreciation. Political and regulatory resistance to data centre expansion in the US could also slow infrastructure investment.

Neoclouds provide GPU compute to customers that may not have the scale or resources to build their own infrastructure. Their business models are capital-intensive, and NVIDIA has supported the ecosystem through strategic investments and financing arrangements. India is increasingly part of this buildout, serving subsidised compute under the IndiaAI Mission and commercial workloads. The IndiaAI Mission had onboarded over 45,000 GPUs by June 2026 and approved 237 projects by August, with 93.18 lakh GPU hours sanctioned. Sanctioned hours do not necessarily translate into sustained usage, so Indian neoclouds are betting on commercial customers to justify their spending.

Unlike US peers backed by large hyperscaler customers such as Meta and OpenAI, Indian neoclouds have limited domestic anchor demand. International customers account for 75 to 80 per cent of Yotta's customer base. Yotta plans to spend over $7 billion on AI infrastructure by the end of FY27 and is targeting a $1.5 billion initial public offering. The IndiaAI Mission utilised less than half its FY26 outlay of ₹10,000 crore, which has affected hardware procurement and deployment timelines. Juspay's co-founder and COO Sheetal Lalwani said the company had been told it would wait three to six months to receive GPUs it is buying with its own cash.

NeevCloud said its engagement with NVIDIA covers technical planning, GPU availability and deployment readiness, while procurement and financing are separate arrangements. Narendra Sen, founder of NeevCloud and RackBank Datacenters, said the market correction reinforces the need for discipline in assessing each project's commercial viability. ESDS said it has no direct commercial or financing relationship with NVIDIA and buys systems from Supermicro, Dell, Lenovo and WWT. Piyush Somani, founder of ESDS, said the company commits capital expenditure only after a customer pays at least 35 per cent of the project cost. NVIDIA offered a revenue-sharing and credit-support model to neoclouds globally in July but later paused some deals, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The Government of India has noted that its compute ecosystem relies on globally sourced GPUs, so changes in chip availability, export controls, pricing or allocation could affect deployment schedules and project economics. Lenders and investors are now favouring projects with confirmed customers, predictable revenues and substantial upfront advances. Sen added that older GPUs could face more pricing pressure as newer generations arrive. Closer to home, ESDS closed at about ₹1,147.25 on November 9, against a September 24 high of ₹1,864.35. E2E Networks ended at around ₹490.50, well below its October 14 high of ₹769.

stories.Headline: Google pushes privacy angle as Gemini-powered smartglasses debut starting at $395
stories.Summary:
Google has launched Gemini-powered smartglasses that are available for preorder starting at $395, with a privacy-focused pitch. The first glasses were made in a collaboration between Google, Samsung, Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, and preorders opened on November 12, 2026. Warby Parker is offering three frames called Alden, Reid and Wren, while Gentle Monster has six styles that start at $449. Google says the devices are designed to address concerns about privacy that have dogged smartglasses since the Google Glass era.

The frames weigh about 41 grams before lenses are added, and the final pricing will depend on lens choice. The glasses have no screens, and users can interact with Gemini by voice or by activating a 12 MP wide-angle camera. Gentle Monster's styles come in dark red, pink, gray and yellow, with clear, tinted, blue or brown lenses. The devices are set to ship and appear on store shelves on December 10. At launch they work with iPhones from the 13 Pro onward, and with Pixel 7 or newer or Samsung Galaxy S or Z series devices running One UI 9 or later.

Google says it has built features to limit misuse of the glasses and to protect people around the wearer. A recording light stays on whenever the camera is active, and the glasses refuse to activate the camera if that light is covered or altered. The glasses also have a physical off switch. Google's terms of use require users to agree not to record people without consent or in sensitive areas, and Google may remotely disable the glasses if those rules are broken. The company says it will not allow Play Store apps to live stream video from the glasses, and it will not permit real-time facial recognition.

Reviewers and the article's author point out that Gemini is not always reliable, and that without a screen it may be harder to verify its output. Privacy concerns are central to the launch, since the glasses automatically redact faces before sending video to Google for processing. Google says images and videos captured by the glasses will not be saved in Gemini history or used to train AI models or target ads. Data on the glasses is encrypted in transit to the cloud but is not encrypted on Google's servers. Those affected include people around the wearer, whom the glasses are designed not to record without consent.

The same week, Google Cloud introduced a separate agentic AI solution called Gemini for healthcare, announced in a press release on Tuesday, November 10. The solution is built on the universal Gemini agent and aims to unify clinical, operational and administrative systems used in healthcare delivery and health plan operations. It brings together information from electronic health records, billing platforms, clinical guidelines and Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services datasets. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said the challenge in healthcare is making data actionable across a highly regulated ecosystem.

Google's smartglasses will support Gemini Guided Vision, which provides conversational audio descriptions for people who are visually impaired. The glasses also let users ask for recommendations or have an event poster added to their calendar. The American Hospital Association estimated that administrative costs account for 25% to 35% of total healthcare spending in the United States. Clinicians spend more than a full day each week on documentation and administrative requirements, according to the release. Superscript CEO Rahul Naidoo said medical providers face a 20% to 40% patient default rate on bills.

Articles leave open how Google's smartglasses will be priced once lenses are included, and the Ars Technica article notes the final figure will depend on lens choice. Google has not yet named the Gentle Monster styles beyond their colors. The sources also do not say when Private AI Compute will come to glasses, or when Samsung Galaxy devices outside the S and Z series will be supported. Whether the Gemini for healthcare solution will be deployed by any particular provider is not stated in the articles.

stories.Headline: Baidu Unveils Latest ERNIE Models Amid Broader Full-Stack AI Lineup, and Debuts Token Exchange to Power Intelligent Organizations
stories.Summary:
Baidu unveiled its latest ERNIE models and a broader full-stack AI lineup at Baidu World 2026 in Beijing, announced on November 12, 2026. The company, listed on NASDAQ as BIDU and on HKEX as 9888, presented new offerings spanning chips, cloud, models, and agents. The lineup includes Token Exchange, a marketplace for model services, and upgrades to the agents DuMate, KOOKO, Baidu Yijing, and Famou. Robin Li, Co-founder and CEO of Baidu, outlined his vision of the intelligent organization in his opening keynote.

ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview has 280 billion total parameters, with 14 billion activated per token, and supports a 1M context window. Its API is available on Baidu AI Cloud's Qianfan platform, and its model weights will be open-sourced by November 25. API pricing is RMB 1 per million input tokens and RMB 4 per million output tokens, with cached input at RMB 0.04 per million tokens. Baidu also introduced the ERNIE Wizshot Micro-Expression and ERNIE Light Deep Thinking application models, available via API on the same platform. Baidu also launched the Tianchi 1024-card Supernode, an all-optical interconnect supernode for high-speed data transmission.

Li said the intelligent organization is the next chapter of AI and that its productivity gains require moving beyond traditional hierarchies. He laid out three principles: breaking down job boundaries, capturing tacit knowledge as a shared company asset, and designing closed-loop processes. Li said jobs will converge into two types, Builders, who create new things, and Sellers, who build emotional bonds and trust. He described the principle of closed-loop processes with a formula: measurability plus looping equals continuous evolution.

Baidu reported that over the past year, the average number of daily active agents inside the company rose from 5,000 to 37,000, an increase of more than 600%. Agents now complete more than 1 million tasks a week, up from 84,000, and Baidu has built 4,300 workspaces and captured more than 20,000 organizational skills. Token Exchange connects model service providers and customers in a neutral, transparent marketplace where buyers can compare services side by side. One month after launch, Token Exchange had onboarded more than 100 model resources and handled a daily average of more than 50 million calls.

Baidu Yijing, a digital human agent, now creates short animated dramas at RMB 0.2 per second of video, with one-click localization for global audiences. DuMate has been upgraded into a unified gateway to Baidu's specialized agents, and its Harness engine and Agent API are now fully open. KOOKO, upgraded from GenFlow 3.0, draws on 1.8 billion professional resources and 750 million academic papers to produce research reports, slide decks, and websites. Famou 3.0 serves customers across 25 of China's 41 industrial categories, and Li said Baidu's Apollo Go now covers 28 cities worldwide.

stories.Headline: Airbnb and Travel Stocks Fall as OpenAI Acquisition Raises New AI Threat
stories.Summary:
Shares of major online travel agencies fell on Tuesday, November 10, after OpenAI acquired Odessia, an automated travel platform, according to a report cited by PYMNTS. The deal prompted investor concern about possible disruption to established booking sites, and Expedia Group dropped nearly 4 percent, Tripadvisor fell more than 3 percent and Booking Holdings slipped more than 2 percent. Unlike traditional aggregators that send users to third-party sites to finish a purchase, Odessia handles trip planning, fare comparison and reservations inside a conversational interface. The platform was built on OpenAI's GPT 5.5 and Codex models and processed about $60 million in travel volume during its first year.

Odessia's founder, Francis Davidson, confirmed the acquisition on LinkedIn and said he will join OpenAI to lead its travel technology work. Davidson previously founded the hospitality company Sonder, which grew to $600 million in revenue, and he launched Odessia in late 2025 with funding from the venture firm Sequoia, individual angel investors and commercial travel partners. In his announcement he said he believed Odessia had built the best AI travel agent on the market. He also said tens of thousands of early adopters used the platform to plan more than $60 million of travel over the past summer. The articles present these statements as his own claims.

The article ties the selloff to growing competition as conversational software shifts toward autonomous commerce, with platforms moving from search assistants to agents that complete multi-step bookings. PYMNTS Intelligence research found that nearly 25 percent of consumers feel comfortable letting artificial intelligence plan their travel itineraries. Established intermediaries such as Booking Holdings and Kayak have been adding conversational tools and native checkout to protect their transaction volumes. Analysts quoted in the piece warn that well-funded AI developers entering direct booking could bypass legacy web portals and change how consumers find, compare and pay for travel. The articles do not report any regulatory response or further steps by the companies involved.

stories.Headline: UK GDP growth hits 0.7 per cent in third quarter on AI boost
stories.Summary:
The UK economy grew by 0.7 per cent in the third quarter, its fastest pace in more than two years, according to figures published by the Office for National Statistics. Investment in artificial intelligence was among the factors behind the increase, which covered the period from July to September. The growth was in line with City economists' estimates and above the 0.4 per cent forecast by the Bank of England. It was the strongest quarter for output since the first three months of 2024. Monthly output rose by 0.2 per cent in September, ahead of a projection of no growth, while August was revised down to zero from an initial 0.1 per cent.

Services, which make up nearly three-quarters of the economy, again led growth, with IT and communications the largest contributor and the single biggest driver this year. The ONS said many businesses reporting the largest turnover increases were involved in artificial intelligence and cloud computing within computer programming. Output from production firms rose by 0.1 per cent in the quarter, while construction output fell by 0.7 per cent. Household expenditure rose by 0.6 per cent as consumers drew on savings, and business investment increased by 0.35 per cent, the strongest private sector investment since 2022. Government spending rose by 0.2 per cent between June and September.

Chancellor John Healey said the UK is showing stand-out resilience, with the economy growing at its fastest rate in almost ten years outside the pandemic. Sandra Horsfield, an economist at Investec, said AI-related services appear to be playing an increasing role in supporting activity, although the UK is not as prominent as some Asian companies in AI chip production. Horsfield calculated that 0.2 percentage points of the 0.7 per cent quarterly growth can be attributed to AI. Analysts also said the rise in investment may be linked to the rollout of AI technology.

The benefits of AI adoption are uneven across the country, according to research published the same week, which found that Yorkshire has the lowest AI adoption rate among SMEs of any UK region. Consumers are affected by rising energy bills and higher inflation, which economists expect to reduce spending power and slow growth in the final three months of the year. Inflation stands at 3.6 per cent and unemployment has dipped to 4.7 per cent, according to the latest official figures. The stronger than expected figures make a further interest rate rise more likely in the coming months, economists said.

The Bank of England raised the base rate to 4 per cent on 5 November, its first increase in three years. The increase followed months of speculation that an oil price shock from the Middle East war could force a rate rise. The ONS full breakdown is set out in its first quarterly estimate of GDP for July to September. The unemployment and inflation figures are due to be updated next week. The articles do not say how the economy will perform in the final quarter beyond the expected slowdown, or whether the Bank of England will raise rates again.

stories.Headline: Korea puts a lens on AI glasses cheating claims in tax exam
stories.Summary:
South Korea's exam authority, the Human Resources Development Service of Korea (HRDK), is reviewing allegations that the top scorer on the 63rd national tax accountant qualification exam used AI-powered smart glasses to cheat. The allegations surfaced online after the candidate missed just one question out of 160 in the first-stage exam. No direct evidence has been made public showing that the candidate wore the glasses or used them. Separately, South Korea's Education Ministry reported finding four cases of students using AI-equipped smart glasses to cheat on school exams. The cases emerged from a nationwide inspection of 5,679 middle and high schools conducted between October 27 and November 3.

The tax exam scores showed the candidate earned full marks in introductory tax law and scored 397.5 out of 400 in the first stage. In the essay-based second stage, the candidate scored 663 out of 800, with an overall average of 82.87 against a passing cutoff of 49.75. Of the 16,856 people who took introductory tax law, 74.21 percent scored below the 40-point minimum to avoid automatic failure. The school cases were recorded at high schools in Seoul, North Jeolla Province and Jeju Island, with three occurring during first-semester final exams and one during second-semester midterms. The Education Ministry will strengthen procedures beginning with second-semester final exams, including collecting restricted devices before tests begin.

Smart glasses will also be prohibited at the College Scholastic Ability Test scheduled for November 19. The HRDK said it is checking with test centers and proctors to see whether they noticed any signs of cheating during the April and July exams. An HRDK official said allegations alone are not grounds to accuse a candidate, but that given public scrutiny the agency is looking into what happened. The official said the agency has found no unusual patterns in the candidate's scores apart from the exceptionally high marks. The Korean Association of Certified Tax Accountants urged the HRDK and relevant authorities to thoroughly investigate the cheating allegations and take appropriate action.

The association said it would take any necessary steps based on the findings. In the school cases, Education Ministry curriculum director Kim Han-seung said teachers identified suspicious behavior partly because they knew their students' usual appearance. Online users questioned whether the tax exam results were possible given the exam's difficulty and strict time limits. One user asked how the top scorer could score 100 in introductory tax law when the second-highest score was in the 80s. A commenter who said they had served as an exam reviewer last year called the public finance and introductory tax law scores physically impossible.

A tax accountant who previously passed the first round with top honors said there are so many tricky questions that even the most expert accountant could not pass. The candidate spent roughly two years preparing for the exam and passed both stages on the first attempt, according to a local news outlet. In the school cases, students were disciplined in several ways, with a Seoul student ordered to complete three days of special education. The Education Ministry's inspection found that one North Jeolla student touched the glasses frame repeatedly during a final exam while a green light reflected from them. In Jeju, a student who switched to smart glasses during a test later admitted wearing the device on the previous day's exams as well.

The school gave that student zero scores on both days and suspended the student for five days. The HRDK has not said when its review of the tax exam will conclude or whether any action will follow. The association has not specified what action it expects. The articles do not say whether the candidate's scores will be revoked or whether any criminal charges will be filed. It also remains unclear what result the HRDK's review of the test center and proctor records will produce.

stories.Headline: How AI Stocks Are Creeping Into Dividend ETFs
stories.Summary:
Data centers built for artificial intelligence are pushing U.S. electricity demand higher, and three utility ETFs offer income investors exposure to the companies supplying that power. The funds are the State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLU), the Fidelity MSCI Utilities Index ETF (FUTY) and the iShares U.S. Utilities ETF (IDU). As of November 9, 2026, their trailing yields range from 2.3% to 2.8%. The article was published on November 9, 2026, by Ryne Mauck at 24/7 Wall St. Their one-year returns were much smoother than the AI headlines would suggest. The U.S. Department of Energy projects that data centers will account for up to 12% of U.S. electrical demand by 2028, driven by AI development.

The Government Accountability Office reported that projection in its study of space-based data centers. Colorado Legislative Council Staff note that a single operating data center can consume over a gigawatt. That same report says a gigawatt is enough to power approximately 750,000 homes. Regulated utilities earn returns that state regulators set, so more demand means more approved spending on plants and power lines. Constellation Energy (CEG) illustrates direct exposure to the trend, according to its third-quarter 2026 earnings disclosure.

The company cited a 20-year, 690 MW power agreement with a cloud provider supporting investment at its Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant. It also cited a 20-year agreement with another tech giant tied to nuclear uprates, which add capacity to existing reactors. The article notes that a utility fund gives exposure to electricity demand, and AI is only one source of it. The Colorado report also lists electric vehicle adoption, onshoring of manufacturing, and electrification of industry and buildings as drivers. XLU is the largest of the three and tracks the utilities in the S&P 500, with $23.1 billion in net assets as of June 30, 2026.

As of that date, NextEra Energy (NEE) made up 13% of the fund, ahead of the next two utilities at 8% and 7%. NextEra's pending combination with another top-ten holding is expected to close in the second half of 2027. On June 30, 2026, Constellation accounted for 6% of XLU, with two other merchant generators at 4% and 2%. XLU's trailing yield is 2.8%, and its September 30, 2026, fact sheet lists a gross expense ratio of 0.08%. FUTY tracks the MSCI USA IMI Utilities 25/50 Index, which adds mid-cap and small-cap utilities to the large caps.

Its July 31, 2026, filing listed 64 positions and $2.3 billion in net assets. As of July 31, 2026, NextEra made up 12% of the fund, Constellation 5%, and another merchant generator 3%. A smaller merchant generator held about 0.9%, and an early-stage nuclear company held 0.4%. FUTY's trailing yield is 2.7%, and it returned 2% over one year and 50% over five years. IDU tracks the Russell 1000 Utilities RIC 22.5/45 Capped Index, and its net expense ratio is 0.37% according to its August 31, 2026, prospectus.

stories.Headline: World's first bionic humanoid robot news anchors unveiled
stories.Summary:
Chinese state news agency Xinhua and robotics firm UBTECH unveiled what they call the world's first bionic humanoid robot news anchors on November 5, 2026, at a forum on artificial intelligence and Chinese modernization in Beijing, held as part of the 7th World Media Summit. The robots, named Xinyan and Xinyu, were jointly developed by the two organizations, with the well-known Chinese director Zhang Yimou serving as lead designer of their visual identities. Built to human scale and customized for news work, they are designed to deliver on-site broadcasts. The launch was presented as a step toward putting a model that combines authoritative news content with embodied AI into practical use.

The anchors draw on Xinhua's AI newsbot "Xinhua Yudian" along with UBTECH's proprietary technologies, including biomimetic skin, embodied AI hardware, operating systems, emotion-driven large language models and mass production capabilities. Together these form what the companies describe as an integrated "brain-expression-control" pipeline. The system can retrieve political news and information in real time from vetted sources, which the companies say helps reduce the risk of misinformation caused by AI hallucinations. Future deployment is planned in educational bases, urban public venues, overseas cultural exchanges and deep space exploration reporting. Xinhua's officials stressed that the robots will assist journalists and editors with presentation, multilingual delivery and on-site interaction rather than become the stars of the show.

Zhang Yimou spoke at the forum about the integration of technology and art, saying he sought a balance between the seriousness and professionalism that news delivery requires and the natural, nuanced realism of lifelike robots. Qian Tong, director-general of Xinhua's New Media Center, said the robots are intended to take on new roles in the newsroom. Zhou Jian, founder, chairman and CEO of UBTECH, described the project as a cross-sector collaboration that combines Xinhua's industry standards and content resources with UBTECH's full-stack technologies and Zhang's design team's work. The summit itself is co-hosted by Xinhua and the People's Government of Beijing Municipality, and aims to build dialogue and consensus among global media organizations on using AI in communication.

A separate report from Business Times in Singapore, dated November 9, 2026, describes a different company's embodied AI robots. It says Keppel is showing its humanoid robot Ken, which is being trained to flip high-voltage switches at the Senoko waste-to-energy plant, alongside a robot dog named Sniff meant to test air for toxic gas in incinerators. The same article says Keppel's agentic AI, which picks data centre sites and spots breakdowns, is already paying its way, making the robots a less central part of its AI story. The two reports involve separate companies and different applications, and the Keppel piece does not concern news anchoring.

stories.Headline: AutoSwift secures close to A$10 million from Singapore's X Star Technology to scale AI WINGMAN
stories.Summary:
AutoSwift, an Australian developer of automotive AI, secured close to A$10 million in strategic investment from Singapore-headquartered X Star Technology, announced on 10 November 2026. The platform in question is AI WINGMAN by AutoSwift, and the funds are meant to accelerate its development and growth. The investment is described as a vote of confidence from international investors in Australian automotive AI. The announcement followed the platform's showcases at the AADA Convention & Expo in Sydney in July and at AIMCONNECT 2026 in Singapore in October. AI WINGMAN is an agentic customer engagement platform that works alongside dealer sales and servicing teams.

AI WINGMAN handles enquiries across web chat, SMS, WhatsApp and telephone, and it helps dealerships respond to customers and identify sales opportunities. It uses dealerships' own customer and operational data to help sales teams win repeat purchases from existing customers. The platform is already used by franchised dealers of BYD, Zeekr, Land Rover and Kia. The investment is intended to support the platform's growth across the Australian automotive retail industry and the wider region. AutoSwift itself is described as an Australian fintech venture that provides AI-powered solutions for buying and financing vehicles.

Lei Shen, Director of AI WINGMAN, said the investment reflects growing recognition of purpose-built AI solutions that transform how dealerships engage customers across the ownership lifecycle. He said dealerships face more intense competition and complex market conditions, and that many sales opportunities are lost through neglected or delayed engagement. Shen said the platform was developed to turn untapped dealership data into actionable insights. Shawn Yang, CEO of X Star Technology, said in a separate statement that the investment reflects the company's focus on AI designed for automotive customer engagement. Yang said the company looks forward to working with AutoSwift to bring the next generation of automotive AI to more dealers.

X Star Technology is a Singapore-headquartered automotive finance technology company with operations across Asia Pacific, Latin America and the Middle East. It is wholly owned by Hong Kong-listed Yixin Group (HKEX: 2858) and serves more than 2,000 automotive dealers, manufacturers and financial institutions worldwide. AIMCONNECT 2026, organised by X Star and held on 11 October in Singapore, brought together over 250 industry leaders from 11 countries. Those attendees included representatives of more than 100 automotive organisations, over 60 financial institutions and around 20 technology companies. Alan Crookes, a former CEO of BMW Group Financial Services for Asia Pacific and a panellist at the event, called backing from X Star a strong signal for Australian innovation.

Dealerships, customers and the automotive retail industry are the parties most directly affected by the platform, since it is designed to change how they handle enquiries and sales. The articles give no figures on how many dealerships or customers currently use AI WINGMAN beyond the named brands. The reports describe the investment as a strategic milestone without giving a timetable or specific targets for growth. The articles do not state what share of AutoSwift the investment represents or what terms were agreed. They also do not say when the new capital will be deployed or which new markets AI WINGMAN will enter.

stories.Headline: BigBear.ai Expands Gross Margin by 878 Bps: What Drives the Gains?
stories.Summary:
BigBear.ai reported a sharp profitability improvement in the third quarter of 2026, with its gross margin rising 878 basis points year over year to 31.2% from 22.4%. The company attributed the gain mainly to a growing contribution from its generative AI platform, which it acquired through the Ask Sage transaction in December 2025. Stronger revenue performance also helped lift results during the quarter. Quarterly revenue grew 31% year over year to $43.6 million, the company's third consecutive quarter of organic revenue growth. Gross profit climbed roughly 83% to $13.6 million from $7.4 million, signaling improving operating economics.

The generative AI platform lets government agencies and critical industries securely access advanced AI models, build agentic workflows and process sensitive information in secure environments. Adoption across federal agencies, including the FBI, NASA, the U.S. Coast Guard and the Department of Energy, supports its expansion. The company secured more than 25 contracts worth over $225 million in value since the second quarter. Its backlog rose 22% sequentially to $330 million, improving visibility into future revenue. Management also raised its 2026 revenue guidance to $150 to $165 million.

The articles do not name a single executive who spoke on the results, but the company's management raised 2026 revenue guidance to $150 to $165 million. Management's outlook ties future profitability to sustained generative AI adoption, a favorable revenue mix and effective cost management. The articles frame those factors as necessary for turning gross margin gains into stronger operating profitability. The company's stated view is that the platform and contract wins support its revenue visibility and growth.

Analysts and data providers cited in the articles, including Zacks Investment Research, emphasized the margin trend and valuation. Shares gained 6.5% over the past month, outperforming the Zacks Computers - IT Services industry. BigBear.ai trades at a forward 12-month price-to-sales ratio of 6.98, a discount to industry peers. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for the 2026 and 2027 loss per share widened to 41 cents and 25 cents over the past 30 days. Its Zacks Rank is #4 (Sell).

BigBear.ai's shareholders and investors are directly affected by these figures, as the articles report adjusted EBITDA remained negative at $9.1 million and selling, general and administrative expenses rose to $31.3 million. Government agencies using the platform are also affected by its expanding adoption. The articles note competition from Palantir Technologies and C3.ai in enterprise and government AI markets. Palantir reported third-quarter 2026 revenue up 96% year over year to $2.31 billion, with a gross margin of about 83.4%. C3.ai reported a fiscal 2026 GAAP gross margin of 31%.

The articles describe BigBear.ai's generative AI platform as an emerging growth and margin catalyst within its business. The Ask Sage transaction in December 2025 brought this platform into the company. Its quarterly revenue has grown organically for three consecutive quarters. Earlier in the articles, the company is described as operating in a market for enterprise and government-focused artificial intelligence solutions. The platform's focus on specialized, mission-ready AI solutions is presented as supporting its differentiation in security and defense markets.

The articles leave open whether the margin expansion will be sustained, since they say profitability challenges persist. They do not state when BigBear.ai expects to reach positive adjusted EBITDA. Future revenue depends on converting its backlog and contract wins, but the articles give no timeline for that. Whether Palantir's scalable software model will widen its advantage over BigBear.ai also remains unaddressed. The articles give no further guidance or outcomes beyond the 2026 revenue range and the consensus loss estimates.

stories.Headline: Public funds ploughing cash into AI will 'own' megatrends shaping economy
stories.Summary:
Sovereign wealth funds and public pension funds are pouring money into artificial intelligence and infrastructure, and a PwC report released on Thursday, November 12, 2026, projects that state-backed investors will reshape the economy. Sovereign wealth fund assets are expected to rise nearly 50% to $22.4 trillion by 2030, up from about $15.2 trillion. Public pension assets are forecast to climb to $36.3 trillion from about $27.6 trillion, and central bank assets to about $20.9 trillion from about $17.3 trillion. The report, which analysed the world's 350 largest public investors, was reported by Reuters and carried by CNBC Africa.

The report says these investors have moved from passive stakes to what it calls principal investors that originate deals themselves and take controlling positions with operational roles. Eric Janson, PwC's global private equity and principal investors leader, said these investors no longer rely only on external managers. Assets are becoming concentrated in a small group, with the top 10 institutions holding about 41% of combined sovereign wealth and pension assets and the top 50 holding 77%. The report says a few dozen large institutions are positioned to set the tone, adding that they will enable, accelerate and own the megatrends shaping the global economy.

In 2025, state investors channelled roughly $66 billion into AI and digitisation, and most of it went to the United States, while flows to China slipped to around $4 billion. The report found Gulf state funds were tilting hard toward the US, pointing to pledges from Qatar's QIA and Abu Dhabi's MGX and ADIA. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund was an exception, cutting foreign allocations to roughly 20% from a peak near 30% as it shifts toward a domestic focus. The article does not describe any formal rule or requirement that these shifts impose on governments or institutions.

stories.Headline: Vanta Buys Pillar to Tie AI Governance to Real-Time Controls
stories.Summary:
Vanta, a San Francisco-based trust platform, plans to buy Pillar Security, a Tel Aviv, Israel-based startup led by a former Aqua Security product manager, to link AI governance with real-time security enforcement. The deal was reported by Calcalist on November 9, 2026, and Vanta's proposed acquisition was covered by GovInfoSecurity on November 11, 2026. Calcalist reported that the deal is valued at approximately $150 million and consists of a combination of cash and shares. Vanta's GRC Senior Director, Khush Kashyap, said the purchase will help organizations discover AI assets, apply policy-based guardrails, block unsafe actions and produce audit-ready evidence. Pillar was founded in 2023 and, according to its own counts, employs 33 people, while Calcalist puts its staff at more than 20.

The transaction would combine Vanta's governance and evidence tools with Pillar's agent discovery, monitoring, red-teaming and enforcement capabilities. Following completion, Pillar would become Vanta's research and development center in Israel, and its team would join the U.S. company. Pillar's technology would be integrated into Vanta's platform, which serves more than 20,000 customers. Kashyap said the combined product would let customers turn written AI policies into automated controls that block unauthorized agent actions at runtime. Vanta's CEO and co-founder, Christina Cacioppo, said customers and regulators want proof that a company's AI does what it claims, and that a policy document alone does not provide that.

Vanta says the deal responds to a gap between knowing what policies require and seeing whether AI agents follow them. Kashyap described enforcement without governance context as producing alerts, and governance without enforcement as producing a paper trail. Pillar's CEO, Ziv Karliner, said the acquisition gives the company access to Vanta's security and governance context and a way to serve a larger customer base. Calcalist reported that Pillar's founders, Ziv Karliner and Dor Sarig, will remain with the company to lead its AI security business. Customers affected include Vanta's more than 20,000 customers and Pillar's customers, which include Fortune 500 companies as well as technology and financial firms.

Kashyap said Vanta's AI governance early-access program is the most requested in the company's history and is six times oversubscribed. She also said daily Vanta agent users have grown 253% over the last three quarters. Vanta's own research, cited by Calcalist, found that 65% of IT and business leaders say their use of agentic AI is outpacing their understanding of it, and that fewer than half have a framework for granting or limiting AI autonomy. Calcalist reported that Pillar raised $9 million since its founding in 2023, with its seed round announced in April 2025 led by Shield Capital, with participation from Golden Ventures and Ground Up Ventures. Karliner previously spent more than four years at Aqua Security, including two-and-a-half years as a product manager.

The articles do not confirm the purchase price, since a Vanta spokesperson disputed the $150 million figure reported by Calcalist and declined to disclose the price. The articles also do not say when the acquisition is expected to close or whether regulators must approve it. Vanta launched its AI governance product in July 2026, according to Calcalist, and its governance tools are used by companies, with auditors at more than 20,000 companies accepting its evidence. Calcalist said Vanta's platform serves more than 20,000 customers, and Kashyap said auditors at more than 20,000 companies accept its evidence. The articles leave open how the combined product will be priced and how Pillar's products will be packaged after integration.

stories.Headline: Australian companies face 'AI washing' claims after wave of job cuts, offshoring
stories.Summary:
Australian blue-chip companies are increasingly citing artificial intelligence as they cut jobs and move work offshore, according to unions and experts, a trend that complicates the government's efforts to support employment in a slowing economy. On Tuesday, Qantas said it would cut 850 jobs and outsource some corporate functions offshore as part of an AI-driven overhaul with consulting firm Accenture, a move that has drawn accusations of "AI washing." The term describes companies attributing layoffs to AI when the primary driver may be broader cost-cutting, such as shifting jobs offshore. Tech companies WiseTech and Atlassian have cut jobs this year and attributed the losses to AI. Telstra has also cut jobs from an AI joint venture with Accenture, with some work moved to India.

Other firms across corporate Australia have slashed domestic headcounts while expanding operations in India, the Philippines and Vietnam, though they did not explicitly mention AI in their announcements. When asked about the Qantas cuts, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said AI "represents an enormous opportunity and a major economic issue." Labour unions argue that Australian workers are not being replaced by AI but by lower-paid offshore employees. The Australian Council of Trade Unions' Melissa Donnelly said unions are concerned that companies are using AI as cover to cut Australian jobs without accountability. The Australian Services Union, which represents affected Qantas workers, accused the airline of "using AI to launder their cuts to Australian jobs."

A Qantas spokesperson said the airline would continue to consult with unions and was focused on "redeployment opportunities" and support for affected staff, but did not respond to the concerns about AI washing. Senator Barbara Pocock of the Australian Greens said on Wednesday she was concerned to see big companies engaging in AI washing, saying AI "is transforming our workplaces and economy but that's no excuse to let it run rampant." Atlassian, WiseTech and Telstra did not immediately respond to requests for comment. University of Sydney Business School professor Uri Gal said a growing number of companies were blaming job cuts on AI and that accepting AI as the primary explanation should be approached with caution. He said that Qantas's decision appeared to reflect conventional outsourcing, since the work is first being transferred to Accenture, primarily in India.

Further job cuts could pose difficulties for Australia's centre-left Labor government, whose approval ratings have steadily fallen in recent polls amid high cost-of-living pressures. The central bank has raised interest rates five times so far this year, to their highest level in 18 years, amid persistent inflation, while the latest data showed unemployment at a five-year high of 4.7%. The Reserve Bank of Australia said this week that AI had not yet led to widespread job losses, though it noted "tentative signs of adjustment," with job ads weakening in AI-exposed occupations. A government spokesperson said it expects Australian workers to benefit from new technologies and that employers should invest in upskilling them to adopt AI.

stories.Headline: Caine Prize clears Zimbabwean author of AI writing allegations and adds new rules
stories.Summary:
The Caine Prize for African Writing has cleared Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza of using artificial intelligence to write his award-winning story, while also announcing new rules to guard against generative AI in future submissions. The allegations were raised in an article by The Atlantic magazine and sparked debate on social media about whether Black authors face unfair AI-related accusations. The prize organizers said an internal review found the evidence clear, so Kundizeza's award stands. Kundizeza said he felt relieved that the allegations had been dismissed and that he was happy to move on. The Caine Prize plans to introduce AI declarations and an AI use policy for entrants.

The organization said it will also require writers to disclose any use of generative AI in their submissions. The rules are meant to address concerns about how such tools may be used in the competition's entries going forward. The prize did not say in the available reporting how the new measures will be enforced. Kundizeza's response was delivered after the prize announced its findings on Wednesday, and he spoke to reporters on Thursday. He said he was grateful for the review and that he hoped the matter would now be closed.

Responsibility for the review and the new policy rests with the Caine Prize organizers, who said the evidence did not support the claims made about his story. Commentators quoted in the reporting described the accusations as having been fueled by broader assumptions about African writing. The matter comes amid wider discussion about how literary prizes and publishers should handle AI-generated writing. The articles do not describe any further steps in the case or any legal action. The Caine Prize's new AI measures are expected to apply to future competitions, and the articles give no date for when they take effect.

stories.Headline: HEARTBOT AI Launches AnyInsight Edge, Ending the Trade-Off Between Private AI and Agentic Productivity
stories.Summary:
HEARTBOT AI has launched AnyInsight Edge, which extends its AnyInsight enterprise AI security and governance platform to on-premises environments and AI servers. The announcement was made in Taipei on November 12, 2026, through a PR Newswire release. The product applies a single control plane to private on-premises models and cloud AI, so enterprises can manage both under one policy. Coverage of the launch appeared in The Manila Times and TNGlobal on the same day.

Enterprises have long had to choose between private large language models, which keep data in-house but lack the productivity of AI agents, and cloud AI, which offers stronger models but cannot always receive regulated data. AnyInsight Edge is delivered as a container with a hardware-agnostic design, and it requires no GPU, leaving compute for model inference. Edge acts as the policy enforcement point in the on-premises AI traffic path and can run in fully air-gapped environments with no cloud connection. Through Edge, on-premises models such as Gemma, TAIDE and Mistral can access AnyInsight's more than 350 ready-to-use AI agents and workflows and over 500 application connectors. Policy-based routing can reach more than 20 leading cloud models when needed.

HEARTBOT AI says the platform is designed for the enterprises that have announced the launch and that the product is aimed at organizations bound by data residency rules, regulation or customer contracts. The company's CEO, Nathan Yen, said that twenty years ago firewalls, intrusion prevention and VPNs converged into UTM, and that AI now faces a similar turning point. Yen argued that enterprises need a control point that enforces policy where AI work happens. He said AnyInsight Edge turns every AI server into that control point.

Organizations that have invested in AI servers and deployed private models are among those affected, because such models often remain isolated chatbots cut off from ERP, MES and CRM systems. The articles describe risks from agents that move data as east-west traffic outside the network firewall and from "shadow agents" and "shadow AI" that IT cannot see. Employees who turn to public AI services on personal accounts are also cited as a source of unmanaged risk. The release gives use cases in manufacturing and semiconductor supply chains, banking and insurance, and government and healthcare. It also refers to Taiwan's AI Basic Act and the EU AI Act.

HEARTBOT AI describes itself as a developer of trustworthy, high-assurance enterprise AI solutions, and says AnyInsight is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022. The company states that its governance and data protection mechanisms are designed on the principles of the EU AI Act and the General Data Protection Regulation. The articles do not report pricing, availability dates, customer deployments or independent evaluation of the product. They also do not say how the EU AI Act or Taiwan's AI Basic Act will apply to particular customers.

stories.Headline: Kazakhstan-linked hackers used AI to steal Tajik government documents, researchers say
stories.Summary:
A hacking group linked to Kazakhstan used artificial intelligence to steal more than 2,000 national security-related documents from neighboring Tajikistan, according to a report published on Wednesday by the Singapore-based cybersecurity company CloudSek. The company said it caught the group, which it said was nicknamed "Silent Lynx," after the hackers accidentally left a server exposed to the internet. The attackers used Hermes, an open-source framework for autonomous AI agents, to carry out the intrusion. CloudSek said the activity was tied to the group's espionage work.

CloudSek's data indicated that the hackers began reconnaissance using Hermes around mid-August and broke into Tajikistan's electronic document system a couple of weeks later. The AI agent then reportedly wrote a custom program to download the files, organize them, and split them into chunks to steal them more efficiently. Exposed data also showed the instructions the hackers gave the agent, which described it as an elite offensive security specialist and red teamer. The company said this shows that instead of typing commands by hand, the attacker told the AI what to do and the AI planned, executed, and documented the attacks. Reuters noted that cybercriminals had previously been assigning break-ins to autonomous AI agents.

Kazakh and Tajik government officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and efforts to reach Silent Lynx were unsuccessful. CloudSek said it found evidence the hackers spoke Russian, worked Kazakh business hours, and often accessed the exposed server through a residential Kazakh internet connection. Other researchers have previously tied the Silent Lynx group to Kazakhstan. The report's findings are based on the data CloudSek recovered from the exposed server, and the article does not describe any further steps by authorities.

stories.Headline: AI hoaxes are deceiving 911 dispatchers, and they're only getting harder to detect
stories.Summary:
In August, a caller made a bomb threat to Wheatland Union High School in Yuba County, California, and the voice on the call was generated by artificial intelligence. Police responded overnight and classes at the school were canceled, though there was no bomb and no one was hurt. Authorities said the call was part of a series of hoax calls, also called swatting, made to schools across the country over the summer. The Yuba County incident stood out because it was an example of a new and growing challenge for emergency responders. Swatting calls can go to 911 or to police departments, with callers reporting a bomb threat, a mass shooting or another life-threatening emergency in order to trigger a massive response, according to the FBI.

Swatting calls made with AI-generated voices or background sounds are making these hoaxes sound more realistic, which makes it harder to tell what is real. Companies such as ElevenLabs, which creates synthetic voice software, offer AI tools that are incredibly cheap and readily available. APCO and the Public Safety Threat Alliance, an information-sharing and cybersecurity group, studied how common swatting is at 911 call centers and published their findings in June. Their report was based on 766 responses from public safety communications professionals, and about 14% of dispatchers said they had been targeted using AI tools. Mel Maier says he thinks that figure will keep rising as the tools become more advanced.

Mel Maier is the CEO and executive director of APCO International, the Association of Public Safety Communication Officials, and he says swatting voices used to be easy to recognize. He says that now they sound natural, can insert pauses, and can use filler words such as "uh" or "um." Maier also notes that people have been killed and injured in swatting attacks. April Heinze, NENA's vice president and chief of 911 operations, says there are hallmarks of a swatting call, including that most swatters do not dial 911 directly. She explains that 911 provides location, a callback number and the name of the phone's owner, and that it is really impossible to spoof your location on 911.

Brandon May, an assistant professor of forensic psychology at the Florida Institute of Technology, says he can clone his own voice on ElevenLabs for less than $20. He says he can change the intonation, the depth or pitch of the voice, and the pauses. May says it is no longer simple to look at an image or hear a voice and tell that it is AI, and that people are duped by this all the time. He adds that elaborate fraud callers using AI chatbots are even tricking people into handing over their life savings. May says the increasingly sophisticated fake voices and sound effects make it especially hard for dispatchers to judge what is real on what he calls high-stakes, high-consequence calls, and he says detection will be nearly impossible.

Swatting calls usually trigger a big, chaotic police response, which redirects public safety resources away from real emergencies. The goal of such calls is to harass or retaliate against their targets, such as a public official. APCO and NENA: The 9-1-1 Association, which both represent 911 dispatchers, say incidents like the one in Yuba County reflect their growing worries about how bad actors could use AI. Heinze says swatting calls are usually made to police departments or courthouses, and the callers are then ultimately transferred into 911 centers. She says trying to trace those calls is impossible, and that the long-running swatting problem now includes this AI element.

APCO and NENA are developing ways to train their members to deal with these new threats, despite the difficulty. Both Heinze and Maier decline to describe the specifics of the training, saying more public information would make it easier to train AI to fool dispatchers. Maier does note that APCO is working on training criteria for caller interrogation, in which dispatchers ask specific questions at such a granular level that an AI cannot take the answers from a public database or a social media post, or guess them. Both Maier and Heinze emphasize that dispatchers will always assume calls reporting a life-threatening situation are real and will keep sending emergency resources to any call for help. Heinze says public safety will have a very strong response even when there are indicators of swatting, because a life-or-death situation means you can never take chances, and the articles do not say when the training will be ready.

stories.Headline: Intel and Altera Simplify Sensor Integration for Edge and Physical AI
stories.Summary:
Intel and Altera announced on November 11, 2026, that they will collaborate on a flexible, real-time sensor bridge for edge and physical AI systems. The announcement came from Santa Clara, California, and combines Intel compute, connectivity and software with Altera FPGAs. The companies say the work aims to help equipment makers connect and act on data from increasingly sensor-rich environments. The partnership targets healthcare, aerospace and defense, and robotics applications. The collaboration centers on modular reference solutions that pair programmable hardware with a consistent Intel compute and software foundation.

The articles say these designs are meant to handle sensor data that must be merged while meeting requirements for timing, performance, power and cost. Some applications need very high bandwidth or flexible form factors that place input and output away from the compute board. In those cases, sensor data must be streamed rapidly into memory for the host Intel processor to use. The companies say this approach should let manufacturers adapt as applications and sensors change and move more efficiently from prototype to deployment. Dan Rodriguez, corporate vice president and general manager of Intel's Edge Computing Group, said customers need a simpler way to turn real-world data into timely action as sensors multiply.

Farhad Shafai, head of business solutions and marketing at Altera, said physical AI systems must sense, decide and act in real time, and that Altera FPGAs supply the connectivity, data processing and deterministic control needed for that. Shafai added that the FPGAs remain programmable as sensors and AI models evolve. Both executives framed the combined offering as a flexible foundation that manufacturers can tailor to their needs. The companies plan to apply the work in three areas. In healthcare, they are jointly developing a reference solution aimed at the strict latency and real-time requirements of advanced equipment.

In aerospace and defense, they are working on reference solutions for next-generation mission systems with a focus on size, weight and power for converged AI and signal-processing workloads. In robotics, they plan to combine Intel compute, connectivity and robotics software with Altera FPGA technology to address complex sensing and timing needs. Developers will reach these capabilities through Intel's Open Edge Platform SDK and an Altera SDK. The articles do not give timelines for when the reference solutions will be released.
