Token pooling reduces those costs by merging similar token vectors, though aggressive compression can discard useful information. Pooling-aware training addresses this by teaching the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged. The method was described in a Hugging Face post dated November 11, 2026, written by Tom Aarsen. The post builds on pooling-aware training studied in work by Stefan Josef and by LightOn.

With pool_factor=4, a normally trained model retained 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10 while cutting document vectors fourfold. Pooling-aware training raised that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget. The post's example arithmetic shows that 200 vectors of 128 dimensions at 4-bit residual quantization need 12.8 KB per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that figure to 3.2 GB. HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering, and it protects the first token from merging by default.

Pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving queries unchanged, and adaptive pooling can use a shared distance threshold instead of a fixed factor. A calibration function, calibrate_distance_threshold, can set that threshold for a target average of 16 vectors per document. The training objective combines the original retrieval loss with a pooled-representation loss, weighting each at one half. The training is implemented in Sentence Transformers through MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss, which wraps CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss.

Gradients from pooled vectors pass back to their member tokens through a straight-through estimator. The example uses a mini-batch size of 64 and a training batch size of 256. The complete script, training_cached_contrastive.py, can be run locally with uv or on a cloud GPU through Hugging Face Jobs. The Jobs example uses an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit, and it can upload the trained model to the user's Hub account.

Articles.Title: Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

stories.Headline: AlphaGenome 2: Deciphering how cells read DNA to better understand disease
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind announced AlphaGenome 2 on November 11, 2026, a next-generation model that predicts how DNA sequences and their variations affect specific human cell types. The model is designed to give scientists a new tool for finding the cellular drivers of disease. The announcement was authored by Adam Gayoso, Natasha Latysheva, Pushmeet Kohli and Žiga Avsec. Its aim is to bridge single-cell biology and human genetics by predicting how hundreds of human cell types respond to genetic variants.

AlphaGenome 2 is a conditional model that predicts DNA effects for one tissue, cell type or state at a time, rather than predicting many tissues in parallel. It takes a million-letter DNA sequence along with a target biological condition, chosen from a reference catalog or generated from a scientist's own single-cell experiment through a cell encoder. The model was trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues, and it also predicts DNA methylation. On the TenK10K dataset of 28 primary immune cell types, it identified nearly twice as many causal variants as the earlier model, at 30% against 16%. It is available today for non-commercial research through the AlphaGenome API and in private preview for commercial research.

Google DeepMind is responsible for building the model, and the company said it reconfigured the architecture to treat cell types differently from the first AlphaGenome. The announcement said the redesign lets the model learn how the same stretch of DNA is read differently across cell types. Google DeepMind also said that a single measurement, such as single-cell gene activity, can let the model predict unmeasured properties such as chromatin accessibility. The company described the model as a step-change improvement in variant predictive performance.

Professor Sarah Teichmann, co-founder of the Human Cell Atlas consortium and Professor of Stem Cell Medicine at the University of Cambridge, was quoted in the announcement. Peter Donnelly, CEO of Genomics Limited, said the company plans to incorporate the model into its Mystra platform and called it an impressive advance. The announcement said researchers studying inflammatory bowel disease can use the model to reproduce a finding that a variant boosts the ETS2 gene in gut macrophages. It also said the model predicted that a variant linked to severe COVID-19 disrupts gene activity more strongly in activated immune cells.

The first AlphaGenome was launched last year, and Google DeepMind later expanded it with AlphaGenome Atlas, which contains predictions for all 9 billion possible single-letter changes in the human genome. The announcement also said the Human Cell Atlas is mapping gene expression for millions of cells. Google DeepMind said it precomputed AlphaGenome 2 predictions for trait-associated variants across hundreds of human cell and tissue conditions. The company said the predictions cover traits ranging from height to type 2 diabetes.

Google DeepMind said it will continue working with researchers at the Wellcome Sanger Institute to profile a wider range of human cell types, developmental lineages and perturbed cellular states. It said it will soon release AlphaGenome 2 Skills in Google Antigravity, its agentic development platform. The company asked researchers to submit use cases by November 30, and said selected projects may be eligible for additional quota and credits. The articles do not say how the commercial private preview will be priced or when it will open more widely, and they give no independent validation of the model's results beyond the company's own benchmarks.

Articles.Title: AlphaGenome 2: Deciphering how cells read DNA to better understand disease

stories.Headline: ChatGPT Plus for veterans and servicemembers
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said in a November 11, 2026 post that more than 20,000 transitioning servicemembers and veterans have claimed a free year of ChatGPT Plus over the past year. The offer was made by OpenAI to these groups, and the company framed the milestone as a chance to look at how veterans are using AI to prepare for civilian careers. The effort began with veterans who work at OpenAI, who know firsthand how hard the transition can be. Beyond the free access, OpenAI Academy and community partners have hosted more than a dozen trainings for nearly 1,000 members of the military community, with seven more scheduled before the year ends.

The free year is offered through ID.me, which OpenAI credited for helping servicemembers and veterans access the offer. Veterans are using the tool to organize job searches, rehearse interviews, and explore career paths they had not considered. Air Force veteran Tilak Bhatnagar used his free year to prepare for a dozen interviews and weigh competing job offers, and he later took a role at a tech company. Air Force veteran Sadarian Bell used it to turn nearly a decade of military healthcare experience into a civilian résumé and practiced interviews aloud using voice mode. Navy veteran Kelli Ramirez used it to publish two books.

OpenAI Academy gives veterans, transitioning servicemembers, and military spouses a place to learn how to use the tools alongside people who understand their situation. The company recently completed a six-event Academy series with Veterans Forge aimed at helping veterans and military families work toward their goals. A workshop in Reston, Virginia drew nearly 100 veterans and active-duty servicemembers, and more than 80 Legionnaires attended three AI training sessions at the American Legion's national convention in Louisville, Kentucky. OpenAI said these sessions, along with workshops alongside AI Collective Hampton Roads and NPower, are shaping what it offers veterans next.

OpenAI said its goal is to help veterans and military families carry the skills they built in service into whatever work they choose next. The company is continuing this work with partners through the rest of the year, including a November 14 event in Nashville with Veterans Forge and Wounded Warrior Project. The post also thanked veterans for their service and for their contributions to their communities. Readers can check whether they are eligible for the free year of ChatGPT Plus through the company's offer page.

Articles.Title: ChatGPT Plus for veterans and servicemembers

stories.Headline: How LinkedIn, Netflix & DoorDash Run Agents, Evals & Inference in Production: QCon AI New York 2026
stories.Summary:
QCon AI New York 2026 has published its full schedule for December 15 to 16, covering the architecture and operational decisions behind production AI systems. Engineers from LinkedIn, Netflix, DoorDash, Figma, and other organizations are scheduled to speak on topics including agent authorization, evaluation pipelines, model serving, and AI-assisted software delivery. The conference is still a few weeks away, and the full ticket price takes effect on December 9. The program targets teams moving beyond their first AI deployments, asking where to enforce agent permissions and how to link offline evaluations to production behavior. It also examines how coding agents change code review, engineering practices, and organizational adoption.

Group registration for teams of three or more closes on November 27, 2026, with savings of $50 to $125 per ticket. Individual tickets cost $1,790 until December 8, the last price before the full rate applies. Tickets can be transferred to a colleague free of charge until December 11, 2026. Engineers who need approval can use a Convince Your Manager page that provides an email template built around the sessions relevant to their work. Nancy Wang, CTO at 1Password, opens day one with a talk on identity and authorization for agents in production, arguing that identity systems assume a human stands behind every credential.

Tara Sainath of Google DeepMind opens day two with a session on audio processing with large language models. Ronak Nathani of LinkedIn presents the company's Kubernetes ops agent, which works across more than 500,000 nodes and 5 million pods. Speakers from Figma, DoorDash, Netflix, Pinterest, Harvey, and Honeycomb also present their own production systems and practices. Figma reports that warm pools cut provisioning latency by 90% and raised availability from 99% to 99.95%. LinkedIn's AI code review system reviews tens of thousands of pull requests a week across about 10,000 repositories, with more than 60% of sampled suggestions accepted.

Netflix serves about 1 million inference requests per second across more than 300 models from one platform. Honeycomb's peak weekday pull request merges rose from about 30 to about 74 between early 2025 and April 2026, and have held steady since. Other sessions come from engineers at Anthropic, Microsoft, BlackRock, Databricks, Datadog, Tessl, LangChain, Baseten, and Google Cloud's DORA team. Topics include agentic standards, sandbox density, SRE agents, AgentOps for financial services, inference with vLLM, voice agents, software factories, and enterprise AI adoption. The full schedule is published on the conference site.

Articles.Title: How LinkedIn, Netflix & DoorDash Run Agents, Evals & Inference in Production: QCon AI New York 2026 - infoq.com

stories.Headline: JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents
stories.Summary:
JioHotstar, the streaming company, published an evaluation of six approaches to helping AI coding agents navigate large codebases, reported by InfoQ on November 11, 2026. The study was led by Abhishek Bansal, a Senior Staff Engineer at JioHotStar. The team compared filesystem tools, Sourcebot, Graphify, CocoIndex Code, Repowise, and an in-house retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. Testing used subsets of SWE-bench and CodeScaleBench, plus a custom question-answering harness built on JioHotstar's own codebase, with Claude Sonnet as the solving model.

The results measured task accuracy, token consumption, agent turns, and tool usability. The filesystem baseline, which relied on locally checked out repositories and standard search and file operations, stayed competitive on concrete tasks. Sourcebot performed better than the baseline on harder SWE-bench Verified tasks while costing less, but on simpler SWE-bench Lite tasks retrieval generally added overhead without consistently improving results. On CodeScaleBench, semantic retrieval helped more when agents had to interpret ambiguous problem descriptions and connect them to implementation details not visible through exact text or symbol searches. The report also found that agents often preferred familiar operations such as text search, file reads and symbol lookups over higher-level abstractions that needed extra verification.

The evaluation did not identify one retrieval approach that won across all tasks, so the team recommends keeping filesystem tools as a baseline, using structural search for concrete code-focused problems, and using semantic indexing for ambiguous or cross-cutting requirements. The engineers also advise measuring tool-use traces alongside accuracy to see whether retrieval reduces unnecessary exploration. Separately, Siddharth Vaithinathan argued in a LinkedIn post that coding agents should also learn the reasoning behind architectural decisions, constraints and past incidents, not just the code, and Tarun Bhargava raised questions about interpreting benchmark results drawn from limited subsets and probabilistic models. The articles do not say what JioHotstar plans to do next with these findings.

Articles.Title: JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents - infoq.com

stories.Headline: Cloud Security Alliance launches verified AI assurance level
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Security Alliance has launched STAR for AI Level 2, a new designation that adds third-party-verified AI assurance to its existing STAR framework. The article, published by IT Brief Australia on 11 November 2026, says the programme is aimed at organisations that want to show their AI systems are governed under recognised standards. It is built on the group's STAR for AI framework and is intended for companies that already hold, or want to combine, certifications tied to information security and AI management. The launch was announced as businesses face growing scrutiny over how they govern, secure and monitor AI systems in operational use.

The new level combines independent certification with automated analysis through the group's Valid-AI-ted for AI process and aligns with its AI Controls Matrix, which sets out controls for AI governance and risk management. Three certification routes are available, depending on an organisation's current status. The first pairs ISO/IEC 27001:2022 with the AI Controls Matrix, the second pairs ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 with that matrix, and the third pairs ISO/IEC 42001:2023 with the matrix for firms already certified under the AI management standard. In every case a Valid-AI-ted AI-CAIQ submission is required. A separate attestation route lets companies seek independent validation of the design and operating effectiveness of their AI controls, building on an existing SOC 2 programme.

Jim Reavis, the group's Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder, said that as organisations adopt AI more quickly, showing responsible governance and effective risk management is essential to building trust. He said the designation gives organisations a way to show their commitment through independent certification and a structured assessment of AI-specific controls. Daniele Catteddu, Chief Technology Officer of the group, said businesses need practical ways to show that their governance practices are keeping pace with adoption. He said the structure helps firms build on established standards while addressing the risks AI introduces, and provides tangible evidence of the controls supporting their systems.

The article places the launch within the group's long-running STAR programme, which organisations have used to document and certify security practices in cloud environments. It notes that ISO/IEC 42001 has become a focal point for firms seeking a recognised management system standard for AI, and that tying the new level to that standard positions the programme alongside frameworks many security and compliance teams already use. The article does not say what happens next or report any figures on uptake. It describes the programme as a formal route for documenting how AI systems are governed and monitored.

Articles.Title: Cloud Security Alliance launches verified AI assurance level - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Adobe previews 10 creative AI projects at MAX 2026
stories.Summary:
Adobe has previewed 10 research projects at its MAX 2026 Sneaks session, covering video, audio, photography, 3D, imaging and design. The projects reflect the company's ongoing research into creative tools and workflows, and some are available for hands-on testing through the Adobe Labs Playground. The announcement was reported on 12 November 2026. The company showed the work as part of its public research showcase, which has long served as a window into ideas that may later shape commercial software.

Four of the previews focus on video. Project Scene Sweep helps editors apply edits consistently across multiple shots by identifying characters, locations and scenes. Screen Test lets creators build a fictional character's appearance, voice and personality, then explore responses through natural language dialogue. Live Set allows changes to a subject, environment or camera while a video plays, and On Cue lets creators set the timing of events in generated video using an editable timing signal. A separate project, Sound Bender, pulls a described sound from a finished mix so users can explore variations and shape it in real time.

Five previews target images and design. Deep Brush interprets the shape, colour and lighting of an image so brushstrokes follow surfaces and light can be painted into a scene, while Sight Span turns a single image into a navigable environment. Hands On places object controls directly on the image canvas, and Rinse Repeat copies edits from one area to another using native Photoshop tools so they stay editable. Link Up uses a drag gesture to place an element in a scene, then adjusts perspective, scale and style and leaves the result as editable vector artwork. Adobe said the projects emphasise automation paired with direct user control, and point to friction it sees in repeating edits, isolating audio and making design changes on the canvas.

Alongside the stage previews, Adobe expanded Adobe Labs to combine research updates, professional workflows and early experiments from across its teams. The new Playground gives users access to selected previews, including Deep Brush and Hands On, as well as a Photoshop feature preview called Custom Filters. The company is putting some experimental work in front of users earlier, and gathering feedback from creative professionals and hobbyists to judge which ideas might become product features. The articles do not say when or whether any of these projects will reach commercial release.

Articles.Title: Adobe previews 10 creative AI projects at MAX 2026 - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Constant AI names Faust Chief Product Officer in reshuffle
stories.Summary:
Constant AI, a fintech that sells software to community financial institutions, has named Angela Faust its Chief Product Officer as part of four leadership changes, according to an IT Brief Australia report published on November 11, 2026. The company also named Lindsay Wescott Senior Vice President of Customer Success and Delivery, appointed Margarita "Maggie" Camacho Head of Product Operations, and created a new Head of Engineering role for Jon Girard. The moves came shortly after Constant AI launched Delinquency Shield, a product that helps credit unions offer payment assistance to members who ask for help before their loans pass 60 days past due. The changes aim to build the product and operations teams around executives with direct experience in lending, servicing and collections. Faust began her career in collections at Credit Union of Texas, where she later became Chief Operating Officer.

Wescott spent 18 years at TD Bank in loan servicing and collections roles, including as Vice President of Transaction Processing. Camacho brings 24 years in the credit union sector, including 17 years working inside credit unions before moving into technology project oversight. Girard has 15 years in software development and consulting, most recently working within client teams. The report places the appointments against pressure on lenders from higher delinquencies and rising loan loss provisions. Delinquency Shield directs members to available payment assistance programmes under an institution's own policies and feeds the outcome back into the lender's core processing system.

Constant AI cited its own analysis of NCUA call report data, which showed that one in four federally insured credit unions with more than USD $500 million in assets set aside more for loan loss reserves than they earned in the first half of 2026. The company says the period between a first missed payment and the 60-day mark is a key window for lenders trying to reduce losses without deepening borrowers' hardship. Wescott's combined role suggests tighter oversight of how clients implement the products, while Camacho's appointment adds an executive who has translated credit union operational needs into technology projects. Girard will lead software development as the company expands its use of AI-assisted coding and process design. Catherine York Powers, President and CEO of Constant AI, said that building agentic AI that protects credit unions' members and loan portfolios requires people who have done the work from the inside.

She said Faust, Wescott and Camacho have spent their careers in lending, servicing and collections, while Girard leads the engineering that turns that expertise into products that scale. Faust, in her own statement, said her start in collections at a credit union showed her what it takes to get a member the right help before a loan falls further behind. She said she was thrilled to join the leadership team at this stage of the company's growth. The appointments put a former credit union operator in charge of product development as Constant AI tries to convince financial institutions that automated tools can handle sensitive borrower interactions while staying within internal policy rules. The report does not say what further product plans or timelines the company has beyond these hires.

Articles.Title: Constant AI names Faust Chief Product Officer in reshuffle - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Hitachi Vantara adds AI analytics tools to VSP One
stories.Summary:
Hitachi Vantara has added new features to its VSP One data platform and Hitachi iQ portfolio, with a focus on object storage, data lakehouse analytics and governed access to enterprise data for AI use. The update was reported on 12 November 2026. The main change is to VSP One Object, which now starts with a four-node configuration intended to lower the cost of entry for organisations building storage for AI and analytics workloads. The release is aimed at companies trying to move AI projects beyond pilot stages into wider operational use.

The company points to a gap between AI adoption and deployment at scale. It cites a McKinsey 2026 State of AI survey in which nearly nine in 10 respondents said their organisations regularly use AI in at least one business function, while 44% said AI was scaling across the enterprise. It also cites IDC research finding that 89% of organisations reported some level of data-quality problem. According to Hitachi Vantara, VSP One Object can provide up to 5.5 times faster access to data for AI, analytics and S3 workloads. Expanded multisite replication and regional features are meant to improve resilience and availability.

Analytics are now available directly on VSP One Object, which can query supported open-format data, including Iceberg, Parquet, JSON and CSV, where it resides. Hitachi Vantara said this supports up to five times faster analytical query performance with 80% fewer CPUs. The approach aims to reduce data movement, which could limit duplicate datasets, data pipelines and the infrastructure needed to manage them. On the AI software side, Hitachi iQ Studio expands access to structured and unstructured data for retrieval-augmented generation, including filesystem and NFS knowledge sources, and adds a Model Gateway, governed Model Context Protocol connectivity, ServiceNow support, role-based access controls, and observability and lifecycle management for AI applications and agents.

Octavian Tanase, Chief Product Officer at Hitachi Vantara, said that AI strategy is now closely tied to data strategy as AI becomes part of more business-critical workloads. He said the company wants to give customers a practical way to build a data foundation for AI, bring analytics closer to their data and scale as demand grows, while keeping the resilience and control enterprises depend on. Hitachi Vantara has also linked the work to its Hitachi AI Factory initiative, which focuses on moving AI systems from experimentation into production tied to business operations. The release reflects a wider trend of storage suppliers repositioning infrastructure around AI requirements, combining storage, analytics and governance into a more unified stack.

Articles.Title: Hitachi Vantara adds AI analytics tools to VSP One - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Data quality and governance lead AI investment priorities in ANZ
stories.Summary:
Organisations across Australia and New Zealand are moving beyond experiments with artificial intelligence and are working to build it into daily operations, from predictive analytics to decision-making. A regional sales director at Melissa, Edmund Ng, argues in an IT Brief article published on 11 November 2026 that AI investment does not automatically produce measurable business value. The underlying data foundation matters more than many organisations assume, because unclear ownership, inconsistent records, fragmented information or poor integration can weaken an AI model's performance. Ng contends that reliable and scalable AI deployment depends on focusing on data quality and governance.

Recent Boomi-Omdia research cited in the article shows a gap between AI ambitions and operational preparedness. More than 70% of Australian organisations and around 65% of New Zealand organisations reported active AI initiatives. Close to 30% of Australian respondents and over 30% of New Zealand respondents said they could not estimate AI success effectively. The study also found that 39% of Australian organisations and 43% of New Zealand organisations lacked a dedicated AI budget, although many were on the verge of increasing AI investment soon. Ng advises that businesses check whether information feeding AI tools is trustworthy, accessible and consistent before buying more tools.

Ng writes that the article is his own analysis, and the articles name the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment in New Zealand as treating data quality as a priority for responsible AI use. Ng says that data validation, de-duplication, standardisation and monitoring should never stop. He also states that governance sets the rules for access management, protection and usage, and that without it departments may define data fields differently. The article notes that around 90% of organisations across ANZ are considering heavy investment in AI risk, governance and compliance, yet fewer than 50% have formal AI governance policies. Ng recommends that responsibilities be defined, data sources documented, and access controls and error review processes put in place.

The article says that over 90% of organisations across ANZ consider data integration and orchestration a priority, but fewer than half use a platform-driven approach. It warns that more than 70% of ANZ organisations found data quality and trust affected by unmanaged shadow integrations built for immediate operational needs. Ng gives the example of a retailer combining inventory, sales, customer and supplier details for demand forecasting, where unlinked datasets could leave the model working with inconsistent product identifiers or outdated stock figures. He also says that over 90% of ANZ organisations are making data quality, privacy and security a priority, with data residency drawing growing attention for sensitive customer details, cloud-based AI services and cross-border operations. Businesses in Australia or New Zealand, he adds, need clarity on where data is stored, who has access, what providers do with it, and which regulatory obligations apply.

Ng recommends categorising data by sensitivity, setting access permissions, and checking whether data suits a given AI use case before deployment. He suggests recording baseline metrics such as duplicate rates, cost per transaction, record accuracy and error rates, then comparing them after implementation. He advises treating data quality, integration and governance as interconnected investments rather than separate technology projects. The article ends by recommending tools for verifying, de-duplicating, correcting and standardising customer details across global markets. It does not report any specific outcome, timetable or regulatory decision that would follow from these findings.

Articles.Title: Data quality and governance lead AI investment priorities in ANZ - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: OutSystems launches AI claims tool for auto insurers
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, OutSystems launched Agentic First Notice of Loss, a prebuilt AI system for auto insurers that extends the company's Agentic Industry Solutions portfolio into insurance. The product is designed to handle the early stages of a claim after a car accident. It links customer-facing applications, AI agents and existing claims systems so that the first report of a loss can be captured quickly. The tool is generally available now.

The system can help policyholders report a loss, gather statements and third-party details, analyze submitted damage photos, check policy coverage and open a claim in the carrier's claims platform through an integration layer. It works with existing claims platforms as well as systems rebuilt on OutSystems technology. The company says it is aimed at reducing the delays that come from legacy systems and scattered data. Decisions on coverage, liability and payments remain with human adjusters, and insurers can adjust business rules, screens and agents to suit their operations.

The company also says the system records agent actions and applies access controls, and it is offering an Insurance Agent Kit with reusable agents for checking coverage and reading claim documents. Luis Blando, Chief Product and Technology Officer at OutSystems, said insurers need AI working in daily claims operations rather than another pilot. He argued that the tool lets insurers take a complete report and guide customers right after an accident while leaving coverage, liability and payment decisions to adjusters. Tom Pelster, Chief Information Officer at PRISM, said the approach shows insurers can build smarter workflows on top of existing core systems instead of replacing them.

Adam DeWitt, Chief Executive Officer of Honk, described how the roadside partner's network can dispatch a tow during the reporting process and offer nearby in-network repair shops. The company cited its State of AI Development in Insurance 2026 report, which found that 35% of insurance IT leaders said AI projects had not started because they took too long, while 42% named legacy systems or scattered data as the main barrier. It also cited InvoiceCloud research indicating that 83% of US consumers would switch carriers after a poor claims experience. Analysts and suppliers have increasingly focused on agentic systems that carry out multistep tasks across software environments, and the article presents this launch as part of that wider push.

Articles.Title: OutSystems launches AI claims tool for auto insurers - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: India's sovereign AI ambitions must go beyond building models - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
India's sovereign AI ambitions must go beyond building models, according to an opinion piece by Abhishek Ranjan, CTO of Blue Machines AI, published by ETCIO on November 11, 2026. The piece argues that India is investing heavily in AI technology, infrastructure and indigenous models to strengthen sovereignty. It states that the IndiaAI Mission, backed by over ₹10,000 crore, has identified 20 indigenous models for support. The mission has also sanctioned 93 lakh GPU hours, and shared national compute crossed 45,000 GPUs in June. The author writes that building models is only part of the challenge, because enterprises must make AI work reliably, securely and at scale.

The article says sovereignty should extend beyond where a model is built or data is stored, covering data sovereignty, model sovereignty and infrastructure sovereignty. It says enterprises need operational control over where AI runs, which models it uses, how it processes information and how it integrates with existing systems. It notes that using an Indian model does not by itself make an AI system sovereign. The author describes inference, the stage where a trained model responds in use, as the point where operational decisions matter most. The piece also says that agentic AI, which executes tasks across applications, requires role-based access, defined execution boundaries, monitoring and audit trails built into the architecture.

The author, Abhishek Ranjan, is the one making these arguments, and the article is an opinion piece whose views are his own. ETCIO states that it does not necessarily subscribe to the views expressed and is not responsible for any damage arising from them. The author calls for collaboration among technology companies, enterprises, infrastructure providers and policymakers. He says technology companies must build deployable and portable AI platforms, and enterprises must evaluate solutions against production requirements. He adds that infrastructure providers must make secure, in-country compute commercially viable, and policymakers must clarify rules on data processing, accountability and deployment.

Those most directly affected are Indian enterprises deploying AI in sensitive workflows, such as banks handling customer enquiries and loan applications. The article uses a banking example to show how latency, data access and reliability requirements apply. It cites the Reserve Bank of India's requirement that payment system data be stored within India as an important reference point for regulated industries. The author also says Indian-language support matters, since customers often switch between Hindi and English, use regional accents and speak over noisy telephone lines. He argues that multilingual accuracy must be tested against such real conditions rather than benchmarks alone.

The article's background is the IndiaAI Mission and the country's broader push for indigenous models, speech technologies and compute infrastructure. The author notes that India must continue developing its semiconductor and computing capabilities, and that domestic AI infrastructure will take time to mature. He states that sovereignty does not mean operating in isolation or rejecting global technology. The piece offers no timeline for the policy clarity it calls for, and it does not say which specific rules or requirements policymakers will adopt next. It also does not indicate what outcomes the proposed collaboration would produce.

Articles.Title: India's sovereign AI ambitions must go beyond building models - ET CIO

stories.Headline: PuppyGraph Secures $10 Million for AI Expansion
stories.Summary:
PuppyGraph, a graph query engine startup for enterprise artificial intelligence based in the United States, has raised $10 million in a Series A round led by Particle Future, with participation from defy.vc. The funding was announced in November 2026, with the Analytics India Magazine report published on November 11, 2026. The round brings the company's total capital raised to $15 million. The announcement came as the company launched the general availability of PuppyGraph 1.0.

The funding is meant to support engineering work and expansion of enterprise sales efforts. PuppyGraph 1.0 lets AI agents query data across up to 3,000 enterprise tables as one unified graph, without copying that data into a separate graph database. The company says agent projects that begin with 30 to 50 tables often struggle to scale when production work requires links across thousands of tables and multiple systems. The platform works with databases, data warehouses, and data lakes, including Apache Iceberg, Databricks, Snowflake, ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, and Microsoft Fabric.

Weimo Liu, co-founder and CEO of PuppyGraph, said in a statement that enterprise data insights will soon be generated by agents. He said those agents will need to move across thousands of tables, follow relationships, and gather evidence across departments and systems. The release includes an AI-assisted schema builder that proposes graph schemas from existing tables for data teams to review and approve. The engine also rejects undefined relationships and sends feedback that agents can use to correct their queries, which the company says prevents unsupported assumptions about how data connects.

The company reports that its annual recurring revenue grew sevenfold over the past year, though it did not disclose a revenue figure. Customers it names include AMD, Palo Alto Networks, Datadog, Netskope, Coinbase, Trend Micro, Baker Hughes, and Sola Security. In a benchmark the company cited, a 10-hop query across billions of edges finished in 2.26 seconds on a four-machine cluster. Developers can try the product through a free Docker deployment that requires no payment method or registration form.

Articles.Title: PuppyGraph Secures $10 Million for AI Expansion - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: NHA Selects EkaCare for AI Voice Scribe in Public Health Facilities
stories.Summary:
The National Health Authority (NHA) has selected EkaCare, a Bengaluru-based health AI startup, as a technology partner for an ambient AI-enabled Voice Scribe that aims to reduce documentation work for doctors in public health facilities. The article, published on November 11, 2026, reports that the selection was made through the NHA's Expression of Interest process for open-source ambient AI voice-to-text solutions for digital health record creation, and that EkaCare demonstrated its product before the NHA's Evaluation Committee. The Voice Scribe listens to doctor-patient consultations and produces structured clinical notes that doctors can review once the appointment ends. Those notes cover complaints, medical history, medications, vital signs, laboratory findings, diagnosis and treatment plans, and they follow specialty-specific templates in Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources format.

The solution is built on two EkaCare technologies: Parrotlet-A 2.5 Pro, an open-weight speech model designed for Indian healthcare conversations, and Lipi, an open-source agentic harness previously called Vaarta. According to the company, Parrotlet-A 2.5 Pro recorded the lowest error rate among the models tested in a benchmark of 6,550 real Indian consultations across five languages. The system supports more than 15 Indian languages, including conversations in which speakers switch between languages, and it will run on NHA infrastructure powered by Amazon Web Services. It will convert consultations into records under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission and is designed to operate inside NHA's air-gapped secure environment, so public health facilities keep control over their health data. Public hospitals can embed the tool in their existing hospital management systems or use a standalone interface and APIs based on the open MedScribe Alliance standard.

EkaCare's Chief Product Officer, Bhaskar Chaudhary, said in a statement that a doctor can speak with a patient in the language the patient is comfortable with and have a structured clinical note ready for review when the consultation ends. The company, which operates as Orbi Health Private Limited, also said that doctors remain responsible for the records. Each note must be reviewed, edited if necessary, and approved by a verified doctor before it is saved and linked to the patient's Ayushman Bharat Health Account, and doctors using the standalone interface authenticate through the Healthcare Professionals Registry. The partnership builds on EkaCare's existing ambient medical scribe, EkaScribe, which the company says more than 1,000 doctors in private practice use.

Articles.Title: NHA Selects EkaCare for AI Voice Scribe in Public Health Facilities - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Can Indian Startups Win The AI Inference Race?
stories.Summary:
Indian startups are moving into AI inference, the stage where trained models respond to new inputs at scale, as the industry shifts focus from building bigger models. Inc42 published the feature on 11 November 2026 under a headline asking whether Indian startups can win the AI inference race. Running models faster, cheaper and reliably for millions of users is proving hard, which is why inference platforms are gaining attention. Companies named in the article include Simplismart, Pipeshift and E2E Networks, which are building different layers of the inference stack. The article frames the business as a bet that companies will increasingly pay for faster, cheaper and more reliable AI.

Simplismart claims it cut inference costs by 53% for voice AI platform Sanas while retaining 99.99% accuracy. For customer support platform Exotel, it claims costs fell to ₹0.90–₹1.30 per minute from ₹2.10 for a closed-model API. The same work cut latency from 1.1 seconds to under 300 milliseconds. Apna, a jobs and professional networking platform, uses inference platforms to run smaller open-source and proprietary models for simpler tasks. Its sister company Blue Machines AI has built its own inference platform for conversational AI, where response speed and handling many users at once matter more.

Abhishek Ranjan, Apna's CTO and also CTO of Blue Machines AI, said businesses need not depend on external platforms for every task. Vishnu Subramanian, founder of JarvisLabs, which E2E Networks acquired, described four ways to consume inference. These are shared model APIs, managed inference, self-managed inference and dedicated infrastructure. JarvisLabs' Token Factory lets businesses access hosted open models through an API and pay per token. Subramanian said the right choice depends on how much control a company needs and how much traffic it handles.

Simplismart raised $14 million in Series B funding in October, with participation from NVIDIA, Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax. E2E Networks offers both managed and self-managed inference. Pipeshift, a startup focused on production inference for open-source models, recently partnered with Neysa to combine its serving layer with Neysa's sovereign AI cloud for Indian businesses. Targeted use cases include voice agents, coding agents and enterprise copilots. Globally, Y Combinator-backed startups Hopper and RouterPlus are also pursuing specific inference problems, one for voice agents and one for an inference marketplace.

The article says the inference opportunity is unlikely to settle into a single category and could span low-latency voice AI, open-model serving, sovereign inference, agent workloads and specialised enterprise deployments. It also notes that the race for smarter models is giving way to running them efficiently at scale. Its own summary states that inference is about finding the right combination of model, hardware and serving configuration for a given business. The article does not say which Indian startups will win or what sustainable business models will look like. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Can Indian Startups Win The AI Inference Race? - Inc42

stories.Headline: Measuring the true capacity of AI seats
stories.Summary:
Mo. Abubakar Lala, chief operating officer of RS Gonzales, a Washington, D.C. digital marketing agency, published an opinion column on Accounting Today on November 11, 2026, arguing that firms need to measure how much of their prepaid AI software capacity goes unused. The column observes that AI vendors are shifting from flat subscriptions to consumption-based token billing, and that many professional service firms are absorbing rising technology costs rather than raising client fees. It cites a 2026 Thomson Reuters report finding that 42% of professional service organizations do not measure return on their AI investments, 40% do not know whether they do, and only 18% actively monitor those returns.

The author disagrees with commentator John Griffin, who had argued that usage- or outcome-based billing is better because it ties fees to outputs. The author's view is that a flat per-seat fee gives a firm a fixed cost ceiling, and that the real gap is the lack of reporting on how much of that fixed capacity is used. A Futurum Group study is cited as finding that 42.3% of enterprise buyers prefer per-seat pricing for generative software, compared with 36.6% for consumption pricing and 21.1% for outcome-based pricing. The author also cites a Zylo study finding that organizations leave an average of 36% of software licenses unused.

To test this, the author compared one billing period's fixed seat invoice of $2,305.50, which includes 6% Washington, D.C. sales tax, with the list-price value of the token usage for the same users, which came to $36,820. Dividing the usage value by the subscription cost gives a metric the author calls "seat yield," roughly 16X in a baseline month. The author stresses that this is a capacity measure rather than a return on investment, since it does not capture work quality, rework or client value, and that the figure is a conservative floor because of how cache writes were calculated. The column proposes "seatsourcing," routing tasks to colleagues with spare capacity on their own named seats without sharing logins, along with three practices: tracking monthly seat yield, setting up internal showback reporting, and enforcing user-level overage caps. The author frames the key question for the coming year as how much already-paid capacity is sitting idle.

Articles.Title: Measuring the true capacity of AI seats - Accounting Today

stories.Headline: SCHMID wins equipment order for glass core substrate plant in South Asia
stories.Summary:
German equipment maker SCHMID Group has won an order for wet-process equipment for a new glass core substrate plant in South Asia, according to a report published on November 11, 2026. The customer is a US company that specializes in glass-based advanced packaging and is moving its technology from pilot production to industrial scale. The order will be booked in the fourth quarter of 2026. SCHMID does not name the customer or the country, and it does not disclose the value of the order.

According to the customer's own public announcements, the plant will be the first advanced packaging site in South Asia built around glass substrates and 3D heterogeneous integration. Once fully ramped up, it is designed to produce about 70,000 glass panels a year, along with glass interposers and 3D integration modules. These products are aimed at AI, data centres, 5G, and aerospace and defence uses. SCHMID will supply equipment for critical wet-process steps that the company says are decisive for yield, reliability and cost. The facility is therefore a notable step toward production of this packaging technology at scale.

Roland Rettenmeier, Chief Sales Officer of SCHMID Group, said that manufacturing glass cores at scale requires processes that deliver precise through-glass vias, reliable metallization and stable yields on large panel formats. He said the company's process know-how and equipment platforms are what make the difference in this area. Glass cores are seen as a possible successor to the organic cores used in today's IC substrates. They are flatter and more dimensionally stable, warp less in large package formats, and allow finer line and space structures, which matters as AI accelerators and chiplet designs require larger packages.

Articles.Title: SCHMID wins equipment order for glass core substrate plant in South Asia - Evertiq

stories.Headline: Imec delivers baseline flows for NanoIC line interposer
stories.Summary:
Imec has delivered the baseline flows for the silicon interposer platform being developed within its NanoIC pilot line, according to an Electronics Weekly report dated 11 November 2026. The milestone provides an early technical view of a key technology for chiplet integration. It is presented as an important step toward more accessible advanced packaging innovation in Europe. The silicon interposer is one of three advanced interconnect technologies being developed within NanoIC, alongside fine-pitch RDL interposers and die-to-wafer hybrid bonding. These technologies are being translated into dedicated process design kits (PDKs) and, ultimately, future low-volume prototyping opportunities.

The reference platform captures the architecture, manufacturing flow and key design characteristics of imec's silicon interposer technology. It includes through-silicon vias, multiple metal routing layers and support for microbump pitches down to 20 µm. The baseline flow forms the technical basis for a dedicated silicon interposer PDK, scheduled for release in early 2027. That PDK will let universities, start-ups and fabless companies explore the technology virtually, using industry-standard EDA environments from Cadence and Synopsys. When launched, it will complement NanoIC's existing PDKs for fine-pitch RDL interposers and die-to-wafer hybrid bonding.

Imec is responsible for the technology, and its representatives described the three interconnect approaches as complementary. Marie Garcia Bardon of Imec said silicon interposers enable the high-density routing needed for advanced compute, while fine-pitch RDL interposers offer a cost-efficient alternative. She said die-to-wafer hybrid bonding enables ultra-dense chip-to-chip connections. Imec senior vice president Bart Placklé said NanoIC provides a common technology foundation that lets researchers, start-ups and fabless companies test interconnect approaches. He said this is intended to help Europe and its strategic markets prepare for next-generation AI, automotive and advanced computing systems.

The article says the semiconductor industry is increasingly turning to chiplet architectures, which combine multiple specialized dies within one package, as AI performance requirements rise. It states that performance depends on the connections between chiplets as well as the chiplets themselves. Silicon interposers act as a high-density routing layer beneath the dies, linking compute chiplets, high-bandwidth memory and other components. The article notes they are relevant to AI accelerators, GPUs and other high-performance multi-die systems. NanoIC's longer-term ambition is to extend virtual exploration through the PDK into physical silicon demonstrators on the pilot line.

The article does not state the cost, the number of participating organizations or the exact size of the pilot line. It also does not give details on when low-volume prototyping opportunities will begin. Whether the early 2027 PDK release will hold is not addressed. The article does not describe any reactions from companies beyond the two Imec quotes.

Articles.Title: Imec delivers baseline flows for NanoIC line interposer - Electronics Weekly

stories.Headline: SK Hynix taps HBM veteran to lead US business as competition intensifies
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix, the South Korean memory chipmaker, has named Hyun Ahn to lead a newly created Americas business unit. The announcement, reported by DIGITIMES on November 11, 2026, comes as competition for custom high-bandwidth memory (HBM) intensifies. Ahn, a former development chief at the company, is identified as the head of the Americas business in a photo caption from TSMC's Technology Symposium in April 2026. The article notes that suppliers are moving closer to US chip designers as demand for custom HBM grows.

The available text is limited, since the full article sits behind a paid subscription, so the details of the unit's scope and staffing cannot be confirmed here. The move signals that SK Hynix is placing a senior executive with HBM experience directly in the United States, where many of the designers of advanced AI chips are based. The report frames the appointment as a response to rising competition rather than a routine reshuffle. Beyond the leadership change, the visible material does not give figures, dates for the unit's launch, or specific customers.

Readers should treat the reported purpose as the company's stated direction and not as a set of measured results. SK Hynix itself is the party responsible for the decision, and the source article attributes the appointment to the company. The article's byline is Sherri Wang of DIGITIMES, based in Taipei. No direct statement from Ahn or from company executives about the reasons for the change is included in the text available.

The broader context is a memory market where HBM, the stacked memory that feeds AI accelerators, has become central to competition among suppliers. Closer contact with US chip designers suggests that custom HBM products are being developed around individual customers' needs. The visible articles do not say what the new unit will do next or how it will be staffed. More to follow.

Articles.Title: SK Hynix taps HBM veteran to lead US business as competition intensifies - digitimes

stories.Headline: Lee Visits Samsung's Onyang Campus, Hails HBM Packaging Hub
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae-myung said on the 12th that Samsung Electronics' Onyang campus in Asan will become a core base for advanced HBM packaging. He made the remark in a congratulatory address at a groundbreaking ceremony for the Chungcheong mega-project, held at the campus in South Chungcheong Province. The article is dated November 12, 2026, though the photo caption refers to a December 12 ceremony. Lee said three advanced investment projects were breaking ground in Chungcheong with great momentum. Lee said the Asan campus will add a new advanced packaging fab worth 6 trillion won, followed by a further 40 trillion won in advanced equipment investment in stages.

He also congratulated the public on the full-scale start of construction for the Chungcheong investments, which include an advanced semiconductor packaging fab and an advanced display production line in Asan. A manufacturing facility for high-performance substrates for AI servers is being built in Sejong. Lee tied the plan to a bold investment pledge made the previous July by companies and the government. Lee said that promise, made just four months earlier, was now becoming reality at the site. Samsung Electronics Chairman Lee Jae-yong spoke alongside him at the ceremony, according to the photo caption.

Lee also said the innovation wave is spreading across the entire Chungcheong region, not only Asan and Sejong. The article reports that the article's original reporting came from Jeon Hee-yoon for Seoul Economic Daily and was AI-translated from Korean. Lee added that preparations for construction are proceeding without disruption on a memory and advanced packaging fab in Cheongju, an AI data center in Dangjin and a biopharmaceutical production facility in Osong. The article does not say when these projects will be completed. It also does not describe any response from Samsung beyond the chairman's presence at the event.

Articles.Title: Lee Visits Samsung's Onyang Campus, Hails HBM Packaging Hub - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Lotte On Teams With Plateer to Run Brand Websites With AI
stories.Summary:
Lotte On, the e-commerce platform of Lotte Shopping, announced on November 12 that it will launch an integrated service helping brands build and run their own online stores, developed with Plateer, an artificial intelligence commerce platform company. The two companies signed a memorandum of understanding on November 11 at Lotte Shopping's e-commerce division in Samseong-dong, Seoul. The service is called "New LECS," short for LOTTE Ecommerce Cloud & Service, and it is powered by Plateer's X2BEE platform. The agreement covers an integrated system for the full range of online selling, including creating direct-to-consumer brand websites, managing several brands on one system, processing online orders and offering overseas services.

The service is aimed at brands that have trouble running their own online stores because of price competition with large platforms, high initial setup costs and a lack of dedicated staff. Under New LECS, brands can open their own stores without making a separate system investment. They also receive support across operations such as product management, promotions, customer service, orders and settlement. AI agents take on repetitive work, including product registration, curated sales events and customer inquiries, which the companies say will ease the operational burden on brands.

Choo Dae-sik, head of Lotte Shopping's e-commerce division, said the service was built to reduce the burden of complex store operations so that brands can focus on their core value and grow by meeting customers directly. He said Lotte's long-accumulated operating experience and distribution infrastructure, combined with Plateer's technology, would be used to build an e-commerce ecosystem in which platforms and brands grow together. Lee Sang-hoon, CEO of Plateer, also took part in the signing. The articles do not give a launch date, pricing or the number of brands expected to join.

Articles.Title: Lotte On Teams With Plateer to Run Brand Websites With AI - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: How companies are using AI to make you spend more money
stories.Summary:
Companies are increasingly using sophisticated tools to set prices, and that practice is drawing new scrutiny from Americans frustrated with rising costs. In a November 11, 2026 PBS NewsHour report, correspondent Paul Solman explained how this technology is changing what consumers pay. A 400-shopper experiment on Instacart found that 75 percent of items in carts were offered at different prices to different shoppers at the same location and time. The price differences reached as much as 23 percent. Instacart halted the experiment after it became public.

Lindsay Owens, who heads Groundwork Collaborative, described how companies can now use algorithms to adjust prices based on personal data. Such data can include a shopper's location, IP address, purchase history, loyalty card use and app logins. Owens' book, "Gouged," expands on that work and draws on Groundwork's review of 315 patents. Walmart plans to install digital price tags in all U.S. stores by the end of the year, which could allow it to change prices quickly. Solman also reported that McDonald's pushes pricing recommendations to franchisees, and that Wendy's once said it would test dynamic pricing.

Walmart executive Dan Bartlett said in an open letter that the company does not and will not use individual customers' personal information to set individualized prices. McDonald's responded to a price-fixing lawsuit by saying its optional tools do not automate, coordinate or fix pricing. Wendy's former CEO, Kirk Tanner, announced plans to test dynamic pricing and daypart offerings along with A.I.-enabled menu changes. Uber did not respond to requests for comment about Uber Eats delivery fees that varied among Solman's colleagues ordering the same meal. Solman's test showed delivery fees ranging from $2.49 to $4.49 for the same location.

Shoppers are the group most directly affected, and Owens said consumer backlash against Wendy's was swift. Surveys cited in the report found that more than 80 percent of Americans believe businesses should charge all customers the same price for the same item. Economist Richard Thaler, of the University of Chicago, said customers who feel treated unfairly may take their business elsewhere. Owens suggested consumers compare prices across channels, use a VPN to change location, or shop without logging into loyalty programs. She also proposed banning the use of shopper data to set prices.

Earlier practices of charging customers the same price have long been part of the economic debate, and Thaler's research from about 40 years ago asked consumers about pricing fairness. In his snow shovel example, a hardware store that raised its price from $15 to $20 after a blizzard was judged unfair by about 80 percent of respondents. Owens said prices once were more tied to the underlying cost of goods plus a fair margin. The report describes these new tools as built on data gathering, cloud computing and machine learning. Solman noted that the use of such pricing technology appears to be growing.

It remains unclear whether public backlash will be enough to stop companies from using personalized pricing, as Thaler said that is an empirical question. The articles do not establish whether Walmart will follow through on its stated policy, nor whether the Uber Eats fee variations were deliberate or random. Owens said outside observers cannot fully see inside companies' pricing processes. Neither the articles nor the report say whether Owens' policy proposals will be adopted. Consumer protection, as Solman concluded, currently seems to rest largely with shoppers themselves.

Articles.Title: How companies are using AI to make you spend more money

stories.Headline: Parenting in the age of AI: Helping kids learn to think for themselves
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is spreading into childhood, from talking toys for toddlers to homework apps for students, according to a FOX 8 report published November 11, 2026. Experts say it offers chances to help children learn but also creates challenges for parents trying to build skills kids will need as adults. Dr. Michael Forbes, chief scientific adviser for Akron Children's Hospital in Akron, Ohio, says AI is already here and people use it without always knowing. Forbes has been writing about parenting in the age of AI, and he says AI is now built into toys, videos and apps children use. AI-powered toys can hold conversations, ask questions and respond to answers, and they never get tired.

Forbes says parents should understand what a toy does before handing it over, since young children may not realize they are sharing personal information. He says parents should learn about AI toys and apps before younger children use them. He also advises parents to experience the technology alongside their children rather than leaving them alone with it. Forbes says middle school is an especially important time for building critical thinking, and he says AI can give answers without teaching how to reach them. He describes struggle and mistakes as desirable difficulties that help the brain learn and remember information.

Forbes says children who lean too heavily on AI may know a little about many subjects without mastering any, which can hurt them when they must explain what they know without a computer. He says students need guidance and accountability from parents and teachers as they move into high school and college. He describes an effective arrangement as a partnership among student, parent and teacher. At Case Western Reserve University, associate professor Peter Shulman says colleges are still deciding how AI should fit into classrooms. He says some faculty allow unlimited use while others prohibit it, and he says the key is students understanding what is acceptable and why.

Forbes says AI can offer individualized tutoring that many families cannot afford from a private tutor, and it can adjust explanations to a student's level. He says the key question is whether AI helps a student understand material or simply produces something to turn in. He warns that AI products may be designed to keep users engaged, comparing this to social media feeds. Forbes also worries that children who spend too much time with machines may miss social skills such as communicating, showing patience and handling disagreements. He encourages parents to ask children how they use AI, what they learned and whether it actually helped them understand.

Forbes says banning AI is not realistic and that families should keep human relationships central. He says AI should enhance human learning rather than replace parents, teachers, friends or real-world experiences. The article does not describe any new law, regulation or policy governing AI in children's products. It also does not report any formal study, survey or data on how many children use AI toys or apps. Whether schools or lawmakers will set uniform rules for AI use by students is not addressed in the report.

Articles.Title: Parenting in the age of AI: Helping kids learn to think for themselves

stories.Headline: Using AI for your resume might help you land a job interview, expert says
stories.Summary:
Job seekers may get a boost from using AI when preparing their resumes, according to a KSAT report published November 11, 2026, by reporter Olivia Dague. The story centers on Jason Pasola, who works for Robert Half, a worldwide staffing company. Many employers now run applications through software that scans for keywords before a person reviews them, a practice Pasola says has grown over the past two years. Pasola's advice is to use AI tools to organize and format a resume, but not to invent or inflate skills.

Pasola told the station that applicants should tailor their resumes to each job description without copying the posting word for word, since that can signal a problem to hiring managers. He named Microsoft and Claude as tools that work well for the task. He also said he believes some qualified candidates are missing out on interviews because they do not use AI tools to bring their abilities forward. The article frames these points as his professional view rather than an official rule or policy.

The report sits within a broader local news roundup and does not describe any new law, requirement or formal change to hiring practices. It notes that Texas is preparing to swear in its first new governor in 12 years, and that Gina Hinojosa is using a digital portal to assemble her team, which the reporter links to the wider shift toward digital applications. The article does not say whether any employer or agency has adopted a specific policy on AI-written resumes. It also does not report on any next steps or follow-up plans beyond the interview itself.

Articles.Title: Using AI for your resume might help you land a job interview, expert says

stories.Headline: Confidential computing and AI agents push KubeVirt VMs forward
stories.Summary:
Confidential computing is drawing new interest from enterprises deciding where their most sensitive AI workloads can run safely, and that interest is giving virtual machines a fresh role alongside containers on Kubernetes. The shift coincides with a milestone for KubeVirt, the open-source project that runs VMs inside Kubernetes clusters, which graduated from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation this week. Its maintainers are now steering the project toward AI isolation, agent sandboxes and confidential computing. Holder and Romanovsky spoke with theCUBE Research at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, and the discussion was broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio. The story was published on November 11, 2026.

The core idea behind KubeVirt is running VMs and containers on the same Kubernetes cluster without maintaining two separate stacks. That pairing matters more in the AI era, and the article notes that Nvidia developers are helping the project integrate dynamic resource allocation for GPU hardware. Romanovsky described the two forms of compute as complementary, with VMs handling heavier lifting and stronger isolation while pods provide scaling for surrounding applications. The project is also being considered as an isolation backend for the Kubernetes agent sandbox repository. Holder said KubeVirt could offer live migration and complex hardware configurations that other isolation backends lack.

Holder is a principal software engineer and KubeVirt maintainer at Red Hat, and Romanovsky is a technical lead and KubeVirt maintainer there as well. Holder said confidential computing is one of the blockers keeping companies with very sensitive data from joining public cloud, and that resolving it would free them to do so. Romanovsky said VMs and containers can even run together as a single application. The article states that Red Hat sponsored the segment and that neither Red Hat nor other sponsors have editorial control over theCUBE content. The piece does not describe any specific timeline for the planned sandbox or confidential computing work.

Articles.Title: Confidential computing and AI agents push KubeVirt VMs forward

stories.Headline: Hardware-Based Location Checks Target AI Chip Smuggling (Texas A&M)
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Texas A&M University published a paper titled "5G CATS," describing a method to verify where AI chips operate after deployment, and the paper appeared on November 11, 2026. The system is meant to counter chip smuggling by pairing a 5G radio, cryptographic engine, and hardware interlock on the GPU package with 5G URLLC base stations. The authors report that their radio profile narrows the 99.9th percentile round-trip spread to 2.60 ms in simulations of an unloaded cell. The paper was listed under the tags on the page, which include chip smuggling, export controls, and GPUs.

The design terminates the radio link inside the package, which removes the host software, PCIe fabric, and baseboard management controller from the verification path. It maps an authenticated challenge-response protocol onto 5G's slot structure and replaces permanent key erasure with short-lived execution leases. It also specifies a cross-check of the chip's reported serving cell against the carrier's own attachment records. In simulations, a tracer rejects every round of a fiber relay from 300 km, compared with 2,000 km for default 5G.

The authors of the paper are Sreevikram Rajaraman, Derek Ladd, Nicholas Heinrich-Barna, Srinivas Shakkottai, and Jeyavijayan Rajendran. The paper is credited as an arXiv preprint, numbered arXiv:2611.13437, from 2026. The researchers state that enforcing export controls on AI accelerators requires verifying where a chip operates after deployment. Their stated aim is to close the timeout slack that an attacker could use to relay traffic over fiber from a restricted region.

The work is directed at AI accelerators and the export controls that apply to them, and the page's tags point to semiconductor security and chip traceability as its audience. The articles do not describe any affected companies, governments, or users beyond these categories. Prior approaches, the authors say, either cross the untrusted host stack or rely on noisy power-line channels that inflate the timeout slack. The page also lists several unrelated technical papers published the same day, which the articles do not connect to this one.

The articles do not say whether 5G CATS has been built in hardware, tested outside simulation, or adopted by any carrier, chip maker, or regulator. They do not report any response from export authorities or industry. The paper is described only as a preprint with simulation results, and the article does not indicate whether it will be peer reviewed or implemented. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Hardware-Based Location Checks Target AI Chip Smuggling (Texas A&M)

stories.Headline: Asia’s AI Boom Has a Timing Problem
stories.Summary:
Asia's AI boom is generating economic gains now, but a blog post by Yasuto Watanabe of the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office argues that the region faces a timing problem as investment, infrastructure, productivity and financial markets move at different speeds. The piece was first published in The Business Times on November 10, 2026, and the author warns that expectations may move faster than the economies supporting them. Demand for semiconductors, advanced electronics and digital infrastructure is supporting exports and investment across ASEAN+3. The author notes that this growing exposure has received less attention than the headline gains. The region accounted for almost half of global exports of AI-enabling goods, such as chipmaking inputs, memory and core computing products, in 2025.

In the first half of 2026, these products contributed roughly two-thirds of the increase in ASEAN+3 merchandise exports. The office projects ASEAN+3 growth of 4.1% in both 2026 and 2027. The post identifies three mismatches, starting with power: AI demand can expand quickly, while new generation and transmission take years to plan and build. In Malaysia, applications for data-center power supply had exceeded 11 gigawatts by December 2024, about 40% of Peninsular Malaysia's generating capacity. Investment can also outpace productivity, because the promised gains depend on changes in business processes, workforce skills and technology diffusion across firms.

The author writes that the office's analysis of the IMF's AI Preparedness Index puts Singapore, Japan, Korea and Hong Kong above 70 on a 0-100 scale, in the same group as the United States. Six of the region's 14 member economies, including the Philippines and Vietnam, score below 50, and those economies may take longer to turn investment into broad productivity gains. The third mismatch concerns markets, which reprice expectations of future earnings quickly, as recent volatility in global AI and semiconductor stocks illustrates. The author says that a change in AI investment plans could simultaneously affect exports, equipment orders, earnings, equity prices and capital flows, and that these effects could reinforce one another.

The office's scenario analysis finds that if US technology investment returned to its more moderate 2024 growth pace rather than maintaining recent momentum, ASEAN+3 growth in 2027 could be 1.5 percentage points below the baseline. The author stresses that this is a scenario, not a forecast, and does not mean AI investment is unsustainable. The post recommends that governments align essential infrastructure with realistic demand projections, that policymakers convert AI investment into broader productivity gains through skills and adoption among smaller firms, and that financial supervisors look beyond direct exposures to suppliers, infrastructure financing, equity markets and nonbank intermediaries. The author concludes that the test of Asia's AI boom will be how much lasting economic value it creates and how well the region manages the risks along the way.

Articles.Title: Asia’s AI Boom Has a Timing Problem

stories.Headline: Nvidia Export Curbs Could Shift AI Demand Toward These Data Center Stocks
stories.Summary:
The articles do not describe a specific announcement by a named party on a particular date that the headline names; the headline refers to U.S. scrutiny of Nvidia's AI chips and tighter export control talk, which the article calls policy noise. Because the article is a Simply Wall St digest about stocks, it offers no concrete event, date, or official action to report. The articles carry too little for the required structure, so this is written as a breaking-style brief. The article, published November 11, 2026, says that scrutiny of Nvidia's AI chips and talk of tighter export controls have drawn attention to where future AI hardware demand might land.

It states that policy noise can shift capital quickly, creating mispricing as traders react to headlines before the business impact is clear. The piece highlights three stocks it says are exposed to this news: Ciena (CIEN), Delta Electronics (TWSE:2308), and Sanmina (SANM). Ciena is described as a US$38.6b network technology business supplying optical networking to telecom operators and cloud providers. Delta Electronics is described as supplying power and thermal systems for high-density AI data centers, with a market value near NT$3.36t.

Sanmina is described as a builder of complex electronics for cloud infrastructure, expanding into metal fabrication for AI racks, high-technology PCBs, transformers, and liquid cooling. The article attributes its analysis to the analyst consensus narrative on Simply Wall St, and it describes Ciena's record backlog as projected to reach US$10b exiting 2026. The article says it was produced with AI automation based on Simply Wall St data and is not financial advice. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Nvidia Export Curbs Could Shift AI Demand Toward These Data Center Stocks

stories.Headline: Rwanda explores AI and science-driven innovation to improve justice sector service delivery
stories.Summary:
Rwanda's Ministry of Justice, the Institute of Legal Practice and Development (ILPD) and the African Institute for Mathematical Sciences (AIMS) are exploring how science, technology and innovation could strengthen the country's justice sector. The aim is to improve efficiency, reduce delays and make justice services easier to access. The discussions were reported by Tech Review Africa on November 12, 2026. They took place at a meeting involving the Minister of Justice and Attorney General, Dr. Emmanuel Ugirashebuja, ILPD Rector Dr. Muyoboke Karimunda Aimé, and Prof. Wilfred Ndifon, who heads the AIMS Research and Innovation Centre. The partners are looking at ways to combine mathematical sciences, artificial intelligence and technical expertise with legal practice knowledge.

Rwanda has already made significant progress in digitising its justice services, particularly through the Integrated Electronic Case Management System (IECMS). As demand for justice services keeps growing, however, the country still needs to process information faster, reduce delays and make services simpler to reach. The institutions noted that new technology could help legal professionals analyse large volumes of information, improve case management and widen access to legal resources. These possibilities would build on the progress already made rather than replace it. The article does not state any specific targets, timelines or budgets for the work.

The discussions follow a recently signed Memorandum of Understanding between AIMS and ILPD, which sets out a framework for collaboration in research, training and innovation. The article describes the Ministry of Justice's leadership and support as central to the partnership. Dr. Ugirashebuja, Dr. Karimunda Aimé and Prof. Ndifon took part in the meeting, and the report presents their talks as exploratory. The article does not describe any formal commitments or decisions made at the meeting.
