stories.Headline: [Graphic News] S. Korea ranks 12th in global AI adoption
stories.Summary:
South Korea's generative AI adoption rate reached 40.6 percent in the second quarter, up 3.5 percentage points from the previous quarter, lifting the country four places to 12th globally. The figures were measured by Microsoft's AI Economy Institute, which tracked the share of people aged 15 to 64 using AI products. South Korea recorded the largest increase among major economies for the third straight quarter. Its adoption rate was also 15 percentage points higher than a year earlier. The Herald report was published on November 12, 2026.

The United Arab Emirates led the rankings at 73.3 percent, followed by Singapore at 64.3 percent, with Ireland and France also placed above South Korea. Globally, the adoption rate rose to 18.8 percent from 17.8 percent in the previous quarter. Adoption stood at 28.8 percent in the advanced Global North, compared with 16.2 percent in the emerging Global South. The gap shows how unevenly the technology has spread across economies.

The article also described differences in how people use AI, depending on where they live. Users in the Global South were more focused on learning and building skills, while users in the Global North more often turned to AI for shopping, searching for information and seeking feedback. The article was written by Nam Kyung-don of The Korea Herald. It did not say what policies or targets, if any, South Korea has set in response to the ranking.

Articles.Title: [Graphic News] S. Korea ranks 12th in global AI adoption

stories.Headline: Seoul warns crypto heists pose wider global security risks in AI era
stories.Summary:
South Korea's Vice Foreign Minister for Strategy and Intelligence, Jeong Yeon-doo, warned on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that recent cryptocurrency thefts carry significant international security implications. He spoke at a cybersecurity conference co-hosted by South Korea and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe at the OSCE headquarters in Vienna. The remarks came after North Korea was accused late last month of stealing more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from the exchange Binance. According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Jeong said such incidents go beyond ordinary cybercrime and touch on wider security concerns.

Jeong called for a wholesale overhaul of the cybersecurity paradigm to suit the AI era, since AI-driven cyberattacks could unfold at an unprecedented pace and scale. He also stressed that security in the Indo-Pacific region and Europe is interconnected, and he underlined the importance of bilateral cooperation. The conference drew about 100 attendees, including representatives from Japan, Australia, Thailand, Afghanistan and Qatar, along with cybersecurity experts and officials from relevant international organizations. The Seoul government has held the conference annually since 2017 to discuss responses to transnational security challenges.

The ministry's account, as reported by Yonhap and the JoongAng Ilbo, attributes the warning to Jeong and presents it as the government's position. The article does not describe any formal response or new measures that Seoul has announced beyond the call for a broader approach. It also does not provide further detail on the Binance theft or on the basis for the accusation against North Korea. Those points are reported as background rather than as developments from the conference itself.

Articles.Title: Seoul warns crypto heists pose wider global security risks in AI era

stories.Headline: Nvidia shareholders sue Huang over affair | Why AI isn't taking over audiobooks just yet
stories.Summary:
Nvidia shareholders filed a class-action lawsuit on Monday, November 10, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, naming CEO Jensen Huang and the company as defendants. The suit followed a day after Huang admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China. The plaintiffs say the chipmaker's stock dropped after the affair and the potential national security risks tied to the woman's former employer, Singapore-based Megaspeed, came to light. They accuse Huang and Nvidia of violating federal securities law and are seeking compensation for heavy losses. On the same day, Nvidia shares fell 4.27 percent on the New York Stock Exchange, wiping out $192.1 billion in market value.

The lawsuit is a direct consequence of that market drop, and its claims center on the securities law that governs what companies must disclose to investors. The plaintiffs argue that the revelations about Alice Huang and Megaspeed were material enough to move the stock, though the article does not describe any specific disclosures that were withheld. The case is still at the filing stage, so no court has ruled on its merits. The article describes the situation as a crisis that is beginning to loosen Huang's grip on the world's most valuable chipmaker. It does not report any response from Huang or Nvidia to the suit.

The lawsuit names Huang personally as well as the company, and the plaintiffs' core argument is that the affair and its national security implications concealed risks that affected the share price. The article presents these as the allegations of the shareholders rather than established facts. Readers should note that the affair itself was described as an admission by Huang, and that the suspicion of Chinese espionage concerns the woman involved rather than any proven conduct by the company. The article does not say how Nvidia's board has reacted or whether any other legal action is planned.

Beyond the lawsuit, the article is part of a wider run of Nvidia coverage in the Korea JoongAng Daily, which reported Huang's admission in an earlier edition. The article does not say what comes next in the litigation or whether additional shareholders will join the suit. Given the size of the market loss, further legal and investor action is possible, but the article itself does not report that. Its context is the broader scrutiny of the chipmaker's leadership and its ties to China-linked business.

Articles.Title: Nvidia shareholders sue Huang over affair | Why AI isn't taking over audiobooks just yet

stories.Headline: SK Group's CEOs to convene to review AI push, align chip and energy businesses
stories.Summary:
SK Group will hold a three-day CEO seminar at its Management System office in Icheon, Gyeonggi, running from Thursday through Saturday, according to industry sources cited on Wednesday. Around 50 CEOs from the group's major affiliates are expected to attend, with the meeting aimed at setting a groupwide AI strategy. The seminar is likely to be presided over by Chairman Chey Tae-won. Executive Vice Chairman Chey Jae-won and SK Supex Council Chairman Chey Chang-won are also scheduled to take part, along with the CEOs named in last month's executive reshuffle.

The central theme is how the group's affiliates can combine their strengths in semiconductors, data centers and energy infrastructure. The agenda is expected to range from SK hynix's memory chip operations and SK Telecom's push into AI data centers to SK Innovation's work on energy infrastructure. Data centers could tie these businesses together, since they need advanced chips, a steady electricity supply and cooling systems. Executives are expected to review how far each affiliate has progressed on AI projects since the most recent New Icheon Forum, and to decide which investments should take priority and which company should lead each project. The meeting will also touch on the group's three-year restructuring drive, including this year's moves to sell SK Corp.'s stake in SK Siltron and merge SK ie technology with SK Innovation.

The seminar is an annual event held each November, and it is one of the group's most important strategy gatherings alongside the June forum. Chairman Chey stressed in September, during a visit to SK Innovation's Ulsan CLX complex, that the affiliates must pool their abilities to meet the challenges of the AI era. Outside speakers, including Kim Dong-shin, CEO of AI communications company Sendbird, are set to address the gathering. Changes in U.S. policy after Democrats took control of Congress in the midterm results could also shape the agenda, since they might affect AI regulations, data center rules and SK Group's U.S. business plans.

Newly appointed CEOs, including incoming SK Innovation chief Cheong Seung-il, are expected to present their strategic priorities for 2027 at the meeting. Their plans for capital allocation and management after the restructuring are expected to draw particular attention. The discussions will also examine how the reshaped businesses can generate stronger profits and better returns on investment. The articles do not say what decisions, if any, will be announced once the seminar ends.

Articles.Title: SK Group's CEOs to convene to review AI push, align chip and energy businesses

stories.Headline: “Not AI manipulation” ‘First hearing’ Kim Se-Eui claims ‘not guilty’ while requesting bail
stories.Summary:
Kim Se-Eui, head of the Garosero Research Institute, appeared at the first hearing of his trial at the Seoul Central District Court on November 11, 2026, where he denied the charges against him. The 26th Criminal Division, presided over by Judge Lee Hyun-Gyeong, heard the case, which concerns defamation under the Information and Communications Network Act and violations of the Act on the Punishment of Sexual Crimes. Kim had been detained and indicted before the hearing. The witness examination of Kim Su-Hyun was held as a closed session to protect the victim's privacy, and spectators were asked to leave before it proceeded.

At the hearing, Kim's attorney said the charges were all denied and that the alleged facts were not false. Kim also argued that a voice recording of the late Kim Sae-Ron, which he had previously released through a press conference and YouTube live broadcasts, was not AI manipulation. He pointed to an analysis report from a Korea University Forensic Center professor, submitted in October, which dated the audio file's creation to two months before his broadcast and one month before Kim Sae-Ron's death. Kim further requested bail, saying the detention warrant's AI manipulation claims were left out of the indictment and that the charges changed the gist of his broadcast. He added that being in custody prevents him from searching materials or reporting, which he called unfair.

According to the article, Kim had claimed in March of the previous year that Kim Su-Hyun had continued a relationship with Kim Sae-Ron since her underage years. Kim Su-Hyun suspended his activities and, together with Kim Sae-Ron's bereaved family, filed a complaint against Kim Se-Eui for defamation. During the investigation, some audio files and materials Kim released were judged to have been manipulated, and he was ultimately detained and indicted on charges including defamation by alleging false facts. The article does not say when a verdict or the next hearing is expected.

Articles.Title: “Not AI manipulation” ‘First hearing’ Kim Se-Eui claims ‘not guilty’ while requesting bail

stories.Headline: AI glasses solve 4 CSAT math questions in 10 seconds
stories.Summary:
AI glasses solved four mock CSAT math questions in under 10 seconds during a brief demonstration at an optical store in Seoul's Myeong-dong shopping area, according to a Korea Times report by Jung Min-ho published on November 11, 2026. The reporter tested Rokid AI glasses on a page of four math questions and saw correct answers and explanations appear in the lenses before he had finished reading the first problem. A separate calculus question involving a definite integral was answered in under two seconds. The test was described as brief and uncontrolled rather than a formal accuracy check.

The concern centers on the College Scholastic Ability Test, which is scheduled for November 19. Data from the Human Resources Development Service of Korea, disclosed in October during a parliamentary audit, showed five cases of AI smart glasses detected at state-run qualification examinations this year. Four of those involved Chinese-manufactured Rokid products, and one involved glasses from the U.S. company Meta. The Rokid glasses use a camera to capture questions, display AI-generated answers through the lenses, and connect to a smartphone, while retailing for 999,000 won in Korea.

One rental service advertises rates as low as 9,900 won a day, making access easier than buying a pair outright. The reporter also tested Ray-Ban Meta glasses, which had no display and instead spoke replies through built-in speakers, a method he judged more conspicuous. He noted that Meta's display-equipped model is not officially sold in Korea. The Rokid glasses showed limitations during his trial, sometimes saying they could not see the question clearly and at other times stopping responses.

He said he did not test whether instructions could persist over a long period or how long the battery would last under repeated use. He added that the glasses' thicker frames and visible lens reflection might give a user away, though spotting those features in a crowded exam room could be harder than in a shop. The reporter concluded that his brief trial did not prove the glasses could get a cheater through an exam undetected, but it showed how quickly they could deliver correct answers. The article indicates that exam authorities face a difficult task in detecting such devices before the November 19 test.

Articles.Title: AI glasses solve 4 CSAT math questions in 10 seconds

stories.Headline: AI glass technology puts Korea's exam supervisors to test ahead of CSAT
stories.Summary:
Authorities in South Korea are preparing staff to spot AI-powered smart glasses ahead of the College Scholastic Ability Test, or CSAT, scheduled for November 19. The Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education said on Wednesday it will train 239 personnel to detect the devices at the city's 228 exam sites. Concern has grown after recent incidents at school exams and university admissions essay tests suggested the glasses could be used for cheating. The Ministry of Education has said it is considering radio-frequency detectors for next year, but none will be supplied for this year's exam.

The ministry plans to assign one staff member to each of the 1,312 test sites nationwide to identify smart glasses. Under the procedures, a supervisor who suspects a student of wearing them before the exam can ask the student to remove them and place them on the desk, and the designated staffer will inspect them and refer unresolved cases to education authorities. Suspicions that arise during a session will be checked after it ends. All electronic devices, including AI glasses, phones, smartwatches and Bluetooth earbuds, are banned at test sites. Possessing AI glasses will invalidate a student's results, and wearing them during the exam will bring a ban from the following year's CSAT.

Choi Hong-won, an official at the Seoul office, said the city has examined different products and prepared training materials for supervisors. Teachers have voiced doubts about the measures. One high school teacher in Cheongju said visual checks could miss discreet devices and that metal detectors may be triggered by ordinary eyeglass frames. A poll released last month by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union found that 82.3 percent of middle and high school teachers surveyed said it would be difficult to identify students wearing smart glasses under the current procedures. The ministry said it would consider criminal complaints over AI-glasses cheating and seek a legal change that would extend the CSAT ban for cheating from one year to three.

Articles.Title: AI glass technology puts Korea's exam supervisors to test ahead of CSAT

stories.Headline: When AI were asked in Japanese about the ‘forced mobilization of comfort women,’ only 56.3% answered “Yes”… compared with 94.9% in Korean
stories.Summary:
When AI models were asked in Japanese whether Japanese military comfort women were mobilized by force, only 56.3% answered yes, according to an analysis by data-tech company Bigvalue's co-CEO Gu Reum dated the 11th. In Korean the share was 94.9%, while in English it was 92.2% and in Chinese 95.2%. The analysis, titled "How Do Language Models Answer on Korea's History, Territory, and Culture," put 50 questions to 27 AI models from 12 developers. Each question was posed 10 times in four languages, and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 was used to judge how closely the answers matched Korea's position.

The same pattern appeared on a second question about whether Koreans conscripted during the colonial period performed forced labor. Affirmative answers were 97.0% in Korean, 93.7% in English and 94.0% in Chinese, but only 54.8% in Japanese. In Japanese, 40.7% of answers on the comfort women question and 41.1% on the labor question gave no clear determination, citing diverse views or divided opinion. Anthropic's Claude and Google's Gemini mostly recognized forced mobilization in Korean but often gave different answers in Japanese. OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Astra and GPT-5.6.1 Terra, Korea's Upstage Solar Mini4 and China's Alibaba Qwen3 235B affirmed forced mobilization in both languages.

Gu Reum said the analysis examined how AI answers contested questions and tested whether a country's language datasets influence those answers. The analysis suggests that Japanese-language training datasets may substantially reflect Japan's perspective on Korea-Japan issues. AI developers and operators do not disclose which sources they use or how they train their models. Gu warned that foreigners may ask AI many questions about Korea, so wrong or differing facts must be prevented from being conveyed depending on the language.

Gu also said it is important for Korea's large language models to learn data consistent with Korea's position. National-level efforts are needed so that foreign models can learn high-quality datasets that faithfully capture Korea's history and culture. Some argue that the government should build foreign-language datasets that properly include information about Korea and release them openly, so foreign AI can be guided toward accurate answers. Concern also exists that incorrect AI answers about Korea's historical issues could spread as if they were facts and influence public perception as AI use grows worldwide. Korea, a latecomer to AI compared with the United States and China, is developing a national flagship AI model, and the industry finds high-quality Korean-language datasets difficult to obtain.

The articles do not establish whether the gaps reflect deliberate bias or how the datasets were actually constructed. They also do not say whether the AI developers have responded to the findings or plan changes to their models. The government's specific plans for building and releasing foreign-language datasets are not detailed, and the articles do not say whether any such effort has begun. The analysis's full detailed findings are available through a link the article points readers to.

Articles.Title: When AI were asked in Japanese about the ‘forced mobilization of comfort women,’ only 56.3% answered “Yes”… compared with 94.9% in Korean

stories.Headline: From infidelity to in-jokes: Jensen Huang affair sparks AI meme wave
stories.Summary:
AI-generated videos and memes pairing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom media reports identify as the other woman, have spread widely online after Huang admitted to infidelity. The article, published on November 11, 2026, says the parodies appeared on Wednesday and draw on a viral clip from a Coldplay concert near Boston in July 2025. In that clip, the stadium's big screen showed the CEO of the software company Astronomer embracing a female executive before the two pulled apart and hid their faces. Online users have also made videos set to the K-pop song "Trouble Maker" and a parody of the elevator scene from the film "(500) Days of Summer," which some call "500 Days of Chip." Puns linking "chip" to a Korean word for a mistress are also circulating.

Huang wrote in an email to Nvidia employees on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife, though the email did not name the woman. The article ties the online attention to a more serious matter, reporting that U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was passing information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times on October 29. Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation to examine whether national security or company secrets were compromised, though it said it has no reason to believe either was. On Tuesday, the board's independent members hired former federal prosecutor Joon H. Kim to lead that inquiry.

The articles frame the memes as a sign of how the affair has become internet entertainment, while the investigation sits behind them. The reporting notes that Korean chipmakers are assessing whether leadership uncertainty at Nvidia could affect their ties with one of their biggest AI-chip customers. The article describes the spy allegations as part of a wider push for tougher U.S. chip curbs on China. Beyond the board's inquiry, the article does not say what the investigation will conclude or when results will be released.

Articles.Title: From infidelity to in-jokes: Jensen Huang affair sparks AI meme wave

stories.Headline: AI Rally Reverses Overnight: Jensen Huang Reportedly Facing Board Ouster, Nvidia Plunges More Than 8% After Hours
stories.Summary:
Shares of Nvidia fell as much as 8.27% after hours on Nov. 11, 2026, to $159.37, after foreign media reported that the company's board was preparing to remove CEO Jensen Huang. The reports also cited fresh allegations of an extramarital affair involving Huang, and they came only after U.S. stocks had closed broadly higher that day. Nvidia had closed the regular session at $173.73, up 2.87%, before the reports surfaced. The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times were the outlets named in the reporting, and the decline spread to other AI-linked stocks in post-market trading. The sell-off followed a day in which the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had surged 5.66%.

The Nov. 11 rally had been driven by cloud computing provider CoreWeave, whose third-quarter results beat market expectations and sent its shares up 24.71%. Anthropic's Nasdaq listing was also set for the 19th, which the articles describe as another catalyst for AI-sector sentiment. On the regular session that day, the S&P 500 rose 98.45 points, or 1.31%, to 7,619.38, and the Nasdaq Composite climbed 400.31 points, or 1.60%, to 25,466.19. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 254.60 points, or 0.49%, to 52,486.49, while the Nasdaq 100 rose 2.28%. Taiwan-listed ADRs also rose, with TSMC's ADR up 4.25%, ASE Technology's up 6.60% and United Microelectronics' up 6.91%.

Nvidia had not publicly commented on the reports as of the articles' publication. Its board, according to the articles, had said on Nov. 8 that it had launched an independent investigation into reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence service. In that statement the board said there was no basis to conclude that national security or Nvidia's confidential information had been compromised, and it expressed confidence in Huang and the management team. The articles note that foreign media sources were the basis for the Nov. 11 reports, and that Korean-language reports were used for some of the foreign-source quotes. Market participants, according to the articles, expected that confirmation would widen volatility in the AI complex, while denial could allow the rebound to continue.

Investors across the AI supply chain were affected, with CoreWeave down 6.76% after hours, Super Micro Computer down 4.40%, IREN down 4.08%, Dell Technologies down 3.83%, Applied Optoelectronics down 3.65% and Nebius down 3.36%. QQQ fell 0.93% and SPY fell 0.49% in after-hours trading. In South Korea, the KOSPI opened at 5,385.94 on Nov. 12, up 0.20%, but turned negative and stood at 5,342.76 at 9:11 a.m., down 0.61%. Foreign investors and institutions turned net sellers in the KOSPI market, while retail investors were net buyers of about $76.2 million. Samsung Electronics, Samsung Electro-Mechanics and KB Financial rose, while SK Hynix, SK Square and LG Energy Solution fell.

The articles provide background on Nvidia's Korean business, including its AI Day event in Seoul, held Nov. 9 at COEX in Gangnam, the second such event held there. Madison Huang, the CEO's eldest daughter and a senior director of product marketing, canceled her planned trip to Korea, and Nvidia officials declined to say how the allegations might affect business in Korea. In October 2025, Nvidia said the Korean government and companies would deploy more than 260,000 GPUs, a plan the articles describe as a large-scale deployment announced last year. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix have expanded HBM cooperation with Nvidia, including HBM4 for the Vera Rubin platform, and industry watchers said the CEO's status could affect that supply.

The articles leave open whether Nvidia's board will actually move to remove Huang, and on what timeline, since so far only foreign media reports exist. They also leave open whether the after-hours decline will narrow once U.S. markets open on Nov. 12, and how the Asian supply-chain stocks will trade after the news develops. Nvidia's official response has not been reported, and the articles do not say how the foreign intelligence investigation will conclude. Whether the reports are confirmed or denied remains unknown, and the articles do not establish what effect either outcome would have on Nvidia's Korean business or its HBM supply plans.

Articles.Title: AI Rally Reverses Overnight: Jensen Huang Reportedly Facing Board Ouster, Nvidia Plunges More Than 8% After Hours

stories.Headline: Meta (NASDAQ: META) Ember Enters AI Price War At A Third Of Rivals’ Cost
stories.Summary:
Meta has released a new artificial intelligence model called Ember, which is aimed at the budget tier of the AI market. According to the article published on November 11, 2026, Ember costs roughly one-third what similar lightweight models charge, and in some cases less, while promising faster response times than many direct competitors. The model is positioned against ChatGPT's Luna and Anthropic's Haiku, both of which have established user bases. Ember is designed to handle roughly 90% of what the most sophisticated frontier models can do.

Meta is pursuing a two-track product strategy, since it is separately trying to compete at the high end against models named Fable 5.2 and GPT 6 Astra. The article says Ember suits repetitive, routine tasks where the value lies in automation rather than complex reasoning. Meta's broader goal, which the company has pursued for years, is to lower model costs so that AI tools reach as many people as possible. The company previously tried to pursue that goal through open-source releases, a strategy analysts say never fully delivered on its promise.

The article attributes the launch to Meta, whose Ember model is presented as a shift from that earlier approach toward balancing capability with low operating costs. Yahoo Finance's Ejaaz Ahamadeen is cited as saying that Muse was the first Meta AI product he found himself returning to daily, a change from earlier releases he found underwhelming. The article does not give a direct statement from Meta about Ember's pricing or rollout beyond the company's stated philosophy. It does not say how many users Ember has gained so far.

Context in the article points to a sobering adoption picture, with a recent report indicating that fewer than 5% of people use AI models for anything beyond a basic internet search. Analysts suggest that even among early adopters, only around 10 to 20% are likely to download and experiment with new AI applications. The article says Apple's anticipated updated Siri AI, expected to reach approximately 3.5 billion active devices, could dramatically shift those numbers. It also notes that Meta holds a significant advantage in personal social data, while enterprise-focused tools like Dots are seen as better positioned in productivity.

Articles.Title: Meta (NASDAQ: META) Ember Enters AI Price War At A Third Of Rivals’ Cost

stories.Headline: Meta Loses 17-Year Infrastructure Veteran Amid AI Buildout
stories.Summary:
Meta is losing Santosh Janardhan, its longtime head of infrastructure, according to a TechBuzz report dated November 11, 2026. He has steered the company's compute operations since 2009 and is stepping down during a critical period of AI expansion. His exit is the second major finance and operations leadership departure in recent weeks, following former CSO Dave Wehner's move to AI startup Fireworks. The departure comes as Meta spends heavily on AI infrastructure and data centers to power its generative AI ambitions. Meta has not announced a replacement and declined to provide details about Janardhan's next moves or the transition timeline.

Janardhan joined the company when it was still Facebook in 2009 and served as head of infrastructure for 17 years. The role oversees server farms, data centers, and custom silicon that runs Meta's AI models, along with keeping billions of users online. CEO Mark Zuckerberg has committed to spending upwards of $37 billion on data centers and compute resources this year. Meta has been building clusters of Nvidia H100 GPUs by the tens of thousands, constructing new data centers quickly, and developing custom chips to reduce dependence on external suppliers. Training large language models requires coordinating GPU clusters, cooling systems, and megawatt-scale power infrastructure.

The article reports that Dave Wehner, Meta's longtime chief strategy officer and former CFO, recently left to become CFO of AI infrastructure startup Fireworks. Janardhan's departure comes within weeks of Wehner's exit, which the article says raised questions about whether top talent sees better opportunities at AI startups. The article describes Janardhan as the architect behind much of Meta's recent infrastructure expansion. The article does not include a direct statement from Janardhan or from Meta about the reasons for his departure. Meta's infrastructure leadership role is described as increasingly strategic as AI workloads consume more compute.

The departure affects Meta's platforms, which serve nearly 4 billion people across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads, as well as the company's AI plans. The article says Meta has warned that community opposition to data center construction could derail those plans. The leadership change also raises concerns among investors about whether senior leaders are seeking opportunities beyond Meta. Competitors including CoreWeave, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google are building out their own AI infrastructure. The article also notes that eBay has blocked Meta's AI shopping agents, which adds to the infrastructure team's challenges.

Janardhan led Meta's infrastructure through a six-hour outage in October 2021 that took all of the company's services offline. That outage cost Meta an estimated $100 million in lost revenue, according to the article. Over his tenure, Facebook evolved from a college social network into a global platform. Meta has recently rolled out Muse with voice capabilities and expressive avatars, which add strain to infrastructure systems. The article also notes that Meta has been racing to catch up with OpenAI and Google in generative AI.

Meta has not named a successor, and the search for a new infrastructure chief will be closely watched. The article says whoever takes the role will inherit responsibility for keeping Meta's social platforms running while building the foundation for its AI future. It is unclear from the article whether Janardhan's exit signals a broader trend of senior departures. The article also leaves open when the transition will occur and where Janardhan will go next. Whether Meta can retain top technical talent as AI startups offer equity upside remains an open question.

Articles.Title: Meta Loses 17-Year Infrastructure Veteran Amid AI Buildout

stories.Headline: LSU and Meta AI partner on five projects across LSU’s campuses, using AI to tackle healthcare challenges - The Reveille, LSU's student newspaper
stories.Summary:
LSU has joined Meta's open science efforts in a partnership that brings five artificial intelligence-powered health projects to campuses across the state. The projects were presented at the Meta Open Source AI for Science Summit in October at Meta's headquarters in Menlo Park, California, which hosted nearly 100 scientists from across the country. Meta is providing $300,000 in financial support for the work, according to an LSU press release. Three of the five projects are taking place on LSU's Baton Rouge campus, each aimed at a different healthcare problem. The announcement was reported by George deBlanc of The Reveille on November 11, 2026.

LSU President Wade Rousse said in the press release that no single campus could carry out this work alone, and that the effort draws on a university system tied to a unified research enterprise with two health sciences centers. He described the partnership as recognition of what LSU can accomplish when it uses all parts of its system. One project, led by Felipe Fronchetti, an LSU assistant professor of computer science and engineering, is building a medical virtual reality training program called COPES. The software uses Meta's Muse Glimmer and Muse Spark AI models to let trainees practice procedures such as chest tube insertions with virtual patients who respond to speech and react to the trainee in real time. The Baton Rouge team received $80,000 of the funding for this program, which Fronchetti said could be especially useful in rural parts of Louisiana with less access to procedure training.

Supratik Mukhopadhyay, an LSU environmental sciences professor, is leading the other two Baton Rouge projects. One, developed with Dr. Sagar Kansara of LSU Health New Orleans, is a tool that predicts future developmental risks for head and neck cancer patients and aims to support drug discovery that could prevent recurrence. It draws on data from institutions including the LSU Health Sciences Center and the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, and Mukhopadhyay said it runs on an open-weight AI model so no data is uploaded to the cloud. The second, called Eyes-On and developed with Dr. Michael Dunham of LSU Health New Orleans, uses cameras in cribs to monitor infants who need breathing support, alerting hospital staff when a baby is distressed or a breathing tube is displaced. Mukhopadhyay said the project relies on Meta's open-weight models and that a clinician needs to trace the tube only once, which avoids the thousands of annotated images most medical AI requires.

Articles.Title: LSU and Meta AI partner on five projects across LSU’s campuses, using AI to tackle healthcare challenges - The Reveille, LSU's student newspaper

stories.Headline: Huawei releases MACaQ, its internal quantizer for local inference
stories.Summary:
Huawei has released MACaQ, an internal quantization tool for running AI models locally, and the project was posted on GitHub on 12 November 2026. The repository describes MACaQ as a model-agnostic quantizer that can handle text, image, video and audio models through llama.cpp, vLLM, Diffusers and PyTorch. It says MACaQ can quantize a 122-billion-parameter model in 64 minutes using 32.5 GB of device memory. The project also claims lower perplexity than MR-GPTQ and DuQuant++, or matching their best Llama-3-8B perplexity with 11 times less quantization time.

Huawei's own page lists the project as an open-source release under the Apache License 2.0. The tool supports several formats and backends, depending on the workload. For text generation it produces 2-, 3- and 4-bit GGUF files for llama.cpp, while vLLM receives W4A4 or weight-only checkpoints. Diffusers handles image, video and audio generation with W4A4 safetensors checkpoints, and PyTorch covers speech generation.

A separate MACaQ-R mode refines the weight codes in an existing quantized GGUF while keeping its native format, so the output runs with a standard llama.cpp installation. The repository also outlines Ascend kernel work through two CANN pull requests, though it notes that full-model execution still requires integration with an Ascend inference runtime. Users are asked to install each backend in its own Python 3.12 environment. The repository credits a team including Lorenz K. Muller, Philippe Bich, Chiara Boretti, Hyun-Min Chang, Jiawei Zhuang and Lukas Cavigelli, and points readers to a paper cited as arXiv 2611.10649.

The published benchmarks include a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B comparison in which the MACaQ-R Q4_K_XL file reports a KL divergence to FP16 of 0.013367, against 0.015731 for Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL, both at 22.36 GB. A Qwen3.8-27B vLLM test shows a W4A4 perplexity of 2.8994 against 2.8463 for BF16, with prefill speed 2.33 times and decode speed 2.58 times the BF16 baseline. The repository had 152 stars and six forks at the time the page was captured. The articles do not say whether Huawei plans further releases or updates beyond what is listed.

Articles.Title: Huawei releases MACaQ, its internal quantizer for local inference

stories.Headline: How Meta is transforming vision-impaired veterans’ lives with AI: ‘A whole new world’
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday at the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, Armsted Chambers, a 70-year-old Marine who served from 1975 to 1995, used his Meta glasses to look up friends he had lost. The glasses were given to him by the company six months earlier, and they have changed much of his daily life since then. Chambers lost his sight after an injury during his service. He said the glasses let him do things he never thought he could do again.

Meta is working to donate 130,000 pairs of its AI-enhanced glasses to vision-impaired veterans, and veterans can request them through bva.org/glasses. The effort is part of a wider push by the company to show how its hardware and AI can help people live more independently. Thousands of veterans are already gaining independence through the program. The glasses can now see what the wearer sees, answer questions about surroundings, translate conversations live, and remember details from earlier in the day.

For Veterans Day, Meta partnered with Honor Flight, an organization that donates trips to war memorials in Washington, and brought roughly 50 blind and low-vision veterans to the capital. During the trip, the veterans used the glasses to read inscriptions aloud and describe the memorials. Dina Powell McCormick, president and vice chairman at Meta, said it had been incredible to spend time with the veterans and hear how the glasses had helped restore their independence. The broader effort grew out of Meta's work with Don Overton, an Army veteran who lost his sight in Desert Storm and helped shape features for blind users.

Chambers says the glasses have had their greatest impact at home, where he now wears them from morning until bedtime. He uses them to read his mail and medicine labels, answer calls from his wife and others, and check the time and weather. He said he no longer has to depend so heavily on others, and that the glasses have lifted his spirits. Meta first launched its glasses in 2021 as camera-equipped wearables, and it added AI capabilities last September. Chambers joked that he would also like them to make him a cup of coffee.

Articles.Title: How Meta is transforming vision-impaired veterans’ lives with AI: ‘A whole new world’

stories.Headline: JioStar’s chief architect on AI discovery at 500M-user scale
stories.Summary:
JioStar, which runs entertainment and live-sports platforms, built a conversational video and cricket-stat discovery assistant into JioHotstar using the OpenAI API. The company's platforms serve more than 500 million consumers and have supported as many as 72.5 million concurrent live-sports viewers. The article, published on November 11, 2026, is an interview with Vijay Seshadri, JioStar's Chief Architect, conducted by Sidharth Sharma, OpenAI's Head of Go-to-Market for ASEAN, at OpenAI's Executive Summit in Singapore. The assistant lets viewers speak or type naturally to find movies and shows, historical highlights, live-match moments and cricket statistics, with results shown in a visual, conversational format. The team built the experience across more than 15 languages in about eight weeks, starting work in October and November ahead of a major cricket tournament in February.

Seshadri said the product had to serve two very different audiences, entertainment viewers who describe what they want in loose terms and cricket fans who want precise updates or ball-by-ball statistics. More than 60% of users rely on voice rather than text, so responses had to be accurate, fast and affordable at scale. He described a three-way tradeoff among accuracy, latency and cost that shaped every engineering decision. He also stressed evaluation systems, combining a pre-launch framework with a production feedback loop that turns user behavior and failures into new test cases.

Seshadri credited a small team of data scientists and engineers with a clear problem statement, and said OpenAI's forward-deployed engineers worked alongside them to identify the essential requirements. The team first decided what the system should refuse to answer, then seeded an evaluation dataset and expanded it with models. One model proposed answers while a second acted as a validator, and the team had to design that validator as its own test problem. Seshadri said Codex helped speed up tasks such as generating test cases, but he maintained that faster building did not remove the need for human judgment.

Looking back, he said he would have invested earlier in monitoring model performance in production, beyond standard latency measures. Seshadri's advice to executives centered on outcomes rather than activity, such as counting generated lines of code, and on the gap between what the technology can do and what an enterprise can absorb. He argued that AI should be used to simplify business processes and engineering systems, and that companies need people with the judgment to validate production systems, not only generic training. The article is part of OpenAI's Executive Function series and reports no further deployment dates or follow-up plans.

Articles.Title: JioStar’s chief architect on AI discovery at 500M-user scale

stories.Headline: Nvidia: AI Is Wearing Down The CUDA Moat, But The Price Already Assumes The Worst (NVDA)
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's stock has fallen sharply since early October, according to a Seeking Alpha opinion piece by deep value investor Tim Travis published on November 11, 2026. The article says the stock closed at a record $239.24 on October 6 and then dropped to $168.89 by November 10, a decline of 29% in five weeks that the author puts at about $1.7 trillion in lost market value. Travis writes that the company trades at a run-rate multiple of roughly 17 times while investors weigh concerns about custom chips and regulatory scrutiny. He describes the CUDA software platform as narrowing at the top end as major AI labs build alternatives, though it remains strong among sovereign, neocloud, and enterprise customers.

Travis states that his base case values Nvidia at around $220 per share, which he says implies a discount of about 25% to intrinsic value. He notes that the downside is plausible if gross margins erode. The article does not describe a new rule or regulation, and the figures it gives are the author's own analysis rather than company filings. Travis says he and his firm have mostly sold out-of-the-money puts on the stock and that he holds a beneficial long position, a disclosure the article includes.

The views belong to Tim Travis, founder and chief investment officer of T&T Capital Management in Coto de Caza, California, and he wrote the piece himself. He identifies two indicators he is watching closely: fourth-quarter gross margin guidance and the growth of customer segments outside the large cloud providers. Seeking Alpha's disclosure notes that the views may not reflect those of the platform and that its authors may not be licensed. The article itself names OpenAI and Anthropic among companies tied to the discussion of custom silicon, and it names CoreWeave as a neocloud customer.

Articles.Title: Nvidia: AI Is Wearing Down The CUDA Moat, But The Price Already Assumes The Worst (NVDA)

stories.Headline: Quanta shifts 2027 capex toward power, the new battleground for AI server ODMs
stories.Summary:
Quanta Computer posted strong revenue and earnings in the third quarter of 2026 and expects operations to keep accelerating in the fourth quarter, driven by AI servers, according to a Digitimes report published on November 12, 2026. The report, filed from Taipei by Aaron Lee, says the company is now shifting its 2027 capital expenditure toward power. The article itself is behind a paid subscription, so only its opening summary is available. Based on that summary, the company's spending plans are changing in a way that reflects where AI server makers see the next constraint. The available text does not give the size of the capital budget or the specific power projects involved.

The headline frames this as a battleground among AI server original design manufacturers, the contract makers that design and build servers for large customers. The shift in spending suggests that power equipment and capacity now matter as much as assembly capacity for these firms. The visible excerpt does not spell out what power investments Quanta plans, which customers they serve, or how the change affects its production schedules. Readers would need the full article for those details.

The report does not include any direct statement from Quanta executives about the spending shift, and no quote from the company is available in the excerpt. The byline credits Aaron Lee, and the article carries the Digitimes name as its source. Beyond the revenue and earnings outlook and the capital expenditure direction, the excerpt offers no further detail about who is responsible for the decision or what they said about it. Any further statements would appear only in the paywalled article.

The surrounding coverage on the same site points to a broader industry theme. Other items on the page discuss rival server makers such as Pegatron and Foxconn expecting strong AI server growth in 2027, and a separate report says the AI bottleneck is shifting from compute to power. Taken together, these reports suggest that power supply has become a central concern across the AI hardware supply chain. What happens next for Quanta, including the scale of its 2027 power spending, is not stated in the available text.

Articles.Title: Quanta shifts 2027 capex toward power, the new battleground for AI server ODMs

stories.Headline: Foxconn sees high-double-digit AI rack growth in 2027
stories.Summary:
Foxconn, the Taiwanese contract manufacturer, reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of more than NT$3 trillion, or about US$91 billion, according to DIGITIMES, which published its report on November 12, 2026. The company also raised its full-year outlook for the year. Its forecast for AI rack shipments calls for high-double-digit growth in 2027. The article provided by the source is partly behind a paywall, so further details are not available. The report describes Foxconn's view of 2027 as cautiously optimistic.

AI racks are the large server units used to run artificial intelligence workloads, and the forecast points to a sharp increase in how many of them the company expects to ship. The specific growth percentage is not given in the text available. Other items on the same page, including Pegatron's expected server growth and Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin shipments, are separate stories and do not form part of Foxconn's stated figures. The forecast comes from Foxconn itself, as reported by DIGITIMES reporter Ninelu Tu in Taipei. The available text does not include any direct statements from company executives beyond the outlook described.

Readers should treat the forecast as the company's own projection rather than a confirmed result. The available material does not explain the reasons behind the forecast or describe how customers or competitors are responding. It also does not say when Foxconn will release its next quarterly results or any updated guidance. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Foxconn sees high-double-digit AI rack growth in 2027

stories.Headline: Baidu CEO Robin Li says commercial AI adoption is only starting
stories.Summary:
Baidu founder and CEO Robin Li said on Thursday, November 12, 2026, in Beijing that the commercial adoption of artificial intelligence is only just beginning. His remarks came at the Baidu World 2026 conference, where the company displayed its Tianchi 1024-card "super node," an AI computing system. Li called for businesses to make greater use of AI agents, even as concerns grow about rapidly rising token budgets and the technology's effect on jobs. The article frames his comments as a push for wider deployment rather than a retreat from spending.

Enterprises in sectors such as finance and manufacturing are reportedly rethinking how their workflows operate as spending on AI climbs. The piece describes this shift as the context for Li's argument that adoption is still in its early stages. The article does not give specific figures for spending increases, token costs, or the number of companies involved. Li, who leads Baidu as its founder and chief executive, made the case for AI agents directly at the event in Beijing.

The reporter, Wataru Suzuki, attended the conference and photographed the computing system on display. The article reports Li's position in paraphrase and does not describe any formal policy change or regulatory response tied to his remarks. The article offers little beyond the conference remarks and the product display, so it does not say what Baidu plans next or how the market is expected to respond. Readers should look for follow-up coverage on how enterprise customers adopt agent-based systems and whether token costs continue to climb.

Articles.Title: Baidu CEO Robin Li says commercial AI adoption is only starting

stories.Headline: SE3 Raises $30 Million Series A Led by Accel for Spatial AI for Drones and Autonomous Systems
stories.Summary:
SE3, a defense technology company that spun out of the Technical University of Munich, has closed a $30 million (around €27 million) Series A round led by the venture capital firm Accel. Keen Venture Partners also took part, and existing investors Lakestar and Seedcamp returned. The article reports the round on November 12, 2026, and notes that SE3 only emerged from stealth in June with €5.5 million in seed funding led by Lakestar, making the new round roughly five times larger. The company builds software that helps drones and ground vehicles understand their surroundings, even when satellite navigation is disrupted.

The software combines sensor data from vehicles made by different manufacturers into a shared three-dimensional picture of the terrain, then uses that picture to coordinate whole swarms, adjusting routes, positions and behavior. Operators can control the system by voice, and it runs directly on the devices instead of relying on outside networks. The article says this matters on the front line in Ukraine, where electronic warfare jams GPS on a large scale and large drone fleets overwhelm the people supervising them. SE3 says it has shipped thousands of systems over the past two years and is working on several contracts with Ukraine and Germany's armed forces, the Bundeswehr.

The company's leaders include CEO Lukas Köstler and CTO Simon Klenk, who both completed PhDs at the university, and chair holder Daniel Cremers, who co-founded the firm. SE3 works as an AI partner to defense contractor Hensoldt and to scale-ups such as Auterion and ERC System, and its software runs on Auterion's Skynode computer. Auterion's CEO, Lorenz Meier, said autonomy only counts if it keeps working when navigation is jammed and one operator oversees many vehicles. Köstler said the technology has to perform under pressure in the field, and Accel partner Matt Robinson praised the team's research background.

SE3 plans to use the money to expand its engineering, commercial and operations teams, and it is opening an office in the U.K. while considering other European markets. From 2027 it also intends to add civilian uses such as robotics and emergency response. The article places the company in a crowded market that includes Helsing, which recently raised $1.8 billion, as well as Anduril and Shield AI in the United States. It also notes that SE3 does not disclose revenue or order volume, and that the shipment figures come from the company itself.

Articles.Title: SE3 Raises $30 Million Series A Led by Accel for Spatial AI for Drones and Autonomous Systems

stories.Headline: Alibaba, Tencent shares fall on report U.S. weighs curbs on remote AI chip access
stories.Summary:
Shares of Alibaba and Tencent fell on Thursday after The Information reported that the U.S. Commerce Department was preparing to finalise rules that would stop Chinese AI companies from remotely accessing advanced chips through data centres located overseas. Alibaba's Hong Kong shares dropped 5% to HK$95.6 by 05:08 GMT, while Tencent slipped 1.5% to HK$403.6. The report said the measure could be announced this month. The article does not say who the sources were beyond the publication itself. The proposed measure would expand existing semiconductor export controls run by the department's Bureau of Industry and Security to seven more countries.

According to the report, those countries include Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. The restrictions are meant to keep Chinese companies from reaching advanced processors remotely and to curb the smuggling of restricted chips into China. The article does not give the full list of the other four countries or the exact text of the rules. The report is attributed to The Information, and the article does not quote any Commerce Department official or any statement from Alibaba or Tencent. The article describes the rules as a response to growing scrutiny of Nvidia's China-related business and to Washington's effort to tighten enforcement of semiconductor export restrictions.

It notes that the reporting comes amid that broader pressure rather than a formal announcement. Nothing in the article indicates whether the companies have commented. The shares' moves reflect the market's reaction to a report, not to a published rule, and the article does not say whether the rules have been finalised. The story sits within a wider pattern of U.S. efforts to limit China's access to advanced AI hardware. The article does not describe any next step beyond the possible announcement this month.

Articles.Title: Alibaba, Tencent shares fall on report U.S. weighs curbs on remote AI chip access

stories.Headline: Nebuly raises $21M Series A to turn AI investments into measurable results
stories.Summary:
Nebuly, a company that builds a platform for measuring the business value of artificial intelligence, has raised a $21 million Series A funding round, as reported by Tech.eu on November 12, 2026. The platform is designed to show how AI agents affect productivity, operational efficiency and revenue across both internal tools and customer-facing applications. The articles describe the platform as covering agents from multiple providers as well as solutions developed internally by enterprises. The reporting frames the product around a simple question that boards are asking, namely what AI is actually worth to the business.

The articles say the platform helps enterprises identify where AI is improving workflows or generating additional revenue, and where additional training could make it more effective. It also lets companies review and adjust the assumptions behind their calculations, so that the figures can be checked rather than taken on trust. According to the reporting, this matters because many organisations have made decisions about spending and hiring based on assumptions about AI productivity rather than on evidence. The articles also note that Nebuly can process enterprise data without sending it to external model APIs, which addresses concerns about keeping company information in-house.

The articles do not give a figure for how many customers the company has or how much revenue it earns. The articles do not name individual people responsible for the raise, and they do not contain direct statements from company executives. The company's own positioning, as described in the coverage, is that it exists to answer the question of what AI is worth to a business. The reporting ties this to a wider trend the articles call "tokenmaxxing," in which the volume of AI usage itself becomes the measure of success.

The coverage presents Nebuly's platform as a response to that trend, since it aims to tie AI activity to measurable business outcomes instead. The articles place the funding within a broader European startup news flow, and they do not describe investors, valuation or future product plans beyond the round itself. They do not say what Nebuly will do with the new capital or when it plans to expand. No further developments are reported in the articles.

Articles.Title: Nebuly raises $21M Series A to turn AI investments into measurable results

stories.Headline: How China and Thailand are shaping the AI future together
stories.Summary:
Youth leaders and experts from China and Thailand have gathered in Bangkok to discuss how artificial intelligence can be made more widely available across borders. The meeting was held under China's Global Development Initiative, and it focused on how education and international cooperation might help shape a more inclusive digital future. The gathering was reported from Thailand's capital by Dusita Saokaew, who covered the discussions for CGTN. The article describes the event as part of a broader push to ensure that the benefits of AI do not stay with a small number of wealthy countries. It is framed around the idea that access to digital technology and the skills to use it should be spread more evenly.

The article presents this equal access as an increasingly important priority as artificial intelligence reshapes economies around the world. It does not list specific figures, dates for new programs, or formal commitments emerging from the Bangkok talks. Instead, it centers on the principle that all countries should be able to take part in the AI era on comparable terms. The reporting suggests that education and cooperation are the main tools being considered for achieving that goal. The piece offers no detailed roadmap, funding amounts, or binding obligations for either government or participating organizations.

Responsibility for the initiative is tied to China's Global Development Initiative, under which the youth leaders and experts convened. The article attributes the framing of the meeting to that initiative and to the participants who gathered in Bangkok. It does not include direct statements from named officials, so any specific positions are reported only at the level of the event's stated aims. The article frames the discussions as an exploration of options rather than the announcement of a finished agreement. Readers are left with a general picture of the cooperation's intent rather than its concrete outcomes.

The article is dated November 12, 2026, and it is published on CGTN's news site. It does not describe what the next steps will be, whether follow-up meetings are planned, or how the ideas raised in Bangkok might be put into practice. Because the report is brief and centered on the event's purpose, the wider context of China and Thailand's technology relations is not explored in depth. Any further developments would need to come from additional reporting, which the source does not indicate is forthcoming.

Articles.Title: How China and Thailand are shaping the AI future together

stories.Headline: In the competition for cultural influence, AI has a default country
stories.Summary:
An article in The Japan Times, published November 12, 2026, reports that artificial intelligence chatbots have a habit of naming Japan when asked open-ended questions about family life, culture or tradition. Researchers at the University of the Basque Country and Cardiff University tested eight AI models by asking them to choose a place on their own, using the prompt "What values shape family life in ______? Choose the place yourself. Be brief." They ran this across 24 languages in 31,680 variations covering festivals, food and family.

Depending on the model, between 43% and 78% of the answers were set aside as referencing home countries, and of the rest, six of the eight models repeatedly picked Japan. The article presents this as a default rather than a favorite. A favorite is chosen over alternatives, but in this test no alternatives were offered, so the choice reflects a built-in pattern instead of a comparison. The article argues that such defaults matter because they rarely get questioned, since users seldom notice when a machine fills an open blank. It also notes that AI chatbots increasingly make choices for users that traditional search engines would leave to them, which changes how cultural influence is distributed.

The article does not say which companies built the eight models tested, and it does not attribute the pattern to any named individual or institution beyond the researchers. The researchers' findings, as described, are the basis for the claim that Japan is a disproportionately common reference point. The article's framing, drawn from the researchers' results, is that this pattern shapes the global contest for cultural influence in a quiet way. The article is part of a broader discussion about how AI is reshaping global cultural competition, and it sits alongside other Japan Times coverage of Japan's international profile. The article itself does not describe any planned responses or next steps from developers, regulators or the researchers.

Articles.Title: In the competition for cultural influence, AI has a default country

stories.Headline: Workday says millions of job applicants can't sue as a group over AI screening - ETHRWorld.com
stories.Summary:
Workday has asked a US federal judge in San Francisco to reject a bid that would let potentially millions of job applicants pursue discrimination claims against the company as a group. The company filed the request late on Tuesday, November 11, 2026, in a 2023 lawsuit brought by four named plaintiffs over its AI-powered screening software. The plaintiffs allege race, sex, age and disability discrimination, and the proposed classes have not yet been certified. Workday says more than 11,500 organizations use its software for functions such as human resources, payroll and procurement.

In a separate filing, Workday also asked Judge Rita Lin to decertify a conditional collective of more than 15,000 people who have opted in to allege age discrimination. The company argues the plaintiffs have not shown it made hiring decisions on behalf of its customers, so there is no common evidence that could support a classwide proceeding. Workday says the lawsuit targets three features, including one that compares an applicant's resume skills with a job posting, which it says most customers never used. The other two grade how well an application matches a posting and search a company's past applicant database for current openings. Lin is scheduled to hold a hearing on class certification in March.

Workday has said its technology looks only at job qualifications and not protected traits such as race or age, and that its products are rigorously tested for potential bias. The company has also been fighting earlier challenges, since Lin rejected its initial attempt to dismiss the case in 2024 and in June mostly denied its bid to toss out amendments alleging violations of California law. Lawyers for the named plaintiffs did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The filings are from Workday's counsel at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe, and the plaintiffs are represented by Winston Cooks.

The case is described as the first of its kind to broadly target the algorithmic decision-making behind AI screening software, which is now common among large employers. Government agencies and worker advocates have worried that such tools can discriminate when built on data reflecting existing biases, yet litigation over their use has been limited, which experts have partly attributed to applicants not knowing when AI is used. The outcome could help shape how similar litigation is conducted. The next major step is the March class certification hearing.

Articles.Title: Workday says millions of job applicants can't sue as a group over AI screening - ETHRWorld.com

stories.Headline: ‘We're Killing Our Own Currency’ - 7 MSP Leaders On How AI Will Change What They Charge
stories.Summary:
The IT Channel Oxygen article published on November 12, 2026 reports on discussions at the Global Technology Industry Association's ChannelCon EMEA in London, where how AI might reshape managed service providers' pricing dominated the agenda. The piece is an interview round-up in which seven MSP leaders were asked how the arrival of AI tools that could make them more efficient would affect what they charge customers. The event, which the article says attracted a record 800 registrations, prompted the headline phrase "We're killing our own currency." The GTIA's chief executive, Dan Wensley, described himself in an earlier interview as a "pure optimist" on the topic, but the article suggests many of the MSPs at the event were less sure.

The leaders' central concern is that AI-driven efficiency will raise customer expectations rather than create a price advantage. One speaker said that if every provider can do more, the extra output becomes a baseline expectation and not a differentiator. Another described a technician whose PC crashed, who asked an AI agent to repair it and had it fixed faster than he could have done himself. Speakers noted that MSPs typically sell per person per month, so marketing that promises to lower a customer's headcount through AI efficiencies undercuts the very unit they charge for. Some predicted that many MSPs would not survive this shift, and one questioned whether the UK needs as many as 10,000 of them.

The article attributes the response to the event's participants, who argued that the industry has relied on a settled playbook for bundling, selling and margins that no longer applies. One MSP leader said that after roughly a decade of learning how to sell managed services, the sector now lacks a established way to build and price outcomes, and called for more collaboration among providers to work out the answer. Another said the community had never been more necessary. The articles do not say how the industry is expected to settle on new pricing models, and the piece points to a separate interview with Redsquid's Phil Callow on the AI pricing question without reporting its contents.

Articles.Title: ‘We're Killing Our Own Currency’ - 7 MSP Leaders On How AI Will Change What They Charge

stories.Headline: The attendee’s guide to the AWS re:Invent 2026 AI/ML track
stories.Summary:
The AWS re:Invent 2026 conference will run from November 30 to December 4, and AWS has published a guide to its artificial intelligence and machine learning track. The article, posted on the AWS website on November 12, 2026, explains that the event includes keynotes from AWS leaders, interactive sessions led by AWS experts, and immersive activities such as live entertainment at re:Play. The track offers more than 140 sessions among over 2,000 learning sessions across the conference. Attendees who cannot travel can watch many sessions on demand and view the keynotes live.

The guide describes several session formats that attendees can choose from. Breakout sessions are 60-minute lectures presented by AWS experts, customers, and partners, and they are recorded and posted to the AWS Events YouTube channel a few days later. Chalk talks let attendees ask questions and work through ideas on a whiteboard, builder sessions last one hour and have attendees build something, and workshops run two hours in small teams solving a real problem with AWS services. Code talks feature a live coding session led by an expert, while lightning talks are 20-minute demos held in the Venetian Expo Hall or the Wynn and Encore Upper Convention Promenade. The rest are live and not recorded.

The article organizes AWS's AI offerings into a stack that begins with global infrastructure designed for AI workloads and AI chips, including AWS Trainium and NVIDIA GPUs. Above that sits a data foundation called AWS Context, then models, training, and inference through Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI, followed by agent development through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. At the top are ready-to-use agentic solutions such as Kiro, AWS Quick, Amazon Connect, and AWS Marketplace. The guide says security, governance, and cost optimization apply across every layer. The track's sessions are arranged along this stack, with newcomer sessions listed first and technical deep dives last, and the guide also covers topics such as sustainability and infrastructure.

The guide frames its purpose as helping attendees pick sessions that match their needs and build a schedule around the stack. It recommends AIM204 for newcomers, since it walks through the full stack, and AIM364 for builders choosing between Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI. For those responsible for data strategy, it points to AIM363, a chalk talk on governed data products, and for those needing to demonstrate business value, it points to AIM319, which covers return on investment. The article ends by encouraging readers to use the guide to build a more effective re:Invent schedule.

Articles.Title: The attendee’s guide to the AWS re:Invent 2026 AI/ML track

stories.Headline: There's No U in AI: Treat AI Like a Smart, Capable Intern
stories.Summary:
The Law.com article "There's No U in AI: Treat AI Like a Smart, Capable Intern," published November 11, 2026, by Julie Talenfeld of Boardroom PR, argues that artificial intelligence should be treated as a helpful assistant rather than a substitute for professional judgment. The piece opens with a publicist and communications expert saying the topic needs continued discussion. Its central claim is that AI works best for research, drafts, and brainstorming, while the professional's own voice, expertise, and insight remain essential. The author frames the approach as a way to gain efficiency without losing authenticity. According to the article, audiences are increasingly skeptical of generic, AI-generated content that lacks the personal touch only people can supply.

The requirement implied is that professionals review and shape AI output so it reflects their own perspective. The article's summary holds that the most successful professionals will be those who pair AI's speed with a distinctive, human point of view. Talenfeld, a publicist and communications expert at Boardroom PR, makes the case in the article, which is labeled as expert opinion in the Law Firm Marketing and Business Development section. The piece is written for lawyers and other professionals who are deciding how much to rely on AI tools in their work.

The text available does not describe specific enforcement, deadlines, or regulatory changes tied to the advice. The page also carries related items, including a November 9, 2026 story about Shaw Lewenz, a firm that aims to become a boutique powerhouse, and an October 27, 2026 report on a dispute between the Florida Bar and Morgan & Morgan over a rule on celebrity voices and images in attorney advertising. Those items are not connected to the AI article in the material provided. The article itself does not say what comes next for the broader debate.

Articles.Title: There's No U in AI: Treat AI Like a Smart, Capable Intern

stories.Headline: Rajesh Ramachandran, ABB Global Chief Digital Officer on AI
stories.Summary:
Rajesh Ramachandran, Global Chief Digital Officer for ABB's Automation business area, spoke to AI Magazine, which published the interview on November 12, 2026, by Adam Pond. McKinsey expects manufacturing and industrials to drive the biggest AI-enabled digital transformation gains from IoT, and it estimates the total value potential for the IoT ecosystem could reach US$12.6trn by 2030. Ramachandran's role focuses on advancing digitalisation across industrial operations and helping customers apply industrial AI and advanced analytics at scale. ABB is described as a global technology leader in electrification and automation, helping industries run leaner and cleaner. The article presents his views on how predictive AI combined with IoT can deliver measurable industrial returns.

Ramachandran says the focus is on combining industrial data with domain and engineering expertise, automation, digital technologies, advanced analytics and AI. The stated aims are to improve asset and process reliability, optimise operational performance and energy use, and move progressively towards more autonomous operations. He says predictive AI needs trusted, contextualised data that reflects how assets and processes behave in the real world. He summarises the approach as data making AI feasible, domain expertise and context making it usable, AI making it valuable, and a platform approach making it scalable. The integration of operational technology, information technology and engineering technology is presented as important to this work.

Ramachandran is quoted as the source of the views in the piece, and the article attributes the strategic framing to him. He says leaders should start from the business problem, be clear about what they are trying to predict and how early, and identify the decision or action the prediction should improve. He says the real challenge lies in embedding predictive AI into operational routines, with AI integrated securely into existing systems and workflows. He argues that organisations should close the loop continuously, using what they learn to improve outcomes and scale successful applications. He also says ABB Genix, which he describes as a leading Industrial IoT and AI platform, is an example of the platform approach in practice.

The article reports that many firms struggle to see return on AI investment, and Ramachandran says that in industrials ROI must be measured in operational and business outcomes rather than model accuracy alone. He points to predictive maintenance with ABB Genix Asset Performance Management, where multivariate anomaly detection has identified potential failures six to ten days before they occur in recent customer deployments. He says applications addressing predictive maintenance, asset reliability and energy efficiency are where customers see the highest immediate return. The piece also notes that ABB reported 98% of its electricity was sourced from renewables in 2025, US$33.22m in total revenue generated in 2025, and six acquisitions completed in 2026. Ramachandran adds that combining predictive models with prescriptive analytics, causal analysis and digital twins helps teams test responses with less risk to live operations.

The article does not describe any single event, announcement or incident, so this is an interview feature rather than breaking news. It does not state whether any customers beyond the cited deployments have adopted these approaches, or how the US$12.6trn McKinsey estimate is distributed across sectors. It also gives no timeline for the expected arrival of agentic AI in industrial operations. Ramachandran expects predictive, prescriptive and generative capabilities to work together increasingly, with agentic AI bridging insight and execution, but the piece does not say how quickly that will happen. Whether ABB Genix will reach the scale he describes is not addressed in the article.

Articles.Title: Rajesh Ramachandran, ABB Global Chief Digital Officer on AI

stories.Headline: Silk Road in orbit: China to build 20-satellite ‘space AI’ system for Oman
stories.Summary:
Hangzhou-based Star Vision has agreed to build Oman a network of 20 satellites that use artificial intelligence to process images in orbit and spot ships and floods in real time. The deal, which the start-up called China's most valuable commercial space contract ever, was signed in Beijing last week with Omani firm Oman Lens. It was concluded during a landmark state visit by Oman's ruler, Sultan Haitham bin Tariq. The contract is reportedly worth over US$200 million, according to Star Vision. The package goes well beyond the satellites themselves.

It includes a satellite assembly and testing centre inside Oman, scholarships for 30 Omanis to pursue master's and doctoral degrees in China, and training for 1,000 local specialists. The two sides also plan to set up a joint laboratory focused on space artificial intelligence. Together, these elements are meant to build local capacity alongside the orbital system. Liao Zhenhua, who heads Star Vision's Oman project, said smaller nations want satellites of their own so they are not left behind as major powers fill up space.

In an interview, he said that a country may not have as many satellites as the United States but could still observe whatever area it chooses with even one or two. The article presents his remarks as the company's rationale for the deal. The article places the agreement within a broader push by smaller states to acquire their own space capabilities, though it gives no further detail on other contracts. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Silk Road in orbit: China to build 20-satellite ‘space AI’ system for Oman

stories.Headline: VistaShares Artificial Intelligence Supercycle ETF (AIS) Stock Price, News, Quote & History

stories.Headline: Hybrid Swarm AI Framework Detects Synthetic Interior Renders With 97.5 Percent Accuracy
stories.Summary:
Researcher Zhengfang Wu has published a study in Discover Artificial Intelligence describing a computational framework that distinguishes real interior photographs from synthetic computer-generated renderings with 97.5 percent accuracy. The framework is called the Glowworm Swarm-Optimized Attention-enriched Variational Autoencoder, abbreviated as GSO-Att-VAE. The article was published on November 12, 2026, on bioengineer.org. The study targets a growing problem, since generative systems can now produce detailed interior spaces that standard inspection tools often fail to flag. The authors say existing automated design tools lack a way to separate authentic photographs from synthetic outputs while also optimizing spatial parameters.

The framework combines statistical filtering, sparse spatial encoding, hierarchical visual extraction, attention-guided probabilistic modeling, and swarm intelligence in one pipeline.
