It is designed to run on edge devices rather than requiring centralized server infrastructure. The study used the publicly accessible Edge AI Interior Spatial Design Dataset hosted on Kaggle, which contains 4,000 synthetic interior scene records and 69 tabular columns. The target attribute, Image_Authenticity, labels each record as either Real_Interior or AI_Generated. Of the 68 predictor variables, the framework uses 58 pre-computed structured spatial metadata attributes supplied with the dataset rather than deriving them from raw pixels.

Images pass through two-dimensional Gaussian filtering, and the numerical attributes are standardized using Z-score normalization. Wu formulated the GSO-Att-VAE framework to address these deficiencies through a unified architecture that couples visual features with structured spatial attributes. The article attributes the design to Wu alone, as the study's sole named researcher. According to the article, the framework's authors frame their purpose as resolving the operational silos that separate image generation, aesthetic scoring, layout planning, and authenticity detection. The article quotes Wu's aim only in paraphrase, stating that the work is meant to close these gaps in a single edge-compatible system.

The article does not report any further statement from Wu beyond the study itself. The article does not report reactions from other researchers, companies, designers, or users of interior visualization tools. It identifies the groups most affected as those relying on automated interior design and architectural visualization, where synthetic or physically flawed renderings can feed into layout analyses and produce implausible recommendations. It also notes that interactive smart interior installations depend on low-latency local processing, which centralized cloud systems cannot easily provide. The article gives no figures on how widely such tools are currently used.

It does not describe any deployment of the framework outside the reported experiments. The article explains that generative pipelines such as StyleGAN variants, diffusion frameworks, and vision-language systems have sped up interior concept creation but typically separate rendering from geometric verification. It notes that classical classifiers for visual authenticity rely almost exclusively on two-dimensional pixels and ignore structured parameters such as room dimensions and illumination vectors. It also states that centralized cloud architectures introduce latency and bandwidth demands that limit real-time responsiveness. The study's own evaluation reported an F1-score of 96.9 percent, precision of 97.3 percent, recall of 97.4 percent, and an area under the ROC curve of 97.2 percent.

On an 800-instance test set, the model correctly identified 392 of 400 AI-generated images and 388 of 400 real photographs. The article's account ends at the reported results and the comparison against classical classifiers and deep learning backbones, which it begins to describe but does not complete in the portion provided. It does not state whether the results have been independently replicated, whether the framework will be released or deployed, or how it performs on data beyond the Kaggle dataset. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Hybrid Swarm AI Framework Detects Synthetic Interior Renders With 97.5 Percent Accuracy

stories.Headline: Global Nursing AI Alliance and American Board of Nursing Artificial Intelligence Present Nursing AI Research at AAAI
stories.Summary:
The Global Nursing AI Alliance and the American Board of Nursing Artificial Intelligence presented five papers at the inaugural Agentic and Trustworthy AI for Health and the Global AI-Ready Nursing Workforce symposium, known as AT-AI4H-NW 2026. The meeting ran November 5 to 7 at the Westin Arlington Gateway in Arlington, Virginia, as part of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence's 2026 Fall Symposium Series. Organizers reported that 23 papers were accepted and presented. The alliance's president, Vanessa Riley, argued that nurses should help shape clinical AI decisions from the start, before procurement. The press release was distributed through EIN Presswire on November 11, 2026.

Several papers focused on how to measure nursing competence with AI. Delaney W. La Rosa and co-authors mapped the literature to the American Board's seven competency domains and found gaps in validated measures of applied AI skills, including equity-related competencies. Simmy King, La Rosa, and Riley used the same framework to build a 105-item self-assessment for an exploratory cross-sectional study. Respondents who reported prior AI education rated themselves higher than those without it, scoring 2.65 against 1.80. Data literacy, analytics, and governance was the lowest-rated domain.

A separate workforce framework was presented by Riley and a team of 29 contributors drawn from nursing specialties, informatics, and data science. The authors identified eight themes for workforce readiness, including nursing leadership in AI governance, accountability for clinical decisions, and adaptation to local care settings. Other sessions addressed nursing education, including an AI Discernment Framework for teaching and learning and a study of graduate students' research skills after an AI research assistant was introduced. Researchers also tested human oversight of clinical AI, evaluating four safeguards across nine reviewers in a nurse-facing patient deterioration testbed.

Sharonda Davis, the alliance's co-director of Acute Care and Surgery, said that AI recommendations must be tested for fit with the care setting, the patient's clinical condition, language needs, and care preferences. La Rosa said AI is becoming a safety and advocacy issue, and that nurses need to be prepared to lead when these systems are designed, evaluated, deployed, and refined. The symposium was co-chaired by Riley and La Rosa along with Hong Qin, Apurva Narayan, and Catherine Fang, and King, the American Board's president, served on the organizing team. The release does not say what follow-up work or future symposia are planned.

Articles.Title: Global Nursing AI Alliance and American Board of Nursing Artificial Intelligence Present Nursing AI Research at AAAI

stories.Headline: New Jersey teen teaches himself machine learning to help families understand children with autism - Tri-State Alert
stories.Summary:
A New Jersey teenager, Shashank Madala, began teaching himself machine learning at age 15 after watching relatives struggle to understand his younger cousin's emotional cues. During family gatherings, adults often guessed at why the boy was upset, and those guesses were frequently wrong. Madala noticed the boy grew less willing to communicate over time. Rather than accept that gap, he set out to see whether technology could help.

With only one computer science class behind him, Madala built an app called Kora, which is free to use. A caregiver can point a smartphone camera at a child and receive several possible readings of the child's expression, such as happiness, sadness, anger, fear or neutrality. The app also suggests how adults might respond. Madala redesigned it to offer multiple possibilities and to admit uncertainty, leaving the final judgment to the adults who know the child best.

The project has drawn recognition at several levels. In December 2025, Kora won first place in the Congressional App Challenge for New Jersey's 10th Congressional District, and it was later displayed at the U.S. Capitol. A 2026 joint legislative resolution from the New Jersey Senate and General Assembly also honored Madala. In an October report, he said the goal was to make adults more attentive, not to expect autistic children to change for them.

Kora now has more than 700 users across 12 countries, with families reaching it through autism therapy centers. Madala continues developing the technology with three other students and hopes to make it available to more schools, therapy centers and families while keeping it free. He also works with researchers at Yale University's Child Study Center on artificial intelligence applications related to autism and communication. Kora is not meant to diagnose autism or replace professional guidance.

Articles.Title: New Jersey teen teaches himself machine learning to help families understand children with autism - Tri-State Alert

stories.Headline: Fewer hours and higher wages – or more burnout and surveillance: employers told to prepare for AI
stories.Summary:
The Australian government has issued a best practice guide on how employers should adopt artificial intelligence at work, and it warns that the technology could either improve or worsen conditions for ordinary workers. Workplace relations minister Amanda Rishworth launched the guide on Thursday 12 November 2026, as large firms cut staff in restructures linked partly to AI. Qantas announced 850 job cuts targeting finance, human resources and marketing roles, National Australian Bank announced 2,500 job losses, and Canva announced 1,200 layoffs. The guide says entry-level work may be the first to be automated.

The guide paints an optimistic picture, suggesting wider AI use could raise productivity, boost wages, offer shorter and more flexible hours, or provide more meaningful work. It also concedes "potential hazards," including intrusive worker surveillance, poor rostering, unrealistic performance standards and possible discrimination. It warns that if basic tasks are automated, the remaining work may become more intense and complex. It also flags that some employers could use expanded monitoring for performance management.

Rishworth said employers must give workers a clear plan about how automation could affect their jobs and the chance to move into new roles. In a speech in Sydney, she said adding AI without consulting workers could increase workloads, because people must navigate an extra step. The guide cautions that younger, older and First Nations workers, along with women and people with a disability, face disproportionate impacts. Labor MP Ed Husic, the former industry minister, asked at a parliamentary hearing on the big four banks who would receive the benefits of higher productivity.

Greens leader David Shoebridge accused the government of watching from the sidelines and said the guidance was too weak. He argued that a worker who loses a job to an algorithm would have no legal recourse under the current approach, and he called for the protections to be written into law. The Reserve Bank this week reported "little evidence to date" of AI disrupting the labour market, while saying future effects were highly uncertain. It noted "tentative signs" of impact on roles such as clerks, computer programmers and call centre workers.

Articles.Title: Fewer hours and higher wages – or more burnout and surveillance: employers told to prepare for AI

stories.Headline: Siemens Q4 profit jumps 32% on AI infrastructure demand; raises growth targets
stories.Summary:
Siemens AG shares climbed to an 11-week high on Thursday, 12 November 2026, after the German industrial group reported quarterly results that beat expectations and raised its medium-term growth targets. Strong demand for AI-related data centre equipment and rail contracts pushed orders to a record for the quarter. The stock rose 4.44% to €289.30 after touching an intraday high of €291.45, its highest level since August 28. It also outperformed Germany's DAX, which gained around 0.9% during the session.

For the quarter ended September 30, net income rose to €2.43 billion from €1.84 billion a year earlier. Revenue increased 11% to €23.68 billion, while profit at the Industrial Business climbed 22% to a record €3.90 billion. The industrial profit margin improved to 16.8% from 15.3%. Orders surged 58% to a quarterly record €34.77 billion, lifting the book-to-bill ratio to 1.47 and the order backlog to €143 billion.

Growth was led by Smart Infrastructure and Mobility, with Smart Infrastructure's revenue rising 16% to €7.24 billion and its order intake jumping 40% on large data centre contract wins in the U.S. and Europe. Digital Industries revenue rose 11% and profit increased 50%, driven mainly by operational improvements in automation. Mobility's orders more than quadrupled, supported by major German rail contracts including a €2.4 billion high-speed train order. Siemens attributed these gains to continued investment in electrification, digital infrastructure and rail transportation.

Looking ahead, Siemens expects comparable revenue growth of 9% to 11% in fiscal 2027 and earnings per share before purchase price allocation accounting of €10.20 to €10.80. The company pointed to investment in AI and digital infrastructure, public investment programmes and a recovery in industrial activity as key growth drivers. For the full fiscal year, net income fell 9% to €9.47 billion, reflecting a €2.1 billion gain from the sale of Innomotics in the prior year. Revenue rose 6% to €83.37 billion, Industrial Business profit increased 13% to a record €13.29 billion, and the proposed dividend rises to €5.50 per share from €5.35.

Articles.Title: Siemens Q4 profit jumps 32% on AI infrastructure demand; raises growth targets

stories.Headline: Europe’s AI Spare Tyre Is Made In China – OpEd
stories.Summary:
In July, an autonomous system of roughly 700 agents, driven by an internal OpenAI model, broke into the servers of Hugging Face, the French-founded AI platform. When the company's engineers tried to reconstruct the intrusion with leading American models, those models refused to help, saying their safeguards could not tell an incident responder from an attacker. The company instead ran GLM 5.2, an open-weight model from the Chinese firm Z.ai, on its own hardware and worked through more than 17,000 logged attacker actions. The opinion piece describing these events was published on Eurasia Review on November 11, 2026.

The article argues that Europe's recent AI disruptions came from American export controls rather than from Chinese technology. In June, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick placed Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 under export controls and barred foreign nationals from using them, and European users waited almost three weeks for access to return. The European Commission's July action plan promises contingency measures for future withdrawals of access. The author proposes three areas of cooperation with China: agent standards, incident-data sharing and sector pilots in cars and telecommunications. He also recommends that ENISA's forthcoming European Blueprint for access to advanced AI in cyber defence include vetted open-weight models, Chinese ones among them, hosted on European hardware.

The author places these ideas against the World Internet Conference summit in Wuzhen, which drew guests from 138 countries. Spain's Yolanda Díaz called for open-source and inclusive AI, and Dame Wendy Hall, co-chair of the conference's AI committee, said Europe remains heavily reliant on American technologies. The article also notes objections raised by others: U.S. agencies have accused six Chinese labs, including Z.ai and Alibaba, of distilling American models, which Beijing rejects, and MERICS warns that Chinese models could create a new dependency. The author counters that these concerns relate to how a model is run rather than where it was trained, since downloaded weights send nothing back to China. The article is an opinion piece by Dr. Imran Khalid, a geostrategic analyst, and the Commission's ENISA blueprint, with contingency measures due before the year ends, is the next step the author identifies.

Articles.Title: Europe’s AI Spare Tyre Is Made In China – OpEd

stories.Headline: Tech industry workers gather to read Pope Leo’s A.I. encyclical
stories.Summary:
In September, at a small cafe in Honolulu, a Zen Buddhist priest named Cristina Moon organized a reading group on Pope Leo's encyclical on artificial intelligence and the human person, "Magnifica Humanitas." The gathering was held during Hawaii Tech Week and drew about 15 people, including tech industry insiders, startup founders, recent graduates and Honolulu locals. Lilinoe Andrews, a Hawaiian language instructor from the University of Hawaii, led the group in an oli, a traditional chant asking for wisdom. Jackson Sayama, a state representative and senator-elect, read the opening paragraph of the encyclical. Participants then read aloud from excerpts Ms. Moon had printed, with a Claude-designed Hawaiian motif on the cover.

Ms. Moon shortened the encyclical's excerpts so the reading lasted 45 minutes rather than an hour. The full encyclical runs 192 pages and five chapters, and it does not address artificial intelligence directly until chapter three. Ms. Moon had first tried to read the document alone but was overwhelmed by its recaps of Catholic social teaching. She was inspired to host the event after a Medium post by Natalie Foster described a similar reading in Oakland, Calif., that used Claude- and human-curated excerpts. Ms. Moon held her event at Hello Again, a coffee shop in Honolulu's Chinatown that uses an automated drink machine so baristas can talk with customers.

Ms. Foster, an economic justice advocate and former president of the Economic Security Project, and Deepti Doshi, a former Meta director who now co-directs the nonprofit New_ Public, organized the Oakland reading. Ms. Foster said the pair advertised the event as lighthearted, but she described the gathering as "more solemn than festive." Ms. Moon said she wanted to show that automation could support what is uniquely human, such as building relationships. Ms. Foster said participants were more interested in artificial intelligence than in religious themes, though she also saw a growing openness to religious expression in the tech industry.

The gatherings have drawn wider interest, including an event at Homeboy Industries, the Jesuit-run nonprofit in Los Angeles that focuses on gang member rehabilitation. Michael Tubbs, the former mayor of Stockton, Calif., helped organize the Los Angeles event, which was co-sponsored by the Aspen Institute's Future of Work Initiative, Common Sense Media, Homeboy Industries, Nefesh LA, End Poverty in California and LA Voice. Mr. Tubbs said he hoped people beyond the tech sector would join the conversation about artificial intelligence. Ms. Foster said that reading the encyclical in person felt like a statement, and that the event served as a reminder of what it means to be human.

Articles.Title: Tech industry workers gather to read Pope Leo’s A.I. encyclical

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Enhances Cellular Immunotherapies Across Diverse Autoimmune Disease Models
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is being applied to cell-based immunotherapies for autoimmune disease, according to a comprehensive review of computational engineering and cellular immunology published on bioengineer.org on November 11, 2026. The review covers systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, and inflammatory bowel disease, which all arise from a breakdown in immune tolerance. Conventional drugs, including broad immunosuppressives, systemic corticosteroids, and biological agents, control acute symptoms but often fail to restore lasting balance between protective and autoreactive immune pathways. They also cause systemic toxicities and leave patients more vulnerable to opportunistic infections. Therapists seek longer remissions by recalibrating immune tolerance while preserving protection against microbial pathogens.

The review describes machine learning as a way to decode cellular heterogeneity, streamline clinical manufacturing, and guide personalized treatment across autoimmune conditions. It identifies three functional roles for artificial intelligence in regenerative immunotherapy, linking molecular observations to clinical delivery. Algorithms first detect subtle cell states and pathogenic subsets that manual classification misses. Computational pipelines then optimize the expansion, characterization, and quality validation of cell products such as mesenchymal stem cells, engineered regulatory T cells, and induced pluripotent stem cell derivatives. Predictive models finally assess donor potency, estimate flare-up risk, and anticipate therapy-induced immune toxicities.

The review's authors are not named in the material provided, and it does not attribute specific statements to individual researchers. The article presents the framework as a systematic, data-driven replacement for empirical therapeutic selection. It frames these tools as a way to tailor interventions to each patient's immune profile across different autoimmune pathologies. The material does not quote any researcher or describe any response from clinicians, regulators, or patients. Patients with the listed autoimmune diseases are the population the review addresses, along with clinicians and manufacturers of cell-based products.

The review describes CD19-directed CAR-T cells as having induced sustained remissions in fifteen patients with severe systemic lupus erythematosus, idiopathic inflammatory myositis, and systemic sclerosis. Complete B-cell aplasia in those patients lasted an average of 112 days after a single infusion. A separate small series of five patients with treatment-resistant systemic lupus erythematosus showed persistent improvement and autoantibody clearance. The article notes that remission persisted even after naive B cells returned. The review explains that artificial intelligence was adopted in these fields because of known problems with cell therapy.

Persistent antigen exposure in inflamed tissue can exhaust T cells, and cytokine release syndrome poses clinical risk. Mesenchymal stem cells face donor heterogeneity, batch-to-batch variability, and replicative senescence during expansion. Deep learning can detect senescent cells from standard microscopy images without destructive staining. Random forest classifiers using transcriptomic and metabolomic signatures can separate high-potency donor lines before expansion begins. The review also describes this as a foundation for further work with pluripotent stem cell platforms, but it gives no timeline, trial results for those platforms, or regulatory decisions, and it leaves open how widely these methods will reach patients.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Enhances Cellular Immunotherapies Across Diverse Autoimmune Disease Models

stories.Headline: Corporate AI Training in Australia: Paloren Trains Whole Departments on Approved AI Tools and Real Tasks
stories.Summary:
Paloren, an AI strategy, implementation, automation and training company, is offering Australian organizations corporate AI training that covers whole departments, according to a press release dated November 12, 2026, republished on FinancialContent. The offer is aimed at organizations planning training for 2027, and it is built around the AI tools each company has already approved and the tasks its teams repeat every week. Paloren delivers half-day and full-day workshops, four-to-six-week department programs and executive coaching. The company is co-founded by Aaron Agius and Alex Agius.

Before any session, Paloren records which tools each team is approved to use, such as Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and which functions are switched on. Cohorts contain six to 16 people, with multiple cohorts for larger groups, and role-specific practice lets finance, operations and customer service teams each work on their own material. Each format includes a baseline exercise, safe practice materials, reusable task instructions, a later independent attempt and a workplace trial with a named reviewer. The article says managers receive work they can inspect rather than just an attendance list. Remote sessions run in Australian working hours, and onsite delivery is available by arrangement.

The training is delivered by founders and senior practitioners at Paloren. The company says organizations can start a discussion by sharing team sizes, approved tools and two or three priority tasks. The article describes Paloren as a business that builds AI into the systems companies already run and trains their people to own it. It notes that course selection for Microsoft 365 users can start from the Word, Teams and Outlook work staff already do.

Paloren's Australian AI Training Price Index, checked on November 10, 2026, found a median published starting price of A$4,900 per group for private team sessions. The index covered 13 offers from eight providers, and session lengths ranged from about one hour to a full day. Because of that spread, the index advises comparing duration and group size before comparing price. The article also notes that it is third-party content and that the publisher makes no guarantees about its accuracy or completeness.

Articles.Title: Corporate AI Training in Australia: Paloren Trains Whole Departments on Approved AI Tools and Real Tasks

stories.Headline: Suno AI Music Review 2026: Can Artificial Intelligence Create Professional Songs and Music Videos?
stories.Summary:
Suno, a platform that generates complete songs from written prompts, has been reviewed in an article published on November 11, 2026, by Rebellion Research. The piece asks whether artificial intelligence can create professional songs and music videos. It describes Suno as one of the most recognizable platforms for this purpose. Unlike earlier systems that produced only instrumental loops or short samples, Suno can generate structured compositions with vocals, lyrics, melodies and instrumental arrangements. The article frames the question as one about whether these tools can replace traditional workflows or simply add new creative options.

Users describe a genre, mood, instrumentation, vocal style or lyrical theme, and the platform generates audio from those instructions. The article's examples include an atmospheric electronic piece with piano and synthesizers, and an energetic rock song with distorted guitars. The technology learns statistical relationships among musical structures, vocal traits and audio patterns, so users guide results through text and revisions rather than arranging instruments by hand. The article says this lowers technical barriers that traditionally required musicians, studio equipment, mixing software and production experience. It also cautions that accessibility does not guarantee artistic consistency, since outputs can have repetitive lyrics, unnatural phrasing or weak vocal delivery.

The article credits Suno with making complete compositions accessible to a broader audience, and says it can speed experimentation for independent creators. It lists strengths such as generating songs from descriptions, producing vocals and lyrics, supporting many styles and offering alternative arrangements. Limitations include the need for repeated revisions and unpredictable links between prompts and output. The article also notes unresolved questions about copyright, training data, licensing and commercial rights, which matter to creators who plan to earn money from their work. It adds that a technically impressive song differs from a commercially successful musical identity.

Finally, the article says that Suno's commercial rights and licensing terms are matters creators should check, rather than assume. Music distribution increasingly depends on visual presentation on platforms such as YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, according to the article. It says a song paired with a static image may struggle for attention against content with movement or narrative. Traditional videos require locations, cameras, performers, editing software and sizable budgets, while generative video systems can create visual sequences from text prompts and reference images. The article notes that building a coherent music video is harder than producing isolated clips, because it requires visual continuity, consistent characters, synchronization with song structure and a complementary aesthetic.

It describes Enkio as a platform designed for that purpose. Enkio's workflow, as described, lets users supply an existing audio track, including a Suno track, and build a video with reference images, visual prompts and scene-level review. According to the article, Enkio's actual output quality, rendering consistency, pricing and reliability require independent testing before performance claims can be established. The article also states that compatibility with Suno audio should not be taken as evidence of an official commercial partnership. It identifies character consistency, synchronization and long-form narrative coherence as the main technical challenges for AI video.

The article argues generative AI could cut costs for independent musicians and digital creators, and that human creative direction remains important. It points to record labels, advertising agencies, social media companies and digital content businesses as parties with incentives to reduce production costs. The article warns that cheaper production may intensify competition for attention, making distribution, originality, branding and intellectual property management more important. The article's final assessment is that Suno is a compelling option for experimenting with AI music, while creators seeking full multimedia productions may need additional tools for visuals, editing and distribution. It says Enkio illustrates how specialized video tools could complement AI music generators, though their comparative capabilities should be tested directly.

It concludes that the key development is the emergence of interconnected AI production workflows. The article leaves open the outcomes of copyright and licensing disputes, the sustainability of revenue for these companies, and how audiences will respond to abundant AI-generated content. It also leaves open how well Enkio and similar tools will perform in practice. Sources cited include the U.S. Copyright Office, the Recording Industry Association of America, YouTube and the companies' own websites.

Articles.Title: Suno AI Music Review 2026: Can Artificial Intelligence Create Professional Songs and Music Videos?

stories.Headline: U.S.-China Engagement Ahead of the Trump-Xi APEC Summit,AI DIalogue
stories.Summary:
The United States and China held a video call on November 6, 2026, with Vice Premier He Lifeng, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, days before the APEC leaders' meeting in China. The call, announced by both sides, centered on carrying out understandings reached by the two presidents in Beijing and Washington. Chinese and U.S. readouts of the call differed in emphasis. A separate phone call between Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Secretary of State Marco Rubio took place on November 11.

Beijing expressed serious concerns about recent U.S. economic and trade restrictions against China. Washington stressed that China must fully and immediately meet its commitments, particularly on agricultural purchases, rare earths and other critical minerals. The U.S. said it would closely assess China's implementation of the Busan arrangement. GE Aerospace announced more than $12.9 billion in agreements on November 6 at the China International Import Expo, including an order from China Eastern Airlines for 202 LEAP-1A engines.

Bessent is responsible for the U.S. statements, which he framed as protecting American workers, farmers and businesses. Foreign Minister Wang Yi described the Rubio call as positive and constructive, while China's readout did not say what Rubio had said. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun dismissed espionage claims linked to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as groundless speculation and malicious smears. Taiwan Affairs Office spokeswoman Zhang Han said cross-Strait semiconductor cooperation serves both sides.

Bessent disclosed the new AI arrangements in remarks on November 11 at the National Committee on US-China Relations' annual dinner. He said the U.S. had set up a dialogue with China on superintelligence, at President Trump's direction, to guard against shared risks. Both countries also expect to exchange best practices for testing advanced AI models before release, and to keep human judgment in command of the technology. A direct channel will let either side promptly alert the other to serious incidents involving its superintelligence models.

Bessent credited Henry Kissinger, who died at 100 and had met Xi in Beijing on his last trip, with raising concerns about superintelligence as a new class of strategic danger. China has already set up several pre-release AI safety mechanisms, including security assessments and regulatory filings for generative AI services. These include red-teaming, adversarial testing and third-party evaluations, under the Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said China and the United States remained in communication about leader interactions later this year.

It remains unconfirmed whether the two presidents will hold a meeting at APEC or whether the Jensen Huang affair will be discussed there. The articles also do not say whether China will meet the agricultural and rare earth commitments the U.S. demanded. Details of the AI dialogue's first meeting and its schedule are not given. Neither country has confirmed a date or format for the planned leader-level exchanges.

Articles.Title: U.S.-China Engagement Ahead of the Trump-Xi APEC Summit,AI DIalogue

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence and Dual Tracers Tackle PSMA Heterogeneity in Prostate Cancer
stories.Summary:
The article reports that a scientific review, published in Frontiers in Oncology, examines how variable target expression complicates diagnosis and treatment of castration-resistant prostate cancer. Its authors are Surilige, Jiacheng Liang, and Ruimin Ren of the Third Hospital of Shanxi Medical University. The review was carried in a November 11, 2026 article on bioengineer.org. It assesses dual-tracer imaging, downstream pathway inhibitors, and artificial intelligence as ways to address target heterogeneity. The article describes this work as a synthesis of existing research rather than a new trial.

The review centers on prostate-specific membrane antigen, a glycoprotein abundant on prostate cancer cells and metastatic deposits. Prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography detects malignant deposits using radioisotope-labeled ligands. Pairing these tracers with fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose captures metabolically aggressive lesions that lack ligand uptake. The article also cites gallium-68 PSFA-01, a heterobivalent tracer targeting both the glycoprotein and fibroblast activation protein, which showed higher lesion detection than monospecific tracers in preliminary human evaluations. Lutetium-177 vipivotide tetraxetan was approved following the VISION and PSMAfore phase III trials, with PSMAfore showing 9.3 months versus 5.6 months of radiographic progression-free survival.

The authors attribute this variability to clonal evolution, epigenetic changes, and lineage plasticity that can drive tumors toward neuroendocrine phenotypes with reduced target expression. They say the review was written by the three named researchers, who evaluate these barriers in the disease. The article does not give a direct quotation from them in the portion provided. It notes that current guidelines, including those from the Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, rely on visual criteria without standardized quantitative thresholds for uptake adequacy. Patients with advanced, aggressive disease, especially those with TP53 and RB1 inactivation, are described as most affected by these diagnostic blind spots.

The article describes preclinical and clinical work on PI3K/AKT and MAPK pathway inhibitors, including phase III trials such as IPATential150 and CAPItello-281 that showed radiographic progression-free survival benefits in biomarker-selected cohorts. It also notes that none of these investigational combinations is currently approved to reverse target heterogeneity. On the artificial intelligence side, the article cites automated segmentation reaching a mean Dice coefficient of about 0.89 and reducing contouring time from 30 to 45 minutes to about 15 seconds. It reports an 82 percent sensitivity for automated metastasis detection with about 1.8 false positives per patient, and an area under the curve of 0.98 for distinguishing malignant hotspots across 72 patients.

The authors caution that most models rely on retrospective, single-center datasets with small samples and lack rigorous external validation across scanners and radiopharmaceuticals. They note that high technical accuracy does not prove improved survival or clinical utility. The article states that large-scale prospective multicenter trials with harmonized protocols remain essential. It does not specify when such trials will begin, which combination regimens will advance, or whether the artificial intelligence tools will reach routine clinical use.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence and Dual Tracers Tackle PSMA Heterogeneity in Prostate Cancer

stories.Headline: Former Chinese Ambassador Cui Tiankai on China-US Relations and AI Governance
stories.Summary:
Former Chinese Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs and Ambassador to the United States Cui Tiankai spoke on November 7 at the "APEC China Year · Greater Bay Area Academic Roundtable" in Shenzhen. He shared his views on China-US relations and artificial intelligence governance. The event was part of the lead-up to the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, which is due to be held in Shenzhen in about ten days. The article reports the remarks as a keynote speech followed by a conversation with Professor Li Cheng of Hong Kong University. The Shenzhen Hetao Institute and the Centre on Contemporary China and the World at the University of Hong Kong invited him to take part.

On China-US relations, Cui called for a relationship of "constructive strategic stability," with cooperation as the priority and competition kept within reasonable bounds. He said China's development has never aimed to replace or challenge the United States. He argued that competition between the two countries should not become a zero-sum game, since cooperation benefits both and confrontation harms both. On AI, he said the two countries have the capability and responsibility to keep the technology under human control and serve the public good. He proposed three steps for an Asia-Pacific framework: establishing AI for good as a guiding principle, building on APEC's cooperation record, and promoting inclusive development and integration.

Cui said the political, economic and social challenges facing the United States have deep structural causes and cannot be blamed on any single leader. He said domestic political developments in the US should not undermine bilateral relations. He criticised Washington for broadening the concept of national security and for politicising scientific, educational and people-to-people exchanges. He called on the US to remove unnecessary barriers to these exchanges and restore normal cooperation, saying even modest progress through dialogue would be worthwhile. On AI, he rejected an approach driven by fear and suspicion toward China's technological progress, saying zero-sum thinking is especially inappropriate in so advanced a field.

The remarks reach people across the Asia-Pacific region, which Cui said is home to nearly 40% of the world's population. He said the region accounts for more than 60% of global economic output and almost half of global trade, with internet penetration approaching 90%. He argued that AI development in such a region carries enormous significance for the world. He said countries at different stages of development should all have opportunities to take part in AI governance and benefit from technological progress. He also stressed that different technological pathways should be allowed to compete fairly, while the guiding principles must be set from the outset.

The speech builds on a July 2026 position set out at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance in Shanghai. At that event, a Chinese national leader called for a people-centred approach and AI for good, and for a fair and equitable global AI governance system. Cui cited that address and its questions about how humanity should coexist with machines and how the benefits of AI can be shared. He drew on APEC's history, noting that the region has weathered natural disasters, financial crises and a global pandemic over more than three decades since the forum was established. He also invoked a classical Chinese passage on understanding and transforming the world.

The articles do not say how the US government has responded to these remarks, and they do not describe any specific policy the US has adopted on exchanges or AI. They also do not set out concrete measures that would result from the Shenzhen roundtable or the APEC meeting. The articles do not say which barriers Cui had in mind, or what form any AI cooperation between the two countries would take. It is also unclear how the other APEC members will respond to the proposals, and whether the three suggestions will appear in the leaders' meeting outcome.

Articles.Title: Former Chinese Ambassador Cui Tiankai on China-US Relations and AI Governance

stories.Headline: Review Finds Artificial Intelligence Aids Healthcare Simulation Debriefing as Supportive Adjunct
stories.Summary:
Researchers Aseelah Alnazawi and Mohammed Almarhabi published a scoping review in Advances in Simulation finding that artificial intelligence currently supports human instructors during healthcare simulation debriefing rather than replacing them. The review mapped international literature on computational debriefing tools used in clinical training. It covered seven eligible studies published between 2023 and 2026, which applied artificial intelligence through automated speech tracking, structured summary reports, and learner dialogue interfaces. The authors concluded that the research is preliminary, exploratory, and mostly limited to single-institution pilot trials. Few of the studies showed objective gains in learner performance, clinical competency, or patient outcomes, so the tools are treated as complementary aids rather than substitutes for facilitators.

Simulation is an established teaching method that lets learners practice clinical reasoning, technical skills, and teamwork without risk to patients. Debriefing, a structured facilitator-led reflective session, is treated as its core component, helping participants analyze their actions and team dynamics. The review noted that traditional debriefing depends heavily on facilitator memory and observation, which strain under complex team dynamics and dense performance data. The authors applied Arksey and O'Malley's framework, with refinements by Levac and colleagues and Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, and followed the PRISMA-ScR checklist. Searches of MEDLINE via Ovid, Scopus, Web of Science, and CINAHL, plus grey literature, identified 46 initial records.

After removing 25 duplicates and excluding 14 of 21 screened citations, seven full-text articles were included. The authors and included studies describe the included work as heterogeneous in design, with three studies conducted in the United States, two in Switzerland, one in Chile, and one in South Korea. Three functional domains emerged: communication and performance analytics, generative systems that assist facilitators with preparation and feedback, and learner-facing reflective dialogue systems. In the analytics domain, Brutschi and colleagues showed speaker diarisation could distinguish individual speakers in debriefing audio, while Armijo-Rivera and colleagues found novice instructors spoke for an average of 56.09 percent of debriefing time. Tscholl and colleagues' automated teamwork reports drew criticism from simulation experts for speaker misattribution, inaccurate behavior categorization, and missing non-verbal cues.

Gonzalez and Nagendran found no statistically significant correlation between student course grades and debriefing duration in screen-based virtual nursing simulations. The review emphasized that human oversight remains essential, and the authors stressed that educators must keep ultimate responsibility for interpreting computational analytics. Because these tools capture audio, transcripts, and performance metrics, the authors raised concerns about data privacy, informed consent, algorithmic bias, and output transparency. They also warned that debriefing depends on psychological safety, so automated systems must not produce punitive or inaccurate evaluations that damage the learning climate. Technical problems reported across studies included poor audio quality, transcription errors, speaker misidentification, and an inability to register non-verbal interactions or emotional subtleties.

Jang and colleagues' nursing study reported improvements in student clinical confidence and domain knowledge, but the authors noted those cohorts were small, single-institution, and lacked control groups. Students, nursing and medical trainees, instructors, and clinical teams in simulation-based education are the populations the review addresses, and the authors call for rigorous evaluation before wider use. The articles do not state how quickly such tools will move into routine practice. They also leave open whether the reported learner gains will hold in larger, multi-institution studies with comparison groups and long-term behavioral follow-up. The articles do not specify which privacy safeguards or consent standards institutions should adopt.

Articles.Title: Review Finds Artificial Intelligence Aids Healthcare Simulation Debriefing as Supportive Adjunct

stories.Headline: Compliance teams failing to check their own AI outputs, says report
stories.Summary:
Compliance teams that skip checks on AI-generated outputs are nearly three times as likely to report a regulatory fine as those that do check, according to a report from regulatory intelligence firm Enhesa. The findings come from Enhesa's State of AI in Regulatory Compliance report, which was covered by Compliance Week and written by Neil Hodge. The article reports that the same teams are also twice as likely to produce an incomplete or incorrect filing, a failed audit, or an audit finding. The coverage was published on November 12, 2026.

The article does not describe any new rule or legal requirement arising from the findings. The report's central point is that the absence of review is linked to worse regulatory outcomes. Compliance teams that do not verify what AI tools produce appear more exposed to fines, faulty filings and audit problems. The article presents this as a pattern in the survey data rather than a proven cause, and it does not set out specific standards or deadlines that organizations must now meet.

It also does not give the size of the sample or the methods used to reach these figures, so readers would need to consult the original report for those details. The research was carried out by Enhesa, which the article describes as a regulatory intelligence firm, and the findings are attributed to its report. Neil Hodge, a freelance business journalist based in Nottingham, wrote the Compliance Week piece. The article does not include direct comments from Enhesa or from any compliance teams named in the survey.

It also gives no account of how the firm or the publication responded to the findings. The article sits within Compliance Week's wider coverage of artificial intelligence governance, which includes a dedicated topic area and related professional certification offerings. Its own related reading includes a practical guide on using AI outputs in compliance decisions. The article does not say what steps Enhesa or Compliance Week plan to take next, nor does it set out any follow-up research or policy response.

Articles.Title: Compliance teams failing to check their own AI outputs, says report

stories.Headline: Meta Taps Former AWS Executive to Lead Infrastructure as AI Spending Surges
stories.Summary:
Meta is replacing Santosh Janardhan, its head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, with David Brown, a former senior vice president at Amazon Web Services. According to a Wednesday, November 11, report by CNBC, Janardhan will leave the company in early 2027 and will remain through the first quarter of 2027 to support the transition. Janardhan, who joined Facebook in 2009, told employees in an internal memo that it was time to pass leadership on. Brown joined Meta in July and will formally oversee the company's infrastructure operations.

Brown will also serve as chief technology officer of Meta Compute, an initiative led by Meta President and Vice Chairman Dina Powell McCormick and technical leader Daniel Gross. The change comes as Meta expands the computing infrastructure needed to develop and deploy AI models. In its third-quarter earnings report, the company said it expects 2026 capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion, covering data centers, computing equipment and supporting infrastructure. Meta also reported negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion for the third quarter. Brown has nearly two decades of cloud computing experience at AWS, where he oversaw compute and machine learning services.

The article notes that Meta is exploring whether to turn its expanding infrastructure into a commercial cloud computing business, which could offer outside customers access to computing capacity and AI services. It describes the appointment as placing a veteran cloud executive in charge of one of the technology industry's largest AI infrastructure investments. The company's cash flow performance drew attention in October, when S&P Global Ratings revised Meta's credit rating outlook from stable to negative and cited that performance. The infrastructure transition also follows another senior departure. Chief Strategy Officer Dave Wehner announced earlier this month that he was leaving to become CFO of Fireworks, an AI training and inference startup.

Articles.Title: Meta Taps Former AWS Executive to Lead Infrastructure as AI Spending Surges

stories.Headline: PARTNER CONTENT: Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data
stories.Summary:
PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was disclosed in 2026 after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, and PHP shipped fixes the following day. The article reports that frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and that the flaw reportedly went undetected for more than a decade. Several security firms saw exploitation attempts before the fixes were released, and Cloudflare reported early attacks hours ahead of the patch. The article frames these events as a sign of how quickly the threat landscape is now shifting for IT and security teams. The piece argues that autonomous IT operations need a governed loop in which software finds risks, ranks them, proposes fixes and carries them out within limits people define.

Routine, low-risk actions can run automatically, higher-impact ones wait for human approval, and some actions are never delegated at all. Every step leaves a reviewable and reversible record. The article says that three problems make this difficult: incomplete visibility into every copy of PHP, the need to hop between separate asset, scanning and attack-surface tools, and the shrinking gap between disclosure and exploitation. It adds that putting an AI agent on top of stale, fragmented data scales these problems rather than solving them. The article is written as partner content, and it presents Tanium's real-time endpoint data as the foundation for trustworthy automation.

It names four qualities such data should have: accuracy, speed, control, and shared truth across IT, security and the system of record. Matt Psencik, a threat research engineer at Tanium, is quoted saying that the installations he worries about most are those a security team does not know it owns. The article also says World Wide Technology, a Tanium partner, hosts a Tanium lab where customers can test approaches before production, and it promotes Tanium Atlas as the product intended to reduce tool-hopping. The article gives practical first steps: find every copy of software, including bundled copies, by comparing the CMDB with what is actually on the network; rank systems by internet exposure and decide in advance which actions are automatic, which need approval and which are never delegated; and pilot one contained, low-risk workflow with approvals and a reviewed audit trail before widening scope.

Articles.Title: PARTNER CONTENT: Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data

stories.Headline: Blackstone’s AI Gets a Voice in Deals, but Not a Vote
stories.Summary:
Blackstone, the world's largest alternative asset manager, has introduced an artificial intelligence chief investment officer that reviews nearly every proposed investment alongside its human deal teams, according to PYMNTS, which reported the story on November 11, 2026. The system draws on more than 14 years of the firm's internal investment memos and committee debates to produce a separate assessment of each potential deal. Bloomberg reported in October that the AI takes part in the review but holds no vote. Nearly every investment now arrives at the Monday committee with two memos, one from the deal team and one from the AI.

The AI assessment becomes part of the committee's regular review, giving executives another perspective before they decide. It cannot approve or reject investments, and that authority stays with the firm's executives. The AI sits on top of tools Blackstone's deal teams already use. Chief Technology Officer John Stecher said in a May interview that reviewing thousands of deal documents once took a weekend and now takes minutes. Rodney Zemmel, the firm's global head of portfolio operations, told Bloomberg that he spends nearly 60% of his time on AI.

Blackstone's arrangement reflects expectations across large enterprises. PYMNTS Intelligence found in a May report, based on a survey of 60 senior technology executives at U.S. firms with at least $1 billion in annual revenue, that 80% to 85% of executives expect AI to augment human decisions over the next five years rather than replace them. None expect full autonomy. The same report found that financial services and insurance firms have reached high adoption in 27 of 75 tracked tasks. Blackstone's Monday meeting follows that pattern, with the AI writing a second memo while Jon Gray and his senior partners make the final call.

Articles.Title: Blackstone’s AI Gets a Voice in Deals, but Not a Vote

stories.Headline: Responsible AI: A Transformation That Belongs to All | General Assembly of the United Nations - Welcome to the United Nations
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has become one of the most discussed issues at the United Nations, with 128 delegations addressing it during the general debate of the eighty-first session. The President of the General Assembly, H.E. Mr. Khalilur Rahman, will convene an informal plenary meeting on responsible AI on 15 December 2026 in the General Assembly Hall at UN Headquarters in New York. The meeting is open to all Member States and observers, and it will be webcast on UN Web TV. Its purpose is to discuss how all countries and people can enjoy the benefits of AI while responsibly managing its risks. The outcome will be a summary of key messages issued by the President after the meeting.

The articles set out three focus areas for the discussion: moving from access to capacity, making AI safe and secure, and bringing existing initiatives into one coherent system. On capacity, the meeting will look at six foundations: connectivity, compute, energy, data, skills and financing. The Secretary-General has proposed a needs-based global fund for AI capacity-building, with $3 billion in initial funding commitments over two to four years. Member States are also encouraged to nominate centres to the Global Network of Centres for Exchange and Cooperation on AI Capacity Building. On safety, the meeting will address nine areas, including risk assessment, testing, incident reporting, human oversight of AI agents and protection of children from AI-enabled exploitation and abuse.

The articles state that the General Assembly has set the course, through resolutions and mechanisms that the President's office and Member States have built. Resolution 78/265, adopted on 21 March 2024, was the Assembly's first resolution on artificial intelligence. The Global Digital Compact, adopted on 22 September 2024 with the Pact for the Future, includes an objective to enhance international governance of AI for the benefit of humanity. Resolution 79/325, adopted on 26 August 2025, established the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance. The articles present these as the mechanisms the Assembly created, and they do not name any other party as responsible for the meeting.

The articles say the President has framed the challenge as one in which benefits and risks are unevenly shared. In June 2025, 77 per cent of the world's co-location data centre capacity was in high-income countries, against 5 per cent in lower-middle-income countries. Around half of all Member States had a national AI strategy in place in 2025, and fewer than one in five least developed countries did. The President said, in his remarks at the close of the general debate on 28 September 2026, that AI had been raised by only five delegations four years earlier. The articles also note that 2.2 billion people remain offline and that AI-generated child sexual abuse material and deepfake-enabled sexual violence are disproportionately harming women and children.

The articles give the background of the first Global Dialogue, held in Geneva on 6 and 7 July 2026, which drew more than 3,000 participants from delegations of 163 countries. The Scientific Panel presented its Preliminary Report there, and the Co-Chairs of that Dialogue identified four areas of emerging convergence, including the view that no single government, company or institution can govern AI alone. The articles also state that the Scientific Panel has 40 members serving in their personal capacity for three years. Member States' views gathered at the meeting are to inform preparations for the second Global Dialogue, which the articles schedule for 3 and 4 May 2027 in New York.

The articles leave open what the meeting will decide, since its outcome is a summary of key messages rather than any binding commitment. They also do not say whether the proposed $3 billion global fund will be fully funded or when it will begin operating. The articles do not state how many speakers will address the meeting or how the President's summary will be weighed in the high-level review of the Global Digital Compact at the eighty-second session. It is also unclear from the articles how the Scientific Panel, the Global Dialogue and the Compact will be made to reinforce one another in practice.

Articles.Title: Responsible AI: A Transformation That Belongs to All | General Assembly of the United Nations - Welcome to the United Nations

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence in the Service of Human Dignity
stories.Summary:
Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas addresses the rapid spread of artificial intelligence, which La Civiltà Cattolica calls one of the most significant transformations of our time. The article, published on November 11, 2026, was written by Giovanni Cucci, SJ, and Aldo Giacchetti. It argues that AI is not merely a more powerful tool but a form of mediation that shapes how people perceive things, make decisions and relate to others. The authors say the question is first anthropological rather than technical, and that every new discovery carries an ambivalent nature. The article itself gives no figures, dates or places beyond the publication date and the encyclical's title.

It does not specify any new rules, requirements or changes to how AI is governed or deployed. Its central argument is that the debate depends on anthropological assumptions that usually remain implicit and must be brought to light. The authors frame the discussion around two categories that the encyclical stresses: the dignity of the human person and the significance of limits. The encyclical is attributed to Pope Leo XIV, and the authors quote it on the point that experiences of vulnerability, suffering and failure allow people to recognize the inviolable dignity of every person. The authors state that finitude is not simply a deficiency to be overcome but a condition within which freedom, responsibility and relationship take shape.

They present this interplay between dignity and limits as the basis for understanding the challenge AI poses. The article is attributed to the two named authors, and the paid-subscriber text carries no further statements from them on responsibility. The article does not report what other individuals, groups or institutions said in response to AI, and it does not identify who is affected beyond the general reference to human persons. Its tags name several figures and companies, including OpenAI, Sam Altman, ChatGPT, Character AI, Adam Raine and Sewell Garcia, but the visible text does not explain their roles in the argument.

Readers are told only that the full piece is reserved for paid subscribers. The visible text gives little further background, beyond noting that Giovanni Cucci is a member of the College of Writers of La Civiltà Cattolica and that Aldo Giacchetti teaches at the Faculty of Philosophy of the Pontifical Gregorian University. The page also lists a related article titled "Woman Unknown" and a related encyclical-themed article, "The Encyclical 'Magnifica Humanitas': The Digital Revolution and Humanity." The article does not state when Magnifica Humanitas was issued.

Beyond these links and the author biographies, the available text supplies no further context. The visible text does not say what follows from the article or whether further publications or responses are planned. It leaves open how the anthropological principles it describes would be applied to specific AI systems or policies. Readers can access the complete text only through a paid subscription, so the remaining arguments and any further facts cannot be assessed here.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence in the Service of Human Dignity

stories.Headline: Introducing usage-based pricing for Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming
stories.Summary:
Amazon Web Services has announced usage-based metering for Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming inference, which lets model providers report actual usage for the AWS Marketplace software charge. The announcement was published on the AWS Artificial Intelligence blog on November 11, 2026, at 06:00 UTC. Deepgram, a real-time speech AI company, is the launch partner for the capability and is bringing usage-based Speech-to-Text and Text-to-Speech billing to AWS Marketplace. The change builds on earlier work between Deepgram and AWS, including bidirectional streaming for real-time inference, AWS Identity and Access Management temporary delegation, and enhanced metrics. Customers continue to pay SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges while an endpoint is provisioned.

The new model adds a companion metadata WebSocket alongside the existing inference stream, and the model server opts in by returning the header X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Supported set to true. The metadata connection is opened at the default path /invocations-bidirectional-stream-metadata, which can be overridden with X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Invocation-Path. Both connections carry the same X-Amzn-SageMaker-Request-Id header so metering records can be matched to the active session. Each metering message is a JSON text frame containing exactly one record, with the Dimension set to inference.count and an integer ConsumedUnits value. Frames are limited to 512 bytes and one message per second per connection, and the optional ClientToken field supports idempotency with a maximum length of 64 characters.

The X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Required header defaults to false, so inference continues if the metadata connection fails, and setting it to true stops inference instead. The articles say AWS is responsible for the service and that the announcement was made by Amazon Web Services. The post presents usage-based metering as a way to align billing with how customers consume streaming workloads. It states that bidirectional streaming differs from request-response inference because a session can last from 30 seconds to 30 minutes and its final usage total is unknown until it ends.

The post recommends that providers discuss negotiated rates and fixed-price contracts through private offers with their AWS account or partner representative. It also says that the SageMaker Marketplace Onboarding Agent Skill includes starter templates for opt-in inference metering. Customers deploying real-time AI models for transcription, contact centers, voice agents, and captioning are affected, because the Marketplace software charge is now calculated from reported usage. Under the post's example, a 12-minute session metered per second of audio is reported as 720 units.

Model providers listing on AWS Marketplace are also affected, since they must define what one unit represents and report units as the session progresses. The article notes that AWS Marketplace prices real-time inference at one per-unit price, shown with up to three decimal places. The background given in the post is that AWS Marketplace software metering for SageMaker AI request-response inference reports a unit count in an HTTP response header, which works only when the billable quantity is known at response time. Bidirectional streaming does not fit that model because usage accumulates during a live session, and hourly pricing would charge customers during quiet periods.

The post says that transport delivery alone does not establish that usage has been billed, and that providers should validate reported units against AWS Marketplace reports and buyer charges. The articles leave open how the metering will be billed in cases that are not covered by the example, and they do not say when additional model providers beyond Deepgram will adopt the capability. The excerpt also cuts off partway through a failure-mode table covering malformed records, so the full handling of those cases is not available in the text provided. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Introducing usage-based pricing for Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming

stories.Headline: Dual-Branch Artificial Intelligence Enhances Forensic Sex Estimation from Adult Chest Radiographs
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Cairo University have developed a multimodal deep learning framework that estimates biological sex from adult chest radiographs by combining image analysis with manually annotated anatomical landmarks. The retrospective study was conducted through a collaboration among the university's Department of Forensic Medicine and Clinical Toxicology, Department of Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology, and Faculty of Computers and Artificial Intelligence. The team evaluated posteroanterior chest radiographs from 563 adult Egyptian patients imaged between August and December 2025. Across the external test cohort, the dual-branch model reached 83 percent overall accuracy, a loss of 0.55, and an area under the ROC curve of 0.8776. Adding structured landmark guidance raised classification accuracy to 90 percent, compared with 71 percent when the model worked without anatomical data.

Forensic sex estimation has traditionally relied on subjective visual assessments and metric evaluations of sexually dimorphic skeletal structures, including the pelvis, skull, clavicles, ribs, and scapulae. Manual assessments by experienced specialists are accurate but time-consuming and depend heavily on expert availability. Posteroanterior chest radiography is among the most frequently performed diagnostic examinations worldwide because it is low cost, quick to acquire, and widely available. Conventional deep learning models applied to these radiographs have mostly learned from image pixels alone, without explicit anatomical knowledge. The training data came from a publicly available chest radiograph repository gathered by the Radiology and Diagnostic Imaging Society of São Paulo and retrieved from Kaggle.

That Brazilian dataset covered adults aged 18 to 89, had a mean age of 50.65 years, and was 58 percent female and 42 percent male. The Brazilian dataset was split 80 percent for training and 20 percent for validation, and augmentation through zooming, rotation, brightness, and contrast changes expanded the training bank from 8,561 to 17,122 images. The independent test cohort comprised 563 Egyptian patients aged 18 to 89, with 324 females (57.5 percent) and 239 males (42.5 percent). The largest age group was 40 to 49 years, with 122 participants (21 percent), followed by 30 to 39 years with 112 participants (20 percent), while the 80 to 89 group had only 17 participants (3 percent). Portable radiographs, images not showing both lungs, and radiographs with bone trauma, fractures, or pathological bone disorders were excluded.

No Egyptian samples were used in training, and the test images received no manual annotations during testing. Images were converted from DICOM files into 3000 by 3000 pixel JPEGs and resized to 128 by 128 pixels before analysis. The researchers, led by the Cairo University team, reported that the anatomy branch accepted 45 numerical features derived from a landmark file in which a senior radiologist marked key skeletal points on a template radiograph. Each rib was described by four coordinate points plus a curve-control parameter, while scapular and clavicular points were also recorded, and left-side annotations were mirrored to form a symmetric template. The image branch used residual convolutional blocks, and features from both branches were merged and passed to a sigmoid output.

The model was trained with binary cross-entropy loss, the Adam optimizer at a learning rate of 0.001, and 20 epochs. For female patients the network reached a precision of 0.79, recall of 0.89, and F1-score of 0.84, while for males it reached precision of 0.82, recall of 0.68, and F1-score of 0.75. The false positive rate was 0.108 and the false negative rate was 0.318. The study's authors stated that the anatomical annotations produced a statistically significant improvement in discrimination.

With landmark guidance, 243 participants were correctly classified and 27 were misclassified, giving a 90 percent accuracy with a 95 percent confidence interval of 86.4 to 93.6 percent. Without landmarks, 209 cases were correct and 84 were wrong, giving 71 percent accuracy with a confidence interval of 66.2 to 76.5 percent. Accuracy was reported as stable at roughly 82 to 85 percent for those aged 18 to 59, but it fell to about 69 to 70 percent for those aged 60 to 79, while results for ages 80 to 89 were deemed statistically unreliable. The authors also reported that the study compared the approach with EfficientNetB0, which reached 52 percent accuracy, and ResNet50, which reached 44 percent accuracy under the same baseline conditions.

The authors noted that large-scale prior models trained on far bigger international cohorts focused their attention on breast shadows, the lower neck, and upper ribs, whereas their own model was validated on real-world clinical images. The article itself does not describe any regulatory response, independent comment, or planned clinical deployment. It also does not state when the findings will be published in a journal or whether the model will be made available to forensic practitioners. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Dual-Branch Artificial Intelligence Enhances Forensic Sex Estimation from Adult Chest Radiographs

stories.Headline: Citrus County Sheriff's Office using AI to help screen calls, save time for emer­gencies
stories.Summary:
Citrus County's Sheriff's Office has begun using artificial intelligence to screen 911 calls at its Emergency Operations Center in Lecanto, Florida. The technology was announced in a November 11, 2026 report by Calvin Lewis, and it lets dispatchers spend more of their time on people who need immediate help. Sheriff David Vincent described an AI operator that handles non-emergency calls so that 911 call takers can stay focused on emergencies. The center receives about 5,000 calls a week, and so far the system has handled about 60 percent of the agency's non-emergency calls. Some residents raised concerns after the sheriff's office announced the change on Facebook.

The system does not replace dispatchers, according to the sheriff, who said the goal is to free them for emergency work. Callers can ask to speak with a person at any point, and true emergencies still reach a human on 911. Vincent said staff watch the calls in real time, and he said there is always a human behind each call. He also said he expects residents will be pleased once the process is in place.

The article does not describe any formal review or changes in staffing that come with the program. Dr. Karni Chagal-Feferkorn, an assistant professor and AI expert at the University of South Florida's Bellini College of Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity and Computing, was quoted on the broader trend. She said more people and organizations are adopting AI, and she named replacement of trained workers as a leading concern. She added that agencies should keep some workers and officers able to handle such calls in case the systems are not available.

The article quotes her on prioritizing and addressing calls as a skill that depends on interacting with people. The article places the rollout within a wider shift toward AI in workplaces, and it reports the concerns as a reason for attention rather than a finding of harm. It does not say what happens next or whether the program will expand. Dispatcher Pontius is quoted describing how calls are answered when there may be an emergency, and the piece presents the tool as another way to manage incoming calls.

Articles.Title: Citrus County Sheriff's Office using AI to help screen calls, save time for emer­gencies

stories.Headline: Winneshiek County Approves Policy Outlining Employee Use of Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Winneshiek County, Iowa, has approved a policy that sets out how county employees may use artificial intelligence in their work, according to a Decorah News report published November 11, 2026. The policy divides information into three levels of risk and gives staff guidance on what they may and may not do at each level. It also approves certain uses of Microsoft Copilot, an AI assistant, for county work. Employees are required to check and verify any work that AI tools have generated before relying on it. The rules are meant to give staff clear limits as AI tools become more common in government offices.

Under the policy, the level of risk attached to a piece of information determines how carefully it may be handled with AI. Only the approved uses of Copilot are permitted, so other tools fall outside the policy's blessing. The verification requirement means that output from these tools is not treated as final until a person has reviewed it. The Decorah News article identifies the county as the body that approved the policy, but the excerpt available does not name the individual officials who drafted or voted for it. It does not include direct statements from county leaders explaining their reasoning.

The available text is limited mainly to the headline and summary points, so the specific wording of the policy and the rationale behind each risk level cannot be confirmed from this material. The article sits alongside other local coverage, including a report about a proposed expansion of a business park district intended to help fund future road work, though the excerpt does not connect that story to the AI policy. The available material does not say when the policy takes effect, how it will be enforced, or whether the county plans further review. Readers seeking those details would need the full Decorah News report or official county records.

Articles.Title: Winneshiek County Approves Policy Outlining Employee Use of Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Can A.I. Help Us Engage More Closely with Art? Some Museums Think So.
stories.Summary:
Several American and European museums are now using artificial intelligence to help visitors engage more closely with art, according to an Observer article published on November 11, 2026. The Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, launched a web-based companion called Ask Rosie when it reopened in June after a 15-month expansion project. Visitors photograph an artwork with the app, which offers information such as the artist's identity and then asks what the user wants to learn. The app adjusts its tone to match the visitor, shifting between academic language and casual phrasing during a conversation. Shayne Hart, the museum's chief digital officer, described how the prompts a visitor gives shape the information the app supplies.

Remuseum, a nonprofit first created within Crystal Bridges to promote innovation in American art museums, released a report titled "Five Ways that A.I. Can Humanize Museums." The report says museums most immediately use the technology to connect information on visitors, donors and members that is otherwise kept in separate data silos. It gives the example of a development officer who must move among a fundraising database, a collections database, a ticketing system and an email platform to assemble one supporter's picture. At the Toledo Museum of Art, the technology tracks where visitors move and linger in the galleries, along with the programs they attend and whether they are members or donors. Adam Levine, the museum's director, said this data will let staff create more personalized experiences, such as inviting frequent visitors of a gallery to a special curator lecture.

Stephen Reily, founding director of Remuseum, said that museum workers and the public already use A.I. extensively, and he argued that curators and policymakers should embrace the technology. Hart described Ask Rosie as designed to meet each guest wherever they are in their art journey. Levine said the museum's policies, safeguards and training mean it does not believe there is any marginal risk in using A.I. to deepen engagement with art. Grace Yao, founder of the San Francisco-area company Artlas, said the app asks visitors whether they are kids or adults, their primary language and where they come from. Yao also said that Artlas users' information is encrypted and not used or shared for anything else, adding the qualifier "not at this point."

Reily said traditional museum experiences were one size fits all, with brochures and wall text written in art historical terms for visitors with higher education levels.
