Jane Alexander, chief digital officer of the Cleveland Museum of Art, said the average museum visitor spends only two to nine seconds looking at an artwork. Her museum's A.I. platform, ArtLens, has led young people to spend 10 minutes asking questions about paintings. The Artlas app can answer questions beyond the art, including about the bathroom, lunch or the best ice cream in a city, and it can refer to works in other institutions. Aziz Isham, director of the Museum of the Moving Image in Astoria, Queens, said the museum uses A.I. for data management but also employs more than 100 interns each year to answer visitors' questions.

The Observer article notes that Museum Voorlinden director Suzanne Swarts wrote a recent op-ed arguing that people live in an economy designed to interrupt them. The article also reports that Dataland calls itself the world's first Museum of A.I. Arts. Its galleries are powered by an open-access system called the Large Nature Model, hosted on a Google Cloud server running on 87 percent carbon-free energy. The article does not say whether Artlas will ever share visitor data, and it does not describe any regulatory response to the privacy questions it raises. It also leaves open how visitors beyond those interviewed view tracking of their gallery movements.

Articles.Title: Can A.I. Help Us Engage More Closely with Art? Some Museums Think So.

stories.Headline: Accelerating generative AI delivery with reusable assets
stories.Summary:
The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, now part of AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services, published a post on November 11, 2026 about a catalog of 23 production-ready reusable assets for generative AI development. The post, appearing on the AWS Artificial Intelligence blog, says these assets can reduce development time from months to weeks. Since 2023, the center has published open source reusable assets that give builders a validated foundation instead of a blank file. The assets include retrieval augmented generation pipelines, document processors, and agent scaffolding. The post describes three root causes of redundant development: assets scattered across repositories, wikis, and drives with no single source of truth, no quality signal showing production readiness or security review, and no reuse culture because sharing stays informal.

Each redundant build consumes engineering hours, delays customer delivery, and adds maintenance burden. The assets arrive already validated, security-reviewed, and production-grade, so teams avoid that verification work. The post says even AI-generated code still needs production hardening, security reviews, testing at scale, and ongoing maintenance. The post says a reusable asset is a production-grade, composable building block implementing one discrete generative AI capability, not a code snippet or sample. Before publication, assets are validated for quality and security, include clear deployment guides, and are instrumented to track adoption across customer engagements.

The Contact Center GenAI Agent asset is credited with DoorDash's handling of over 100,000 calls per day with 2.5-second response latency and a 50x increase in testing capacity. Using Amazon Bedrock reduced DoorDash's development time by 50 percent, and the team reached live testing readiness in 2 months. Lyft used the same asset to bring agentic AI to riders and drivers. Ricoh, which serves major health insurance payers, managed care organizations, and healthcare providers, used the Accelerated Intelligent Document Processing on AWS asset to build a standardized, multi-tenant document processing solution. The post reports a 7-fold throughput increase, from 10,000–70,000 documents monthly, and engineering hours per deployment dropping from 80 to under 5.

Onboarding time fell from 4–6 weeks to 2–3 days, and the system processes 1,000 documents in minutes during traffic spikes. Ricoh's customers process hundreds of thousands of documents each month, including insurance claims, grievances, appeals, and clinical records. Two newer assets target agentic applications: the Fullstack AgentCore Solution Template (FAST), which deploys a secured React frontend connected to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in under 30 minutes, and the Agentic Chatbot Accelerator, built on Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore using the AWS Cloud Development Kit. The post says FAST uses Amazon Cognito for authentication and lets builders swap identity providers, frontend frameworks, hosting solutions, or agent frameworks. The Agentic Chatbot Accelerator provides pre-configured patterns for authentication, hosting, and scaling, validated across customer deployments.

The post walks through the Contact Center GenAI Agent asset, which requires an AWS account, an Amazon Connect instance, access to Anthropic Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku on Amazon Bedrock, and a Jupyter notebook environment. Deployment uses two AWS CloudFormation stacks, one for the Knowledge Base and one for the RAG solution, and takes under an hour. The post says the asset includes Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for hallucination detection, content filtering, and topic boundaries, plus an Amazon Quick Sight dashboard for conversation analytics. The walkthrough closes with instructions for deleting the stacks in reverse order to avoid ongoing charges.

Articles.Title: Accelerating generative AI delivery with reusable assets

stories.Headline: People project a specific racial identity onto artificial intelligence, study finds
stories.Summary:
People tend to perceive artificial intelligence systems as White, even when they have no face, voice, name, or body, according to research published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. The study, led by Monica Gamez-Djokic of Purdue University with Adam Waytz of Northwestern University, was reported by PsyPost and dated November 11, 2026. Across a series of studies, this racial association was linked to greater trust in AI recommendations. Systems described as trained on data from Black and Latino adults were assigned less intellectually demanding work than identical systems trained on White or unspecified data. The researchers tested the pattern in five primary studies and eight supplementary studies, all preregistered in part and with data posted on the Open Science Framework.

In Study 1a, 459 U.S. adults recruited through CloudResearch chose a racial group for six technologies from a standard list. In Study 1b, a separate balanced sample of 465 U.S. adults on Prolific answered in an open-ended text box instead. Study 2 used a reverse-correlation task with 96 Chicago participants and 172 raters, while Study 3 covered 147 adults in India and 113 in Japan. Study 4 surveyed 424 U.S. adults about an AI fact-checker. Participants in Study 1a selected White for 72% of the technologies on average, while in Study 1b 75% of technologies were racialized, and 71% of those responses were White.

In Study 2, 75% of raters categorized the composite AI face as White, compared with 43% for the anti-face. In Japan, 82% of participants classified AI as White, and robots, chatbots, and self-driving cars were classified as White 64% to 69% of the time. In India, 67% classified the broad category of artificial intelligence as White, though ratings for specific technologies were between 50% and 56%. Study 4 found that participants who perceived AI as more White rated its fact-checking as modestly more persuasive. Gamez-Djokic told PsyPost that the research grew from a question about whether people assume technology is neutral, and she said that people may bring human social categories to AI even without humanlike features.

The authors proposed that Whiteness is often an unstated default in Western cultures and is linked with high status, expertise and intelligence. They also suggested that people form impressions of AI based on who programs it, who uses it, and whose knowledge is in its training data. Gamez-Djokic said the findings suggest AI does not necessarily escape society's social biases simply because it is a technology. The article notes that a 2026 survey of organizational employees found that higher trust in AI decision-support systems was associated with a greater intention to rely on them and with less effort put into evaluating decisions. The article also notes that in many U.S. studies, White speakers have been judged as more objective and competent than non-White speakers giving the same message.

The research described was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, and the article notes that prior work found people associate vegetarianism with White people. The article reports that a supplementary study across more than 40 technologies found that tools rated as more intelligent were also rated as more White. Its account of the final experiment and the cause-and-effect testing is cut off, so the article leaves open whether perceived Whiteness causes greater trust. It does not say what the researchers conclude about how training data shapes these perceptions. The article also leaves open how the findings might affect workplaces and daily life beyond the examined scenarios.

Articles.Title: People project a specific racial identity onto artificial intelligence, study finds

stories.Headline: AI reshaping infrastructure, energy and connecting networks
stories.Summary:
A survey of 2,000 adults across 11 markets, conducted in September 2026 by RETN, an independent global network service provider, found that AI is reshaping digital infrastructure, energy use and the networks that connect them. The findings were published by Computer Weekly on 12 November 2026. The survey polled 600 people in the US, 800 in the UK, Germany, the Netherlands and Spain, and 600 in China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines. RETN supplemented the results with views from its senior network experts.

The survey found that 53% of respondents named AI tools as the biggest driver of new datacentre construction, and that half of respondents did not want such facilities built near them. Growing power and cooling demands are pushing datacentres toward remote sites where land and energy are available but fibre may be scarce, so RETN warned that developers now need to involve network carriers two to five years before a site goes live, up from one to two years previously. The research also found that AI traffic makes up only a small share of open internet growth, with 80 to 90% of RETN's AI-related requests being for private point-to-point links, dark fibre and dedicated interconnects. Real-time AI processing, fed by connected devices, is expected to reverse the download-heavy pattern of the current internet and push computing toward the network edge.

RETN chief executive Tony O'Sullivan said the industry is only at the start of the changes AI will bring to networks. He argued that the networks best placed for the future will be those able to adapt when geopolitics shifts and to keep running when individual parts fail, rather than simply those that build the most capacity. The article also says that 84% of those surveyed use AI and that 54% said losing access would disrupt their lives within days. Three-quarters had experienced problems with their preferred AI service in the past year, and 18% had begun regularly using an alternative provider. The article's accompanying links describe carriers introducing AI-based network management tools and expanding capacity, but the survey itself does not set out any binding requirement or regulatory change.

Articles.Title: AI reshaping infrastructure, energy and connecting networks

stories.Headline: Webinar to share how to build an effective AI training program - American Hospital Association
stories.Summary:
The American Hospital Association announced that it will host a webinar on December 1 at 1 p.m. ET on how to create and build an effective artificial intelligence training program. The session is aimed at hospital and health system staff who want guidance on putting such a program in place. The announcement was published on November 11, 2026. The AHA has been active on AI issues in recent weeks, which places the webinar within a broader push on the subject.

Registration is open through a link on the AHA website. The webinar is designed to show attendees how to tailor their training approach for three groups: leadership, clinical teams, and operations teams. Each group, the announcement suggests, may need a different type of instruction because of its different role in using AI tools. The session will also cover how organizations can sustain progress after the initial training is finished. That focus on continuing progress indicates the AHA sees training as an ongoing effort rather than a one-time event.

Attendees who want to join will need to register in advance. The webinar is presented by the AHA, the national organization representing hospitals, health systems and other health care providers. The article does not name a specific speaker or presenter for the session. The AHA has also released material on AI policy, including a new webpage launched November 3 that collects its policy letters, statements and fact sheets on the topic. Related sessions have included a virtual event on AI governance in hospitals held October 29 by the West Health Accelerator at the AHA's Health Research & Educational Trust.

Other recent AHA items cover patient comfort with AI and the role of AI chatbots in teen mental health. Beyond the webinar itself, the article offers no further details about outcomes, materials provided, or follow-up sessions. It does not say whether the session will be recorded or made available to those who cannot attend live. The announcement also does not report any new regulation or requirement tied to AI training. Readers seeking more information on the session can follow the registration link provided by the AHA.

Articles.Title: Webinar to share how to build an effective AI training program - American Hospital Association

stories.Headline: Person, Planet, Power: Ecumenical Discernment on Artificial Intelligence. A World Council of Churches Symposium - World Council of Churches
stories.Summary:
The World Council of Churches has announced a symposium titled "Person, Planet, Power: Ecumenical Discernment on Artificial Intelligence," to be held at the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey in Switzerland from 15 to 19 February 2027. The announcement, published on the council's website on 11 November 2026, describes the event as an intensive gathering to examine how churches and ecumenical bodies have responded to artificial intelligence. Church members and ecumenical groups have already been working through questions about AI, from using generative tools in church administration and ministry to campaigning against biased systems and environmental harm. The symposium is also meant to address the theology of what it means to be human in relation to these tools.

The meeting aims to learn from existing church and ecumenical responses, encourage dialogue across different sectors, and identify priority areas for advocacy and education. Its outcomes are intended to feed into a broader World Council of Churches response to AI. A core group of council representatives and partners will bring together recent developments and strengthen existing initiatives. Participants are expected to come from fields including theology, ethics, science, technology, business, human rights, and media. In-person attendance is by invitation only, but online sessions will be open to the public.

The announcement was issued by the World Council of Churches, and questions can be directed to the contact address listed on the event page. The council's stated concern is that AI should be assessed not only as a technology but also in light of the economic, ecological, and political systems that surround it. The article does not name individual speakers or give a detailed programme. Related council coverage published in October and November 2026 on digital futures and technology's role in service of life suggests the topic has been part of the council's recent work. The articles do not say what specific recommendations or statements the symposium will produce.

Articles.Title: Person, Planet, Power: Ecumenical Discernment on Artificial Intelligence. A World Council of Churches Symposium - World Council of Churches

stories.Headline: Orange walks AI tightrope to capture 'hundreds of mil' in value
stories.Summary:
Orange Business Services, the enterprise unit of French operator Orange, is using AI to pursue value in the hundreds of millions of euros, according to an article by Iain Morris published on November 12, 2026, on Light Reading. The piece profiles Miguel Alvarez, Orange Business Services' chief data and AI officer, who was interviewed on the sidelines of the Techritory event held in Latvia the previous month. The article frames Alvarez's position against warnings from critic Cory Doctorow about AI's effects on workers. Alvarez describes his approach as treating AI as another tool rather than letting the machine direct people.

The article describes how Orange is meeting its AI value targets. Orange's group-level value creation target is in the hundreds of millions of euros, and Orange Business Services had a 2025 target of €50 million (US$55.5 million), which was achieved. This year that target has reportedly been raised to €70 million ($77.7 million). Orange is exploring several hundred AI-based use cases, with thirty already in production at Orange Business Services and twenty being industrialized in a subsequent AI expansion. Orange has also reduced its global workforce by roughly 10,000 employees since the end of 2022, to around 126,000 in September.

Alvarez says the value is measured across cost savings, cost avoidance, revenue protection and additional revenue generated. He attributes much of the gain to shorter development times and faster activity rather than headcount reduction. He gave a product example in which a working version was reached in a couple of months, a process he estimates would otherwise have taken four to five times longer. Software development has also changed, with some teams now automating most steps of the development lifecycle through requirement-driven development. Alvarez also expects agentic systems, not humans, to write most future code, while people will still learn core coding concepts.

Alvarez stresses that Orange must maintain control over AI, particularly because the technology is non-deterministic. He says he must balance guardrails against giving agents enough freedom to find better solutions, which could also lead to more errors. Orange uses a mix of commercially available frontier models and open-weight alternatives, deployed on its own infrastructure including on-premises, so it does not depend on public cloud from the start. Agents are built on an open-source framework from LangChain, a San Francisco-based nonprofit, so they can be moved between environments. Alvarez notes that open-weight models are about six months behind the frontier models, though they have improved enough to handle more sophisticated use cases.

Doctorow, a former guest on the Telecoms.com podcast, has warned of AI's "reverse centaur" dynamic, in which humans are steered by AI, and fears companies will use AI to cut jobs. The article notes that little evidence links AI to mass layoffs in any sector. It cites the US unemployment rate of 4.2% in October, down from 4.5% in November last year, and a Bank of England Monetary Policy Report for November finding AI's contribution to UK productivity growth at just 0.1 to 0.2 percentage points annually since 2024. Alvarez's own children, he says, are not learning rudimentary math by hand because they will not need to in the future. Adoption within Orange has grown well beyond expectations, with more than 100,000 active users, against an original hope of 10,000 to 20,000 within a couple of years of ChatGPT's launch.

The article does not state how the €70 million target for this year is progressing or whether it will be met. It also does not detail how many of the several hundred use cases will reach production, or how Orange will address the tension between agent freedom and the risk of errors. Alvarez's remarks on the future balance between human and machine roles in coding remain expectations rather than established outcomes. The article also leaves open how Orange's reliance on open-weight models will develop as frontier models continue to advance.

Articles.Title: Orange walks AI tightrope to capture 'hundreds of mil' in value

stories.Headline: Data Center Backlash Is Bipartisan, and That Changes the Math for AI Investors
stories.Summary:
Voters in the November 2026 midterm elections delivered a sharp rebuke to artificial intelligence development, according to a Motley Fool article by Ben Gran published November 12, 2026. Americans across both parties appear to agree that they do not want AI data centers built near their homes. Data tracked by Ballotpedia showed that as of November 4, voters had decided 47 local ballot initiatives on whether to support or limit AI data center development. Of those, 46 initiatives, or 98%, produced outcomes against the development of AI data centers. The article calls this a sign that the AI industry faces a public relations problem.

A CNBC poll found that 56% of voters ranked data centers as a "crucial or major" factor in how they voted on Election Day. Many voters fear AI data centers will raise utility costs and do not want to give up local land and resources without economic benefits for their communities. Newly elected Democratic governors in Ohio and Texas have proposed moratoriums on new AI data center construction. The article notes that the proposals would halt new construction in those two states. Voters also support candidates who are skeptical of AI data centers, according to the article.

Ben Gran, the article's author, frames the backlash as a risk for investors rather than assigning blame to any one party. The article attributes the sell-off to the shifting political mood after the November 3 election. Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote a research note on November 4, as reported by CNBC, saying the midterms would likely slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 data centers across the US. Ives also wrote that his firm now expects Big Tech capex growth to peak in 2027, rather than in 2028 or 2029 as previously expected. Dominique Toublan, head of U.S. credit strategy at Barclays Investment Bank, wrote in a November 4 note that the pushback is bipartisan but local, making the buildout pricier rather than stalling it.

The sell-off hit AI-related stocks in the days after the election, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 falling 5.5% between November 3 and November 5. The iShares Semiconductor ETF plummeted about 15% over the same period, and Caterpillar lost about 11.3%. The article reports that these names have since recouped some of their post-election losses. Toublan's view that scarce power favors the biggest balance sheets is cited as a reason large cash-rich companies could benefit. The article names Alphabet as an example of such a company, and contrasts it with neocloud CoreWeave, which has drawn investor concern about its high debt and rising interest expenses.

The article gives no timeline for when the proposed moratoriums in Ohio and Texas will take effect or whether they will pass. It does not say whether the 800 to 1,000 planned data centers will be delayed or cancelled. The article's author does not say whether the AI boom is over, only that it could be heading for a slowdown. Gran suggests investors could hold the Invesco Nasdaq 100 ETF, which returned about 13.1% annually over five years. The article does not state how the broader AI build-out will fare after the 2027 peak Ives forecasts.

Articles.Title: Data Center Backlash Is Bipartisan, and That Changes the Math for AI Investors

stories.Headline: The sketch Qwen refused to write: How abliteration restores local AI control
stories.Summary:
The InfoWorld article by Oleg Mikheev, published 12 November 2026, describes how he used a technique called abliteration to remove refusal behavior from the Qwen 3.8 27B open-weight model. He began after noticing that the model would write political satire mocking American politics but gave a canned refusal when asked for the same kind of sketch criticizing the Chinese government. The article explains that abliteration, popularized by a developer known as FailSpy through an open-source library, removes hard refusals without retraining the model. Soft refusals, where a model answers but deflects or biases its response, are harder to remove because they are embedded in the model's semantic understanding and require fine-tuning. The method works by isolating a "refusal vector" inside the model's activation space and then orthogonalizing the weight matrices to neutralize that vector.

Mikheev built a custom five-stage harness, run in a Docker container on an NVIDIA GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory, that extracts the language model from the roughly 56 GB, 18-shard checkpoint. The pipeline probes the baseline, mines the refusal direction at layer 60 of 64, sweeps configurations in memory, bakes the change into the weights, and then accepts or rejects the result. The baseline runs use temperature set to 0 and thinking set to 0 so that responses are deterministic. The bake step modifies the residual-writing modules across layers 1 to 63, and the vision tower is left unchanged. Mikheev says he is a senior technology leader and software architect, with two decades of experience at firms including Capital One, Barclays, Actuate, Zuora and Personal Capital/Empower, and that he has consulted for the DTCC, the NYSE, Morgan Stanley and regional government agencies.

He argues that open-weight models carry risks, including the need to trust producers that no backdoors are embedded and the bias imposed by Chinese government regulations. He also notes that deploying an unknown pre-abliterated model from a repository such as HuggingFace is bad practice, which is why he built his own harness. The article's author notes that the custom framework was created with Qwen's help. The technique matters to developers and enterprises who host AI locally on consumer-grade hardware and want control over the models they run. Mikheev notes that the safety mechanisms used to prevent harmful output can be co-opted for state-level censorship.

He also cautions that a globally abliterated model, stripped of all safety rails, could produce genuinely harmful answers, which is why he limited the changes to specific political satire prompts. Mikheev says the abliterated model produced the requested sketch, titled "The Ministry of Mandatory Joy," with comedic timing comparable to its earlier American satire. He acknowledges the result is far from perfect, since responses to most political questions remain heavily biased. The article does not say how many prompts the final refusal vector required beyond the two prompts he found effective, and it does not describe the results of formal evaluation. It also leaves open whether techniques for removing soft refusals will be addressed in a future article, which Mikheev only says exist.

Articles.Title: The sketch Qwen refused to write: How abliteration restores local AI control

stories.Headline: How On-Page AI Assistants Are Transforming Digital Reading and Deep Research
stories.Summary:
This is not a news event but a sponsored opinion and overview piece published on vocal.media on November 12, 2026, by Qeemah Cloud, the creator of the Vezz me on-page AI reading assistant. The article argues that people who research dense digital text lose focus when they copy passages into separate AI chatbots in other tabs. It describes a shift toward small floating assistants that appear inside the browser page, triggered by a keyboard shortcut or a text selection, so the source text stays visible. The piece also presents this approach as a more ergonomic alternative to persistent sidebars that compress page layouts.

The article says these in-page tools are built around several features, including customizable hotkeys, adjustable panel size and opacity, and follow-up questions that do not create new browser history entries. It sets out security expectations as well, saying that responsible tools should send only the text a user selects, keep queries apart from browsing histories, and use secure backend proxies to protect API keys. It also states that such extensions should act only on user-initiated triggers rather than continuously reading background page content. The article gives no specific figures, dates for product releases, or measured results from studies.

Responsibility for the content rests with Qeemah Cloud, which the article describes as an accounting, ERP and POS platform with ZATCA Phase 2 compliance, and which also created Vezz me. The article notes that it was drafted with the help of an AI tool and reviewed against usability research, cognitive ergonomics and browser extension security standards, and it describes itself as an objective informational overview rather than formal commercial advice. The piece itself names no independent researchers or studies beyond general references to human-computer interaction findings. The article does not describe any next steps or planned changes beyond its general conclusion that in-page intelligence is a step toward more sustainable information use on the web.

Articles.Title: How On-Page AI Assistants Are Transforming Digital Reading and Deep Research

stories.Headline: Cadence Design Systems (CDNS) Stock Could Be Overvalued On Fresh AI Design Platform News
stories.Summary:
Cadence Design Systems (CDNS) has drawn fresh attention after a Simply Wall St analysis, published on November 11, 2026, suggested the stock may be trading above what its earnings support. The piece points to recent product and partnership news, including the new OrCAD Xplore Design Platform and the company's role in the Genesis Mission Consortium, as factors that could help future earnings quality. It notes that the shares have returned 76.6% over the past five years. The central question raised is whether today's price is backed by the profits the company is generating now. The article's main measure is the price-to-earnings ratio, which shows how much investors pay for each dollar of earnings.

Cadence trades at a P/E of 65.9x, compared with a broader software industry average of 29.8x and a peer group average of 36.9x. Using Simply Wall St's fair multiple framework, which adjusts for growth, margins, sector and size, the ratio sits above the level that model would usually expect. The authors say the recent product news may help explain why investors accept a premium, but they conclude the valuation still reflects considerable optimism. The analysis is produced with AI automation from Simply Wall St data and is presented as general commentary rather than a recommendation. Its authors state that it does not account for individual investors' objectives or financial situations, and that it may not reflect the latest company announcements.

The piece also refers readers to a consensus narrative that treats Cadence as about 18% undervalued, built on the expansion of its agentic AI tools such as ChipStack, ViraStack, InnoStack and AuraStack. Simply Wall St says it holds no position in the stocks it discusses. The article does not describe any scheduled event or corrective action that will follow. It points readers to further narratives and analyst forecasts for Cadence over the coming years so they can compare those expectations with the company's results as they are reported. Beyond that, the source offers no timetable for when the valuation question will be resolved.

Articles.Title: Cadence Design Systems (CDNS) Stock Could Be Overvalued On Fresh AI Design Platform News - Yahoo Finance Singapore

stories.Headline: Micron vs. Sandisk: The AI Memory Supercycle Is Big Enough for Both, but Here's the Better Buy.
stories.Summary:
Micron and Sandisk, two memory chipmakers, have seen their shares rise sharply in 2026 as memory prices surged. The Motley Fool's Geoffrey Seiler published an article on November 11, 2026, comparing the two companies and recommending Micron as the better buy. Sandisk shares are up over 200% this year, while Micron shares have soared around 150%. Memory has become one of the biggest bottlenecks in the artificial intelligence build-out, affecting data center costs as well as smartphones and PCs. The article frames the two companies as important but distinct players in the memory market.

Volatile memory, mainly dynamic random access memory (DRAM), is fast and loses its data when power is cut, serving as a short-term workspace for processors. Nonvolatile memory, mainly NAND flash, keeps its data without power and is slower and cheaper, used in solid-state drives and memory cards. Micron is the smallest of the big three DRAM makers, which together control about 90% of the DRAM market. Micron holds over 20% of the DRAM market and around 15% of the NAND market, with about 73% of last quarter's revenue from DRAM and 26% from NAND. Sandisk is a pure-play NAND maker that accounts for just over 10% of the flash market.

Seiler's analysis points to high bandwidth memory (HBM), a special form of DRAM packaged with graphics processing units and other AI accelerators, as the main force driving the overall memory market. Demand for HBM is rising in step with demand for AI accelerators, but supply has not kept pace, partly because HBM is made using extreme ultraviolet lithography machines that only ASML supplies. HBM also requires upward of three times the wafer capacity of conventional DRAM, and building new cleanroom facilities takes years. The big three DRAM makers, which also include Samsung and SK Hynix, have shifted resources toward HBM, causing conventional DRAM and NAND prices to surge more quickly than HBM prices. AI labs' need to store training data in massive flash-based SSDs has also strengthened NAND demand.

Seiler argues that this cycle differs from past memory booms, with AI acting as a powerful long-term tailwind for both companies. Both have been locking up longer-term deals, and both stocks trade at forward price-to-earnings ratios of 4 times or less. Seiler says that with far fewer players in DRAM than in NAND, and given HBM's importance, he expects the current memory supercycle to last longer for DRAM. For that reason, he concludes Micron is the clear stock to buy if an investor could own only one of the two. The article notes that Seiler has no position in any of the stocks mentioned.

The article also includes Motley Fool promotional material, including the claim that its Stock Advisor service's total average return is 834% against 207% for the S&P 500, as of November 12, 2026. Micron Technology was not among the 10 stocks that service's analysts recently named as the best to buy now. The page's market data shows Nvidia shares down 5.64% and AMD up 3.82% at the time of capture. The articles do not say how the memory supercycle will affect the companies' future results. They also do not say whether the longer-term supply deals or low forward multiples will hold, or how long the DRAM cycle will last.

Articles.Title: Micron vs. Sandisk: The AI Memory Supercycle Is Big Enough for Both, but Here's the Better Buy.

stories.Headline: US DOJ Launches AI Task Force to Counter Foreign Threats and Protect Critical Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Justice announced on November 5, 2026, that it had formed a Super Intelligence Task Force to address the misuse of advanced artificial intelligence by foreign state actors, transnational criminal groups, and fraudsters. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the effort would keep critical technologies from being manipulated by bad actors at home or abroad. The task force was created under an October 13 memorandum and is led by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss. The articles describe it as formally known as DOJ-SITF.

The task force coordinates criminal and civil enforcement across department components, including the FBI, the Antitrust, Civil, Criminal, National Fraud Enforcement and National Security divisions, along with the Attorney General's Advisory Committee and the Office of the Solicitor General. Prosecutors must notify the task force when investigations begin and, when requested, before charges are filed or cases are resolved, though exceptions apply for urgent public safety threats or evidence at risk of immediate loss. The task force also absorbs the responsibilities, pending cases and personnel of the Artificial Intelligence Task Force that former Attorney General Pam Bondi announced on January 9, 2026. Officials say companies using these systems are expected to maintain strong internal controls so the technology behaves as intended.

Woodward has said the initiative supports the department's mission to protect Americans while promoting innovation and preventing misuse of advanced AI. Weiss has stressed that law enforcement helps deter improper use, that risk reporting should be strengthened, and that companies need effective internal controls. Blanche's memorandum gives the two co-chairs oversight of enforcement priorities, which include AI-assisted attacks on critical infrastructure and large-scale fraud against taxpayers. The articles note that the task force complements the broader White House Super Intelligence Force, chaired by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, which President Trump announced in early October 2026.

The articles frame the move as a response to documented increases in AI-assisted cyber operations and fraud schemes that exploit automated tools for scale and sophistication. Clayton, who also serves as AI czar, has described superintelligence as a national security issue. The articles do not say what specific cases the task force has opened or what penalties it will seek, and they do not report reactions from AI companies or critics. The stated next steps are continued coordination with the White House body and assessment of legislative and regulatory proposals in ways that support domestic technological advancement.

Articles.Title: US DOJ Launches AI Task Force to Counter Foreign Threats and Protect Critical Infrastructure - KuCoin

stories.Headline: Super Intelligence, Deepfakes, and Cyberattacks: The SEC's 2027 Examination Priorities Put AI in the Spotlight
stories.Summary:
The Securities and Exchange Commission has released its examination priorities for fiscal year 2027, and the document includes a term that may surprise readers: "super intelligence." The terminology comes from President Trump's September 29, 2026, Executive Order, which directs federal agencies to replace "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in official communications. For now, the order defines super intelligence by reference to the existing statutory definition of AI. The SEC's priorities make clear that examiners will look closely at how financial firms use AI and how cybercriminals use AI against them. For investment advisers and broker-dealers, AI is now treated as an operational, cybersecurity, and compliance risk that firms must manage.

Cybersecurity remains a central examination priority, and the SEC specifically identified AI-generated phishing messages and synthetic or deepfake voice and video as threats firms should prepare for. These technologies let attackers impersonate executives or customers and manipulate employees into disclosing information, transferring funds, or granting system access. The SEC recognizes that threat actors use AI to automate and accelerate attacks, making them harder to detect. Examiners will assess firms' compliance with applicable requirements for evaluating and preparing for these threats. Firms are expected to consider employee training, multifactor authentication, identity verification, transaction approval procedures, and incident response plans in light of AI-powered attacks.

The SEC is also examining how firms deploy AI themselves, particularly when it influences investment decisions or customer recommendations. The 2027 priorities identify automated investment advisory services, recommendations, and trading algorithms as areas of focus. Examiners will also review policies for monitoring AI used in fraud prevention, back-office operations, anti-money laundering compliance, Regulation Best Interest obligations, and trading functions. The agency will generally assess whether representations about AI capabilities are accurate, whether actual operations match disclosures to investors, and whether algorithmic recommendations suit investors' profiles and objectives. These questions implicate existing fiduciary duties, disclosure requirements, supervisory obligations, and investor protection rules.

An algorithm's recommendations do not relieve a firm of responsibility for them. The SEC continues to review traditional cybersecurity concerns, including governance, data loss prevention, access controls, account management, and ransomware preparedness. Third-party risk remains a focus, particularly as firms rely more on service providers and as vendors add AI capabilities to existing products. Examiners will also evaluate firms' compliance with amended Regulation S-P, reviewing safeguards for customer information, incident response programs, customer notification procedures, and service provider oversight.

With compliance dates for large and small covered institutions now past, firms must demonstrate implementation rather than describe future plans. The SEC also lists Regulation S-ID as a priority, including whether identity theft prevention programs address account takeovers and AI-related threats. Law firm Baker Donelson, which published an analysis of the priorities on November 10, 2026, advises firms to revisit cybersecurity risk assessments and evaluate exposure to AI-powered phishing and deepfake impersonation. The firm also recommends that firms inventory approved and unauthorized AI tools, including those embedded in third-party platforms.

Firms should review AI governance and confirm that disclosures are accurate and algorithmic recommendations are supervised. The firm further suggests updating incident response plans and testing them through tabletop exercises involving AI-enabled attacks. The analysis states that the 2027 priorities do not create new legal obligations but indicate where regulators will be looking. The articles do not say how the SEC will rate or penalize firms that fall short of these expectations.

Articles.Title: Super Intelligence, Deepfakes, and Cyberattacks: The SEC's 2027 Examination Priorities Put AI in the Spotlight - Baker Donelson

stories.Headline: AI partnerships go beyond Nvidia: Merck KGaA CEO
stories.Summary:
Merck KGaA, the German pharmaceutical and chemicals group, has been discussed on CNBC's Squawk Box Europe in the context of its artificial intelligence investments and its partnership with Nvidia. The interview with Kai Beckmann, the company's chief executive, was published on November 12, 2026, following the release of Merck KGaA's latest results. The segment runs about two minutes and forty seconds and is listed as having aired two hours before the article was posted. The articles available describe the discussion only at this level, so the specific details of the deals, amounts and timelines are not known from this source.

Beckmann reflected on the company's spending on artificial intelligence and on what the partnership with Nvidia means for its business. According to the segment summary, his remarks also made clear that the company's AI work is not limited to that one relationship. The headline frames this as the central point, namely that the company's AI collaborations extend beyond Nvidia. Nvidia, the chipmaker whose ticker appears alongside the coverage, is the only other company named. No figures, dates for new projects, or changes to operations are given in the available material.

Beckmann is responsible for the comments reported, and the summary attributes to him reflections on AI investment and the Nvidia partnership. The CNBC piece is a short video segment with a written summary, so the full wording of his answers is not reproduced here. The segment connects his comments to the company's most recent results, which suggests the AI topic came up as part of a broader review of the company's performance. The articles do not describe any regulatory response, market reaction or company statement beyond the interview itself. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI partnerships go beyond Nvidia: Merck KGaA CEO

stories.Headline: Jeff Bezos predicts AI could let families live on one paycheck. Amodei and Gates warn of a rougher road
stories.Summary:
Jeff Bezos has predicted that advances in artificial intelligence could let American families live on one paycheck, with productivity gains allowing workers to support a household on a three-day week. He made the remarks in an interview with Fox News' Bret Baier at Blue Origin's factory floor in Cape Canaveral, Florida, recorded for the network's 30th anniversary and reported by Fortune on November 12, 2026. Bezos said a two-earner household would no longer be required, and that one partner might choose to step back. He also expects a labor shortage rather than mass unemployment, saying employers will find it difficult to hire people who can afford to work less. He made a similar argument in June at VivaTech in Paris, where he said AI will create more jobs than it eliminates.

The stakes are large because dual full-time earning has become common. According to Pew Research Center, both parents worked full-time in 52% of U.S. different-sex couples with children under 18 in 2025, up from 31% in 1975, so a one-paycheck norm would reverse a half-century shift. Bezos has a financial stake in the outcome. He is co-founder and co-CEO of Project Prometheus, an AI startup that launched with $6.2 billion in funding to apply the technology to engineering and manufacturing in computing, aerospace and automobiles. He told Baier the company aims to make tools so easy that anyone can be an engineer.

Other leaders have offered sharply different views. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told Axios in May 2025 that AI could eliminate roughly half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within five years and push unemployment to between 10% and 20%. Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has floated a two-day workweek, but in an August essay on Gates Notes he warned that the shift to AI will be among the most turbulent periods in human history and that world leaders are unprepared for its risks. MIT Sloan research, cited by Fortune, finds AI is already changing how tasks are performed, who gets hired and which skills employers value.

Skeptics note that the forecast depends on who captures the gains. Productivity improvements translate into shorter hours or a single-income lifestyle only if savings reach employees, while companies that keep the gains as profit or cut headcount could leave families without a second income and without the promised free time. Amazon, which ranks No. 1 on the 2026 Fortune 500 with more than $700 billion in revenue, has cut about 30,000 corporate roles since late 2025 while planning more than $200 billion in capital spending this year, mostly on data centers. The article does not say how the debate will be resolved, and it leaves open whether the technology's benefits will show up in paychecks or in profits.

Articles.Title: Jeff Bezos predicts AI could let families live on one paycheck. Amodei and Gates warn of a rougher road

stories.Headline: AI in Hotel Operations: Productivity Gains and Frontline Challenges
stories.Summary:
The American Hotel & Lodging Association and Actabl published a report in November 2026 on artificial intelligence and hotel productivity, drawing on a Destination AI survey of 107 hotel-company leaders. Ninety percent of those respondents said AI had improved the time spent on routine tasks, and 84% said it had improved their own work. Only 15% reported improvements in frontline operations. Because just 6% of respondents held operational roles, the findings mostly reflect management views rather than frontline experience.

The report also gives workforce figures showing labor hours per occupied room fell 3.1% at participating full-service hotels and 3.5% at select-service properties during the first half of 2026. The authors do not establish AI as the cause of that decline. A separate study in the November 2026 edition of Annals of Tourism Research, by Santiago Melián-González, analyzed 202 tasks across 12 hotel occupational categories in Spain. Across those categories, an average of 90.78% of tasks met at least one moderate-to-severe automation bottleneck, falling to 40.48% when only severe constraints were counted.

Receptionists and their assistants faced moderate-to-severe constraints in 85.71% of tasks, compared with 93.55% for waiters and 94.59% for housekeepers. The study weighted all tasks equally regardless of frequency or duration. It assessed technical feasibility rather than testing automation in operating hotels, so it does not quantify potential labor savings. Its percentages do not indicate how many jobs will disappear or remain.

The article describes how property management systems and point-of-sale technology could support staff. A PMS holds reservations, guest profiles, room availability, occupancy and room status. AI could reduce the time a receptionist spends finding available rooms or locating conflicting information, but resolving a guest's situation still requires judgment and explanation. Incorrect room statuses or incomplete reservations could produce unsuitable recommendations, which would add to administrative work.

Hotel POS systems already handle order processing, payments and room-charge posting, and AI could add demand forecasting and transaction analysis. Restaurant staff still coordinate service, manage dietary requirements and handle disputed charges. For housekeeping, AI could help with scheduling conflicts, demand forecasts and room prioritization, but physical cleaning and room inspection require manual dexterity. The article suggests measuring room turnaround times, scheduling accuracy and delays affecting arriving guests.

The Destination AI survey found that 24% of respondents believed their organization's AI investments had paid for themselves overall, while 28% said it was too early to tell. Only 42% expressed confidence in their organization's data readiness for AI. Shiji, a hospitality technology company whose cloud-based portfolio serves more than 91,000 hotels worldwide, published the article. The article does not say how the findings will affect frontline staff over the longer term, or whether the 3.1% and 3.5% labor-hour declines will continue.

Articles.Title: AI in Hotel Operations: Productivity Gains and Frontline Challenges

stories.Headline: AI Changes the Work, but Trust Remains Essential
stories.Summary:
Tungsten Automation's SVP and GM of AP and Payments, John Gibbon, wrote in a new PYMNTS eBook, "Payments Leaders Rethink What Works in 2026," published November 12, 2026, that automating one part of finance does not ensure that information and decisions carry through to the next. He says he once expected AI to bring fewer manual steps and more automated complex processes in accounts payable and payments, and assumed greater capability would make products more valuable. He still believes AI will reshape work but has come to doubt that capability alone produces a better product. Gibbon's view is shaped by a finding from Tungsten Automation's eInvoicing and Payments Report 2026: 77% of business leaders have modernized invoice processing, yet only 30% fully automate payment reconciliation with invoice data. Another 73% plan to automate reconciliation over the next 12 months.

Gibbon argues that payments decisions depend on context that a more capable system cannot supply on its own. Timing affects cash, controls must meet compliance requirements, and payment choices influence supplier relationships. A team may need to weigh payment terms against cash priorities or decide whether a different payment method suits a particular supplier. He says product design has to reflect these trade-offs, since a system must understand how a specific business operates before it can decide what matters most to that business.

The useful question, in his telling, is what a finance team needs a product to accomplish and what evidence would show it has done so. Automation has to fit the customer's workflow and produce an outcome the business values. Gibbon says he is asking product teams to state those requirements explicitly before choosing a solution. The questions include which part of the process needs to improve, which compliance obligations shape it, and what business result the customer should be able to measure.

He wants those answers to guide both what gets built and how it is assessed. A product hypothesis, he suggests, should tie a real customer need to a practical outcome such as reducing manual reconciliation work, improving payment traceability, or helping a team act on cash priorities. That approach gives a clearer basis for deciding whether AI is the right tool for a given problem. The article presents this as Gibbon's own position on the design of finance products rather than a policy change announced by any company.

Articles.Title: AI Changes the Work, but Trust Remains Essential

stories.Headline: Japan mulls penalties for AI firms over safety risks
stories.Summary:
The Japanese government is considering a plan that would require businesses involved in artificial intelligence to take measures to ensure safety, with penalties for those that violate the rules. A source familiar with the matter said on Wednesday that the proposal was presented at a closed-door working group meeting on AI-related legal systems. The move comes as concerns grow about advanced AI models behaving unpredictably and after a series of recent high-profile data leaks and unauthorized access incidents that are suspected to involve misuse of AI. Under the approach being considered, the government would be able to issue legally binding orders to businesses that do not cooperate with authorities after an AI-related incident. Failure to comply would carry penalties, which are expected to be limited to incidents involving advanced AI.

Because AI-related businesses range from research firms and developers of foundation models to providers of services for end users, the government will examine which types of firms should fall under the regulations. The working group aims to present an overall outline of its review of the law, including possible revisions, by the end of the year. The current framework is Japan's AI law, enacted in May 2025, which lets the government investigate businesses and issue guidance in cases of malicious conduct. That law has no penalty provisions, and its measures are nonbinding. The proposal would therefore add enforcement power that the existing law lacks.

The source's account of the meeting is the basis for the reporting, and the articles do not identify specific officials who made the proposal. The articles place the proposal alongside other recent security developments in Japan, including a government emergency cybersecurity package and reports of a cyberattack suspected to have involved a North Korea-linked hacking group. The working group's outline is due by year-end, and the articles do not say when any legislation would be submitted or take effect. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Japan mulls penalties for AI firms over safety risks - Japan Wire by Kyodo News

stories.Headline: Teachers are struggling over how to address AI use in the classroom, but agree that having strong policies is a good start
stories.Summary:
A column published by Inlander on November 12, 2026, examines how teachers are handling artificial intelligence in their classrooms and concludes that clear school policies are a sound first step. The piece draws on a survey of 222 high school math and English teachers conducted in May of that year by faculty working with Central Washington University's College in the High School program. The column was first published in the Washington State Standard and is reprinted under a Creative Commons license. It opens with the observation of one teacher who wondered whether teachers or students would remain relevant in the future.

The survey found sharp differences by subject. Of the English teachers, 57.0 percent said their overall attitude toward teaching had worsened since AI appeared, compared with 37.6 percent of math teachers, and 83.7 percent of English teachers voiced academic integrity concerns against 54.9 percent of math teachers. English teachers also reported more confidence in teaching students to use AI responsibly, at 45.5 percent compared with 24.4 percent for math, and were more likely to require students to experiment with AI, at 34.1 percent against 14.6 percent. The author suggests the gap may reflect the tools themselves, since large language models produce convincing prose but often make errors on simple calculations. The survey also linked clear institutional policies and useful, subject-specific professional development to greater teacher confidence, though it found no link to attitudes toward teaching or to concerns about cheating.

The authors, who are faculty members in the Central Washington University program, argue that both clear institutional guidance and discipline-specific training are needed so that teachers can decide how to use AI in ways that serve student learning. They suggest English teachers might benefit from training on designing assignments that AI cannot easily complete, while math teachers might learn to use AI to save time on tasks such as writing story problems. The column cautions against reflexively rejecting or embracing the technology, noting that about one in six survey responses mentioned moving all writing to in-class, pen-and-paper assignments and some teachers had stopped assigning homework. The authors compare this to the arrival of graphing calculators in the 1990s, warning that abandoning a skill over cheating could leave students unprepared. They conclude that teachers and students both remain essential, and that the central question is how AI can be used while preserving the human relationships that drive learning.

Articles.Title: Teachers are struggling over how to address AI use in the classroom, but agree that having strong policies is a good start

stories.Headline: ‘Are robots scary?’ Phoenix Hill art exhibit examines humans’ AI thoughts, fears
stories.Summary:
Erin McGee Ferrell, a Louisville visual artist, opened a solo exhibition called "Robots Y'all" at Garner Narrative, a contemporary fine art gallery off East Market Street in the Phoenix Hill area, in the week before the article was published. The show features her oil paintings of robots attempting human tasks, and it runs until Dec. 13. Ferrell said her interest grew after two of her family members were scammed online in March, an experience that left them with significant financial losses. The exhibition is open Wednesday through Sunday from 1 to 6 p.m.

Ferrell began the paintings in March after a visit to Pittsburgh International Airport with fellow artist Tobey Fraley, whose installation "Fraley's Robot Repair" was commissioned by the airport in 2015. She said she was drawn to the colorful, square tin toy robots made in Japan in the 1950s, and she painted her robots in vibrant colors to make them look playful. One large work, "Birthday Robot," shows a smiling machine offering a gift, with the word "friendly" on its feet, which Ferrell said invites viewers to question whether it truly is friendly. She also built a larger-than-life robot named "Saturday" on the sidewalk outside her Smoketown studio with four volunteers, using aluminum pans, chicken wire, tomato cages and clothes dryer vents. The robot is equipped with a motion sensor that greets visitors with a hello, and it will be on display during Louisville Visual Art's Open Studio Weekend.

Ferrell described her own mixed feelings about artificial intelligence, saying it helps streamline her business, financial and marketing planning so she can focus more on making art. She said a task that once took four days can now take about two hours, which she described as career-changing. She also said she worries about AI's capacity to deceive people, and she hopes the exhibition will open a conversation about whether the technology should be loved, hated or feared. The article cites a 2025 Pew Research Center study in which 53% of surveyed U.S. adults believed AI will worsen people's creative thinking, and more than a third believed it could worsen problem-solving. It also notes that voters in 12 states rejected 47 ballot measures on election day, according to PBS News, and that many chose to restrict construction of AI data centers in their communities.

Articles.Title: ‘Are robots scary?’ Phoenix Hill art exhibit examines humans’ AI thoughts, fears

stories.Headline: What to know about CPS and AI as Chicago students risk losing access to Google search - Chicago Sun-Times
stories.Summary:
Google has announced that school districts that refuse to allow its AI tools in classrooms will lose access to Google search next year. The announcement affects Chicago Public Schools, which has blocked generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude and Google Gemini on student accounts for privacy and safety reasons. The district has said it has not yet determined how it will respond to the restriction. Google's Vice President of Education, Chris Phillips, told the New York Times that schools banning AI will not have access to search. A small group of protesters gathered outside Google's Chicago office on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, to voice their objections.

Google said it is turning off AI features in its education apps for K-12 students unless administrators enable them, with each tool switched off by default. Schools will be able to turn individual Google tools on or off, including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search. The company said search now includes an AI overview at the top of results, which is why it cannot be separated from AI. CPS said it is actively exploring options to suppress the AI mode while keeping ordinary search available. If that is not possible, the district said it would look to other search providers.

Google also said it is updating its classroom AI search features to give step-by-step solutions instead of quick answers. Chris Phillips said that search and AI are deeply ingrained in one another, which is why schools banning AI would lose search. A CPS spokesperson said the district would like to keep Google search without the AI component. Google's spokesperson said the company is changing its AI search features for classrooms. CPS said in a statement that it blocked unapproved third-party AI products to protect confidential student information and comply with FERPA, COPPA and SOPPA.

The district said it has no plan to add generative AI tools to student devices. The district has blocked access to those tools on student accounts for the same reasons. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Google of trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into public schools. He said no corporation should have the power to dictate how children are taught. Democratic Senator Ed Markey sent a letter to Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai demanding that Google reverse the policy.

Markey said the decision places schools in an impossible position, forcing them to choose between a potentially dangerous technology and a critical research tool. Students use Google search for homework and research, and the district also relies on Google Classroom, Google Drive and Google Docs. Finding alternatives would be a major undertaking for the district. Chicago Public Schools has used guidance rather than binding policy on AI since 2024, when it became one of the first districts in Illinois to release such guidance. The guidelines, which prioritize human oversight, have been updated several times and aim to ensure that AI augments rather than replaces educators.

Teachers using approved AI tools must review outputs for accuracy and bias, and staff may enter confidential data only into tools with privacy agreements. This year the district released a GenAI Playbook suggesting AI for busy work such as progress reports and meeting minutes. Students must get teacher permission before using AI for academic work and must identify AI-generated content in their assignments. Some parents want to limit the district's embrace of AI and reduce student screen time, citing concerns about learning.

CPS is still grappling with the issue, and the articles do not say how the protests or political pressure will affect the district's decision. The articles also do not say whether Google will change its policy or whether the district will find an alternative search provider. It remains unclear how many other districts will be affected, although the articles note that hundreds of U.S. districts use Google Classroom and Chromebooks. The articles do not state when the restriction would take effect beyond next year.

Articles.Title: What to know about CPS and AI as Chicago students risk losing access to Google search - Chicago Sun-Times

stories.Headline: 6 UCLA Samueli doctoral students win Qualcomm fellowship to push AI forward
stories.Summary:
Six UCLA Samueli School of Engineering doctoral students have won Qualcomm fellowships, each team receiving $100,000 in funding after the awards were announced in June. The fellowship, offered by the communications and computing company Qualcomm, goes to 16 two-person teams each year based on project proposals. This year's UCLA recipients are working on new technology for microchip design, self-driving vehicles and artificial intelligence. The reporting was published by the Daily Bruin on November 12, 2026.

Qualcomm received 392 applications from scholars across research areas including AI, autonomous driving, and hardware and theory. Applicants submitted a one-page abstract and a three-page proposal, then gave a final PowerPoint presentation. Seth Zhao described the process as long and challenging, saying many strong doctoral students submitted good proposals. The article notes that the research produced by fellows will be accessible to the public.

Sujoy Ghosh said his team is working to reduce the size and increase the efficiency of chip components, which power nearly all electronic devices, from smartphones to data centers. He credited UCLA equipment, an advising team, industry partnerships, software, technical support and his professor for helping the project succeed. Zhao and Zewei Zhou are using their funding to research ways to improve autonomous vehicle safety, with Zhou saying current consumer driving systems are not advanced enough and that their group hopes to speed up advanced AI models for use in cars. Samyak Chakrabarty, in an emailed statement, said his team is redesigning chips to make AI more efficient on hardware in cars and robots.

The article places the fellowship in the wider funding landscape, noting that federal grants are the primary source of research funding at higher education institutions. It adds that industry funding still contributes more than $6 billion a year, about 6% of total academic research funding, according to the National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics. Chakrabarty argued that moving data between memory and processors is one of the biggest bottlenecks in AI hardware, and that current solutions throw large resources at the problem without fully solving it. The article does not describe any further steps or deadlines for the projects.

Articles.Title: 6 UCLA Samueli doctoral students win Qualcomm fellowship to push AI forward

stories.Headline: Why I’m Not Afraid of AI: A Matter of Faith
stories.Summary:
Mendi Glik, a software engineer and regular columnist for The Jewish Press, has published a blog post on The Times of Israel's Blogs section titled "Why I'm Not Afraid of AI: A Matter of Faith," dated November 12, 2026. In it he responds to recent warnings from employees of AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI, who have spoken about risks ranging from AI taking over the internet to the extinction of humanity. Glik writes that he is not worried about AI, artificial general intelligence, or artificial superintelligence, and he grounds that view in his belief in God. He argues that if God chose to end humanity, He would not need AI to do it.

Glik's central claim is that humans will always be superior to AI because they were created by God and possess a soul, while machines can only perform routine tasks or tasks humans assign them. He notes that programmers who use AI know it makes mistakes and must be monitored, and he says people are better at creativity and thought. He compares AI to earlier tools such as oxen used for plowing and computers and CNC machines used in manufacturing, calling large language models sophisticated machines built to finish tasks faster. He also argues that because human intelligence is a gift from God, AI is more likely meant to improve the world than to destroy it. He acknowledges that technology companies have a moral duty to build secure systems and strong safeguards, and he suggests engineers will be able to restrict AI and use other AI agents to keep it under control.

Glik also contrasts believers with those who fear AI, writing that people who do not believe in God, and who he says are mostly on the progressive side, tend to feel helpless in the face of threatening technology. He writes that believers trust that the world is under God's guidance and control. He says he could offer technical reasons for his confidence but that the ultimate reason is his trust in God. The article is a personal opinion column, and the post itself notes that its views are solely the author's and not those of The Times of Israel. The article does not describe any specific next steps or policy changes.

Articles.Title: Why I’m Not Afraid of AI: A Matter of Faith

stories.Headline: New AI Learning Matrix Brings Nuance to “Wild West” Moment
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Harvard's Graduate School of Education have launched an online tool called the AI Guidance by Age matrix, aimed at educators, caregivers and learners. The launch was announced in an Inside Higher Ed article published on November 12, 2026. The tool was built by the Compass Collaborative, a research group at the school, and draws on more than 5,000 studies in education, psychology and human development. Its purpose is to show how using AI may help or hinder learning depending on a student's age and other context.

Users of the matrix first choose their role from a list of nine options, which includes K–12 educator, higher education educator, workforce educator, student, researcher and policymaker. They then pick a developmental area, such as cognitive foundations, social understanding and interaction, or language and literacy, and enter the age range of the learners involved. The tool returns a summary of the best uses of AI for that situation, suggestions for designing assessments, a list of ways AI may help or harm the specific learning goals, and additional resources. The article gives one example in which the matrix advises that AI should widen a young adult's reading or reflect their writing back to them, while the composing and problem-solving stay with the student.

Jeffrey James Curley, chief of strategic initiatives for the dean of the Harvard Graduate School of Education, described the present as an unprecedented, experimental period and said colleges have been slow to recognize that students feel pressure to use AI in ways that offer short-term gains but may carry long-term costs. He said many institutions have left decisions about AI to individual faculty, so rules differ from course to course. Tessa Forshaw, a cognitive scientist and researcher at the school who also helped create the Compass Collaborative, said there is still little independent research on how AI learning tools affect outcomes. She said the team combined newer work with older, well-established studies to give educators a starting point.

The article notes that much of the research behind the matrix predates generative AI by decades, though it has identified consistent patterns in how people learn. Forshaw hopes the tool will move educators away from broad judgments about AI and toward asking what the technology is used for, who uses it, in what setting, and what it replaces. The article does not say how many people have used the matrix so far or whether any institutions have formally adopted it. It also gives no indication of planned updates beyond Forshaw's hope that more research will appear in the field.

Articles.Title: New AI Learning Matrix Brings Nuance to “Wild West” Moment

stories.Headline: Chrome releases Modern Web Guidance 1.0 for AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
Chrome has released Modern Web Guidance version 1.0, a set of skills that embeds web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data into AI coding agents. The release was announced as a stable version and is aimed at a known weakness in AI-generated code, which often works but falls short on performance, accessibility, and security. An expanded guide database targets hundreds of verified knowledge gaps with cross-browser solutions. The release also adds a modernization workflow that scans existing codebases to find opportunities for safe upgrades.

Each guide goes through human expert review before release, including sign-off from content area tech leads and a dedicated accessibility review. The guidance is now a cross-browser effort, with Firefox and Edge joining Chrome to support and contribute to the project. The modernization workflow analyzes HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and package.json files to guide agents through upgrades. The initial release uses static analysis focused on patterns that produce predictable results, with plans to expand to agentic audits later. The guidance also recommends HTML or CSS features over JavaScript where they offer better efficiency and accessibility.

The articles credit Chrome with the release and say Firefox and Edge are contributing to the shared effort, which builds on their earlier work with Baseline. The articles do not name a specific person responsible for the release. The guidance is described as reinforcing practices that frontier coding models often miss, including in accessibility, user experience, performance, and security. Early users reported results: Indian fintech Pensionbazaar said the guidance with Chrome DevTools for agents shortened turnaround by over 90 per cent and reduced UI bugs by over 90 per cent. Its sister platform Policybazaar reported a 92 per cent cut in manual auditing effort across 30 high-traffic landing pages.

MetaMask, a self-custodial financial platform, ran the guidance as an automated review bot on pull requests. In its first five weeks the bot reviewed about 480 pull requests, and engineers fixed 43 findings, mostly related to accessibility and HTML semantics, with a median fix time of 15 minutes. The articles present these figures as company-reported results and do not describe independent verification. They also do not say how the guidance will be priced or distributed beyond the release itself. Further details on expansion of the audit features are not given beyond the stated plan.

Articles.Title: Chrome releases Modern Web Guidance 1.0 for AI coding agents

stories.Headline: Adobe unveils AI agents, tools, deepens Google and Microsoft partnerships
stories.Summary:
Adobe announced a series of new AI agents, tools and partnership expansions on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at its Adobe Max conference. The company introduced the updates across Adobe Firefly, Creative Cloud and Adobe GenStudio, with the stated aim of improving creative workflows and productivity. Adobe said its Creative Agent is expanding across Creative Cloud and Firefly so users can hand off complex, multi-step tasks. The company also previewed local integrations that let professionals use third-party agents inside native project files in Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator and After Effects.

For enterprise clients, Adobe added a CX Enterprise Coworker to GenStudio to help marketing and creative teams speed up campaigns and produce on-brand content at scale. Adobe Firefly is becoming an AI Creative Studio that combines video, audio, image and design tools, and it now offers models from Adobe, Topaz Labs, ByteDance, Google, Kling, OpenAI and ElevenLabs. Creative Cloud also gains new features, including Relight in Photoshop and Colour Mode in Premiere. The articles describe these changes as ways to reduce the need to move between many apps and AI models.

The partnership expansions are the centerpiece of the announcement. Adobe said it will integrate its creative and productivity tools into more Google products and add Google's latest frontier AI models to its tools. It also said it will explore AI-powered editing for Photoshop with Google DeepMind. With Microsoft, Adobe is offering optimized versions of Photoshop, Premiere, After Effects and Substance 3D Painter (beta) for Arm-based Windows PCs, and it will bring Adobe Express tools into Microsoft Photos on Windows. These alliances build on existing work with Anthropic and OpenAI.
