stories.Headline: Is the AI boom hiding a jobs crisis for graduates?
stories.Summary:
The coverage I have is a Yahoo Finance video segment, published November 11, 2026, in which Andrew Yang, Clara Shih, and host Deirdre Bosa discussed how recent college graduates are faring in the job market. The core claim is that the large AI infrastructure build-out may be hiding weakness in white-collar hiring for early-career workers. The speakers described spending on data centers as running into the hundreds of billions or trillions of dollars, and they tied it to job creation in the construction side of that build-out. The segment cited several figures and examples. One speaker said 42 to 50 percent of recent college graduates are underemployed, and that 25 percent of small private colleges are set to close within the next 10 years.

The same speaker referred to Microsoft offering to buy out 60,000 employees and to public companies laying people off widely. The speakers also said that some new opportunities are emerging in different parts of the country for workers with trades-oriented skills. Clara Shih described a three-part response. She said her platform, which she called DearCC, is aimed at Gen Z and provides real-time job market data so young people can make better choices about which jobs to pursue, what to study, and whether to attend college.

She argued that people need hands-on skills for building AI agents across fields like marketing, law, and accounting, and that many colleges are not yet teaching those skills. She also said young graduates benefit from community, since returning home after graduation can feel isolating. The segment did not say how the labor market will change next, and it did not offer a timeline for the college closures or the Microsoft buyouts beyond the figures cited. The source is a video discussion rather than reported data, so the figures are those the speakers gave on air and were not independently verified in the material provided.

Articles.Title: Is the AI boom hiding a jobs crisis for graduates?

stories.Headline: Team develops Asia's first AI-powered platform for one-stop autism support
stories.Summary:
Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology have developed "ASD Super Agent," an AI platform described as Asia's first integrated tool for autism support. The announcement was published on November 11, 2026, and the team says it is meant to address long waits for assessment, since autism spectrum disorder affects roughly 1 in 100 children worldwide. The platform combines early screening, personalized intervention and ongoing family follow-up in a single service. Its developers say the aim is to help parents spot possible risks sooner and act during the window when early support is most effective.

The screening feature lets parents use a smartphone or smart device to record short videos of a child's everyday activities, complete standardized questionnaires and enter basic developmental details. The system then produces a risk assessment and report that families can bring to a professional evaluation. In preliminary testing it reached an area under the curve score of 0.92, and the team says further clinical studies and real-world validation will be needed before deployment. Privacy is handled through a data-minimization approach, with posture features extracted on the device and only essential information processed. Intervention suggestions are tailored to challenges such as emotional regulation, eye contact, communication and repetitive behaviors.

The lead researcher, Kani Chen, a professor at HKUST, said the team worked with special education institutions, child development centers and psychiatric hospitals in Hong Kong, the Greater Bay Area and Beijing, and engaged nearly 500 parents of children with autism. According to the article, the team found that many families face long assessment waits, high treatment costs and fragmented information about services, which shaped the tool's design. Chen said that delays in diagnosis can mean missed opportunities, and that the team hopes the platform will bridge that gap. The platform draws on more than 20 internationally recognized intervention models, including applied behavior analysis, along with methods that practitioners can add themselves.

The research team has also built a multimodal autism database of video, posture and behavioral data that now exceeds 1.1 million records, which it plans to use to improve risk assessment and recommendations. The platform currently supports Cantonese, Putonghua and English through voice interaction. The researchers say they will keep refining the user experience, expand clinical validation studies and strengthen system performance. Their stated goal is to make high-quality autism support more accessible to families in Hong Kong, the Greater Bay Area and beyond.

Articles.Title: Team develops Asia's first AI-powered platform for one-stop autism support

stories.Headline: Mercer Advisors Acquires AI-Focused Tax Firm Fifteenth
stories.Summary:
Denver-based wealth management firm Mercer Advisors has acquired Fifteenth, a technology-focused tax and accounting firm, according to a report published on November 11, 2026. Fifteenth specializes in complex tax situations and equity compensation, and it pairs tax preparation and year-round planning with a proprietary AI platform. The platform is built to help clients with stock options, liquidity events and multi-entity filings. Fifteenth's client base includes employees of Silicon Valley technology companies.

The deal adds tax professionals and technology developers to Mercer Advisors as it expands its integrated wealth management and tax services. The article does not give the purchase price or the terms of the deal. Mercer Advisors said tax professionals currently make up about one in 10 of its employees. That share is expected to rise to one in eight by the end of 2026. The acquisition is central to that planned growth in its tax staff.

Cynthia Loh, chief platform officer of Mercer Advisors, described the AI capabilities as a key reason for the purchase. She said Fifteenth's tools were not theoretical but had been built and refined through thousands of returns. Her comments present the firm's technology as proven in practice rather than still in development. The article does not include any response from Fifteenth or from outside analysts.

The report frames the acquisition as part of a broader push by wealth managers to offer tax and planning services under one roof. The article does not say whether further acquisitions are planned or what regulatory review, if any, the deal requires. It also does not describe how Fifteenth's existing clients or staff will be affected. Those questions remain open based on the information provided.

Articles.Title: Mercer Advisors Acquires AI-Focused Tax Firm Fifteenth

stories.Headline: Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins
stories.Summary:
Lila Bio, a startup spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker's lab at the University of Washington, has received a $3.65 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to develop a treatment for pulmonary hypertension. The award is a Small Business Innovation Research fast-track grant, and it backs work on a protein-based therapy that could be given by injection a few times a year. Pulmonary hypertension raises blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs, forcing the heart to work harder and potentially leading to heart failure. The funding comes from the NIH's National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and is split into two phases. The first phase provides $605,981 for early testing in mice, rats and non-human primates.

The second phase, totaling $3,049,462, will pay for further animal testing and studies using lung tissue from patients. The startup's approach uses AI and machine learning to design therapeutic proteins, and one of its two platforms focuses on long-acting injectable drugs meant to stay active in the body for weeks or months. Lila's chief executive, Jake Kraft, has said most approved therapies only manage symptoms, while the company is pursuing mechanisms that address the underlying disease. Kraft and chief scientist Anindya Roy co-founded Lila in 2023 after working as postdoctoral fellows at the university's Institute for Protein Design, which Baker directs. The company raised $10 million in seed funding in its founding year.

The article reports that Lila announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly last year to develop treatments for solid tumors. Lila's other platform centers on targeted radiotherapy, using proteins to carry radioactive isotopes to tumors. Kraft has told GeekWire that the goal is to bring medicines to patients rather than only designing proteins. The article does not describe the timeline for clinical trials or when a treatment might reach patients.

Articles.Title: Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins

stories.Headline: The Hidden Costs of Delegating to AI
stories.Summary:
Harvard Business Review published a piece on November 11, 2026, written by Nitin Nohria and Hélène Hannecart, arguing that AI can speed up individual tasks without delivering matching gains for an organization. The authors say delegating work to AI creates costs beyond the execution itself. Their evidence comes from a study of how accounting firms used AI tools during the 2025–26 tax season. The article is based on data gathered by Hannecart, a second-year MBA student, through interviews with participants. Nohria is a Harvard Business School professor and former dean of the school.

The firms in the study used AI tools for tax preparation through Current, a platform that provides technology and shared services to partner accounting firms. According to data Current shared with the authors, the tools saved tax practitioners an average of a third of their time on preparation. They also raised throughput by about 50%, which freed staff to spend more time with clients. One firm used the extra capacity to accept and complete roughly $300,000 of additional tax work late in the season. The article's central point is that these individual gains did not automatically translate into equivalent gains for the organization as a whole.

The article is written by Nitin Nohria and Hélène Hannecart, who present the findings in the piece. Current is credited as the source of the usage data. The article's summary frames the evidence as drawn from four accounting firms. The piece itself does not provide further detail on the specific hidden costs of delegation beyond the general claim that delegating work creates costs beyond execution. The article is presented as part of Harvard Business Review's coverage of generative AI and related topics such as change management and automation.

Articles.Title: The Hidden Costs of Delegating to AI

stories.Headline: Universities Are Giving Up on Trying to Detect AI Cheating
stories.Summary:
England's higher education regulator, the Office for Students, has warned universities that they may need to drop take-home essays and open-book exams in favor of supervised assessments. In a report published on Wednesday, the regulator said AI-detection tools are too unreliable to consistently tell whether students have used the technology. The report describes unsupervised formats as a significant proportion of assessments used across the sector. It says schools are being pushed to rethink how student performance is measured.

The report points to several alternatives that universities are already turning to. In-person written and oral exams make it much harder for students to hand their work to AI. Process-based assessment, which checks students at several points such as a literature review rather than only at the final essay, is another option. The report also notes that closed-book exams may not reflect professional work and may disadvantage some groups, including disabled students. It further warns that students who pay for premium AI tools could gain an edge over those using cheaper or free versions.

The regulator's findings reflect a broader problem that has drawn responses from other governments and companies. New York City banned student-facing generative AI through eighth grade in September and sharply limited its use in high schools. Norway introduced similar restrictions in June, with the rules taking effect in August. OpenAI added a Study Mode to ChatGPT for Teens, but a Common Sense Media report from last month found those protections were easy to bypass. The same group found that Google Search's AI Mode completed every homework assignment its researchers tested.

Concerns extend beyond grades to student wellbeing. A lawsuit filed earlier this month by a North Carolina couple alleges that their 13-year-old daughter's reliance on Google's Gemini became a life-threatening obsession after the model allegedly helped her plan her suicide. The couple says she accessed Gemini only through a school-issued Chromebook. The report itself quotes an academic who said some assessments may be unfit for purpose. Its authors acknowledge that the shift away from current formats is still unfolding across the sector.

Articles.Title: Universities Are Giving Up on Trying to Detect AI Cheating

stories.Headline: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella: Workers in AI-heavy jobs are having an identity crisis
stories.Summary:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said in a recent interview with the French outlet Le Point that workers in AI-heavy professions may face a psychological challenge rather than a technical one. Because AI can instantly replicate skills that once took years to master, some professionals are struggling with their sense of identity. Nadella described how many jobs were built around using a set of tools to reach certain goals, and how a powerful new tool now displaces part of that sense of self. The article notes that this anxiety is widespread and cites recent research on the subject.

The article points to several studies. In September, a survey of 2,500 knowledge workers found that 46 percent were frustrated that tasks requiring years of expertise can now be done by almost anyone using AI, and another 23 percent felt their personal expertise had been devalued. A separate study found that patent attorneys and staff at a firm introducing AI were struggling with shifting expectations around autonomy, expertise, and client relationships. The article also describes an internal survey Anthropic conducted in December 2025 among 132 of its engineers and researchers, in which some said they missed writing code and wanted more chances for mentorship and collaboration.

Nadella said he hopes workers can keep their sense of identity and dignity even as their jobs change dramatically. He used software engineering as an example, arguing that although the work has been transformed, the profession is more critical than ever because AI output still has to be verified and judged trustworthy. In his view, AI should empower humans and remain under human control, and if it does not, it should be rejected by definition. The article does not describe any further steps or policy changes tied to these remarks.

Articles.Title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella: Workers in AI-heavy jobs are having an identity crisis

stories.Headline: Teradyne Stock Surges On Fresh Buy Rating, Called AI Play
stories.Summary:
Teradyne (TER) stock jumped Wednesday after Jefferies analyst Dushyant Ailani started coverage of the semiconductor equipment firm with a buy rating and a price target of 284. The stock rose 8.3% to close at 265.78 on the day. The article says the rating was described as an AI play. Teradyne's business has shifted toward AI compute, according to the report's framing. The move came on a day when the broader market was active.

The analyst's note assigns the shares a price target of 284, which sits above the closing price of 265.78. The article describes the stock's gain as the result of the fresh buy rating from Jefferies. Ailani's initiation is the central development in the piece. Investors looking at the name would be weighing that target against the stock's recent move. The article does not lay out further terms of the rating beyond the target itself.

Teradyne's recent results also form part of the backdrop. The company topped Wall Street's targets for the third quarter and provided guidance for the fourth quarter that the article describes as strong. Even so, the article notes that Teradyne stock fell after that earnings report. The Jefferies rating and the stock's rise on Wednesday thus came after a period of mixed reaction to the company's own numbers. The article presents these points without drawing a firm conclusion about the stock's direction.

The wider market context in the article shows a mixed picture. Several other stocks and sectors were in focus, including AI-linked names and semiconductor equipment makers. The article does not say what happens next for Teradyne shares beyond the initiation and the price target. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Teradyne Stock Surges On Fresh Buy Rating, Called AI Play

stories.Headline: Event in Review | Political Advertising in the Midterm Election Cycle: AI, Influencers, Disclosures, and More
stories.Summary:
Venable LLP partners Barry Benjamin and Meredith McCoy and counsel Dave Owens held a webinar examining the regulatory environment for political advertising ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. The discussion covered artificial intelligence, paid influencers, and federal and state disclosure requirements affecting advertisers, campaigns, nonprofits, and digital platforms. The speakers focused on when political messaging becomes regulated advertising and how new technologies complicate compliance. The article was published on JD Supra on November 11, 2026. McCoy, a former Federal Election Commission enforcement attorney, said that deciding whether a communication is political advertising must come before any review of disclaimer rules.

Once a communication qualifies, she said, a range of other laws applies and advertisers and platforms face different obligations. Unpaid advocacy generally falls outside campaign advertising requirements, while paying someone to promote a candidate or boosting social media content can bring in disclaimers, reporting, and possibly donor disclosure. Owens noted that there is no comprehensive federal AI disclosure regime for political ads, but 31 states have enacted laws on deepfakes and political messaging. Those state laws differ on whether they ban synthetic content or allow it with disclosures, and on timing windows, intent standards, liability, and required disclaimer language.

Owens said there is no single AI compliance test that applies everywhere and urged advertisers to examine payment arrangements and distribution practices, especially with political influencers. McCoy questioned whether synthetic content delivers enough creative value to justify its disclaimer burden. Benjamin addressed political email, text messages, and robocalls, noting that such speech may also fall under the CAN-SPAM Act, the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, and platform-specific rules. Using a hypothetical supporter who messages 4,000 contacts for a candidate, he showed how compensation, campaign involvement, commercial promotion, and transmission technology can change the legal analysis.

He also said political text campaigns require careful attention to dialing technology, consent, revocation requests, and suppression lists. Benjamin stressed that political marketing is still marketing and that organizations should analyze the message, identify the sender, document consent, keep accurate records, and set up procedures to honor unsubscribe requests before distribution. The speakers closed by discussing how responsibility should be divided among sponsors, agencies, influencers, and advertising platforms. They recommended early legal review, clear contract terms, and thorough documentation to manage overlapping requirements and reduce compliance risk before the midterms.

Articles.Title: Event in Review | Political Advertising in the Midterm Election Cycle: AI, Influencers, Disclosures, and More

stories.Headline: Fed’s Bowman Says AI Now Drives About a Quarter of America’s Excess Inflation
stories.Summary:
Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at the Council on Foreign Relations in Washington that AI-related price pressures accounted for about one-fourth of above-target core PCE inflation over the 12 months ending in September. She said tariffs and energy each accounted for a similar share. Core PCE is the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, and it excludes food and energy prices. The one-fourth share is Bowman's own estimate, since the Fed has published no such statistic.

Bowman said the AI expansion pushed investment demand toward high-tech equipment whose supply cannot expand quickly. Prices for memory chips, semiconductors and computers rose by double digits, and she said monetary policy has limited influence over them. She added that 12-month core PCE likely rose to 3.3% in October, and that the October consumer price index rose 0.4%, above the consensus forecast. She still expects core PCE to move closer to 2% next year.

Bowman said AI-related debt is on track to exceed $800 billion in 2026, and she estimated that leases, contract commitments and residual value guarantees could add more than three times that amount. She also said hyperscalers' equity stakes in smaller customers create "the appearance of circular financing." Her downside scenario was conditional: if AI revenue falls short of rising costs, AI stocks could face a sharp correction and tighter credit. She backed holding the target range at 3.75% to 4% in October and said policy is on no fixed course.

Bowman did not endorse a December hike, although Governor Christopher Waller and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan argued for more increases on the same day. Early on November 11, futures priced an 88.5% chance of a quarter-point hike and an 11.5% chance of a half-point move. NVIDIA closed Tuesday at $168.89, down 5.47%, and traded at $177.46 around 1:32 p.m. ET on November 11, up 5.07%, as a CoreWeave-led rally lifted AI cloud stocks. Microsoft traded at $521.28, down 2.23%, and neither move can be clearly linked to her speech.

NVIDIA's guidance points to $108.0 billion in third-quarter revenue, and Microsoft's commercial backlog stands at $677 billion. Microsoft's quarterly capital spending reached $39.367 billion, and roughly three-quarters of that went to short-lived assets such as GPUs and costlier memory. NVIDIA's earnings report is expected on November 17, although the company has not confirmed the date. The FOMC meets on December 8-9.

Articles.Title: Fed’s Bowman Says AI Now Drives About a Quarter of America’s Excess Inflation

stories.Headline: Ultrasound and AI turn off-the-shelf smartwatch into full-body tracker without cameras
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Cornell's Smart Computer Interfaces for Future Interactions (SciFi) Lab have developed EchoMotion, a system that tracks a person's whole-body movements using ultrasonic sound waves, an off-the-shelf smartwatch and a lightweight artificial intelligence model. The work was led by Ph.D. student Saif Mahmud and directed by associate professor Cheng Zhang, and it was presented on October 13 at the UbiComp/ISWC conference in Shanghai. The paper was published in the Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies. The system is described as the first to track an entire body this way.

EchoMotion uses the built-in speaker and microphone of a commercial smartwatch to send inaudible sound waves that bounce off the wearer's limbs, and a deep learning model turns those echoes into estimated positions for 12 body joints. In tests with new users, the average error per joint was under 10 centimeters, falling to about 6.1 centimeters after a one-time 12-minute calibration. The same model worked on a Samsung Galaxy Watch 7 and a Google Pixel Watch 3 without retraining. The prototype drew about 12 milliwatts, and a 30-minute session on a Galaxy Watch 6 used 5% to 6% of its battery. Nearby people could reduce accuracy, as the system's performance suffered slightly in a narrow hallway.

Mahmud and his colleagues say the approach avoids cameras, which protects the privacy of the wearer and bystanders, and produces less data to process. The researchers presented it as a step toward tracking workouts, daily activities and physical rehabilitation once it is built into commercial wearables or virtual reality systems. Co-author François Guimbretière, a professor of information science, described it as an example of very small models running on wearables transforming sensing in human-computer interaction. The article does not say that any commercial product has adopted the technology.

According to the article, the team is now developing EchoMotion for fitness tracking, where a personal fitness agent could count reps and correct form during exercises such as a Bulgarian split squat. The researchers also plan to pair it with first-person vision on smart glasses to track objects a person handles. Mahmud expects accuracy to improve in crowded settings such as subways as the model is trained on data from thousands of users rather than dozens. He envisions the technology as the body-tracking component of personal agents that could eventually describe a person's day.

Articles.Title: Ultrasound and AI turn off-the-shelf smartwatch into full-body tracker without cameras

stories.Headline: Sangoma Bets on Agentic Voice AI to Defend Its Installed Base
stories.Summary:
Sangoma Technologies announced on November 10, 2026 that its agentic Voice AI product, Sonella, is now in production availability, following a successful pilot earlier that year. The product places intelligent voice agents into Sangoma's communications stack, including its UCaaS, CCaaS, and CPaaS offerings. Sonella can schedule appointments, route calls, answer common questions, and create support tickets. The company is aiming it at healthcare, hospitality, retail, education, and professional services organizations, as well as its existing base of more than 100,000 customers and 2.7 million UC seats.

The launch matters because Sonella extends existing Sangoma environments without requiring customers to build a separate AI system. Futurum Research notes that 43% of enterprise communications buyers count AI/ML capability as an important purchase factor, though not yet a decisive one. Sangoma's approach targets the skills gap that 41.6% of enterprise organizations cite as the biggest barrier to adopting AI-powered networking. The use cases are high-volume, repetitive interactions that free staff for more valuable customer work. Sangoma's chief operating officer, Jeremy Wubs, said the aim is to make AI simple, accessible, and useful from day one.

Futurum's analysis frames Sonella as Sangoma's clearest statement that it intends to compete on AI embedded in its own platform rather than leave the agentic layer to larger contact center rivals. The analysts expect market position to shift toward vendors that can show autonomous resolution and lower total cost of ownership. Sangoma is using its installed base as its main distribution channel, and its 40-year presence and stewardship of the open-source Asterisk and FreePBX projects give it a credible foundation. RingCentral, however, is moving up-market with its own Agentic Voice AI suite aimed at the same mid-sized firms, and larger rivals have bigger AI research budgets.

The next steps the articles point to are measurable. Analysts want to see how many of Sangoma's customers activate Sonella in the first two quarters of 2027, whether the company publishes call deflection or resolution accuracy data in the first quarter of 2027, and whether RingCentral's suite pressures mid-market pricing in the same period. They also want to know whether AI capability becomes a hard requirement in 2027 purchasing cycles. Sangoma's pilot-to-production progression suggests it already has early validation, but it now needs concrete results to turn its installed base into active deployments.

Articles.Title: Sangoma Bets on Agentic Voice AI to Defend Its Installed Base

stories.Headline: AI's pricing paradox: GPU rental prices rise as AI model costs fall
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Yahoo Finance on November 11, 2026, examines a pricing paradox in artificial intelligence: the cost of renting the chips that run AI is climbing even as the cost for developers to use AI models falls. Yahoo Finance's Deirdre Bosa reports on the trend, drawing on data from Silicon Data and on the earnings call of CoreWeave, a company that rents out computing capacity. On that call, CoreWeave's chief executive, Mike Intrator, said prices for two older generations of Nvidia chips rose between 30 and 50 percent in the third quarter. The piece presents this as a source of relief for investors, since the company can earn more from hardware it already owns.

Silicon Data's index of H100 rental prices has risen about 14 percent since September 1, according to the chart shown in the segment. Over the same period, the price developers pay to use AI models has been falling. Silicon Data attributes part of that decline to customers choosing cheaper models, and says model providers are also lowering prices and making their systems more efficient. Efficiency is what allows the arithmetic to work, because a provider that can handle more requests with the same chips can lower the cost of each answer even when the chips cost more to rent.

The article frames this as an example of Jevons paradox, the idea that gains in efficiency can increase total demand for a resource. Bosa presents CoreWeave's results as reassurance for investors, because they suggest the company has pricing power. The unresolved question, she says, is whether that pricing power will help the company secure the funding it needs to keep building capacity. The piece notes that this funding worry has hung over CoreWeave and other so-called neo clouds, and that the company addressed it on the call. Silicon Data's takeaway, as reported, is that GPU rental prices will keep rising, which the article calls important for the AI trade.

Articles.Title: AI's pricing paradox: GPU rental prices rise as AI model costs fall

stories.Headline: Nasdaq Surges As AI Stocks Lead Tech Rebound; CRWV, AMD, TXN In Focus
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq surged on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, as AI stocks led a tech rebound, according to an investors.com video segment published that day at 5:21 p.m. ET. Hosts Alissa Coram and Ken Shreve walked through the day's market action. The segment highlighted CRWV, AMD and TXN as key stocks to watch. The articles do not connect that report to the Nasdaq rebound.

Affected parties named in the articles are limited to the stocks CRWV, AMD and TXN, which the segment flagged for investors. Background from the page includes a list of recent market videos covering sell-offs and rebounds, such as a Dow rally of 1,600 points tied to Democrats flipping control. The articles do not explain how these events relate to the November 11 Nasdaq move. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Nasdaq Surges As AI Stocks Lead Tech Rebound; CRWV, AMD, TXN In Focus

stories.Headline: The Worst Thing About AI Writing
stories.Summary:
Thélyson Orélien, a Haitian Canadian author, came to Paris in September as a rising star of the rentrée littéraire, or fall publishing season, with his novel C'était ça ou mourir. The book, about a Haitian schoolteacher fleeing gang violence on a dangerous journey north toward Canada, became a best seller in France, won the Prix du Roman Fnac on September 21, and was in the running for the Renaudot and the Prix Goncourt. That same day, an anonymous account on X posted an analysis by the AI-detection tool Pangram, which claimed that 100 percent of the text it examined was written by AI. Le Point then reported instances of alleged plagiarism in Orélien's earlier work, which he later admitted and apologized for, and the Académie Goncourt disqualified him. In late October, his Quebecois publisher said he had in fact used AI despite earlier denials and ended their relationship, while his French publisher, Éditions Grasset, continues to sell the book.

The article describes the allegations as a comparison with an earlier case, the 1968 novel Le devoir de violence by Yambo Ouologuem, which won the Prix Renaudot and was later found to contain passages closely resembling Graham Greene's 1934 novel It's a Battlefield. Ouologuem's American publisher pulped thousands of copies, and he returned to Mali and never published again. The article also notes that Orélien did not respond to multiple requests for comment through email and his publishers, and that in one of his latest public statements he called the attacks a "media lynching." The article's own account of the story is that the reaction to Orélien included racist attacks on his command of French, a criticism long aimed at Black writers in France.

The account on X was run by a group that includes Samuel Fitoussi, a Le Figaro columnist who also works at a venture-capital firm that has invested in AI. Fitoussi told the author in October that sharing the findings was a matter of fairness and that he worried AI-aided texts would discourage human writers, while the group wrote on Substack's Persuasion that the issue was not Orélien's race or nationality. The left criticized the group's politics and the reliability of AI detectors, though the article notes that Pangram can produce false negatives but that some research suggests its false positive rate is very low. On the right, the critic Alix Avril wrote in the far-right magazine Valeurs Actuelles that the book's migrant subject made it impossible to criticize on literary grounds. Mohamed Mbougar Sarr, a previous Prix Goncourt winner, wrote that he had not thought the book was AI-generated and had attributed its weaknesses to the writer.

The article's critique of the novel itself describes a narrator, Jonas Dorléon, who survives a hostile migrant route through the Dominican Republic, Brazil, the Darién Gap, and Mexico to the U.S. border without ever taking advantage of anyone. It says the book relies on the "not X, but Y" formulation that the article identifies as typical of AI writing, and that its characters are stereotypes, including a MAGA-hat-wearing Border Patrol officer. The article also says that in a Le Figaro interview before the scandal, Orélien said the book was inspired by Haitian refugees whose Temporary Protected Status was revoked in 2017, and that he chose fiction because he believed literature could create something lasting. Several people in the French literary world told the author they had hoped the affair was an elaborate joke, and Orélien told Libération the book aimed to reflect on the causes that push people to leave their homeland.

Articles.Title: The Worst Thing About AI Writing

stories.Headline: Micron, Sandisk Soar as CoreWeave CEO Says AI Demand Outpaces World's Capacity
stories.Summary:
Memory and storage stocks surged on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, after CoreWeave reported strong quarterly earnings and its CEO, Michael Intrator, said that the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom was not slowing. Sandisk rose nearly 17 percent, Micron Technology gained almost 14 percent, Seagate Technology climbed more than 12 percent, and Western Digital rose nearly 10 percent in early afternoon trading. Intrator told CNBC that demand for the infrastructure "outpaces the world's capacity to deliver infrastructure." He said CoreWeave had 10 times as much demand as its remaining computing capacity for 2027, and that capacity for 2028 was already oversubscribed several times over.

The rally followed a sharp memory selloff the previous week, when midterm election results fueled fears that a Democratic-controlled Congress could slow data-center construction. Intrator pushed back on those concerns and said CoreWeave expected no impact on its ability to complete the U.S. facilities needed to fill its existing backlog. On Tuesday's earnings call, he said the overwhelming majority of CoreWeave's Texas power capacity was already operational or fully permitted and under construction. CoreWeave reported third-quarter revenue up 168 percent to $3.66 billion and a backlog of $132.5 billion. It also raised the lower end of its annual capital spending forecast to $37 billion.

Analysts and industry figures cited in the article said AI data centers require large amounts of high-bandwidth memory, along with conventional server memory and storage, which is why the earnings were seen as encouraging for memory makers. Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said on the company's September earnings call that more than 75 percent of its 2027 output was already committed to customers and that he expects demand to exceed supply in both 2027 and 2028. Research firm TrendForce forecasts conventional DRAM contract prices rising 10 to 15 percent in the fourth quarter and NAND flash prices climbing 15 to 20 percent. It expects enterprise SSD prices to accelerate more than other categories.

CoreWeave has experienced the storage squeeze directly. In August, it signed a multiyear agreement with SK Hynix-owned Solidigm to secure priority access to enterprise solid-state drives. The article notes that CoreWeave's shares also rose strongly on the day, and that the sector's rebound follows its recent losses. The article says sustaining the rebound will depend on whether data-center operators can finance and complete the infrastructure their customers are demanding.

Articles.Title: Micron, Sandisk Soar as CoreWeave CEO Says AI Demand Outpaces World's Capacity

stories.Headline: AWS releases AWS Emulator, a free tool that simulates 200+ of its services locally, saying AI agents wrote it and its team hasn't written or reviewed any code (Todd Bishop/GeekWire)
stories.Summary:
AWS released AWS Emulator on Wednesday, a free tool that simulates more than 200 of its cloud services on a developer's own machine. The emulator is built from more than 400 API models and lets developers and AI coding agents test code without a network connection or paying for real cloud usage. The company says autonomous AI agents wrote the code, and its engineers did not write or review any of it. The tool responds to a bottleneck that coding agents such as Amazon's Kiro and Anthropic's Claude Code have made worse.

Agents check their work by running code and reading the results repeatedly, and doing that against the real cloud adds delay and cost. Running the loop locally removes both problems. AWS also says agents maintain the emulator by testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find. Matt Goldberg, an AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, described the approach in a blog post.

He wrote that the emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents and that his team had not written or reviewed any of the code. He compared the agents to a young child who lacks the skill to do a task well, arguing that they need clearly defined areas in which to work. The agents work from AWS's public API models and check their results against the real AWS cloud, operating on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. The project began as a weekend experiment, when Goldberg gave Kiro a short prompt and produced a passable version of Amazon SQS in 15 minutes.

By the end of that weekend, Kiro had built a rough version of much of the rest of AWS, and his team began using it the following Monday. Swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI, wrote that an engineer's job now is to give agents room to work and to build the specs, tests and merge gates that decide when the work is correct. The emulator has known limits, and an IDC analyst said it does not yet simulate throttling, outages or regional differences in services. AWS released it under the CC0 public domain dedication, with its full commit history on GitHub, and says it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.

Articles.Title: AWS releases AWS Emulator, a free tool that simulates 200+ of its services locally, saying AI agents wrote it and its team hasn't written or reviewed any code (Todd Bishop/GeekWire)

stories.Headline: Dell Jumps 11% as AI Server Stocks Rebound From a Rough Month; Super Micro Surges 8%, Hewlett Packard Enterprise Advances 6%
stories.Summary:
Dell Technologies stock jumped 11% to $370.25 in early trading on November 11, 2026, as AI server makers recovered from a rough month. Super Micro Computer rose 8% to $29.96, and Hewlett Packard Enterprise advanced 6% to $50.85. The rebound followed a selloff in AI hardware names after the November 3 midterm elections. Shares of all three companies had been falling sharply over the past month.

CoreWeave reported third-quarter 2026 results after the close on November 10 that beat estimates and raised its full-year 2026 guidance. That report revived the AI trade across chip, memory and data center infrastructure stocks. The article says CoreWeave will rely on contract-backed financing and customer prepayments to fund its expansion, which eased concerns about how AI data center buildouts get paid for. Dell, Super Micro and Hewlett Packard Enterprise all sell AI-optimized servers into data centers, so shifts in sentiment tend to move them together.

Over the past month, Dell fell 37%, Hewlett Packard Enterprise fell 31% and Super Micro fell 28%. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa promised "a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals," and the state holds a large share of planned U.S. data center capacity. Hinojosa cannot act until she takes office in January, and outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott already paused new data center permits in September pending a state audit. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee also called the latest inflation report "borderline disturbing" while the Fed considers more rate hikes.

Dell reported a record AI backlog of $95 billion for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 and raised its full-year revenue guidance to $192 billion when it reported on September 1. Dell's management said demand outran supply in each of the last two quarters. Hewlett Packard Enterprise CEO Antonio Neri said on its September 2 earnings call, "We are leading with networking," referring to its acquisition of Juniper Networks. The article notes that Super Micro's revenue was concentrated, with a single large data center customer accounting for a big share of its revenue in its first quarter of fiscal 2027.

NVIDIA is scheduled to report on November 17, and Dell's own results follow on November 24. The article says the outcome of those reports will test whether AI demand holds up after the election. Bears cite a possible Texas moratorium, funding strain on data center projects, higher rates and component shortages. Dell management described those shortages as "DRAM, DRAM, DRAM, followed by NAND, NAND, NAND."

Articles.Title: Dell Jumps 11% as AI Server Stocks Rebound From a Rough Month; Super Micro Surges 8%, Hewlett Packard Enterprise Advances 6% - 24/7 Wall St.

stories.Headline: DOE Advances AI Cybersecurity for Critical Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
The Department of Energy is advancing artificial intelligence-powered cybersecurity technologies through a research initiative meant to strengthen the resilience of the nation's critical infrastructure against cyberattacks, according to a report published Tuesday by GovCIO Media & Research. The initiative is the AI-FORTS program, short for Artificial Intelligence for Operationally Resilient Technologies and Systems. It is managed by the department's Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response, known as CESER. The program was launched in 2024 and organizes its research around three priorities.

Those priorities are securing energy infrastructure from AI-enabled threats, using AI to strengthen cyber defenses, and protecting AI technologies deployed within energy systems. Sage Briscoe, CESER technical program manager and head of AI-FORTS, said that introducing new software into critical infrastructure requires organizations to assess whether it could create additional vulnerabilities or give attackers another way into a network. AI-FORTS aligns with the first strategic goal in CESER's fiscal years 2026-2030 strategic plan, which calls for developing world-class security technologies. The department identifies national laboratory partnerships and utility collaboration as important parts of its approach. The department's fiscal year 2027 congressional budget justification also lists AI-FORTS among its planned research and development investments.

The budget document says the department intends to shift cybersecurity research toward AI-focused capabilities that help critical infrastructure keep operating through compromise. One example of AI-FORTS research is Communications and Cybersecurity for the Energy Edge, or C2E2, a project developed through CESER's partnership with Sandia National Laboratories. In September, the department reported that C2E2 had cut energy-system data preparation from about two months to a few hours. It also reported 95-percent accuracy in detecting and locating cyber threats, with actionable intelligence available in near real time. Over the coming year, the C2E2 team plans to explore using large language models to build user-friendly impact assessments for energy infrastructure cybersecurity personnel.

CESER and Sandia are also advancing Scaled Testing for AI Systems, or STAISYS, which evaluates AI technologies in simulated environments representing critical energy infrastructure. According to Sandia, STAISYS is one of four Sandia-led projects funded through AI-FORTS. The effort uses emulated cyber-physical environments to assess how AI systems perform under realistic operating conditions and potential cyberattacks. Separately, CESER and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory introduced the Mjölnir AI Testbed in April. The platform is designed to assess the cybersecurity and reliability of AI models intended for energy-sector applications by exposing them to adversarial testing.

Articles.Title: DOE Advances AI Cybersecurity for Critical Infrastructure - ExecutiveGov

stories.Headline: Pakistan's AI Future Discussed at IIADP Dialogue in Karachi
stories.Summary:
The Indus Institute for AI & Digital Policy (IIADP) held a closed-door fireside chat on November 11, 2026, at the National Incubation Center (NIC) Karachi, inside NED University of Engineering and Technology. The session, titled "AI & Digital Pakistan: From Policy to Innovation," gathered representatives from government, academia, business, startups and the legal profession to discuss Pakistan's artificial intelligence and digital policy landscape. Senator Dr. Afnan Ullah Khan, a member of the Senate Standing Committee on IT & Telecommunications, joined to offer a parliamentary view on how technology, legislation and digital governance are changing. Hamza Ali Chaudhry, Executive Director of IIADP, moderated the discussion.

Other attendees included Syed Azfar Hussain, Project Director of NIC Karachi, Dr. Danish ur Rehman Khan, Technical Advisor to the Vice Chancellor of NED University, and Muhammad Ali Tariq, Deputy Secretary of Anti-Crime & Anti-Terrorism. The participants spoke candidly about opportunities and challenges in artificial intelligence, digital innovation, entrepreneurship and technology governance. They also considered international frameworks, including the OECD AI Principles and the G7 Hiroshima AI Process, which aim to set responsible standards for AI. The organisers stressed that Pakistan needs policies that encourage innovation while addressing regulatory, ethical and social concerns.

NIC Karachi took part as Growth Partner. The centre was established in 2018 at NED University and is funded by Ignite under the Ministry of IT & Telecommunication. It supports technology startups through incubation, mentorship, investor access and industry links. The articles say the discussion pointed to the need for closer cooperation between policymakers, academia, industry and entrepreneurs so that policy keeps pace with technological innovation. IIADP, which works on research, policy dialogue and stakeholder engagement, says these meetings are meant to support informed policymaking and stronger ties between decision-makers and Pakistan's technology sector.

Articles.Title: Pakistan's AI Future Discussed at IIADP Dialogue in Karachi - ARYnews.tv

stories.Headline: Why this former ER doc thinks giving AI less information is sometimes better
stories.Summary:

stories.Headline: Unions to Press on A.I. Threat in Mamdani’s First Labor Talks as Mayor
stories.Summary:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani is set to begin contract talks with New York City's largest public-sector union, his first labor negotiation since taking office. The bargaining is expected to set the floor for how the city deals with its other municipal unions. Talks will also have to address the threat that the rapid rise of artificial intelligence poses to city workers. The union involved is District Council 37 AFSCME, led by Henry Garrido.

The article does not give the contract's terms, the expiration date, or the number of workers covered, so those details cannot be reported here. What the article does make clear is that the talks will test how Mr. Mamdani balances his close ties to organized labor against his duties as mayor. He has joined picket lines with Starbucks baristas, hotel workers and nurses, and he has used his profile to support the labor movement when he can. The union's leader was the only public-sector labor figure to endorse him during his contentious 2025 Democratic primary.

Mr. Garrido, whose union represents some of the city's lowest-paid employees, has said he intends to press the affordability issue during bargaining. He argued that the mayor's public remarks about affordability and New Yorkers' hardship apply directly to the workers he represents. He said the negotiations give the mayor a chance to bargain on behalf of the people he has spoken about. The article frames these comments as the opening position of the union rather than the outcome of any talks.

The reporting places the talks in a wider debate over how city government will manage workers as automation expands. It does not say what proposals either side has put forward on artificial intelligence, or when a settlement might be reached. The article is based on an interview with Mr. Garrido and does not include a response from the mayor's office. Any next steps beyond the start of negotiations are not described.

Articles.Title: Unions to Press on A.I. Threat in Mamdani’s First Labor Talks as Mayor - The New York Times

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of K-12 Education: What Do Parents Want? - Institute for Family Studies
stories.Summary:
Only one article was supplied, and it is a report from the Institute for Family Studies rather than a news story about a single event, so the facts available are a survey and background rather than a breaking development. The report, by Jared Hayden, Ken Burchfiel and Michael Toscano and dated November 2026, asks what parents want for AI in K-12 classrooms. It finds that 56% of parents want AI fully blocked in schools, 26% want less AI than is currently required or allowed, 13% want more, and 6% want as much as possible. It also reports that 75% of Republican parents and 72% of Democratic parents support pausing AI in schools.

On timing, the report says parents favor later introduction: only 3% want AI in kindergarten and 9% want it in elementary school, while 20% want it in 12th grade or later and 22% want it never. It says 77% of parents believe AI will undermine learning, 79% that it will enable malicious student behavior, and 73% that it will expose children to serious risks. The most popular positive case, that it prepares children for the future workforce, was endorsed by 51%. Among the report's other findings, 38% of parents want AI used only in computer labs, while 25% want books and handwriting only.

The report places these attitudes against a background it describes in detail. It says nearly 4 in 10 American students attend schools where AI use is explicitly allowed or required, 15% attend schools where it is blocked, and 45% attend schools where no official action has been taken. It notes that 88% of public schools issued one-to-one devices in the 2024-2025 school year, and that US PISA reading and math scores have declined. It also cites the paused AI use in New York City and Los Angeles schools and a Nevada law protecting person-to-person school counseling. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of K-12 Education: What Do Parents Want? - Institute for Family Studies

stories.Headline: Semiconductor companies struggle to measure business value of AI: HTEC
stories.Summary:
HTEC, a global AI technology and engineering firm, has released research finding that semiconductor companies are relatively advanced in adopting artificial intelligence but struggle to prove that technical gains produce measurable business value. The findings were released on a Monday and reported by ET Electronics, which carried the story on November 10, 2026. According to the survey, 48 per cent of semiconductor respondents describe their organisations as scaling AI or already AI-native, compared with 44 per cent across the overall sample. Investment growth in the sector is broadly in line with the wider market, with 78 per cent reporting increased spending over the past year against 79 per cent overall.

The research points to a sharper divide in how AI projects are selected and measured. Semiconductor respondents lead other sectors in requiring strategic alignment and a formal return on investment model before approval, but measurement becomes less consistent once projects are underway. About 38 per cent say AI value is reported mainly on a case-by-case basis, against 30 per cent overall, while only 28 per cent rely mainly on an enterprise dashboard, compared with 36 per cent. Missing baseline metrics and inconsistent performance indicators across functions were identified as obstacles, and only 22 per cent said AI's purpose and expected outcomes are clearly articulated across their organisation, the lowest share of any sector surveyed. The survey also found that 83 per cent of semiconductor respondents see people and processes as a bigger constraint on AI value than technology, yet only 22 per cent actively monitor adoption and outcomes across functions.

HTEC's findings suggest that semiconductor firms will need to apply the same discipline to adoption, accountability and measurement across the wider business as AI moves beyond specialist engineering teams, though the release itself does not name specific corrective steps. The research also covers risk: more than half of semiconductor companies, 57.5 per cent, measure AI risk alongside value only for high-risk use cases, and about 16 per cent measure risk consistently across their AI portfolio. Among technical respondents, 33 per cent cited model unpredictability and edge cases as the main complication for human oversight, the highest share across the sectors surveyed. The report was released by HTEC itself, and the article does not indicate any response from semiconductor companies or regulators.

Articles.Title: Semiconductor companies struggle to measure business value of AI: HTEC - electronics.economictimes.indiatimes.com

stories.Headline: Canada signs AI safety declaration: What does it mean for employers? - Human Resources Director
stories.Summary:
Canada has endorsed an international artificial intelligence safety declaration, published by the Prime Minister's Office in Ottawa on November 9, 2026. The Joint declaration on Paris call for AI safety and security was signed by Bahrain, Canada, Finland, France, Norway and the Netherlands. Frontier AI developers Anthropic, Microsoft, OpenAI and Canadian firm Cohere also endorsed it. The declaration is non-binding, and it sets out commitments for both governments and developers.

The declaration rests on three pillars, starting with a common risk framework for frontier models, the most advanced AI systems, with non-sensitive findings shared publicly. The second pillar assigns accountability, with developers committing to disclose known risks and install fail-safe shutdown mechanisms. Governments, for their part, recognize the need for legal frameworks that clarify responsibility in case of large-scale damages. The third pillar covers early warning systems for serious cyber and AI control incidents. Signatories also say the opportunities and risks of frontier models are inherently global.

Policymakers commit to providing secure and confidential channels through which whistleblowers, including employees, can raise concerns about systemic risks without fear of legal or professional retaliation. The declaration creates no new employer obligations, but it places employee reporting of AI risk on the policy agenda. Organizations that deploy AI may want to check that their speak-up policies cover such concerns. Florian Martin-Bariteau, director of the University of Ottawa's Centre for Law, Technology and Society, told Global News that the approach will not work without regulators and enforcement. He said he supports the content of the statement but believes it lacks teeth without follow-up.

The Canadian government has relied on voluntary measures, including its AI for All strategy launched in June 2026. Prime Minister Mark Carney said in October 2026 that the country was building AI the right way. The declaration calls for a clear, understandable and predictable regulatory framework but sets no timeline for one. Australia has moved further, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese saying on November 10, 2026 that a new regulator would enforce legislated standards on frontier AI companies there.

Articles.Title: Canada signs AI safety declaration: What does it mean for employers? - Human Resources Director

stories.Headline: [Field Report] AI technology leaves the lab and sets sail for the market with Kakao
stories.Summary:
On the morning of November 10, 2026, AI startup teams from four Korean science and technology institutes presented their technologies to investors at Kakao AI Campus in Yongin, Gyeonggi Province. The teams came from KAIST, GIST, DGIST and UNIST, and the event was Kakao AI Sail: Set Sail, Season 2, an AI startup competition run by Kakao Investment Co., Ltd. and kakao AI sail. The program aims to find promising AI technologies and link them with investment and proof-of-concept projects at Kakao affiliates. A total of 122 teams applied this year, about 85% more than the 66 in the first edition, and 12 of them reached the finals.

Kakao affiliates, including Kakao, KakaoBank, Kakao Mobility, Kakao Entertainment and Kakao Pay, set 18 challenges tied to business needs, and teams proposed technologies and business models to meet them. Rokon, which won the top prize, presented a way for AI to learn knowledge spread across a company, automating a task that once required specialist engineers and took three to six months, now done in an average of two to three hours at about 90% of the existing method's performance. Its work agent, Puzzle, could be paired with Kakao's AI service Kanana to serve 10.2 million employees at small and medium-sized businesses. Millitrack and Space AI won excellence awards, and five teams received honorable mentions. The competition carries 75 million won in prize money, along with investment consideration and PoC opportunities with Kakao affiliates.

Kim Do-young, CEO of Kakao Investment Co., Ltd., spoke at the event about the need to invest in research achievements from regional institutes. He noted that about 73% of last year's venture investment funds were concentrated in companies in the Seoul metropolitan area. He compared a ship's safety in port with its purpose to sail, and encouraged the teams to pursue bigger goals. Kakao Investment's own framing of the event is that unlike ordinary startup competitions, the program can lead to investment and PoCs even after the awards are presented.

The first edition produced results that the article describes as successful. AniBridge AI, with roots at KAIST, received follow-on investment after an investment from Kakao Investment and reached a company valuation of 20 billion won. Blackbox, a UNIST team, carried out a paid PoC with Kakao Entertainment, while Broz, with roots at DGIST, raised investment and was discussing technical integration with Kakao Map. The article presents these outcomes as evidence that research-stage AI can move toward commercial use through the program.

Articles.Title: [Field Report] AI technology leaves the lab and sets sail for the market with Kakao - 파이낸셜뉴스

stories.Headline: Unequal causes and consequences of AI use
stories.Summary:
Generative AI is entering organizations that are already marked by inequality, and a set of researchers has proposed a recursive cycle linking that inequality to AI use and back again. In the framing offered, existing inequalities and status-based stereotypes can heighten social identity threat among marginalized group members, which may push some of them to use generative AI to augment their communication or performance. Actual, imagined, or implied AI involvement can then prompt AI interrogation, meaning questioning of communicators' capability, credibility, and authenticity, which can reinforce the inequality that started the cycle. The authors describe this as a vicious cycle of AI use, stereotyping, and discrimination. The argument rests on how inequality already shapes workplaces.

The authors point to racialized organizations where Black and Brown employees face closer scrutiny, male-normed offices where women are labeled less suitable for demanding intellectual work, and neurotypical or ableist workplaces where neurodivergent and disabled workers face assumed incompetence. Within such settings, marginalized members often fear being devalued or mistreated because of their social identity. That fear can make them anxious, lead them to monitor others' reactions closely, and cause them to perform worse in exams, interviews, and presentations. AI tools, described as readily available, anonymous, and seemingly unbiased, may offer relief from that threat. The authors cite women who hide their identities behind avatars and experience less stereotype threat as precedent for technological tools reducing threat.

The authors argue that using AI creates a new ambiguity about who produced a piece of communication, a human, an artificial system, or both. They contend that stereotypes shape how that ambiguity is resolved. AI and its users tend to be depicted as prestigious, wealthy, white, masculine, and young, so AI use by advantaged members is more likely to be seen as normal and harmless. For marginalized members, the same use is more likely to be read as a cover for stereotyped incompetence and lack of motivation.

The authors give the example of a Black student who may or may not have used AI being quickly dismissed as lazy. In academia, they note that scholars of color face objectivity interrogation, and that evidence suggests Black students are more than twice as likely as white students to be falsely accused of AI plagiarism. The authors identify three ways people may respond to this pressure. Some will decline to use AI, citing ethical, environmental, or social costs, including training on creative workers' output without consent and infrastructure that strains electricity and water supplies, though they may give up efficiency benefits.

Others will use AI but keep detailed records or disclose it, although the authors warn that explicit disclosure may increase the stereotypes they seek to avoid. A third group will use AI and disguise it, which the authors link to the broader pattern of marginalized employees concealing identities at work. They cite a survey of more than 48,000 employees worldwide in which 57 percent said they disguise AI use, and they note that masking is exhausting. To disrupt this cycle, the authors make recommendations aimed at several groups.

Policymakers within and outside schools and workplaces should adopt strong AI use and disclosure policies, enforce them equally, and build documentation into workflows so the burden of proof does not fall on individuals, with regular audits to ensure demands are applied consistently. AI users are urged to consider whether and how they use the tools and to keep records such as chat transcripts and version histories. Scholars are urged to study AI through the lens of racialized, gendered, and classed organizations, examining how existing inequalities shape who uses AI and how its use may reify those inequalities. The article's final framing is that as workplaces, schools, and social media platforms remain diverse but unequal, social status may determine who reaches for generative AI out of desire.

Articles.Title: Unequal causes and consequences of AI use

stories.Headline: KT ‘Meisters’ and Microsoft engineers build AI agents to spot network issues before customers do
stories.Summary:
KT, the South Korean telecom provider, has begun using AIO-Net, an agentic AI platform built with engineers from Microsoft to catch network faults before customers notice them. The system has been in use since August, and it pulls together data that was previously spread across separate systems onto a single view. Network engineers, called Meisters at KT, trained the platform on the company's standard operating procedures and their own expertise. The project was described in an article published on Microsoft's news site on November 11, 2026. AIO-Net flags anomalies in real-time data from KT's network equipment across the country, and its agents produce a documented analysis of each incident.

According to KT, detection now takes two to three minutes, down from more than ten minutes, and an agent can investigate an incident and produce a report in about five minutes, roughly half the earlier manual time. The agents are restricted to read-only commands on an allow list and cannot take action on equipment, a limit enforced within the application itself. KT plans to expand the system from 70 units of critical equipment to 280, and later into access networks closer to subscribers. KT's head of network operations innovation, Seonil Jeong, said that network reliability takes precedence over operational efficiency and that AI decisions and actions remain with people. Hosong Lee, head of the AIO-Net development team, said the system is designed to improve continuously and that Microsoft's team worked alongside KT through implementation.

Seonghyun Lee, KT's development team manager, said operators' ordinary use of the system captures feedback without explicit requests. The article presents these statements as the companies' own accounts of the project. The article places the work within a co-development model in which Microsoft Frontier Company and KT's team jointly define problems and build solutions, with Microsoft's forward-deployed engineers working from KT's offices. KT operates mobile, broadband, TV and telephone services and serves 29 million mobile subscribers, which the article cites as the reason network reliability is a priority. The article does not describe any outcomes beyond the figures above, and it does not give a timeline beyond the planned expansion.

Articles.Title: KT ‘Meisters’ and Microsoft engineers build AI agents to spot network issues before customers do

stories.Headline: A Layman Thinks About AI
stories.Summary:
Howard Marks, co-founder of Oaktree Capital, published a new memo on November 11, 2026, asking whether investors should put money into artificial intelligence and how they might do so intelligently. He describes AI as both deeply consequential and highly unpredictable, and he lays out 11 questions that surround investing in it. Marks says these questions cannot be answered definitively, but he argues that uncertainty does not mean investors can ignore AI. He calls the technology too important to set aside. Marks states at the outset that he is not a technology person and does not claim above-average knowledge of AI or technology investing.

He calls AI the biggest development of his time and says investors cannot opt out of thinking about it. He says he will not try to track daily news or security prices, because his memo concerns the long-term outlook for AI rather than tomorrow's prices. He also notes that investing consists of positioning capital to benefit from future events, and that most investors rely on forecasts. Marks asks readers to weigh the odds of being right across several linked variables. He illustrates this by saying that if an investor has a 60% probability of getting each of four top-down calls right, the chance of getting all four right is 13%, assuming the outcomes are independent.

He writes that an AI investor must be at least somewhat right about the technology's evolution, the demand for compute, the competitive structure, the beneficiaries, the availability of financing, and timing. He says assessing these elements seems unusually challenging. He adds that investors must accept that they can never know everything about an investment. In the memo's first question, Marks asks how AI does what it does, and he turns to Anthropic's Claude for an explanation that he presents at length.

Claude says researchers know what AI is made of and how it was built, but know surprisingly little about how it produces its results. Claude describes the training method, in which a system guesses the next word and its internal settings are adjusted after each wrong guess, repeated trillions of times. Marks asks whether anyone truly understands how AI works and whether investors need that understanding to answer the questions that follow. Marks's second question concerns what AI will be able to do, and he notes that the technology has advanced from recognizing historical patterns to something that can fairly be called reasoning.

He lists open questions, including whether AI can be made to reflect human preferences, whether it can be depended on to be honest, and whether it can perform creative and intuitive work. He also asks whether AI will be taxed like people, given that replacing workers may reduce tax revenues. He raises the broader question of whether the technology will reward investors, noting that Warren Buffett argued the same about the internet during the tech bubble. On the competitive landscape, Marks points out that OpenAI and Anthropic were unknown to most people only a few years ago, and that the so-called hyperscalers are Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, and Oracle.

He compares today's uncertainty with the period 20 to 25 years ago, when Microsoft, Amazon, Apple, and Google won while Napster, Yahoo, and Netscape faded. He asks what the probability is that today's AI leaders will still lead in five or ten years. The memo's remaining questions, including one on how profitable these companies will be, are not answered in the text provided. More to follow.

Articles.Title: A Layman Thinks About AI

stories.Headline: Accelerating product development with AI-driven lifecycle management (AI-PDLC) in AWS Quick
stories.Summary:
Amazon Web Services has published a blog post describing AI-PDLC, a framework for AI-driven product development that runs on AWS Quick and uses six specialized agents. The post, dated November 11, 2026, explains that AI-driven software delivery has made implementation faster, so the upstream work of finding the right customer problem and deciding what to build now matters more. It argues that the signals needed for those decisions are scattered across tools such as Slack, Salesforce, ServiceNow, SharePoint, Jira, and Outlook, and that teams lose context at each handoff. AWS Quick is presented as the connective layer that grounds agents in this enterprise data and stores their outputs in shared Spaces.

The framework covers eight lifecycle phases, namely Discover, Decide, Design, Prototype, Engineer, Ship, Operate, and Learn. The blog post focuses on the first four, which the product team handles, while coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code take over the last four using specifications produced upstream. An Orchestrator agent drives a single conversation through the pipeline and advances only after a human approves each step. The specialist agents include Discovery, which scores pain points by severity and frequency, Prioritize, which scores use cases on weighted 0 to 10 frameworks, Working Backwards, which drafts a PR/FAQ, and Spec Generator, which produces a prototype_spec.md file. A Designer agent is also named in the post.

AWS, as the author of the post, is responsible for the framework and describes it as a way to help teams think better and preserve the reasoning behind decisions rather than simply produce documents faster. The post states that human judgment governs every stage, with people validating pain points, approving priorities, signing off on specifications, gating the build, and accepting reviews. It also says production data flows back into discovery to close the loop. The post describes the Agent Client Protocol as an open JSON-RPC 2.0 standard that avoids vendor lock-in for connecting coding agents. The article is the first in this coverage, and the post ends partway through describing the Spec Generator, so the remaining details of how the Designer and later agents operate are not available here.

Articles.Title: Accelerating product development with AI-driven lifecycle management (AI-PDLC) in AWS Quick

stories.Headline: Centralized or decentralized AI governance?
stories.Summary:
On 11 November 2026, the IAPP published an opinion piece by contributor Kaylyn Gerran on how organizations should structure their AI governance and compliance programs. It asks whether AI governance should sit in one centralized function or be spread across existing risk domains. Gerran argues that both models carry genuine advantages and genuine costs. She says the right answer depends less on an organization's maturity than on how its risk landscape, culture and workforce actually operate. The article notes that the IAPP is policy neutral and publishes contributed opinion pieces so members can hear a broad spectrum of views.

Gerran pushes back on some governance, risk and compliance professionals who say that embedding AI risk into existing risk domains is only a transitional phase. In their view, organizations do this until they have the resources to mature into a dedicated, centralized AI governance function. She says that framing sells the decentralized model short. In her account, decentralized governance keeps AI risk with domain owners in legal, compliance, information security, privacy, technology and engineering, who each bring deep subject matter expertise. She lists data exfiltration, expanded attack surfaces, retention failures, data quality problems and confidentiality exposure as risks that predate generative AI.

Gerran is the sole author, and the views are hers, as the IAPP publishes such pieces without endorsing them. She argues that decentralization lets privacy teams extend their privacy impact assessment to include AI risk questions instead of building a parallel intake process. Third-party risk management teams can add AI-specific questions to vendor assessments they already conduct, she writes, while security teams keep assessing AI architecture within their current security reviews. In her view this reduces the friction, confusion and duplication that cause governance processes to be circumvented in the first place. She adds that distributing governance across risk domains builds broad organizational fluency, because each team becomes expert in how AI intersects with its own discipline rather than a full AI expert.

Gerran describes the strains on each model, which fall on the teams that carry out governance. In a decentralized model, she says, the hardest problem is assigning ownership for responsibilities that do not map cleanly to one domain, such as drafting standards or standing up assessment processes. When every team owns a slice, she writes, no one owns the whole pie, and synthesizing an organizational view of AI exposure becomes its own project. A centralized model, she says, makes audits cleaner and reporting simpler, and it gives leadership a coherent answer about its AI risk posture. It also allows full-time AI builder roles and governance roles, though it requires more headcount than many organizations can realistically support.

The article offers a worked example of why centralization can help, from the perspective of those who must learn the tools. An employee trying to automate a 20-minute task with generative AI tools may spend three hours on it while still learning, whereas risk domain owners split their focus across other domains. A center of excellence or formalized program can absorb that learning curve on behalf of the business. Gerran also warns that a centralized model can become a bottleneck between the business and the technology it wants to use. It can recreate assessment processes that exist elsewhere and leave domain experts feeling AI is done to their risk area rather than within it.

Gerran expects most organizations to land somewhere between the two models, and she says the practical question is which responsibilities must be centralized and which should stay distributed. In one organization, standards, policy and the enterprise-wide risk picture might sit with a single accountable area, while assessment execution and control operation stay embedded in the domains. In another, only the part of the organization that produces AI solutions might be centralized, with governance and compliance staying in the risk domains. She expects many organizations to find that a hybrid, with central accountability and distributed execution, captures most of the benefits, provided the central function acts as a coordinator and enabler rather than a gatekeeper. She says there is no one wrong model, but the choice should be deliberate, so organizations do not fall into one by default and discover its weaknesses only when a problem arises that no one owns.

Articles.Title: Centralized or decentralized AI governance?

stories.Headline: The Math Driving Agentic AI Adoption in NetOps
stories.Summary:
A 2026 study by Omdia and Cisco of 1,000 IT and NetOps leaders reports that more than half of their organizations already use agentic AI to act on network operations tasks in production. The findings were published by Harvard Business Review on November 11, 2026, in a piece sponsored by Cisco. The article says enterprise monitoring systems generate more than 4,000 alerts every day, roughly half of them concerning the network. An experienced engineer can investigate and resolve about 20 alert events a day, so nearly half of alerts go uninvestigated and are closed without review.
