stories.Headline: AI1000: Bot Access and Blocking Reveal an AI Readiness Divide Ahead of Holiday 2026
stories.Summary:
Retailers were ranked on AI shopping readiness in a new benchmark released November 12, 2026, by ReFiBuy and Digital Commerce 360. The quarterly AI1000 index, which covers 1,000 leading online retailers in North America, combines AI traffic measures with bot-access and commerce-protocol signals. The Q3 edition reports an average score of 39.9 out of 100. Costco is the biggest climber, rising 182 places to No. 325, while GoPro and Scheels gained 173 and 168 places respectively.

The results point to a divide between retailers that welcome AI shopping agents and those that do not. Only 13 of the 100 largest online retailers rank in the AI1000 top 100, and all five leaders sit outside the top 100 by sales for the third straight edition. Nixon leads on AI readiness, followed by Online Labels, Everlane, CustomInk, and Brooklinen. Adoption of the Universal Commerce Protocol, which lets AI agents complete checkout for shoppers, also varies widely, with 55% of jewelry retailers showing endpoints compared with 3% of automotive parts and accessories retailers.

ReFiBuy CEO Scot Wingo said some major platforms, including Amazon and eBay, are deliberately blocking bots, and a larger group of retailers appear to be blocking them too. He said it is unclear whether those decisions were strategic or came from IT or infrastructure teams without input from commerce staff. Wingo warned that such blocking will significantly reduce discovery traffic for holiday 2026. The release advises commerce and security teams to set separate permissions for search crawlers, model-training crawlers, and shopping agents, and to test whether approved agents can retrieve useful product data.

The release also recommends that retailers maintain accurate, consistent product data, including current availability and delivery terms for holiday shoppers, ahead of planning for 2027. ReFiBuy offers an ACO audit to identify catalog gaps and monitoring to track how agents discover products after updates. Retailers in the index can view their personalized Q3 report at refibuy.ai/ai1000 after verifying a work email. The company describes itself as the inventor of Agentic Commerce Optimization, a term it uses to frame this work.

Articles.Title: AI1000: Bot Access and Blocking Reveal an AI Readiness Divide Ahead of Holiday 2026

stories.Headline: Photon Joins SpaceX Super Intelligence Partner Network to Help Enterprises Put AI to Work
stories.Summary:
Photon Group, an enterprise AI consulting and engineering firm based in Dublin, has joined the SpaceX Super Intelligence Partner Network, known as SpaceXSI, and has set out the focus of the collaboration as helping enterprises adopt AI across software engineering and business workflows. The announcement was published on November 12, 2026. Photon is a Launch Partner in the network, which was announced on October 22, 2026, and it takes part in the network's Transformation Partner program. Photon says it will bring consulting and engineering services that help clients find relevant use cases, redesign workflows and put SpaceXSI capabilities into existing systems. Its Forward Deployed Engineers will work inside client environments to support implementation and adoption.

For agent-based solutions, Photon will also offer PHTN.ai, its Enterprise Agent Management platform, which is built to orchestrate, govern and monitor AI agents. The partnership will concentrate on three areas: software engineering, where development teams adopt AI within their delivery processes, supported by training and workflow redesign; business workflow transformation, where industry-specific processes are targeted and AI capabilities are built into the systems employees already use; and agent deployment and oversight, where PHTN.ai supplies orchestration, human-review controls and visibility into agent actions. The platform is described as domain-aware and LLM-agnostic, meaning it works across different models, frameworks and cloud environments. Clients can set human-review requirements and monitor agent activity as deployments grow. Photon's Universal Agent Harness serves as the shared foundation for these functions.

Srinivas Balasubramanian, Photon's chief executive, said clients want to know where AI can improve their business and how to move it into production, and that Photon will handle the business problem, the engineering and the adoption work. Mukund Balasubramanian, the company's president and chief technology officer, said that building an AI workflow and running it reliably are linked responsibilities, and that PHTN.ai controls what agents can access, which actions they can take and when a person must review their work. Toni Adams, head of partnerships at SpaceX Super Intelligence, welcomed Photon to the network and said the two companies look forward to helping customers adopt AI across software development and business operations. Photon describes itself as serving 40% of the Fortune 100 across banking, financial services, retail, consumer goods, healthcare and automotive. The release provides no financial terms, timeline for specific client results, or details on how the partnership will be measured.

Articles.Title: Photon Joins SpaceX Super Intelligence Partner Network to Help Enterprises Put AI to Work

stories.Headline: Struggling marijuana farms pivot to becoming AI data center sites to escape falling weed revenue
stories.Summary:
Struggling marijuana farms are considering converting their cultivation facilities into AI data center sites, according to Arizona Public Media, as the cannabis industry declines. Sales in the cannabis industry peaked in 2024, and oversupply has driven prices down, prompting some growers to sell their facilities or convert them into "mini data center nodes." Moe Asnani, former owner of two Tucson D2 Dispensaries, told the public broadcaster that he is leaving the cultivation side of the business. Asnani said the facilities could be repurposed, and he described the idea of smaller nodes where people control their own data. The reporting was published on November 12, 2026, by Tom's Hardware, with Jowi Morales as the byline.

Cannabis farming is both power- and water-intensive, and Forbes looked at a 32,850-square-foot facility in Kalamazoo, Michigan. That facility is currently wired for 1.5 megawatts, which can be expanded to 2.5 megawatts in under a year and to 15 megawatts in the long term. The building is also provisioned for fiber internet and equipped with a state-of-the-art HVAC system for climate control. Data centers often demand two to three times more power than cultivation facilities, and upgrades could take up to five years. The concept is described as "adaptive reuse," meaning existing buildings are repurposed rather than building new sites.

Tucson City Council member Paul Cunningham described the concept as a more palatable alternative to massive, purpose-built data center sites on the outskirts of town. Cunningham said he is open to exploring the option if existing buildings can be used without being invasive. Niki Krear, vice president of acquisitions at real estate investment trust New Lake Capital Partners, said operators look for a balance of affordable power, dense fiber networks, and favorable tax policies. Krear spoke to MJBizDaily about the criteria for site selection.

Growers facing increased competition, costs, and taxes are the group most directly affected, as the articles describe them as cash-strapped and seeking to unload unprofitable properties. Neighbors may also oppose such projects, as data center operators seeking smaller sites may face NIMBY, or "not in my backyard," fights. The articles note that the lack of economies of scale could cost operators more, and that OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly interested in such sites as hyperscale projects face community opposition. The article also notes that data centers are often viewed negatively, and that no one wants to build a brand-new one.

The articles say the cannabis oversupply in Arizona is the background to the decline, with more cannabis grown in Arizona than Arizonans use. Growers have seen falling demand, and the Tucson council member's remarks reflect local opposition to new purpose-built data centers. The articles do not give a figure for how many growers are considering the conversion or how many have completed one. The articles also do not state whether any specific sale or conversion has been agreed upon, what zoning or regulatory approvals would be needed, or whether any current projects have begun.

Articles.Title: Struggling marijuana farms pivot to becoming AI data center sites to escape falling weed revenue

stories.Headline: Adaptive Neural Subspaces with Geometry-Aware Quadrature for Interface Problems
stories.Summary:
The articles here are a single preprint abstract posted on Research Square, a platform where manuscripts appear before any journal peer review, with a timestamp of November 11, 2026. The preprint describes a new machine learning method for solving interface problems, which are mathematical problems involving boundaries where material properties change abruptly. The authors combine neural networks, numerical quadrature schemes, and adaptive subspace approximation, and they say the neural network is used to build the basis functions of a finite-dimensional subspace on which the discrete solution is then computed. They also say the method can handle singularities that arise at such interfaces when paired with high precision integration. The abstract reports that the approach achieves high accuracy in simulations, though it gives no specific figures.

The method includes an a posteriori error estimator derived from the hypercircle technique within the subspace approximation framework. According to the abstract, this estimator serves as the loss function used to adaptively refine the neural network parameters. The authors say the design of these loss functions depends on a high precision numerical integration scheme to reach the reported accuracy. The source does not provide the names of the authors, the institutions involved, the specific test problems, or any quantitative error comparisons against other methods.

The preprint lists no competing interests. Because it has not yet been peer reviewed by a journal, its claims about accuracy and singularity handling have not been independently checked. The articles do not say whether or when the work will be submitted to a journal or what follow-up the authors plan. Details on those points would need to come from the full text or from later publication.

Articles.Title: Adaptive Neural Subspaces with Geometry-Aware Quadrature for Interface Problems

stories.Headline: Incremental prognostic value of CT radiomics and deep learning beyond complete tumor volume in non-small cell lung cancer: a reanalysis of LUNG1
stories.Summary:
A reanalysis of the publicly available LUNG1 dataset, published in BMC Medical Imaging by Qiang Zhao, Shanwu Ma, F. Chen and colleagues, tested whether CT radiomics and deep learning add to survival prediction in non-small cell lung cancer beyond a simple measure of tumor volume. The team worked with 420 patients from the NSCLC-Radiomics collection, 372 of whom had died, and the work was shared early as an accepted, citable article before final typesetting. The study compared complete gross tumor volume alone, 107 radiomic features extracted from original images, a fixed pretrained 3D convolutional neural network, and a fusion of radiomic and deep learning features. Model evaluation used repeated five-fold cross-validation, with preprocessing and model fitting restricted to training patients to avoid data leakage.

The researchers also checked whether a fixed 96-millimeter cubic crop covered each tumor fully, and found that it cut off part of the tumor in 64 of the 420 patients. On the initial fold assignment, the mean concordance index was 0.585 for tumor volume, 0.567 for volume plus radiomics, 0.571 for clinical plus radiomics, 0.514 for the frozen network and 0.569 for fusion. Across 20 repetitions, the mean concordance index was 0.588 for volume alone, 0.577 for volume plus radiomics and 0.568 for fusion. The authors reported that the confidence intervals for the radiomics-minus-volume and fusion-minus-volume differences crossed zero, and that harmonizing scans across reconstruction kernels with ComBat in a 295-patient subset gave no clear improvement. A separate 46-patient cohort from NSCLC Radiogenomics, with 14 deaths, was too small for comparative validation.

The authors, affiliated with the Center for Precision Cancer Medicine and Translational Research at Tianjin Cancer Hospital Airport Hospital in Tianjin, China, concluded that in this cohort the complete-volume radiomic and fusion models did not show a stable gain in held-out survival prediction over complete tumor volume. They said their findings support measuring the full tumor contour, validating without leakage, and replicating the work in an independent, population-matched cohort. The study was funded by the China Association for Promotion of Health Science and Technology, and the authors declared no competing interests. The articles do not describe any planned follow-up study beyond that recommended replication.

Articles.Title: Incremental prognostic value of CT radiomics and deep learning beyond complete tumor volume in non-small cell lung cancer: a reanalysis of LUNG1

stories.Headline: Hub: More streamers using AI to search for content
stories.Summary:
Hub Entertainment Research released new data on Thursday, November 12, 2026, showing that streaming viewers are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence chatbots and similar programs to find something to watch. According to the survey, two in five streamers now use tools such as ChatGPT and Google's AI Mode for recommendations and to search for particular shows and movies across different platforms. That share rises to 57 percent among streamers aged 16 to 34. The research was conducted in October and drew on responses from more than 1,600 U.S. consumers.

Among those already using AI for entertainment discovery, 57 percent said the technology works better than traditional search engines. Viewers in this group also feel that the built-in search and discovery tools on streaming platforms often fail to connect them with the content they want at a given moment. Personal recommendations still lead as the most common discovery method, with 29 percent of streamers finding a new favorite through word of mouth from family or friends and 21 percent crediting movie and TV trailers. Only 14 percent credited a streaming service's own algorithm. The data also found that younger viewers are finding older shows: nearly one in four streamers aged 16 to 24 said a classic TV series was their top new discovery over the past year, compared with 11 percent of viewers over 35.

Hub Entertainment Research Senior Consultant Jason Platt Zolov, in a statement, said viewers have plenty to watch and simply need better ways to find it. The articles place this finding within a broader push by connected TV platforms to add AI to their search and discovery features. Samsung announced in August 2025 that its smart TV home screen would get an AI-powered makeover aimed at more personalized recommendations, and earlier this year it said it was partnering with Nielsen's Gracenote metadata business to improve those recommendations. Google has incorporated Gemini into newer versions of its Android TV platform since last year, and LG, Roku and Apple have made similar moves. Amazon has long used its Alexa assistant on Fire TV devices to help viewers find content across its own platforms and some partner apps.

Articles.Title: Hub: More streamers using AI to search for content

stories.Headline: GREP: Grounding Generated Room Evaluation in Principles
stories.Summary:
A new research paper titled GREP, short for Grounding Generated Room Evaluation in Principles, was posted on November 11, 2026, by a team of seven authors led by Mohan Cao. The work addresses a gap in how computer-generated furnished rooms are judged, since existing evaluations look only at narrow perspectives or fixed questions. The authors say this leaves no reliable way to assess overall scene quality. They describe the paper as one of the cs.CV, cs.AI and cs.GR categories on arXiv, a preprint server. The core of the approach is a three-tier philosophy rather than a set of predefined questions.

The first tier, basic physical validity, checks whether a scene obeys physical constraints. The second, visual coherence, examines whether objects agree in scale, style and composition. The highest tier, human-use logic, requires that object arrangements match everyday human habits. Guided by these principles, an evaluation agent identifies issues from the scene context, gathers evidence, and produces scores and reports. According to the authors, GREP reached 87% agreement with the majority preferences of human judges, which they say substantially outperforms baseline evaluators.

They also report that GREP's written reports, when used to refine scenes, improved scene quality, while score-only and no-feedback baselines showed slight declines. The paper further suggests that as planning ability improves, recent models such as GPT-5.6 Sol can begin to challenge the pipelines and guidance imposed on them, yet still lack the ability to resolve the resulting conflicts. The authors expect stronger models to plan well and also adapt more flexibly to external guidance and constraints. The paper is available as a PDF and HTML version, with a project page linked by the authors. The articles do not say what follow-up work, adoption or peer review is planned.

Articles.Title: GREP: Grounding Generated Room Evaluation in Principles

stories.Headline: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories
stories.Summary:
A research team led by Fei Lin and 17 co-authors posted a paper on arXiv describing BEAKER, a new benchmark for testing how well multimodal large language models can act as "embodied brains" in self-driving chemical laboratories. The paper's abstract was published on November 11, 2026, and it addresses a gap the authors see in existing tests, which mostly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific knowledge. BEAKER contains 1,000 question-answer samples spread across 11 image and video task types. The authors say all questions and annotations were manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied artificial intelligence experts, without AI-assisted generation.

The benchmark covers the judgments needed to carry out chemical experiments, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, recognition of equipment, states and safety conditions, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. The researchers evaluated 28 models in total, drawn from general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized and embodied categories, in an offline, single-turn setting. The results indicate that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures shown in videos. However, the paper reports that they still struggle to turn actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to identify fine-grained apparatus, states and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures.

The paper is credited to the 18 authors listed, with Xue Yang among them, and the abstract does not single out any one author as responsible for the findings beyond that authorship. According to the abstract, the authors frame BEAKER as a diagnostic tool, and they say it exposes a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception that laboratory execution requires. The abstract does not describe any planned follow-up work, release timeline or specific next steps. What the authors hope will happen is that future multimodal models for self-driving laboratories will be measured against this benchmark. The source material offers no further details on how the benchmark will be adopted or what it will change in practice.

Articles.Title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories

stories.Headline: ModalSearcher: Weaving Visual Evidence into Autonomous Cross-Modal Deep Search
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers has posted a paper on arXiv, a preprint server, describing a system called ModalSearcher that lets multimodal AI models search for information across text and images. The paper was listed on November 11, 2026, and its authors are Zhihan Yin, Ruyi Li, Chengyu Fang, Yifeng Yao, Nonghai Zhang, Pengfei Xiong, Terry Zhang, Huishuai Zhang and Dongyan Zhao. The work addresses a limitation of current models, whose built-in knowledge is static and incomplete, which hurts performance on questions about new information or those requiring several steps of evidence gathering. The authors describe the approach as autonomous cross-modal search, in which an agent chooses between reasoning on its own, text-to-text search, text-to-image search and reverse-image search.

The system relies on a training pipeline called ModalSearch-Pipeline, which builds an interleaved multimodal knowledge graph of questions with paths of varying depth and mixed modalities. According to the abstract, the procedure hides entity names and image targets that would reveal shortcuts while keeping clues needed to disambiguate the answer. The researchers trained the agent with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a live Web environment, and they also built a benchmark called ModalSearch-Bench. The abstract states that the 8-billion-parameter ModalSearcher-8B improves average accuracy by 16.2 points over Qwen3-VL-8B under the same agentic workflow across five multimodal knowledge-intensive question-answering benchmarks. It also reports consistent gains on independently constructed active visual-search benchmarks.

The paper is credited to the nine authors listed above, and the articles do not name any institution, funder or company that sponsored the work. The abstract reports the results as the authors' own experimental findings, and it does not indicate whether independent parties have reviewed them. The articles also do not say whether the code, model weights or benchmark will be released publicly. The research is presented as a preprint, so it has not been described as peer reviewed in the material provided. Any further developments, such as publication in a journal or conference or release of the models, are not covered in the articles.

Articles.Title: ModalSearcher: Weaving Visual Evidence into Autonomous Cross-Modal Deep Search

stories.Headline: DreamRealm: Exploring and Materializing Hallucination Worlds for Trustworthy Vision-Language Models
stories.Summary:
DreamRealm is a post-training framework for multimodal large language models, introduced in a research paper posted to arXiv and listed on doi.org on November 11, 2026. The authors, Benlei Cui and eight co-authors, say the work addresses visual hallucinations, where a model gives wrong answers when correct responses depend on subtle visual details. The paper describes an approach that explores latent hallucinated responses, makes minimal edits to original images so the responses become valid, and trains the model to match each response to its supporting image. A data pipeline named RealmForgePipe mines hallucinations from a target model and materializes them through image editing. The authors built a dataset called the Realized Hallucination Dataset, or RealmSet, using hallucinations mined from Qwen3.5-9B.

Their training objective, named RealmMatch, builds a likelihood score matrix across image and response combinations and combines supervised learning with bidirectional contrastive losses. The aim is to reinforce correct matches and suppress mismatches between images and responses. The paper says these steps are meant to make supervision target the model's own perceptual confusions rather than generic visual contrasts. According to the paper, DreamRealm improves performance over the original Qwen3.5-9B model across six visual perception and hallucination benchmarks. The reported gains include 7.26 percentage points in HallusionBench accuracy and 11.34 percentage points in MMVP pair accuracy.

The authors also present ablation studies on their data construction and training methods, which they say support the conclusion that hallucination assignment is a promising paradigm. The paper runs 28 pages including supplementary material, and the authors have released code and a model. The article does not describe any independent review, outside reaction, or deployment plans beyond the released code and model. It also does not indicate whether the results have been peer reviewed or published in a conference or journal. The authors frame their findings as a promising direction, and any further validation would depend on follow-up work by the research community.

Articles.Title: DreamRealm: Exploring and Materializing Hallucination Worlds for Trustworthy Vision-Language Models

stories.Headline: AttriSwarm: Orchestrating Agent Swarms for Cross-Page Visual Attribution
stories.Summary:
Researchers Suifeng Zhao, Zida Liu, Lei Sun, Xun Wang, Daojian Zeng, Jun Gao and Sujian Li have published a paper describing AttriSwarm, a framework for cross-page visual attribution in multimodal large language models. The work appeared on doi.org on November 11, 2026, and it addresses answers that are synthesized from evidence spread across several document pages. The authors say that when such answers are assembled from many pages, the connection between a conclusion and its supporting visual evidence becomes hard to see, which makes verification and trust difficult. Their system is built to restore that connection.

According to the abstract, cross-page attribution requires two steps: identifying the pages that support an answer and locating fine-grained evidence regions within those pages. Existing methods either process multiple pages jointly or refine evidence step by step in a single trajectory, which the authors say can pollute context across pages and add heavy sequential overhead in interactive settings. AttriSwarm separates these tasks among distinct roles, with a leader agent handling global reasoning across pages and subagents performing page-by-page attribution in isolation and in parallel. To support training and evaluation, the authors also built AttriDoc, a cross-page question-answering dataset that links supporting pages to annotated evidence regions.

The authors report that role-specific training on AttriDoc improved AttriSwarm over its training-free version. Averaged across three open-source backbones and three datasets, the gains were 18.94 percentage points in answer accuracy, 29.34 percentage points in page-level F1, and 23.04 percentage points in region-level IoU. The paper itself is credited to the seven named authors, and the abstract describes the results as the authors' own findings. The article content does not say how the work will be used beyond the research setting, nor does it describe any further releases or follow-up steps.

Articles.Title: AttriSwarm: Orchestrating Agent Swarms for Cross-Page Visual Attribution

stories.Headline: New Relic launches AI agent for Kubernetes troubleshooting
stories.Summary:
New Relic, the observability company, announced the New Relic Autopilot Kubernetes Agent, an AI tool meant to simplify troubleshooting of Kubernetes clusters, according to a TechGig report published on November 11, 2026. The agent is aimed at site reliability engineers and platform engineers who manage these clusters. It is described as a domain-specific extension of New Relic Autopilot, the company's suite of SRE agents. The report says it was unveiled that day and is currently available in public preview.

The agent runs more than 90 specialised diagnostic detectors across Kubernetes events, object descriptions, logs and APM traces to isolate root causes. It then generates context-aware remediation code, which engineers review and execute themselves. The article notes that the tool connects to New Relic's Ground Truth context engine, which is built on OpenTelemetry. It is designed to diagnose common and complex infrastructure failures such as noisy neighbours, compute resourcing problems, scheduling failures, network errors and cloud misconfigurations, including issues with Application Load Balancers and ingress.

Human-in-the-loop options are included so engineers can keep oversight during investigations. Brian Emerson, chief product officer at New Relic, said the agent brings specialised, agentic AI directly into the engineer's containerised workflows. He said the aim is to remove guesswork from complex cluster incidents while engineers stay in control. The article presents this as the purpose of the launch and does not include further assessments from outside the company.

It does not say how the agent will be priced, when it will reach general availability, or how widely it has been tested. The report describes the agent as fitting into standard SRE and platform engineering workflows rather than replacing them. It also notes that the agent works within New Relic's existing observability platform, which is why it draws on the company's telemetry data. Beyond the public preview, the article gives no timeline or next steps.

Articles.Title: New Relic launches AI agent for Kubernetes troubleshooting

stories.Headline: Platform ownership shapes AI infrastructure strategies, CNCF report finds
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData released their Q3 2026 Technology Radar report on November 11, 2026, at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026. The research looked at how developers view observability, infrastructure as code, and storage technologies. Its central finding is that the way an organisation structures its platform engineering is closely tied to how it approaches AI infrastructure. The report covers tools across these three areas and tracks which of them earned an "Adopt" position.

The report ties platform ownership to AI choices. Among organisations where individual teams manage their own tooling, 54 per cent of developers use hybrid approaches for AI workflows, compared with 43 per cent where multiple teams collaboratively provide platform capabilities. Only 5 per cent of organisations building custom internal developer platforms use hybrid approaches. Among those building custom platforms, 38 per cent use a separate dedicated AI platform, while 33 per cent extend their existing developer platform.

Where platform teams curate third-party tools, 25 per cent rely primarily on AI vendor platforms. Liam Bollmann-Dodd, principal market research consultant at SlashData, said that centralised teams tend to make deliberate decisions about extending existing platforms or building dedicated AI environments. He added that distributed teams are more likely to adopt hybrid approaches. The report's findings on technology adoption were drawn from developer ratings and recommendations gathered by CNCF and SlashData.

Prometheus and OpenTelemetry earned "Adopt" positions in observability, with 80 per cent of developers rating Prometheus four or five stars for maturity. Ninety-two per cent of current and former OpenTelemetry users said they would likely recommend it, and Fluent Bit was the most recommended observability tool at 99 per cent. In infrastructure as code, OpenTofu and OpenFeature earned "Adopt" positions, and 96 per cent of OpenTofu users said they would likely recommend it. Carina earned the "Adopt" position in storage, while Crossplane, Atlantis, and cdk8s landed in "Trial."

Articles.Title: Platform ownership shapes AI infrastructure strategies, CNCF report finds

stories.Headline: Airbnb CTO details multi-party AI agents for customer support
stories.Summary:
Airbnb's Chief Technology Officer, Ahmad Al-Dahle, discussed the company's deployment of multi-party AI agents to handle customer support, according to a Stack Overflow blog post republished by TechGig on November 11, 2026. The report describes how Airbnb is using several AI agents working together to manage support requests. Al-Dahle's remarks were covered in a short news item that gives few further details about the system's design or rollout. The available account is brief and does not describe the scale of the deployment or its results.

The coverage says that rigorous evaluations help engineers balance latency and accuracy in AI systems. That balance matters because a support agent must answer quickly without giving wrong responses. Al-Dahle also said that AI coding tools require a higher level of judgment from software engineering teams. The articles do not state specific figures, thresholds or timelines for these requirements. They also do not describe any formal change to Airbnb's policies or processes beyond the engineering shifts described.

Al-Dahle is identified as the speaker, and the account of his views comes from a Stack Overflow blog post that TechGig summarized. According to the report, Airbnb is reshaping its engineering organization to put generative AI into use across its platform. The item does not describe any response from outside parties or any criticism of the approach. It also gives no indication of the company's intentions beyond the general effort to adapt its engineering teams.

The item places Airbnb's work within a wider industry move toward generative AI in software and customer service. It does not say what follows next, such as product launches, follow-up statements, or further evaluations. stories.Headline: AI chatbots are recommending fake retail websites, study finds
stories.Summary:
A study by IP protection firm Podqi, shared exclusively with The Verge, found that AI chatbots can direct shoppers to imposters and other risky websites. Podqi tested ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity with shopping questions about 151 brands during two testing periods in September. The study was reported on November 12, 2026. The brands included fashion labels Lululemon, Birkenstock, Stüssy and Madhappy, along with homeware brand Le Creuset. Podqi wrote its own prompts rather than using real user conversations.

Across 6,795 answers, Podqi found all three engines cited or showed risky sites, which it defined as fake sites impersonating retailers or selling knockoffs, reregistered old brand domains, and dead sites that others could buy and reuse. Gemini showed risky sites in 4 percent of answers, the lowest of the three. Perplexity performed worst at 15 percent, while ChatGPT showed them in 8 percent of answers. ChatGPT offered warnings about risky sites 24 percent of the time, the best of the three. Queries about larger companies had risky sites in answers about half as often as those about smaller brands.

Podqi CEO and cofounder Trevor West said consumers should verify a source before entering personal or credit card information. Google spokesperson Jessica Levis Boord said Gemini performed best among the products tested and that links to sources are displayed so people can verify information. OpenAI spokesperson Taya Christianson said the company is improving safeguards to make potentially deceptive sites less likely to appear in shopping results. Perplexity spokesperson Jesse Dwyer said the company is consistently among the most accurate AI on credible research benchmarks, while not claiming 100 percent accuracy.

AI companies market chatbots for researching, comparing and discovering products, and the article says citing fake sites is a headache for brands and retailers. The article notes the risk could grow for consumers ahead of the holiday shopping season, when people look for in-stock items and the best prices. It also says more consumers are likely to use AI to shop this year, including from brands or sites they do not already know. In Podqi's test, prompts about regional brand websites triggered risky sites more often than other categories.

The article says that in one conversation Perplexity named the wrong page as Stüssy's official website and called it the best starting point for guaranteed authentic items. The article also says the tested engines at times listed fake regional sites for brands that have none. It does not say whether any of the risky sites were used to defraud shoppers, nor whether the companies will change their systems on a set schedule. It also leaves open how much more often consumers will encounter such sites during the holiday season.

Articles.Title: AI chatbots are recommending fake retail websites, study finds

stories.Headline: Google finds technical debt derails AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
Google researchers have reported that outdated code comments and references to closed bugs can pull AI coding agents off course, a problem they call "agent distraction." The findings were highlighted in an article by Google senior staff software engineer Sam Saccone and senior staff data scientist Madhuri Garikapati, reported on November 11, 2026. According to the authors, stale technical debt such as old TODO comments and obsolete bug references gets read by agents as context, which can misdirect their work. At best this raises token consumption and execution time, and at worst it can lead agents to flawed logic and decisions. The study focused on TODO(bug/...)

comments, which often outlive the bugs they point to. Google analysed distributed traces from thousands of engineers and hundreds of millions of agent steps. About 13 per cent of sessions exposed agents to inline TODO or FIXME references, and agents acted on the referenced bug in 6 per cent of those cases. In 41 per cent of these unprompted detours, agents worked on tickets that were already closed, while in 57 per cent they addressed open bugs outside the developer's request, which the researchers classed as scope creep. These detours added 70 per cent more steps, 77 per cent more tokens, and 105 per cent more wait time per session.

Most prompts did not mention the referenced bug at all. To counter the problem, Google built scanner agents that search its codebase for obsolete TODOs, sometimes examining years of git history to confirm a comment is out of date. Once confirmed, the agents submit a pull request to remove the reference. Over six months this approach removed thousands of obsolete references, and human reviewers accepted over 95 per cent of the resulting changes.

The researchers concluded that presubmit analyzers, codebase scanners, and automated agents can reduce agent distraction and improve the effectiveness of AI coding agents. Reactions on X and LinkedIn echoed the findings, with one user noting that "comments are context too" and another comparing the behaviour to junior developers working at machine speed while raising token costs. A LinkedIn user took the high human acceptance rate as evidence that cleanup automation can work without losing human judgment. The articles provide no further details on whether Google plans to extend the cleanup tools beyond its own codebase.

Articles.Title: Google finds technical debt derails AI coding agents

stories.Headline: Mirendil Raises $1B to Democratize Frontier AI R&D
stories.Summary:
Mirendil, a San Francisco company, announced on November 12, 2026 that it had raised $1 billion in a Series A round. The round was led by Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital, with participation from Battery Ventures, Doerr Capital, Gil & Co, Google, M13, Pear VC, and S32, along with other new and existing investors. The announcement was distributed through a PR Newswire release. The company said the funding would help it make frontier AI research and development more widely accessible.

Mirendil described its recent work as evidence that AI agents doing hands-on tasks can reduce how much a team's size limits what it can build. According to the release, one researcher used agents to pretrain a competitive coding model, Mirendil-Base, from scratch in 3.5 months with less than $10M in compute. The company then post-trained that model into Fern, which it said can hold up to 10 million tokens of context. Its platform, Lor, is in private beta and is meant to let teams run hundreds of agents writing code and running experiments for days at a time.

Mirendil said it uses Lor every day. The company framed the new capital as a way to move toward a world where one person can take on work that once required a team, and a team can take on work once requiring an institution. Mirendil said it wants to accelerate science and technology more directly than it has before. The release also said the company remains a small team with a narrow focus and invited people to join it or to contact it about building with its tools.

The release is a paid press release, and the article notes that inquiries should go to the distributor. The article is a press release reproduced on Yahoo Finance and does not include independent reporting, valuation figures, or details on how the $1 billion will be spent. Related items listed on the page mention earlier Mirendil deals, including a reported $100 million-plus Google Cloud arrangement, but the article itself does not confirm the terms of those deals. The page offers no further information on next steps beyond the company's stated plans to expand its tools and team.

Articles.Title: Mirendil Raises $1B to Democratize Frontier AI R&D

stories.Headline: Anthropic CEO predicts AI could help cure major diseases within 10 years
stories.Summary:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in a 42-minute investor roadshow video released on November 10, 2026, that artificial intelligence could make diseases such as cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease and mental illness relics of the past within less than a decade. He also spoke of an "age of miracles" in which scientific advances could solve long-standing problems. His remarks came as Anthropic expands its work in biological research and drug development. The article's own coverage places them against a background of ongoing company activity and expert debate. In an October 27 company update, Anthropic said it had set up research partnerships with six organizations developing medicines and had started its own drug discovery programs.

Some of this work targets rare childhood diseases, including forms of muscular dystrophy. Anthropic acknowledged, however, that most of it remains preclinical, meaning the potential treatments have generally not reached human testing. The article presents this as the current state of the research rather than evidence of a finished medical result. Amodei's optimism echoes a view held by other technology leaders. Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis, speaking at the Indian Institute of Science, said developing a new drug typically takes about 10 years and suggested AI could cut that to months or even weeks.

He pointed to AlphaFold, which has generated predictions for more than 200 million protein structures, while acknowledging that predicting structures is only one part of making medicines. Researchers must still confirm that compounds work as intended, have suitable properties and avoid harmful side effects. The pharmaceutical industry has been more cautious. Jeff Leiden, executive chairman of Vertex Pharmaceuticals, told The Wall Street Journal that Vertex had evaluated about 50 AI companies using a database of 10,000 drug compounds, and none had independently produced a working drug. He rejected claims that AI could cure 90% of human diseases within seven years, calling them "complete BS."

The article notes that drugs must still pass laboratory research, preclinical studies, human clinical trials and regulatory review before they are proven safe and effective. The article concludes that AI may help researchers identify targets, analyze biological data and speed early-stage discovery, but that these abilities do not remove the scientific uncertainties of developing treatments. Amodei's prediction, it says, reflects the possibilities he sees rather than an established medical timeline. Whether such expectations become treatments for the world's most difficult diseases within a decade remains, in the article's words, an open question.

Articles.Title: Anthropic CEO predicts AI could help cure major diseases within 10 years

stories.Headline: Anthropic releases Mythos 5.2 for improved bug hunting
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has released Claude Mythos 5.2, an access-restricted AI model, alongside Claude Fable 5.2, announcing the release on Monday, according to a report published on November 11, 2026. The new model is reported to improve vulnerability discovery and to reduce sandbox escapes compared with its predecessor, Mythos 5.1. Mozilla found that Mythos 5.2 roughly doubled the vulnerability discovery results of Mythos 5.1 in Firefox. The company also reported that the model achieved an 89.6 per cent success rate in CVE Rediscovery across 1,829 CVEs, up from 78.3 per cent for Mythos 5.1.

Mythos 5.2 reduced sandbox escapes to 3.1 per cent in more than 1,800 scenarios, a sharp drop from 21 per cent for Mythos 5.1. One security company found that one in six confirmed bugs uncovered by Mythos 5.2 had gone unnoticed by other frontier models. Claude Security, Anthropic's code vulnerability scanner, now uses Mythos 5.2 for Claude Enterprise customers. Fable 5.2 shares the same underlying model as Mythos 5.2 and triggers 60 per cent fewer cybersecurity blocks than Fable 5.1 for legitimate work.

Direct access to Mythos is reserved for vetted organisations through Anthropic's Cyber and Life Sciences Verification Programs. Anthropic internally evaluates the model's vulnerability identification ability to be roughly on par with Opus 5.5, according to the reporting. The articles attribute the performance figures to Anthropic and to Mozilla's own assessment of Firefox results, and do not describe any independent verification beyond those reports. The articles do not say what further releases or access changes the company plans next.

Articles.Title: Anthropic releases Mythos 5.2 for improved bug hunting

stories.Headline: Frida Kahlo’s Image Has Become a Global Brand. A Viral AI-Generated Ad Makes Things Worse.
stories.Summary:
A viral AI-generated advertisement for the fashion brand Les Énervés, which has roots in Paris and Bali, has drawn sharp criticism for its portrayal of the Mexican painter Frida Kahlo. The ad was first posted to Instagram in October and began spreading widely on X this month. In it, a bubblegum-chewing Kahlo drives a bus through Paris carrying the Mona Lisa and Vincent van Gogh, with his ear replaced by a steel prosthetic. The depiction shows her downing several drinks before driving, though the real artist struggled with alcohol and drug addiction.

The brand says the ad was directed by its founder, Wakim Krari, and produced using what it calls "AI, and a lot of patience." Its website adds that the bus was recreated as a Renault TN, a model that might have been seen in Paris when Kahlo staged an exhibition there in 1939. Les Énervés presents the ad as a statement of reclamation, saying that a hundred years after her 1925 bus accident, Kahlo is the one driving. The soundtrack moves from an Édith Piaf song to Britney Spears's "Gimme More," and the brand's website hints that a new chapter with a new muse is coming soon. Responsibility for the content rests with the brand and its founder, who have framed it as a tribute.

The article's author says the ad disrespects the dead, and notes that a post with 46,000 likes made the same point. The piece also points to other AI-generated Kahlo content, including a video that recasts her as a Spice Girl and a chatbot that answers as her. The author argues that Kahlo carefully built her own self-image, including her unibrow, men's clothing, and Tehuana skirts, in ways that resisted the expectations placed on a 20th-century Mexican woman. The commercial spread of her image on items ranging from Barbie dolls to tequila bottles is described as already wearing down those nuances. Curator Mari Carmen Ramírez, of a Tate Modern show called "Frida: The Making of an Icon," has said her image has become subsumed by artists and activists.

The article also raises concern about how AI can distort art history, using the ad's sidelining of Diego Rivera as an example. Kahlo's 25-year relationship with Rivera was complicated, marked by love and frustration, and he betrayed her by having an affair with her younger sister. Kahlo died at 47 in 1954, when she was far less famous than she is today, so she cannot respond to the ad. The author concludes that the brand appears to have found its next target, and that its promised new chapter reads like a threat.

Articles.Title: Frida Kahlo’s Image Has Become a Global Brand. A Viral AI-Generated Ad Makes Things Worse.

stories.Headline: Why bond king Jeffrey Gundlach is steering clear of the AI 'blast radius'
stories.Summary:
DoubleLine founder Jeffrey Gundlach said on November 12, 2026, that he is avoiding the AI stock sector. He made the remarks at Yahoo Finance Invest, where he described a strategy he has followed since about September. Gundlach said he has been trying to stay clear of what he calls the "blast radius" of the AI trade. The statement came after a sharp selloff in technology shares.

Gundlach said investors should not own the S&P 500 or any cap-weighted index, because of heavy concentration in AI and AI-adjacent companies. He said such concentration is roughly 60 percent, or about half of the market, depending on the statistics used. Gundlach said he is low in equities compared with his historical weighting, holding only about 30 percent. He said the only equity holding he recommends is an equal-weighted S&P 500. He also said he likes bonds and has a barbell approach to them.

Gundlach placed responsibility for the strategy on his own judgment and on his shift away from the sector after sensing what he called the dark side of the mania. The articles give no further direct quotes from him beyond those describing his positioning. He described his move as a rotation he made in the aftermath of that shift. He said he intends to remain in that position for a while. The articles do not name any other party responsible for his decisions.

The articles report that fears about the AI trade intensified after the Democratic blue wave on Election Day, which could see newly elected Democratic senators and governors disrupt AI expansion. On November 5, the S&P 500 lost 4.4 percent, erasing $3 trillion in market value. The Dow fell 1,280 points, its worst single-day decline since 2020, and the Nasdaq dropped 4.8 percent, dragged down by Micron and Sandisk. Nvidia's CEO, Jensen Huang, has also resigned following reported affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and a fellow Nvidia executive.

Investors across the market are affected, since the tech-heavy indexes and Nvidia's technology and financial commitments sit at the center of the AI boom. The articles state that any disruption to Nvidia is what AI investors least want to see. Tech names continued trading with a downward bias after the selloff. The articles say the AI sector had been crushed under the weight of its own expectations.

The articles note that Gundlach has previously voiced caution about AI spending. Other coverage cited in the article carries headlines describing his comparison of Nvidia's $500 billion AI financing push to bonds backed by bananas. Other headlines describe him calling for almost nothing in AI stocks and saying he wants out. The articles also mention that the Yahoo Finance page lists the S&P 500 at 7,627.93 and the Nasdaq at 25,473.16 at the time of the snapshot.

The articles do not say whether Gundlach will change his allocation or when he might do so. They do not state what happens next for Nvidia's leadership or who will succeed Huang. The articles leave open how the newly elected Democratic officials will act on AI expansion. They also do not say whether the selloff in tech shares will continue.

Articles.Title: Why bond king Jeffrey Gundlach is steering clear of the AI 'blast radius'

stories.Headline: Jaeger previews AI-assisted troubleshooting, GenAI trace visualisation
stories.Summary:
Jaeger, the distributed tracing project that has graduated from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, has begun previewing its first AI-assisted troubleshooting and generative AI observability features. The announcement was published on November 11, 2026, by TechGig, and the features are available as experimental options in Jaeger v2.22. The preview is aimed at engineers who need to find faults in systems spread across many services. It is described as the project's first integrated work of this kind.

The main addition is Ask Jaeger, a natural language assistant built into the product, which lets engineers investigate traces through conversation. A separate opt-in Model Context Protocol endpoint offers nine tools for discovering services and traces, examining errors, mapping service topology, identifying critical paths, and inspecting individual spans. The preview also includes built-in diagnostic skills for root-cause analysis of errors and for detecting N+1 query problems, which give AI agents repeatable investigation workflows. Teams can enable these capabilities after downloading Jaeger and following the project's AI sidecar integration guide.

The article also describes new views built on OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. These views are meant to help teams study model interactions, agent activity, retrieval operations, token usage, system instructions and tool execution within distributed traces. The features are presented as experimental, and the article does not name specific individuals responsible for the release. It also does not say how the features will move from preview to general availability or when that might happen.

stories.Headline: Validation architect crucial for AI in software testing
stories.Summary:
AI agents can generate hundreds of tests in minutes, but they cannot decide which of those tests truly matter, according to Donovan Brady, vice president of developer relations at Leapwork. He made the point during the SD Times Live! AI in Test Supercast on November 5, and the article was published on November 11, 2026. Brady argued that organisations can hand testing work to agents without giving up accountability for quality. Vaclav Vincalek, a virtual CTO and founder of Recurrent Patterns Podcast and Media Services, also spoke at the event and questioned the wider push to treat AI as a teammate.

Brady described three ways AI agents can go wrong. They may generate incorrect tests because they lack business context, run tests at the wrong moment, or make what he called silent repairs, where an agent rewrites a failing test so it passes and hides a defect. He gave the example of asking an AI for 500 tests when perhaps only 100 are needed or tied to critical customer journeys. To address this, he proposed a "validation architect" role, a QA professional or SDET who would own business intent, critical journeys, risk priorities, coverage expectations, escalation rules, and release decisions. Agents would handle execution, such as proposing and maintaining tests, selecting suites, running them in CI/CD pipelines, and gathering evidence.

The architect would review what ran, failed, was skipped, or remained unproven, while a person keeps the final release call. Brady's advice is to begin with standing policy, requirements, approved outcomes, mandatory evidence, and escalation rules to decide what agents may do on their own. He said mechanical repairs, such as a moved button, can be left to agents, but changes to expected outcomes should be flagged for the requirement owner. He also cited a case where a 1 per cent failure rate might be acceptable on an ordinary day but not during an event like Black Friday, a judgment he said agents do not inherently make.

Brady called this approach "continuous validation," sitting between continuous integration and continuous deployment, and recommended starting small with one critical journey such as checkout. The article reports that Microsoft reportedly uses Leapwork for Dynamics 365 and Power Platform testing in Azure DevOps pipelines, cutting regression cycles from weeks to hours. Vincalek was more sceptical about the returns from AI. He compared using AI in code to driving a fast car one cannot explain, warning that it can cause harm quickly.

He said that if companies produced ten times more with AI, profits should be ten times higher, which he has not observed, and he noted that model makers still sell tokens to software firms rather than building their own ventures. He urged measuring quality over quantity and seeking technology that helps skilled people deliver better results. Brady also stressed that workflows must be re-engineered rather than having agents attached to old processes. The article notes that Leapwork Play, a Playwright-based tool with built-in agents and MCP support, became generally available on September 30.

Articles.Title: Validation architect crucial for AI in software testing

stories.Headline: Copilot in Visual Studio upgrades to Microsoft SDK
stories.Summary:
Copilot Chat in Visual Studio has been moved onto the Microsoft Copilot SDK, the same technology that powers GitHub Copilot CLI and VS Code. The change takes effect with Visual Studio 2026 version 18.12, and the article was published on November 11, 2026. Developers who update will get the new engine, which the article says improves how tasks are resolved across various models and gives shorter, more focused answers. Testing reported in the article found that the new experience resolved up to 21 more coding tasks than before. The .NET team built a benchmark from real C# project issues to measure the effect on .NET developers, and the new engine resolved 157 tasks within it.

That benchmark covered .NET Framework, .NET Core, Azure, Aspire, WinForms, and desktop applications. The article adds that the engine has also been tested with C++, Python, and other languages. The change also alters how developers work with Copilot in practice. Users can steer Copilot in the middle of a task and see the cost of each request. Copilot is meant to behave more consistently across Visual Studio, VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the GitHub Copilot app, and an agent skill written once is said to work on all four without modification.

Specialized agents are available for debugging, profiling, fixing build failures, modernizing .NET applications, and speeding up C++ builds, and built-in skills add .NET and Azure expertise. The article does not name a specific person as responsible for the change, and it attributes the benchmark work to the .NET team. Users who prefer the earlier experience can still revert to the previous Copilot Chat in the settings. The article does not describe any further rollout plans or next steps beyond the release described above.

Articles.Title: Copilot in Visual Studio upgrades to Microsoft SDK

stories.Headline: The Executive Guide to Scaling Agentic AI in Healthcare
stories.Summary:
Healthcare has long met rising demand by hiring more people, but that approach is no longer feasible. In a Healthcare Dive survey of 150 U.S. healthcare executives, 83% cited reducing operational cost as a reason to invest in agentic AI, and 52% cited staffing shortages. The article's author, Michael Serbinis, founder and CEO of League, argues that AI agents can give every member and patient an always-on care team. He calls this the infinite care team. Serbinis describes the vision as a future where people receive answers and care at any hour.

The survey found that 89% of executives call agentic AI very important to their strategy, yet only 16% have reached broad deployment. Trust is the main barrier, as 99% would delay a launch by months rather than go live without full guardrails. Executives favor starting small, with 75% wanting to deploy one use case before expanding. Benefits navigation leads at 54% overall and 59% among payers, while providers lean toward appointment scheduling at 53%. Serbinis recommends starting with one use case on a platform built to support later ones.

Serbinis states that League is launching two solutions at HLTH this year, AI Front Door for payers and AI Care Companion for providers. AI Front Door offers members one entry point through chat, text or in-app, with benefits navigation, care finding, care gap outreach and health coaching agents. AI Care Companion lets health systems target populations such as chronic conditions or post-surgical care, with agents handling scheduling, symptom check-ins and escalation to on-call teams. Both solutions run on League's platform, which the article says has five built-in safeguards and is governed by the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Organizations can launch in as little as 12 weeks.

Executives told Healthcare Dive that three requirements would give them confidence to launch: built-in healthcare compliance (49%), automatic escalation to a person (48%), and runtime controls on agent statements and actions (46%). The article says League's platform meets these requirements, and its safeguards include approved-knowledge-only answers, guardrails, eval-gated releases, full-context handoffs and continuous oversight. The platform adheres to HITRUST r2, SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, HIPAA and PIPEDA standards. League reports more than 1.8 billion healthcare interactions across the 70 million people it reaches worldwide. Serbinis says these solutions are informed by that history.

League is the source of the article, and it is a sponsor of Healthcare Scene. Serbinis is founder and CEO of League, and before League he cofounded and led Kobo and founded DocSpace. He also chairs the Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics and is a founding board member of the Vector Institute for Artificial Intelligence. The article notes that the League platform is used by the largest payers, providers and consumer health brands. The piece itself is a sponsored article, and it explicitly frames League's products as the answer to the barriers described.

The article says that AI Front Door and AI Care Companion will be shown live at HLTH in Las Vegas, November 15 to 18, at Booth #2836. Attendees can also see the Forge console, which tracks completions, escalations and accuracy by use case. A live AI Care Companion webinar is offered for those not attending HLTH. The article does not report independent outcome data or the results of any deployment. It also does not describe how the 12-week launch timeline or the five safeguards perform in practice, leaving those claims unverified.

Articles.Title: The Executive Guide to Scaling Agentic AI in Healthcare

stories.Headline: Six planning patterns for AI agents aid goal decomposition, debugging
stories.Summary:
AI agents can use six planning patterns to break a goal into manageable steps, and a recent guide says this structure also makes the applications easier to debug. Planning here means deciding which actions are needed to reach a goal, such as splitting up a request, choosing tools, and gathering results. The guide advises developers to examine the task first and pick a pattern that fits it, rather than forcing a problem into whatever reasoning approach is currently popular. Fixed workflows suit predictable, repeatable jobs like generating reports or checking forms, while model-driven plans fit requests that vary widely or where the agent must adapt to information it retrieves. The six patterns are a fixed workflow, plan-then-execute, ReAct-style tool use, routing to specialists, parallel work, and draft-evaluate-revise.

A fixed workflow follows steps the developer has chosen in advance, which makes it predictable. In plan-then-execute, a model proposes steps that the application or another model then carries out. ReAct-style tool use alternates between reasoning about the next step and taking an action, adjusting as results come in. Routing sends requests to suitable workflows or specialists, parallel work splits tasks into independent subtasks that are combined afterward, and draft-evaluate-revise has an agent produce a draft, check it against criteria, and revise it. The guidance also says a plan is a proposal rather than a guarantee, so developers must validate actions and results, and set stopping conditions such as maximum steps or time limits.

The article lists several common mistakes, including overplanning simple tasks, treating a plan as a guarantee, giving agents too many choices, forgetting stopping conditions, and relying on models for exact arithmetic. It points to guidance from OpenAI on building agents, which describes orchestration as handling multiple steps and tool use, and to Anthropic's guide, which distinguishes predefined workflows from more flexible agents. The author recommends making plans observable and testable, with steps stored or traced so developers can see what happened, and includes a simple Python example of a predictable research plan in which code handles calculations and models interpret user criteria. The article's central conclusion is that the simplest approach fitting the task is often the most effective, since it helps the system reliably reach a verifiable result.

Articles.Title: Six planning patterns for AI agents aid goal decomposition, debugging
