AI Governance by Vanta is designed to follow an AI agent through its full life cycle, covering discovery, vulnerability testing, behavior controls and proof of governance. Entire jobs can now be handed to the latest Vanta Agent, which brings staff in when a decision needs human judgment and can be used inside Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and Slack. Chief Product Officer Jeremy Epling, who was due to demonstrate the products at a keynote, said security teams are usually held accountable for AI with the same headcount they had before it arrived. He said that while many tools can list the AI running in a company, Vanta also checks whether that AI is doing what a customer approved.

The company also named Fredrick "Flee" Lee its new chief information security officer, effective November 16, after he led security at Reddit Inc. Vanta said Lee is expected to act as "customer zero" in shaping the product road map. The company's early access program for AI Governance opened in July and has become its most requested product, with a waitlist now six times oversubscribed. Vanta claims to be the only vendor tying an AI agent's live security telemetry directly to an organization's compliance controls. Vanta has been valued at $4.15 billion since July 2025, when it raised $150 million in a Series D round led by Wellington Management Co. LLP.

Articles.Title: Vanta launches AI Governance, Risk Quantification and a Vanta Agent for entire jobs

stories.Headline: AI-Powered MedChain Framework Secures Healthcare Data Using Blockchain and Advanced Cryptography
stories.Summary:
Researchers have introduced an artificial intelligence-enabled framework called MedChain, built to secure sensitive healthcare data during transit, classification and storage. It combines blockchain technology, advanced cryptography and smart Internet of Things devices, and it was developed by KKKUMARI KALA.M and MPM. Priya at the Vellore Institute of Technology in Chennai, India. The study appeared in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, under its Medicine and Public Health section, and the news report on it is dated November 11, 2026. The review process ended with acceptance in October 2026, after the researchers first submitted the work in June 2026.

The framework proposes a decentralized architecture in which consensus-based authentication customizes data protection strategies according to the sensitivity of each patient record. The framework starts with C-score Min-Max normalization, which standardizes and preprocesses heterogeneous healthcare records before any classification takes place. It then applies a novel Fuzzy Intensive Support Scalar Vector Machine, designated FI-SSVM, which computes the Absolute Confidential Feature Scaling Behavior Rate to sort records into sensitive and non-sensitive categories. The Spectral Sensitive Fit-Whale Optimization Algorithm handles mutual feature selection, and a Long Short-Term Memory Generative Adversarial Network, or LSTM-GAN, uses generative data augmentation to identify sensitive margins. For transmission and storage, an Integrated Data Hash Indexing Policy catalogs sensitive records on the dedicated MedChain blockchain network.

Those records are encrypted at the block level with a Multi-Parity Starvation Foldable Advanced Encryption Standard cipher, while the Medi-Consensus Chain Link Policy Key Management scheme governs consensus and cryptographic keys. Access control and identity verification are regulated through the Metaverse-Master Proofing Registry Authentication Policy, which executes Secure Handover Mutual Peer-to-Peer protocols. The published documentation describes a seven-part architectural model covering sensitive data classification, mutual feature selection, generative adversarial network augmentation, block-level encryption, key management, peer-to-peer authentication and decentralized ledger management. Its protections apply to three states: data moving across connected channels, records undergoing classification, and stationary data held in storage. The authors conclude that combining automated machine-learning classification, blockchain immutability, high-level encryption and a decentralized structure improves data visibility, traceability and administrative efficiency in next-generation healthcare ecosystems.

In the standard declarations, they state that all presented assessments are solely their own rather than institutional endorsements. The article cites no outside experts, regulators or hospitals reacting to the framework, so the only voices on record are the authors themselves. The paper is cited as Kala, M. K., and Priya, M. (2026), titled AI-enabled medchain framework for secure healthcare data management, Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, volume 9, article 1919907. Correspondence for the paper is directed to M. Priya.

The people the framework is meant to serve are those whose personal health records are gathered by wearable health monitoring devices and Internet of Things hardware during continuous remote patient monitoring. The article describes the work as an original structured engineering framework developed to overcome vulnerabilities in modern distributed medical architectures. The research addresses weaknesses created by the rapid spread of Internet of Things technologies and wearable health monitoring devices in modern healthcare systems. These connected instruments allow continuous remote patient monitoring and real-time collection of personal health records.

Large-scale deployments, however, frequently face security hurdles including privacy compromises, data breaches and authentication failures. They also face elevated feature dimensionality, which complicates the secure handling of sensitive patient health information. The architecture's feature selection step is meant to counter this high dimensionality and to prevent model overfitting during data processing. The article does not report any deployment, hospital trial or performance results for MedChain, so how well it works in practice remains open.

It gives no timetable for further testing or adoption, and it names no healthcare provider or regulator that has agreed to use the framework. The framework is presented as a design for scalable healthcare ecosystems, but no figures on accuracy, speed or cost are given. The authors' conclusion rests on the combination of artificial intelligence classification and decentralized immutability, and the article does not say how that claim will be independently checked. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI-Powered MedChain Framework Secures Healthcare Data Using Blockchain and Advanced Cryptography

stories.Headline: Autonomous Business: Joule Work, Joule Assistants, and the SAP Business AI Platform
stories.Summary:
The SAP Connect event in Las Vegas saw SAP unveil the integration of Joule Work, a new AI user interface, Joule Assistants for specific business domains, and the SAP Autonomous Suite, all under the theme of the "autonomous enterprise." The consolidated SAP Business AI Platform combines the cloud portfolio, the Business Technology Platform, the Business Data Cloud, and the AI Core Framework. SAP says Joule Work is already in productive use across its own roughly 110,000 employees and has produced productivity gains averaging 20 percent in key administrative and logistics areas. Joule Work also lets users start and carry out cross-system tasks in natural language on mobile devices and on the desktop. The assistant relies on the SAP Knowledge Graph, which maps more than seven million data fields and relationship networks within the S/4 universe, to reduce errors in business-critical operations.

SAP has also released Joule Studio, a low-code and pro-code environment in which business users and developers can pick from more than 70 language and AI models and build multi-agent workflows using the visual orchestration platform from its partner n8n. To control third-party agents, SAP points to the Agent2Agent protocol and the Model Context Protocol, and it offers the AI Agent Hub inside the LeanIX enterprise architecture solution as a central directory of active agents. The governance structure is certified to ISO/IEC 42001, and the Business Transformation Management toolset, made up of SAP Signavio, LeanIX, and WalkMe, is available to analyze process bottlenecks and monitor AI use. SAP also entered the payments market with SAP Pay, powered by Tereina, which processes payments and reconciles them within the ERP workflow without manual file exports.

The company said this reduces manual file handling and dependencies on external processing while giving customers more control. Christian Klein, the chairman of SAP's Executive Board, called the launch a groundbreaking moment for enterprise AI and said the autonomous enterprise has arrived in business. Customers cited at the event included Novartis, Morgan Foods, Nestlé, and PwC. Christoph Bürki, head of procurement at Novartis, said a pilot of the Joule Sourcing Assistant has been launched and that AI agents are meant to handle labor-intensive manual tasks.

Luca Dell'Orletta, global head of IT innovation and enterprise architecture at Nestlé, said the company is running an SAP S/4HANA transformation across 140 countries. Peter Wied, director of complexity management at Maschinenfabrik Reinhausen, said after 28 years as an SAP customer, the Early Adopter Program for Joule Work Desktop produced more momentum in a few months than in all prior years. The articles also describe a commercial shift. Customers are being moved from predictable flat rates toward usage-based billing built on AI Units, BTP Capacity Units, and AI token prices, with prepaid credits that expire at year end if unused.

The author writes that investors fear autonomous agents will devalue traditional per-user licenses, which is why SAP is seeking new revenue sources. According to the German-speaking user association DSAG, 43 percent of its members have already implemented specific AI projects, and 77 percent of companies actively using AI rely on non-SAP solutions from providers such as OpenAI, Microsoft, or Anthropic. The author links this to SAP offering AI innovations mainly through the "Rise with SAP" cloud subscriptions and to the restrictive SAP API Policy, Version 4.2026, which governs bulk data extraction for external agents. The articles state that under the European Union's AI Act, the user company remains liable for erroneous decisions made by autonomous agents.

Articles.Title: Autonomous Business: Joule Work, Joule Assistants, and the SAP Business AI Platform

stories.Headline: Roundhouse AI Expands Dashboard to Solana, Broadening Reach Across the AI Agent Economy
stories.Summary:
Roundhouse AI, listed on the London Stock Exchange under the ticker LSE:RHAI, has extended its Dashboard to cover transactions on the Solana blockchain. The move adds Solana to Base and Ethereum, bringing the company's coverage to three major networks and allowing it to record a wider range of payments made by AI agents. The company reported the change in an article published on 11 November 2026. Solana adds immediate scale to the platform. In the 30 days to 2 November 2026, the Dashboard recorded 821,915 x402 payments on Solana, worth US$341,261 in value and involving 1,425 distinct paying wallets.

Across all three networks, Roundhouse has now logged more than 202 million x402 payments, with a combined transaction value of about US$45.6 million. According to DefiLlama data cited by the company, Base and Solana together made up roughly 98% of cumulative x402 payment volume by value since May 2025. Roundhouse describes its goal as becoming a trusted data and reputation layer for autonomous AI agents. The Dashboard offers a searchable record showing which agents are paying, who receives the payments and what those payments are worth. The company says this dataset underpins its planned Agent Reputation Scores and its proposed aGDP Index, which are intended to give greater insight into the emerging agent economy.

Chief Executive Matthew Lodge described the Solana integration as a major step toward a more complete picture of the market. The articles provide the company's own framing of the expansion and give no independent assessment of its significance. They also note that Roundhouse made its AIM debut roughly a month before this announcement, with its shares reported to have risen more than 17% on that debut. The articles do not set out any further timetable for launching the Agent Reputation Scores or the aGDP Index.

Articles.Title: Roundhouse AI Expands Dashboard to Solana, Broadening Reach Across the AI Agent Economy

stories.Headline: AI, accountability and the economics of evidence
stories.Summary:
Benjamin Guin, who works in the Bank of England's Strategy and Policy Approach Division, published a post on Bank Underground on 11 November 2026 arguing that artificial intelligence changes the economics of evidence. Most discussion of AI in organisations, he says, focuses on productivity, on the idea that cheaper analysis should improve decision-making. His argument is that an important consequence lies elsewhere, because a wider range of people can now produce professionally presented analysis where the relevant information is accessible. Responsibility for decisions, however, remains concentrated and changes more slowly than the production of analysis. The post therefore concludes that the comparative advantage of institutions may increasingly lie in deciding what evidence to trust and act on.

The post describes the gap as two blades of a pair of scissors, shown in a stylised chart that is not drawn to data. The falling blade is the cost of producing analysis, while the flatter blade is accountable attention, meaning the capacity of those responsible for a decision to assess evidence, choose what to rely on and justify that choice. Controlled studies find that AI assistance speeds up professional writing and analytical tasks by 25% to 40%, and the cost of obtaining a given level of AI capability has fallen dramatically. The Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority's 2026 survey found that 86% of UK financial services firms already use AI, up from 58% in 2022. Its use now extends beyond data and modelling teams into compliance, legal and operational functions.

Under the Senior Managers and Certification Regime, responsibility in UK financial firms is assigned to named individuals through statements of responsibilities, the documents that map specific duties to each senior manager. The post notes that these responsibilities can be reassigned through formal processes, but the capacity for accountable decision-making does not automatically grow as more analysis is produced. Directors' duties do the same for boards, while statutory objectives constrain regulators. The post's example is a regulator that receives 100 responses to a rule review rather than ten. Staff or AI can summarise them, but the person responsible must still decide which claims are reliable enough to influence the final judgement and be able to explain that choice.

The post says that professional presentation, references and structure were once useful, if imperfect, signals of effort and quality because they were costly to produce. As AI lowers those costs, the signals may become less informative for organisations receiving reports, applications and other material. It points out that similar concerns have been raised elsewhere in the public sector, where AI-generated complaints, appeals and claims have been argued to risk overwhelming administrative processes. AI may also broaden participation, letting individuals and organisations contribute evidence and perspectives that might otherwise not have been brought forward. Canada's recent national AI consultation drew tens of thousands of responses from over 11,300 respondents, which the government analysed using large language models.

The post illustrates the point with the duty to review rules. The Financial Services and Markets Act 2023 inserted into FSMA 2000 a statutory duty on the UK financial regulators to keep their rules under review, in section 29 – 3RA, and to publish a statement of policy on how they do so, in section 29 – 3RB. The Financial Conduct Authority finalised its Rule Review Framework in January 2024, and the Prudential Regulation Authority published its statement on the review of rules in February 2024. Both include channels through which firms, trade bodies and members of the public can submit evidence that a rule is not working as intended. The PRA framework asks that feedback be supported by relevant and verifiable empirical evidence where possible, with underlying assumptions clearly set out, which the post calls a verification filter rather than a volume filter.

The post says the argument becomes an empirical question, turning on whether the cost of integrating evidence falls as quickly as the cost of producing it. If it does, institutions may be able to absorb much of the additional volume, and some forms of verification may become cheaper. One proposed test is the volume of submissions received and the share meeting the verifiability standard, since growth in submissions could outpace growth in verifiable ones if the mechanism operates as described. The post suggests institutions may need to invest more in the frameworks, processes, people and systems used to assess evidence, and that the familiar debate over centralising or decentralising may be the wrong axis. It leaves open how much weight to place on competing evidence and what is sufficient to justify action, since those judgements may remain harder to automate.

Articles.Title: AI, accountability and the economics of evidence

stories.Headline: AI Development And Its Role In Eurozone Capital Investment
stories.Summary:
European investment in artificial intelligence is gaining momentum, according to an analysis by S&P Global Market Intelligence published on November 11, 2026. Inflation-adjusted spending on intellectual property rose 15% between early 2022 and the second quarter of 2026, compared with 8% for total investment. Imports of processors, memory and data-processing equipment have accelerated and now make up 7% of total imports, reflecting both higher demand and higher prices. The analysis also points to data center projects as further evidence of an expanding AI-related capital base. Together these trends suggest that the investment cycle is moving from experimentation toward deployment.

Adoption among eurozone firms more than doubled between 2023 and 2025, with stronger spending on software, data and computing infrastructure alongside it. Large firms lead the way, with 58% of companies with 250 or more employees using AI, and usage is expanding across all firm sizes. Northern and northwestern economies generally sit at the front of adoption, while several southern and eastern eurozone economies remain at an earlier stage. The article warns that this gap could widen regional differences in productivity and investment. European initiatives, the analysis notes, are focused on mobilizing private capital, expanding computing capacity and improving access to power, land and finance.

The analysis is produced by S&P Global Market Intelligence, which provides data, news, research and analysis on global public and private companies. The article does not name a single official responsible for the trends, and it attributes the policy efforts to European initiatives in general terms. It describes the data as showing both broad diffusion of AI across regions and sizes and a persistent lag in some member economies. The article does not say what specific policy changes are planned or when they would take effect.

Articles.Title: AI Development And Its Role In Eurozone Capital Investment

stories.Headline: Phota Labs uses AI to turn everyday photos into professional-looking shots
stories.Summary:
A new iOS app called Phota Labs uses artificial intelligence to act as a personal photo assistant that turns everyday snapshots into images that look like a professional photographer took them. The app is designed to keep the authenticity of each picture while improving it. Unlike typical editing tools, it focuses on fixing the shot itself rather than only enhancing a photo after it was taken. The article, published by TechCrunch on November 12, 2026, describes the app as free at launch.

The startup was founded by Cecilia Zhang and Zach Xia, who met at Adobe while working on computational photography products such as Project Indigo, Lightroom, and Photoshop. They saw a gap in the market, since editing tools struggle with photos that were poorly captured to begin with. Users can pick from photography styles that range from subtle edits that keep the original lens and composition to dramatic transformations with fish-eye effects or alternative angles. Phota Labs says it built its own personalization technology to preserve people's identity, which it contrasts with general generative AI tools that can alter a person's appearance. Images edited with the app carry invisible watermarks that flag them as AI-altered when shared on social platforms.

Zhang described the app as a proactive assistant that looks over a camera roll and works out how a photo could have been taken for a given scene. Xia stressed the company's focus on authenticity and said beta users saw the results as better versions of real memories rather than AI-generated images. The founders also reported that users took more photos because they knew the app could enhance them later. The company initially targets people who take many photos and share them on social media, with a broader audience such as retirees and parents envisioned over time. The startup raised a $5.6 million seed round led by the venture firm a16z last year, and it plans to explore a freemium model after building an initial user base and to launch an Android app in the future.

Articles.Title: Phota Labs uses AI to turn everyday photos into professional-looking shots

stories.Headline: Thoughtworks CEO makes case for cross-vendor AI agent control plane
stories.Summary:
Thoughtworks expects its first commercial customers to have its Agent/works control plane for AI agents in production in the first quarter of 2027. The platform was launched in June at the Databricks Data + AI Summit in San Francisco, and it runs in a customer's own environment on any cloud. Thoughtworks engineers set it up as part of an engagement, and Thoughtworks already runs its own AI/works agentic software development platform on Agent/works. The company is also completing ISO certification of the platform. A Singapore organisation is among a handful of early users testing the platform.

Mike Sutcliff, chief executive of Thoughtworks, spoke to Computer Weekly in Singapore and said the company was not yet naming its alpha and beta customers. He said he hoped to announce the Singapore customer before Christmas. Sutcliff argued that cloud providers, large language model developers and software-as-a-service suppliers each have control planes that cover only their part of the AI supply chain. He said customers have to work across LLMs, clouds and SaaS products at once. He described the platform as a way to see how many agents an organisation has, what they do, what they cost and what value they generate.

The platform taps each provider's native tools where they make sense and applies one set of controls across an organisation's agentic AI estate. Thoughtworks is targeting enterprises that are moving more agents out of pilots and into production. Sutcliff said every layer of that supply chain is changing week to week, from frontier and open-weight models to the tools and governance that control them. He said clients do not want to wait, but they also do not want to invest heavily if the technology will improve within weeks. He also said they do not want to put anything into production unless they know it is safe and secure.

Sutcliff advises clients to design every AI system to be responsible, which means doing what it is meant to do and treating the people it affects fairly. He said the first question is whether the company can do something, the second is whether it should, and the third is how it should do it. He also pointed to the difficulty of deploying agents across environments whose technical boundaries are undefined. Sutcliff cited personal agents from companies such as Meta that worked on Amazon's marketplace one day and failed the next after Amazon changed something. He added that organisations also need to protect themselves from attackers, and he noted that Singapore telco StarHub is building a trust layer to identify and block rogue AI agents.

The articles say sovereign AI has come up repeatedly in Computer Weekly's interviews with CIOs across Asia, where organisations want more control over their access to models and model weights. Sutcliff said that a company needing only seven languages could stop using the parts of a model that handle 72, which would improve token efficiency. Organisations can also run open-weight models on their own hardware, either by renting capacity from a neocloud or by buying their own datacentre equipment. Sutcliff said people are looking for resilience so that an agentic capability, once part of a business process, cannot be withdrawn without consequence. He also said that a net exporter of tokens is a net importer of capital, and noted that SK Telecom is building a gigawatt-scale AI cloud with Nvidia in South Korea.

Software development remains the most advanced use of AI among Thoughtworks' clients, according to Sutcliff, who said engineers have had about 18 months to try tools such as Cursor and GitHub Copilot. Organisations are also using AI to redesign operating models and business processes. Thoughtworks applies AI internally across its own work, and its platform is part of how it builds software for clients, including more than 20 Singapore government agencies. The company is also rethinking discovery, the process of understanding a client's problem before prescribing a fix, and Sutcliff asked whether AI could shorten that work from 10 to 12 weeks to three to four weeks. The article ends by noting that passing work to agents risks people losing the skills to judge it.

Articles.Title: Thoughtworks CEO makes case for cross-vendor AI agent control plane

stories.Headline: Democrats Invoking Specter of AI Apocalypse To Justify New Wave of Costly Government Benefits - American Enterprise Institute
stories.Summary:
Democrats in Washington have proposed a new wave of government benefits, justified by fears that artificial intelligence could cause widespread job losses. The American Enterprise Institute, a conservative think tank, published an article on November 12, 2026 criticizing the push. The piece argues that politicians often respond to perceived crises by expanding federal benefit rolls, citing the Great Recession, the Covid-19 pandemic, and climate change as past examples. It notes that these AI-related job losses have not appeared in the data, since unemployment has stayed below 4.5 percent for 60 consecutive months, the longest such stretch on record.

The article points to a proposal to automatically pay extended unemployment checks in response to AI-related fears. It says that current practice requires Congress to pass a new law before extended unemployment benefits are authorized during recessions, and that the proposal would remove that step. The article also raises the question of whether new taxes on data centers could pay for expanded benefits. It notes that voters considered 47 ballot measures on data centers this year, most of them restricting construction, and that only one, in Harwood, North Dakota, favored allowing them.

The article's authors, affiliated with the American Enterprise Institute, are the ones making these criticisms, and they argue that the proposals misjudge the situation. They describe the doomsday framing as coming from advocates who have promoted benefit expansions before. They also quote a recent New York Times report stating that lawmakers are exploring ways to bolster the economic safety net before it is too late. The authors contend that the same pattern has recurred across multiple crises over the past two decades.

The article is one of several recent AI-related pieces the institute has published, alongside work on welfare payments to households headed by illegal aliens and a critique of Democratic spending promises. It draws a comparison between current Democratic promises of expanded taxpayer benefits and similar guarantees made in the Soviet constitution. The articles do not say what action Congress will take on the proposals. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Democrats Invoking Specter of AI Apocalypse To Justify New Wave of Costly Government Benefits - American Enterprise Institute

stories.Headline: Our AI Leaders Want to Play God. First, They Should Believe in One.
stories.Summary:
Spencer Klavan, a writer and host of the Young Heretics podcast, published an opinion piece in The Free Press on November 10, 2026, arguing that leaders in artificial intelligence need some form of religious belief. The piece, titled "Our AI Leaders Want to Play God. First, They Should Believe in One," was republished on November 12, 2026. Its central claim is that tech executives who hope to reshape human nature cannot explain why human nature is worth keeping. Klavan frames this as a practical problem rather than a moral lecture.

Klavan points to the ambitions of prominent figures in the technology industry, many of them successful American businessmen, who are drawn to using advanced technologies to refashion the human species. He notes that Elon Musk has said for more than a decade that humanity might serve as the biological boot loader for digital superintelligence, a launch pad that could be discarded. The article suggests that the rapid growth of AI has convinced many of these figures that a turning point in human evolution is approaching. Klavan argues that without a religious or moral framework, such efforts could go badly wrong.

The author's concern is that these leaders lack a basis for deciding what should be preserved and what should be changed. He writes that the risk is that transhumanist dreams could veer into dark outcomes, and he argues that some kind of religion would help guard against that. Klavan is himself a host of the Young Heretics podcast and co-hosts Klavans on the Culture with his father, Andrew Klavan, for the Daily Wire. His most recent book is Light of the Mind, Light of the World. The article is filed under the Faith section, and the text available to this reader does not describe any specific policy, regulation or follow-up action.

Articles.Title: Our AI Leaders Want to Play God. First, They Should Believe in One.

stories.Headline: AI and ethics - beware techno-hesitation and the perils of mistaking Risk Management for fairness
stories.Summary:
A study by King's Business School found that many organizations using AI-based recruitment tools treat their risk management activities as if they amounted to fairness. Most participants were neither enthusiasts nor dedicated sceptics, but they moved between two positions that ultimately supported adoption of the technology. The first, techno-optimism, presents AI as a way of reducing or exposing biases already present in current hiring approaches. The second, techno-hesitation, has organizations acknowledging the risks and limitations of AI while rarely rejecting its use on that basis. Under techno-hesitation, organizations reframe ethical questions about discrimination as legal, reputational or managerial risks they believe they can control.

As a result, ethical concerns become part of the justification for continued AI use, provided people can persuade themselves that the risks are being managed effectively. Evgenii Arsentev, an AI Transformation Executive and independent researcher at Arsentev.AI, says the two worldviews are fundamentally mismatched. Fairness concerns the person who was rejected, whereas risk concerns the organization's exposure, and swapping one for the other changes who the question is about. Risk is measured through complaints, claims, regulatory attention and press coverage, but a candidate filtered out by a model is never told, so they do not complain. Organizations read that silence as evidence of fairness, even though the harmed party is invisible to the control.

Arsentev argues that treating bias as a technical glitch turns discrimination into a defect rate, which is never zero and is instead managed to an acceptable level. Someone is therefore implicitly choosing a tolerable level of discrimination without saying so or defending it, and cost questions get optimized while rights questions are resolved. Swathi Young, Chief Technology Officer at lottery operator Allwyn Corp and founder of The AI Blueprint implementation methodology, says risk management asks teams to satisfy legal requirements, while fairness concerns whether they accept the outcomes. Fairness is hard to measure and defend in the boardroom, whereas risk has owners, budgets and legal cover, so teams translate "is this discriminating?" into "what's our exposure?"

Vendors encourage this by making "bias-tested" a procurement checkbox rather than an outcome anyone verifies, and pressured procurement teams treat the model's score as cover. Lianne Potter, Chief AI Security and Ethics Officer at AI consultancy Northstar Intelligence, says that describing a system as anti-biased feels more contained than admitting it may reproduce discrimination, even if the risk is no lower. Potter says AI is a tool for pattern matching and that humans are not codifiable, so putting people into that framework will never be fully accurate. She illustrates this by noting that an applicant tracking system might read her CV as showing a flip-flopper because of her apparent career changes, failing to understand roles built on one another in an unusual background such as hers as a digital anthropologist. Arsentev gives three reasons organizations accept the risks yet rarely reject AI, and only one of them is cynical.

The first is organizational grammar: risk registers have owners and budgets, while ethics committees typically have neither authority nor money. The second is genuine ambiguity, since discrimination cannot be seen in a model's output without building tests, running counterfactuals and sampling outcomes. The third is that adoption is already decided, so hesitation becomes a ritual that lets people acknowledge the problem and continue. Arsentev says the short-term danger is that nothing visible happens, because the absence of complaints is read as success. Over the medium term, the drift accumulates until a regulator, journalist or litigant finds the exposure all at once.

Over the long term, discrimination can become documented, governed, insured against and defensible in process terms, which is harder to dislodge than plain prejudice. Potter warns that governance can become performative, with audits treated as evidence that a system is safe until investigation shows otherwise. She also says responsibility cannot be outsourced to vendors, since HR is responsible for how a tool is used, security for safeguarding it, legal for legal exposure and governance for oversight. Arsentev adds that vendors owe evidence rather than indemnities, meaning access to test systems on an organization's own data before and during deployment. Young says the same pattern appears wherever AI scores people, including in lending, benefits and performance management.

Arsentev says recruitment is simply where the pattern is most visible because employment law has a vocabulary for discrimination. He lists credit decisions and pricing, insurance, fraud and risk flags, benefits and eligibility triage, tenancy, and visibility and reach on platforms as other settings where a model allocates something scarce and the losing person never learns why. In these settings the harm is statistical and silent, so it can only be found by deliberately looking, and looking is optional, unbudgeted and nobody's job. The articles say a follow-up article will examine what organizations can do to avoid unquestioned bias becoming embedded in recruitment and other processes without proper oversight.

Articles.Title: AI and ethics - beware techno-hesitation and the perils of mistaking Risk Management for fairness

stories.Headline: Tracking Anthropic-discovered vulnerabilities
stories.Summary:
Seven months into Project Glasswing, the security firm VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs it attributes to Anthropic, which is roughly 0.5% of the 93,450 CVEs published this year. Only two of those have been exploited in the wild, according to the firm's data. The findings come from an update published on November 9, 2026, by VulnCheck's Patrick Garrity, who has followed the project since its launch on April 7. Anthropic had said the project identified thousands of high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities and was disclosing them to open source maintainers. Garrity's count covers CVE records, GitHub advisories, Linux kernel commits and Anthropic's own ledger.

Anthropic's public ledger lists 37,966 reported findings, but only 7,349 of them, or 19.4%, have been made public. Just 217 have been marked fixed, and 1,654 have been marked as duplicates, which VulnCheck says is about eight times the number of fixes. Another 419 have been withdrawn. Since September 8, Anthropic has added nearly 11,813 findings while recording only 15 additional fixes.

Over the same period, the claimed true positive rate rose from 91.4% to 94.2%, a change Garrity says is hard to square with the high number of withdrawn and duplicate reports. He also notes an apparent bug that inflates the count of disclosed findings, which readers can check with the ledger's "disclosed" filter. Garrity does not attribute these outcomes to any particular person at Anthropic, and he frames his findings as a critique of the project's public reporting. In his view, the ledger's numbers show a widening gap between discovery and remediation, and he questions whether the claimed accuracy figures account for duplicates and withdrawn findings.

Anthropic's October 8 announcement of its OSS Scanner, a self-service tool, acknowledged that about 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities had been found but only about 6,000 manually reviewed. The company said reports from the tool are generated without human review and may be incorrect or invalid. Garrity cites curl's maintainer, Daniel Stenberg, who said that of 34 published reports the project had reviewed, it rejected 19 as vulnerabilities and confirmed six as low severity, with nine still awaiting assessment. The articles do not describe any further steps Anthropic plans to take in response.

Articles.Title: Tracking Anthropic-discovered vulnerabilities

stories.Headline: Qualcomm CEO: AI won't replace your smartphone anytime soon
stories.Summary:
Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said on November 12, 2026, that artificial intelligence will not replace the smartphone anytime soon. Amon made the remarks at Yahoo Finance Invest, where he discussed the phone's near-term outlook alongside other AI hardware. The article notes that Meta, OpenAI, Snap and Tesla are each developing AI-related hardware, including glasses and humanoid robots. Amon's comments came as the broader technology market was moving on the same day. The article is written by Brian Sozzi, Yahoo Finance's executive editor.

Amon said the phone market is currently weak because of memory prices, and that the market has been down in 2026. He expects 2027 to be flat to down for phones. Qualcomm reported that its smartphone processor revenue fell 26% year over year to $5.14 billion in its fiscal fourth quarter. Across the full 2026 fiscal year, smartphone sales made up $24.07 billion of Qualcomm's $37.21 billion total semiconductor revenue. Full-year sales dropped 13% from the prior year, while automotive chip revenue rose 89% to a record $1.99 billion.

Amon described how AI agents will operate phones on behalf of users, and said certain workloads will eventually move to agents. He said phones will remain a central processing hub for content and sensing, even as workloads shift to glasses and other personal AI devices. He pointed to traction in glasses, AI keychains such as the Muse, and watches, along with more processing on the phone. Amon said the phone is not going anywhere and that workloads will shift, eventually producing a more powerful phone. He added that Qualcomm survived several transitions in which many mobile companies failed.

Phone makers and their component suppliers are affected by the weak phone market, and Qualcomm's handset business has been hit by industrywide memory shortages. Apple's transition toward in-house modems also reduced demand for Qualcomm's chips. Qualcomm remains a major handset player while diversifying into automotive technology and advanced AI chips. Handset chips remained Qualcomm's largest business in its most recent quarter, according to the article. The article also notes that Qualcomm's stock, ticker QCOM, was among those listed alongside the companies discussed.

The article reports that Amon's remarks were made at Yahoo Finance Invest and cite Qualcomm's reported fiscal results for the fourth quarter and full year 2026. It also references Qualcomm's earlier presence at the Computex forum in Taipei, Taiwan, where a photo from June 3, 2024, accompanies the story. The article includes several unrelated Yahoo Finance links about CrowdStrike and other companies, which are not part of Qualcomm's results. Other market headlines on the page, such as Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO, are separate from this story.

It is unclear from the article when Qualcomm's next quarterly results will be released or how its handset revenue will change after 2027. The article does not say whether Apple's modem transition will continue or how quickly agentic AI will affect phone usage. It also does not say when the glasses, AI keychains or other devices discussed will reach mass adoption. The article leaves open whether the phone's processing role will hold as AI workloads move to other devices.

Articles.Title: Qualcomm CEO: AI won't replace your smartphone anytime soon

stories.Headline: VR pioneer Jaron Lanier says Silicon Valley is sabotaging itself by poorly pitching AI and treating areas designated for data centers as sacrifice zones (Jaron Lanier/New York Times)
stories.Summary:
Jaron Lanier, a virtual reality pioneer who says he coined the term, published an opinion essay in The New York Times on November 9, 2026, arguing that Silicon Valley is undermining its own artificial intelligence work. The piece, titled "I Am a Silicon Valley Pioneer. We Are Sabotaging Ourselves," was republished online on November 11, 2026. Lanier writes that he works on and uses A.I. and finds the newest large models genuinely useful, but he says the industry is misdescribing them.

Lanier recalls that around 2013, when virtual reality went mainstream, leaders such as Mark Zuckerberg and Marc Andreessen talked about it in ways that alienated the public, and he argues the same mistake is being repeated with A.I., only on a larger scale. He points to a filing by the A.I. lab Anthropic, made ahead of a planned initial public offering valued at more than a trillion dollars, in which the company warned its models could present "catastrophic or existential risks." He also says that Americans, according to the results of the most recent election, now disapprove of A.I. more than almost anything. He calls the disapproval unnecessary, saying it stems from the culture surrounding the technology rather than the technology itself.

Lanier places much of the blame on the insular culture of the leading A.I. companies and their executives, whom he says often frame the technology as a threat that could kill people or strip them of livelihood and meaning. He also criticizes some technologists for treating areas where they want to build data centers as sacrifice zones. Drawing on decades of conversations with A.I. pioneers, including his former mentor Marvin Minsky, he says he is entitled to think of A.I. as "tools not creatures," more like a calculator than a living being, since there is no definitive evidence that it is conscious. He argues that this framing leads to more useful products and offers a practical route to making A.I. safer. The article's content beyond this point was not available in the material provided, so the remaining details of his proposals are not reported here.

Articles.Title: VR pioneer Jaron Lanier says Silicon Valley is sabotaging itself by poorly pitching AI and treating areas designated for data centers as sacrifice zones (Jaron Lanier/New York Times)

stories.Headline: The cybersecurity-AI conundrum: One expert’s perspective
stories.Summary:
Health Data Management published an interview on November 12, 2026, in which Mark Hagland spoke with David Finn, principal at Cyberhealth Integrity, a Dallas consulting firm, about the state of healthcare cybersecurity as artificial intelligence becomes a lasting part of it. Finn, who has about four decades of experience in healthcare IT governance and management, described the current moment as fraught and said the threat landscape has changed fundamentally, driven by four forces that amplify one another, with AI the first he named. He said AI has not created new kinds of attacks but has made existing ones faster, more targeted, and harder to detect, noting that a spear-phishing campaign that once took about two weeks of research can now be built in roughly 45 seconds. He also said attackers are using AI-assisted malware designed to evade the detection tools organizations have recently installed.

Finn argued that organizations need strong AI governance and controlled deployment, moving deliberately rather than rushing because of fear of missing out. He pointed to widespread "shadow AI," with clinicians using their own AI tools on personal phones, and said that hospitals must learn to govern and manage those deployments. He said healthcare has historically handled IT governance and data governance poorly, recalling that when he rolled out an electronic health record system in one health system in 2002, he had to build a governance structure himself. He also said that AI adds new components to secure, including the data used to train models, the models themselves, the prompts that feed them, and the application programming interfaces that call them, and that any hospital claiming not to use AI likely does not know what its systems are doing, since the EHR itself may be using AI. He added that vendors must be included in these efforts.

Finn placed responsibility for these decisions with healthcare leadership, saying the matter is a leadership problem rather than a purely technical one and belongs in the boardroom instead of only the IT department. He said clinical and financial leaders often do not understand the technical issues, while IT staff do not always understand how the data is used. He also warned that AI systems drift over time and need continuous monitoring, auditing, and documentation after deployment. Finn said he would rate his own confidence in the sector's readiness at about two on a scale of one to five, and that AI investments are not yet paying off, partly because they are fed data that has not been well managed for two decades. He urged leaders to adopt AI to solve specific problems rather than because competitors have it.

Articles.Title: The cybersecurity-AI conundrum: One expert’s perspective

stories.Headline: Obsidian expands AI agent security with runtime policy enforcement
stories.Summary:
Obsidian Security announced its Runtime Policy Decision Engine on November 11, 2026, giving security teams centralized control over AI agent actions before they run. The engine uses context about who is behind an agent, its access and the third-party applications involved to allow or block actions. It can also require human approval where supported. Context from apps, identity systems and customer labels feeds a single Policy Decision Engine, and each enforcement point applies its decision before the agent's action reaches the app. Obsidian builds on its existing AI agent discovery and governance coverage.

The engine checks allowed actions against centrally managed policies, using identity, employment and application context along with customer-provided data classification labels. Three new components extend it: a runtime policy for OpenAI Codex, the MCP Security Proxy and the Policy Decision API. The MCP Security Proxy checks agent tool calls before they reach business applications and keeps app tokens out of the AI client. The Policy Decision API extends Obsidian's decisions to customer-operated gateways and custom agent tools. Discovery and governance now also cover agents built into Salesforce Agentforce, Databricks, GitHub, Microsoft 365, Snowflake, ServiceNow and Workday.

Hasan Imam, CEO of Obsidian Security, said that an agent can hold valid credentials and use an approved tool yet still take a costly action. He said Obsidian has spent years mapping the chain of authority across third-party applications, and that policies are defined once and enforced at the moment of action. Avivah Litan, a former Distinguished Gartner Analyst, said enterprises need a single policy layer that follows agents across SaaS applications, data platforms and developer tools. Kenny Johnson, Principal Product Manager for Security at Cloudflare, said that connecting Cloudflare to Obsidian's Policy Decision API lets customers apply decisions informed by identity, access and data involved in agent traffic.

The announcement affects enterprises facing agent risk from employees using coding platforms and from vendors embedding agents in their products. Developers can keep using their preferred coding tools while security teams maintain oversight across multiple vendors in one console. Enterprises that route agent traffic through API, AI and MCP gateways can enforce the same decisions there rather than rebuilding policies in each gateway's format. Obsidian is partnering with Cloudflare and its MCP Server Portal to provide policies for agentic access to third-party applications through the Obsidian MCP Proxy.

Obsidian's discovery and governance capabilities cover platforms including Codex, Claude Code, Cowork, Cursor, Microsoft Copilot, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex and n8n. They also cover agents built into Snowflake, Databricks, ServiceNow, Workday and other applications. Developers have been adopting coding agents faster than guardrails can be put in place, often across several vendors at once. Many applications now ship AI features that often arrive switched on, and users can build agents in-app, frequently without a security review. The articles do not say when the new capabilities become generally available, what they cost, or how customers will measure their results.

Articles.Title: Obsidian expands AI agent security with runtime policy enforcement - Help Net Security

stories.Headline: After math, will AI upend science, too?
stories.Summary:
Mathematicians have spent 2026 grappling with a run of AI breakthroughs, and scientists in other fields now wonder whether they are next. In March, theoretical physicist Matthew Schwartz of Harvard University warned his peers at the American Physical Society's annual meeting that AI would do a lot of science, and many physicists in the audience reacted with skepticism and derision. Since then, AI-powered advances have unsettled mathematicians, with models from OpenAI disproving a long-standing conjecture by Paul Erdős in May. In August, AI models effectively solved the Navier-Stokes problem, and in October OpenAI released 722 AI-generated preprints covering about 370 open problems.

Scientists now routinely use AI for coding and increasingly for analysis, but the article reports that no truly novel deep physics insight has yet come from these tools. In late October, OpenAI and Anthropic each announced independent progress on a difficult problem underlying the mathematics of the Standard Model of particle physics. That same month, a separate assessment found the latest AI models were nearly flawless at solving research-level theoretical physics problems that an expert might work out in a day. Researchers interviewed by Scientific American disagreed about what AI will be able to do in their fields, but they agreed that science is on the cusp of massive change. Mark Histed, a neuroscientist at the National Institute of Mental Health, said there is a lot of uncertainty.

Large language models were once so weak that they struggled to add two-digit numbers, but within four years they became good enough to pass eighth-grade math tests. The article says the most popular AI models, all of which are large language models, can now produce superhuman quantitative reasoning, even though they tend to write merely good prose. Mathematics suits these models because exact solutions exist and proof-verification software such as Lean can confirm a result is true. N. M. Anoop Krishnan, an engineer at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, notes that science lacks such a verifier. He is skeptical that models can make comparable autonomous discoveries in science, because scientists rely on negative results and tacit knowledge that rarely appear in published literature.

Krishnan also points out that AI-designed materials must still be synthesized and validated in the physical world, and high-profile AI-sourced materials results have so far been unphysical or trivially novel. The article notes that the most promising evidence of AI speeding up materials science turned out to be completely fabricated. Leslie Schoop, a physical chemist at Princeton University who consults for Anthropic, said these past results may not predict future performance. She has tried to get AI models to predict a novel structure her lab discovered through serendipity, intuition and repetition, and none have succeeded. Histed believes the hard questions in neuroscience will not be solved by adding intelligence, and he argues that the field needs more and better data.

Histed also warns that chaos may limit neuroscience and other complicated fields, because the data needed to estimate downstream nonlinear functions could exceed what can be acquired before the heat death of the universe. Schwartz began in December 2025 feeding graduate-level physics problems to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.5 model, which he said returned answers in two minutes rather than two weeks. He documented the experience in a paper he called the most important he has written. Last month he and his collaborators released 36 preprints across 22 areas, on topics including the geological history of Earth's atmospheric oxygen and the demographics of sunspots. In one case, the model claimed it had improved earthquake forecasting by 15 percent, a claim an independent expert refuted.

Schwartz predicts that the content of any theoretical physics paper could soon be generated by AI, though Schoop is not convinced that AI capabilities will keep rising at their current rate. Two years ago the article's author argued that AI would become just another tool for scientists, but he says the past nine months have been humbling. In math, humans in some cases no longer understand the answers models produce, but that is not yet true in science. The author believes AI is poised to disrupt the jobs of all knowledge workers, including scientists and science journalists. Schwartz says his wife hates AI, but as a scientist he feels he cannot avoid using the best available tools to solve problems.

Articles.Title: After math, will AI upend science, too?

stories.Headline: US workers are fighting to protect their jobs from AI – and winning
stories.Summary:
Public workers in Oakland, California, took a strike vote on 22 October 2026 to press for protections against AI, and 94.1% voted in favor. Their union, the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers Local 21, feared that AI tools could increase surveillance and inaccurately rate their performance. The city and the union then reached a tentative three-year agreement, and the strike set for 5 November was put on hold. The deal requires the city to retrain or reassign workers displaced by AI instead of firing them. The agreement also includes other AI-related protections for city workers.

Julian Ware, an Oakland spatial data administrator and union member, said the city should be deliberate about how it engages with AI products. He argued that new tools can cost more, be harder to implement, and produce poorer results. John Samuelsen, president of the Transport Workers Union and a New York City subway track inspector, said automation is the ultimate threat to jobs. Liz Shuler, AFL-CIO president, said unions are using contract talks to set guardrails that policymakers have not. Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, said AI does not belong on big-rig trucks, in hospitals or in schools.

A survey by Ernst and Young, conducted from July to August 2026, found that nearly 70% of state and local government agencies have adopted or are implementing generative AI. Researchers call the monitoring tools bossware, and an October report co-authored by Kung Feng describes them. Such tools rank and evaluate workers, track location and activity, monitor productivity, and scan biometrics for timekeeping. Gonzalez said Amazon used algorithms to push warehouse workers to dangerous speeds, and that strategy is now reaching the public sector. The tools also use cameras, wearable devices and sensors, and some predict employees' emotions.

Steve Catanese, president of Service Employees International Union Local 668, which represents more than 10,000 statewide public-sector workers, said Pennsylvania's 2025 pilot with OpenAI gave workers no guarantees. The union then pressed Governor Josh Shapiro to adopt a policy requiring employee input and supervision of state AI use. In Columbus, Ohio, the Transport Workers Union won contracts in 2024 giving it veto power over any Central Ohio Transit Authority plan to deploy autonomous vehicles. In New York, a law effective December 2025 protects state agency workers from AI displacement. Keith Brown of the Alameda Labor Council said workers have faced AI harms for a long time.

Public workers in Florida and New York are trying to block Waymo and city governments from deploying autonomous vehicles, calling them unsafe and a threat to jobs. Samuelsen said his union supports systems that aid collision avoidance and bus and train timing, but he worries about safety. He said some airlines are experimenting with drones to inspect aircraft instead of human mechanics. In California, Governor Gavin Newsom signed the No Robo Bosses bill and a second bill banning workplace AI surveillance tools on 30 September. The No Robo Bosses bill bars employers from relying solely on automated systems to discipline or fire workers.

The articles leave open how the Oakland agreement will be finalized, since it is only tentative. They do not say whether the Pennsylvania union's expected 2027 contract negotiations will produce new AI terms. The articles also do not state how the Florida and New York efforts against autonomous vehicles will end. Whether the California bills will be enforced in practice is not addressed. Unions say more fights are coming, and Feng said the contest over technology in the workplace is ongoing.

Articles.Title: US workers are fighting to protect their jobs from AI – and winning

stories.Headline: Delegation by default: should UK justice reverse its drift to private AI?
stories.Summary:
The Nuffield Family Justice Observatory has published Delegated by Default?, a report by Dr Natalie Byrom setting out 26 recommendations grouped under four themes. The report argues that UK justice has handed a growing share of digital services to private vendors by default rather than by deliberate choice. It describes this as a policy choice. The report was published days after the Civil Justice Council released 15 recommendations on 29 October on how parties should use AI in civil court documents. Together the two reports show a gap, because the Civil Justice Council's remit covered what lawyers and witnesses file, not the AI that judges use.

The Nuffield report does not call for an end to private supply, saying it is not an argument against digital or AI-mediated justice or against private-sector involvement. What it wants reversed is the default. The report says the drift came from financial pressure, the troubled HMCTS court modernisation programme and the rapid arrival of generative AI. Byrom sees the turn to the market as an understandable consequence of the court reform programme failing to achieve its aims. She judges the regulatory and governance framework for AI to fall far short of what such reliance requires.

The Ministry of Justice has rolled out a locked-down edition of Microsoft Copilot to judges, yet the report finds limited public information on how it was judged safe, what it is for, who checks its use and how litigants can object. David Lammy said at a Microsoft AI Tour event in London in February that the ministry had been one of the fastest growing government users of Copilot. The April 2025 judicial guidance referred to Copilot Chat on judges' devices, but the October 2025 guidance replacing it does not mention Copilot. The report also says the Justice AI Unit received more than £12 million of extra funding for next financial year, and it counts eight family law providers on LawtechUK's tracker, three of which plausibly offer dispute resolution. The report's concern is that general-purpose language models can get facts wrong, invent material and introduce subtle shifts in meaning.

It argues that judges acting as a human check is unreliable because fluent AI outputs make users less likely to scrutinise them. It wants public evidence about disregarding Microsoft's advice against using Copilot where it could affect legal status or rights. The current judicial guidance states that judges are not generally obliged to describe preparatory work done in producing a judgment, which sits awkwardly with calls for litigants to contest AI use. The Civil Justice Council's final report, chaired by Sir Colin Birss, recommends a Practice Direction and a declaration from witnesses of fact that AI did not generate or influence their statements. The reports name several groups as affected.

Litigants in person in family cases are turning to generative AI for advice and documents, with limited redress when it gets the law wrong. The report warns that sycophantic tools may affirm and enflame vexatious litigants and domestic abusers. Judges and legal advisers are answerable for anything issued under their name. The Ministry of Justice and HMCTS are asked to assess vendor lock-in and sovereignty risks before buying. The report cites research finding that users of sycophantic chatbots grew more convinced of their own rightness.

The Law Society Gazette reports that the paper also cites studies finding people who search with generative AI reach official sources less often. The report proposes four themes of reform: a new national commission to oversee AI in justice, funded public legal information, published evidence and approved tools for court AI, and shared standards with monitoring and a route for litigants to object. It recommends an oversight committee for judicial AI with a budget of at least £1 million a year. The articles leave open whether the ministry, courts service and judiciary will adopt these measures, how a single framework can cover the different bodies that govern court participants, and what in-house capability would cost. They also leave open whether any future review of legal services regulation will take up Byrom's suggested registration regime for UK-built AI tools.

Articles.Title: Delegation by default: should UK justice reverse its drift to private AI? - Resultsense

stories.Headline: Harvey Partners with Djøf Forlag to Add Danish Legal Sources
stories.Summary:
Harvey, the legal AI company, announced on November 11, 2026, a partnership with Danish legal publisher Djøf Forlag to add licensed Danish legislation, executive orders and preparatory works to its platform. Jurabibliotek licensees will be able to research and draft from those materials alongside their own documents. The Jurabibliotek legislative content is scheduled to become available in Harvey at the start of 2027 at no additional charge. Access requires a license to Djøf Forlag's digital platform, and the collection will sit alongside Danish public sources already available in Harvey.

The collection covers consolidated acts, the executive orders issued under them, amendments and preparatory documents. Lawyers will be able to move from a statutory provision to the regulations implementing it and to material showing legislative intent, with each answer citing its source. Harvey gives examples such as checking what preparatory works said when a provision was introduced and drafting Danish-law advice from the licensed sources together with a firm's prior work. The content can be used in Harvey Assistant, Agents, Vault, Workflows and the Word Add-in, next to a team's own notes and matter documents.

Djøf Forlag Digital Director Bjarke Madsen said the publisher has supplied Danish legal sources for more than 65 years, and that customer demand for making them available in AI-powered legal tools motivated the partnership. The agreement follows Harvey's data partnership with Gyldendal Rettsdata in Norway and builds on its work with Danish firms including Kromann Reumert, which went live with Harvey across the firm in 2026. At Accura, Executive AI Officer and Head of AI Christian Høyer Ørum described a regulatory-advice process that starts with the act, checks executive orders and returns to preparatory works when interpretation matters. He said the integration will let Accura perform those steps in the tool it already uses, making the work faster and more consistent.

For Danish firms, the practical significance lies in linking licensed authority with internal work product. Because each answer cites its source, an AI-assisted draft can be traced back to the act, executive order or preparatory document supporting it. This keeps legal verification attached to the research and drafting process. The articles do not describe further rollout timelines beyond the January 2027 availability date for the legislative content.

Articles.Title: Harvey Partners with Djøf Forlag to Add Danish Legal Sources - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang was AI's rock star before dramatic career unravelling
stories.Summary:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after two affair revelations rocked the company and its global standing. The news came days after reports, first published on 29 October in the New York Times, that he had been involved with a businesswoman. The resignation followed a second report, published on Wednesday, that he had also had an affair with a company colleague. The articles describe the sequence of events as a dramatic unravelling of a career once seen as almost untouchable.

Huang, who had been named by one article as among the most valued figures in technology, was seen as a central figure in the AI boom. His departure creates uncertainty in a global stock market that had already been unsettled in recent weeks. Nvidia, which dominates the market for microchips used to power AI, is still valued at nearly $4 trillion despite the scandal. The company is described as a linchpin in the United States' race for technology leadership with China. Huang's estimated fortune is put at $145bn (£109bn) by the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Huang admitted after the first revelation that he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologised for hurting his family. US officials allege that Alice Huang, no relation, a businesswoman linked to Singapore-based firm Megaspeed, is a Chinese intelligence asset. The second affair involved Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who has worked at the company for 18 years. A board meeting followed the reporting of the second affair, leading to the announcement that Huang was stepping down. The articles do not state who will formally lead Nvidia on an interim basis.

Donald Trump initially backed Huang to remain in his role and described him as "honourable". After the resignation, Trump said Huang had done "a fantastic job" and proposed Tim Cook of Apple as a suitable replacement at the head of Nvidia. Stephen Witt, author of the biography Thinking Machine, described Huang as a demanding boss and said the fallout would be bad for his family. Customers of Nvidia include Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all of which spend heavily on its products.

Huang was born in Taiwan in 1963 and moved to the west coast of the United States at the age of nine. He trained as an electrical engineer at Oregon State University and later earned a master's degree from Stanford University. He met his wife, Lori Mills, at college, and they married in 1985, eight years before he founded Nvidia. The couple have two children, Madison and Spencer, who both hold senior roles at the firm. The articles say Huang had worked to present himself as a family man, and that the company began as a supplier of chips for gaming before shifting to AI.

Articles.Title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang was AI's rock star before dramatic career unravelling

stories.Headline: While many Americans resist, China embraces AI data center boom
stories.Summary:
Chinese state broadcaster footage and CBS News reporting show that the AI data center construction boom in Ulanqab, a city in Inner Mongolia, is well underway, with multistory facilities going up on what was once farmland. CBS News correspondent Anna Coren visited the site, and the images aired by Chinese state television were dated October 16, 2026. The project, described as the biggest and fastest growing infrastructure effort in China right now, is said to cover an area roughly the size of a small American city. Trucks, cranes and thousands of workers are building dozens of facilities in the region, more than in any other part of the country.

Officials are betting that the area's cheap and abundant power will help China overtake the United States in artificial intelligence. The energy supply mixes fossil fuels, which remain the main source, with wind and solar, and Ulanqab's frequent winds and year-round cold keep costs down. The Financial Times, citing experts, says data centers in China cost about one-fifth as much to build as those in the United States, largely because land and labor are far cheaper. As many as 30,000 workers have been brought in from across China, a welcome development in a country facing an economic slowdown and high youth unemployment.

Huawei, Alibaba, ByteDance, DeepSeek, Baidu, Z.ai, ZData and VNET, which CBS describes as China's biggest AI companies, are all active in Inner Mongolia. Local residents interviewed by CBS, including a farmer who has grown potatoes and corn in the area for more than 40 years, said the changes have been positive and did not affect his land. Henry Wang, founder and president of the Center for China and Globalization, told CBS that opposition to data centers is essentially unheard of in China, in contrast to the growing movement against them in American neighborhoods. A United Nations survey from last year reportedly found that as many as 80 percent of Chinese people support data center construction, although the government tightly controls protests and media messaging.

According to the article, Chinese AI models are believed to be about six months behind their American rivals, partly because of restrictions on high-end microchip sales, but that gap is narrowing. China has more than double the United States' power generation capacity, and Wang argued that access to power, rather than chips, may decide the global AI race. In his words, whoever clears that power bottleneck first gains the advantage, and China currently has the edge. CBS presents this as a contrast with the United States, where community resistance to data centers is growing.

Articles.Title: While many Americans resist, China embraces AI data center boom

stories.Headline: Scaling AI value without losing control: Lessons from Frontier Firms
stories.Summary:
Microsoft published a blog post on November 12, 2026, summarizing research from IDC, which it commissioned for the fourth year running. The study surveyed more than 5,200 senior IT and business leaders across 28 industries about what it takes to scale AI value. Its central finding is that results are widespread but value at scale is not, and it names the top 10% of organizations on IDC's AI maturity scale as Frontier Firms. Those firms are the focus of the report's lessons.

Frontier Firms report an average 4x return on AI, compared with 2.7x for slow adopters, the bottom 30% on the scale. Of Frontier Firms, 39% see returns of 5x or more, against 4% of slow adopters. Only 61% of organizations are highly confident they can measure AI's business value and ROI, versus 93% of Frontier Firms. Sixty-five percent of organizations have an established process to govern agents, yet only 60% have high confidence in addressing AI security and governance risks. Sixty-seven percent say their workforce reports high trust in AI, but only 20% have a comprehensive, organization-wide skilling strategy.

Kathy Lange, Research Director, AI, Data and Automation Software at IDC, says organizations that scale AI value manage investments, models, agents, governance and skills as one discipline. Microsoft's Alysa Taylor, Chief Marketing Officer for Commercial Cloud and AI, writes that the lesson is to manage models, agents, governance and measurement as one accountable system, and that value and control are not a trade-off. Eric Tabor of KOHLER and Tracy Schaefer of Conagra Brands are quoted on skilling and governance, and Mike Adams of Black & Veatch is quoted on his company's goal of becoming a Frontier Firm. Lakshman Yerramalla of Bristol Myers Squibb says the RABIT agent helps teams make better decisions, and project managers who use it save an estimated 20% of their time.

Organizations now use AI in 6.5 business areas on average, led by IT infrastructure, cybersecurity and customer service. Sixty-six percent of leaders say AI has delivered substantial or transformative results, but only 48% are scaling that value across multiple business units. Thirty-six percent of organizations are still piloting agents. Frontier Firms report a 3.8x return from agents versus 3.0x for slow adopters, and these returns are leader-reported, with the research showing association rather than cause. Ninety percent of Frontier Firms exceeded planned AI spend, and 96% are rolling out agents at scale.

The article says that 87% of Frontier Firms have a process to govern agents, versus 51% of slow adopters, and 80% have an organization-wide AI skilling strategy, versus 3% of slow adopters. Trust and security, leading-edge technology and model performance tie at 44% each as criteria for choosing an AI platform. Leaders point to creativity and innovation (41%), customer-facing work (39%) and analytical work (39%) as areas agents free people to pursue. Seventy-one percent of organizations expect AI budgets to rise 10% or more in the next 12 months. Microsoft says its own Frontier Transformation work with customers follows these disciplines, and that IDC Executive Analyst Shari Lava will lead three sessions at Microsoft Ignite on Nov. 18.

The article does not give the full methodology beyond the survey size and the July 2026 survey date, and it does not say how the Frontier Firm figures were computed. It also does not give the full InfoBrief, which it says will follow. Available materials include a global infographic, The Real Business Value of AI, and regional infographics for Europe, Asia Pacific and the Americas. The article states these returns are leader-reported and show association rather than cause, but it does not say whether the research will examine causation further.

Articles.Title: Scaling AI value without losing control: Lessons from Frontier Firms

stories.Headline: These AI trends will shape health IT strategy in 2027
stories.Summary:
Healthcare IT News published an interview on November 12, 2026, in which Merlin Gackle, vice president of global healthcare at HGS, a global technology and AI services company, outlined what he expects artificial intelligence and automation to do to health IT in 2027. Managing Editor Bill Siwicki conducted the interview, which describes hospitals and health systems looking to use AI to improve efficiency, cut costs and ease workforce pressures. Gackle expects organizations to move AI beyond isolated uses and into everyday clinical and administrative work. He named three developments he considers most consequential for the coming year. The first is expanded AI automation across provider departments, with more tools connecting directly to electronic health record platforms such as Epic.

The second is greater automation of revenue cycle management, where AI would handle claims processing, invoicing to payers and patients, and collections, while accounting for each patient's coverage, whether commercial, Medicare Advantage, Medicare or Medicaid. Staff would then focus mainly on exceptions that fall outside automated ICD-10 coding or need further attention. The third is wider use of voice- and chat-enabled AI agents to help patients schedule, receive reminders and reschedule appointments, which Gackle says could reduce administrative costs and recover revenue lost to missed visits. Gackle says the organizations that gain the most value will be those that build on early AI successes instead of moving to new projects too quickly. He argues that once a system proves value from one application, it should look for further capabilities that improve the experience for clinical staff and patients.

For hospitals with a strong EHR platform, he recommends tools that make diagnoses, procedures and upcoming appointments easier for clinicians to access and act on, ideally through a centralized database or connected applications and APIs. He also says chief information officers should prioritize secure single sign-on across these applications and invest in data analysis tools that keep patient information current, accurate and compliant with HIPAA and personally identifiable information requirements. The article sits within a broader push by health systems facing financial strain, workforce shortages and rising expectations for patient experience to show measurable returns from AI. Related coverage in the same publication addresses turning stalled AI pilots into gains, a health system reporting a 5.1 percent revenue increase from autonomous coding, and another system citing a return on investment from AI scheduling.
